en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Minor Readings from the Minor Collection.
The Introduction to the Work:
I go for refuge to the Buddha;
I go for refuge to the Dhamma.
"I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
This is the exposition of going for refuge, which begins the Minor Collection (Khuddaka).
Now, in order to explain, analyze, and clarify its meaning according to the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Minor Collection, this is said:
Having paid homage to the Three Jewels, who are most worthy of veneration,
I shall compose a commentary on the meaning of some of the Minor Works (Khuddaka),
although, due to their profound depth, it is exceedingly difficult to do so.
This commentary on the teaching by one such as I is for those who have not yet awakened to it.
Nevertheless, even today the determination of the ancient masters remains unbroken;
for the Teacher’s ninefold dispensation stands exactly as it was.
Therefore, relying upon the true Dispensation and the ancient exegesis, I desire to compose this commentary on the meaning;
it is out of great reverence for the True Dhamma, and not from a desire for self-exaltation.
"Not for the sake of disparaging others; listen to that with concentrated mind.
Since it was stated there, "I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of some of the *Khuddaka* [texts]," first, regarding the *Khuddaka*:
Having established [the categories], I shall later provide an explanation of their meaning. "Khuddaka" refers to a portion of the Khuddakanikāya;
"Khuddakanikāya" refers to a portion of the five Nikāyas. The five Nikāyas are:
the Dīgha, Majjhima, Saṃyutta, Aṅguttara, and Khuddaka.
These five Nikāyas are profound both in their doctrine and in their meaning.
Among them, the thirty-four discourses beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta constitute the Dīghanikāya.

The one hundred and fifty-two discourses beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta constitute the Majjhimanikāya. The seven thousand discourses beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta [constitute the Saṃyuttanikāya].
The Saṃyutta Nikāya consists of seven hundred and sixty-two suttas.
The Aṅguttara Nikāya consists of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven suttas, beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta.
[Also included are] the Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, and Petavatthu.

The *Theragāthā*, *Therīgāthā*, *Jātaka*, *Niddesa*, *Paṭisambhidā*, *Apadāna*, *Buddhavaṃsa*, *Cariyāpiṭaka*, and the *Vinaya* and *Abhidhamma Piṭakas*—or, setting aside the four *Nikāyas*, the remainder of the Buddha’s word is the *Khuddakanikāya*.
But why is this called the *Khuddakanikāya*? Because it is a collection (*samūha*) of many small (*khuddaka*) divisions of the Dhamma (*dhammakkhandha*).
And by way of dwelling. For it is the dwellings of groups that are called a "nikāya. As for the scriptural authority from both the Teaching and the world, there are such passages as:

"Monks, I do not see even a single other group so fickle in mind as these animals, monks—the *poṇika* group, the *cikkhallika* group," and so forth. This is its [meaning] regarding the Khuddaka Nikāya.
A single portion. These "Minor Texts" (*khuddaka*) intended to be explained, analyzed, and clarified according to their meaning are included within the Sutta Piṭaka;

and the ninefold division of the Minor Texts (*khuddakapāṭha*), beginning with the *Saraṇa*, *Sikkhāpada*, *Dvattiṃsākāra*, *Kumārapañha*, *Maṅgalasutta*, *Ratanasutta*, *Tirokuṭṭa*, *Nidhikaṇḍa*, and *Mettasutta*, is the first among them.

This is according to the method of recitation transmitted through the lineage of teachers, not according to what was actually spoken by the Blessed One. For according to what was spoken by the Blessed One:

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra, I have wandered without finding [peace], Seeking the house-builder, suffering again and again from birth. (*Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ, sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ; Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.*)”
“House-builder, you have been seen; you shall build no house again.
All your rafters are broken, the ridge-pole is demolished;
the mind has reached the unconditioned and attained the destruction of craving.”

These two verses are the beginning of the entire word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*). And they were spoken merely by way of mental formulation, not by way of vocal utterance. But by way of vocal utterance, it was said:
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest to the ardent, meditating brahmin;”
"Then all his doubts vanish,
when he understands phenomena together with their causes"—
this verse is the beginning. Therefore, I shall begin the commentary on the meaning from the very start of this ninefold Minor Text (Khuddakapāṭha), which is the beginning of these Minor Texts.
The Purification of the Source.
And this is its beginning: “I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha. This is the outline for its commentary on the meaning:
“By whom, where, when, and for what reason was the Triple Refuge spoken?”
In some cases it was stated from the beginning, while in others it was not stated from the beginning.
Having performed the purification of the introduction,
one should thereafter analyze here the going for refuge to the Buddha and the one who goes for refuge.
“One should illuminate the distinction and non-distinction, as well as the fruit and what is to be understood;
this method is considered to apply to the pair beginning with ‘the Dhamma’ and ‘the refuge.
In the case of the successive analysis, one should also point out the reason.”
"And this Threefold Refuge should be made clear by means of similes.

Regarding that, for the first verse, there are five questions: by whom was this Threefold Refuge spoken? Where was it spoken? When was it spoken? For what reason was it spoken? And although it was not mentioned at the beginning [of the Sutta], why was it stated here at the beginning?
The answer to these is as follows: "By whom was it spoken? It was spoken by the Blessed One; it was not spoken by disciples, nor by seers, nor by deities.

"Where? At Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana. "When? When the Venerable Yasa, together with his companions, had attained Arahantship, and the sixty-one Arahants were giving a teaching on the Dhamma in the world for the welfare of many beings. "Why?
For the sake of going forth and for the sake of full ordination. As it is said:

“And furthermore, monks, one who is to be given the going-forth and the full ordination should first have his hair and beard shaved off, be clothed in saffron robes, arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, pay homage at the feet of the monks, sit in the kneeling position with hands joined in reverential salutation, and be told: ‘Speak thus: “I go for refuge to the Buddha…”’”
“I go for refuge to the Buddha, I go for refuge to the Dhamma, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.

Why was this said from the very beginning? Because when the ancient teachers were committing this ninefold teaching of the Teacher into the path of recitation by organizing it into the three Piṭakas, they [did so] because by means of this path, gods and humans [attain] the state of lay followers (*upāsaka*).

Or they enter the Dispensation by means of their state as renunciants; therefore, it should be understood that because it constitutes the path for entering the Dispensation, this is stated at the beginning of the Minor Readings (Khuddakapāṭha).
The clarification of the introduction is finished.
1. Explanation of the Three Refuges:
An Exposition on the Buddha.
Now, regarding what was stated—“One should explain the going for refuge to the Buddha and the one who goes”—therein, among all phenomena...

Based on the continuity of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) which has been cultivated by the attainment of the unsurpassed liberation characterized by unimpeded knowledge, the Buddha is designated as a "distinction among beings" (sattavisesa) from the standpoint of conventional designation (paññatti).

Alternatively, based on the perfect enlightenment regarding the Truths (saccābhisambodhi), which is the proximate cause for omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), he is designated as such from the standpoint of conventional designation. As it is said:

"A 'Buddha' is that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), without a teacher, who by himself perfectly awakened to the Truths regarding phenomena never heard before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers."
This, first of all, is the analysis of the Buddha according to meaning.
According to the phrasing, however, it should be understood by way of such methods as: “He is a Buddha because he has awakened (bujjhitā);

he is a Buddha because he awakens others (bodhetā),” and so forth. And this has been said: “In what sense is he ‘Buddha’? He is a Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the world.”

He is called "Buddha" because of omniscience; he is called "Buddha" because of all-seeing vision; he is called "Buddha" because of not being led by others; he is called "Buddha" because of being fully blossomed;

he is called "Buddha" by way of having exhausted the taints; he is called "Buddha" by way of being free from defilements; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from lust; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from hatred;
he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from delusion; he is called "Buddha" because he is entirely free from afflictions.
He is called "Buddha" because he has gone upon the path that leads to the one goal; he is called "Buddha" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment;

he is called "Buddha" because of the destruction of non-intelligence and the attainment of intelligence. This name "Buddha" was not given by his mother, nor by his father, nor by his brother, nor by his sister, nor by friends and ministers, nor by kinsmen and relatives.
"It was not made by recluses or brahmins, nor was it made by deities;
this is a designation realized at the root of the Bodhi tree by the Blessed Buddhas, simultaneously with the attainment of omniscient knowledge—namely, 'Buddha'.
And here, just as in the world one who understands is called "an understander," so too one who has awakened to the truths is "Buddha. Just as...
Just as winds that wither leaves are called "leaf-dryers," so too, because he awakens people, he is called "Buddha. He is called "Buddha" by virtue of omniscience;
this means he is called "Buddha" by means of an intelligence capable of awakening to all phenomena. He is called "Buddha" by virtue of seeing all things;
this means he is called "Buddha" by means of an intelligence capable of awakening to all phenomena. He is called "Buddha" by virtue of not being led by others.
It is called "Buddha" because he has awakened by himself, without being awakened by another.
It is called "Buddha" in the sense of blossoming, because, like a lotus, he has blossomed through various qualities. He is called "Buddha" as one whose taints are exhausted;
thus, by abandoning those states that cause the contraction of the mind, he is like a person awakened from sleep, having awakened from the sleep of all defilements.

"Buddha" is what is meant. It is stated "he has gone along the path that goes in a single way (ekāyanamaggaṃ gata), thus he is a Buddha," because the root *budh* has the sense of "understanding" (*buddhi*) as well as the sense of "going" (*gamana*).
This is said to show that just as a person who has traveled a road is called "gone," so too he is called "Buddha" because he has gone along the path that goes in a single way.
Furthermore, he is called "Buddha" because he alone has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddho*).

He is not called "Buddha" because he was awakened by others; rather, it is said that he is "Buddha" because he himself has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-sammāsambodhi*).
Because he has destroyed non-intelligence (*abuddhi*) and attained intelligence (*buddhi*), he is "Buddha. *Buddhi*, *buddha*, and *bodha* are synonyms for this.
In this regard, just as a cloth is called "blue" or "red" due to its connection with the qualities of blueness or redness, so too is he called "Buddha."
Thus, it is said in order to make known that one is called "Buddha" due to the possession of the qualities of wisdom (*buddhi*).

Following that, for the purpose of making it understood that this designation "Buddha" is a conventional description (*paññatti*) that conforms to such meanings as "this is not his name," the meaning capable of establishing the word "Buddha" for all these terms should be understood according to this method.
This is the analysis of the Buddha even from the perspective of the phrasing (*byañjana*).

Now, regarding the analysis of the act of going for refuge and so forth: in the context of "going for refuge" (*saraṇagamana*) and the rest, it is called *saraṇa* because it destroys (*hiṃsati*) fear; for those who have gone for refuge, by that very act of going for refuge, fear [is destroyed].
The meaning is that he harms, scatters, expels, and suppresses terror, suffering, miserable destinies, and defilement.
Alternatively, he is called *Buddho* because he harms the fear of sentient beings by engaging them in what is beneficial and turning them away from what is harmful;

[he is called] *Dhammo* because he enables crossing over the wilderness of existence and because he bestows consolation; and [he is called *Saṅgho*] because he causes even small deeds to yield the attainment of vast fruits.
The Saṅgha. Therefore, by this method as well, that Triple Gem is the refuge.

Going for refuge is a state of mind (cittuppāda) that has destroyed and shattered the defilements through faith and reverence toward them, which proceeds with the mode of taking them as its supreme resort, or is independent of others.
A being endowed with that [state of mind] goes for refuge to it, saying with such a state of mind as described: "This is my refuge; this is my supreme resort."

The meaning is: "It approaches this [truth] in such a way. And as for approaching it, one does so either by formal undertaking, as did Tapussa, Bhallika, and others, saying: "Venerable sir, we go to the Blessed One for refuge and to the Dhamma; may the Blessed One accept us as lay followers";
or by entering into the status of a disciple, as did Mahākassapa and others, saying: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am his disciple."

Or, as in the case of Brahmāyu and others, by being inclined toward that [the Buddha], such as when it is said: “When this was said, the brahmin Brahmāyu rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and extending his hands in añjali toward the Blessed One, three times uttered this inspired exclamation: ‘Homage to that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One!
Homage to that... [as before] ...the Perfectly Enlightened One!’”—thus for those devoted to the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhānānuyogin).

It functions in many ways according to its object and its function— either by the surrendering of oneself like [the Bodhisattvas], or by the eradication of the defilements of going for refuge like the Noble Persons (ariyapuggala).
This is the exposition of the going for refuge and of the one who goes for refuge.
The Elucidation of the Differentiation and Non-differentiation of the Fruit:
Now follows this elucidation of the differentiation and so forth mentioned in the statement, “I shall elucidate the differentiation and non-differentiation, as well as the fruit.
For a person who has gone for refuge, there are two kinds of differentiation in going for refuge: that which is blameworthy and that which is blameless.

It is blameless (*anavajja*) at the time of death; it is blameworthy (*sāvajja*) when directed toward another teacher in the manner described, and also when directed toward that [Buddha] in a manner contrary to what was described.

Both of these types [of refuge-taking] belong only to worldlings (*puthujjana*). For them, the refuge is defiled (*saṃkiliṭṭha*) due to the occurrence of ignorance, doubt, and wrong knowledge regarding the qualities of the Buddha, as well as due to the occurrence of disrespect and so forth.
Noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), however, possess an unbroken refuge and an undefiled refuge.
And they are as follows. As it is said: "It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should name another teacher.
But ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) remain those whose refuge is unbroken for as long as they do not reach a breach of their refuge.
For them, a breach of refuge is indeed blameworthy; it is a defilement that yields undesirable fruit. [That which is] blameless...
Because it is without karmic ripening, it is fruitless; however, in terms of its non-destruction, it yields only a desirable fruit as its result.
As it is said:
"Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, they shall not go to a plane of misery."
“Having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the host of devas.

In this regard, the intended meaning of the verse should be understood as follows: those who have gone for refuge by means of the complete eradication of the defilements of going for refuge will not go to the states of misery (*apāya*); however, others will not go [to the states of misery] by virtue of their going for refuge.
This, then, is the explanation of the fruit of both distinction and non-distinction.
The Elucidation of What Is to Be Understood.

In this "Elucidation of What Is to Be Understood," the challenger says: "Regarding the phrase 'I go for refuge to the Buddha,' one who goes for refuge to the Buddha would either be going to the Buddha or going to the refuge; in either case, one of the two terms is redundant."

Why? Because there is an absence of two objects (kamma) for the action of going. For here, grammarians do not accept a double-object construction (*dvikammakatā*), as they do in cases such as "he leads the goat to the village.
If it is argued that [the verb] has a purposeful object (*sātthaka*) just as in "He goes to the eastern direction; he goes to the western direction," and so on—[we reply: no.
No, because the state of having a common locus (*samānādhikaraṇabhāva*) for those who have gone for refuge to the Buddha is not intended here.
For if that state of having a common locus were intended, even one who approaches the Buddha with a hostile mind would have gone for refuge to the Buddha;
for he would have gone to that very refuge which is specified as "the Buddha. As it is said: "This indeed is the secure refuge; this is the supreme refuge."
If it is argued that this is simply a case of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇatta*) based on the wording [of the verse], we say no; because that very state exists in that very context.

For it is precisely in that context—within the lines of the verse—that this Three Jewels, beginning with the Buddha, are intended as being in a state of coreferentiality in the sense of "the supreme refuge and security," due to their unfailing nature in providing protection from fear for those who have gone for refuge.
However, in other instances, there is a connection with the verb "to go" (*gami*).
The argument that [the term *saraṇagamana*] is not intended because its establishment is difficult when [the compound is taken as a genitive] is not a proof. If it is argued:

"In the passage, 'Having come to this refuge, one is released from all suffering,' even though there is a connection with the act of going (*gamisambandha*), the state of being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇatta*) is established because the taking of refuge (*saraṇagamana*) is proven," [we reply:

No, because that would entail the same fault mentioned previously. For even in that case, if there were a state of apposition, then [the phrase] "this refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha" [would follow].
If one were to argue that even someone with a hostile mind could come and be liberated from all suffering, then the same fault previously mentioned would apply;
nor is it a valid argument to say, "We have no interest in this because of its defect. For example, in the passage:

"Indeed, Ānanda, by coming to me as their spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta), beings subject to birth are liberated from birth," it is through the power of the Blessed One’s spiritual friendship [that this occurs].
Beings who are being liberated are said to be "liberated by coming to a spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitta*).
Likewise, here too, one who is being liberated through the power of taking refuge in the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha is said to be "liberated from all suffering by coming to this refuge.
This is how the intended meaning (*adhippāya*) should be understood in this context.

Thus, in every respect, it is not logical that either the Buddha, the refuge, or both are the "object of going" (*gamanīya*). Furthermore, the "object of going" must be that which is intended by one who says, "I am going," as indicated by the act of going itself;

therefore, the reasoning (*yutti*) for this matter must be stated here. It is said: Here, the Buddha alone is the object of going. However, the mention of "refuge" is for the purpose of showing the manner of going—that is, "I go to the Buddha as my refuge.
By means of this [formula]: "He is my refuge, he is my ultimate resort, O Father, the provider of safety and welfare," [the manner of going is shown].
"By intention, I go to this, I associate with it, I serve it, I attend upon it; or rather, I know it thus, I understand it.
For those verbal roots whose meaning is "going," "understanding" is also their meaning. If it is argued that this is incorrect because the word *iti* is not employed here, that is not so.
In this regard, it might be said: if the meaning here were indeed thus, then [one would say], "Form is impermanent, form is impermanent..."
In such passages as "one understands form as it really is," the particle *iti* might be employed;
however, it is not employed here, and therefore this [interpretation] is incorrect. But that is not so. Why? Because its meaning is possible.
Just as in such passages as "He who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha," the meaning of the particle *iti* is possible here as well. It is not...

And because the word *iti* is employed everywhere to indicate the existence of a thing, the meaning of the word *iti*—even when it is not explicitly used—should be understood here as it is in cases where it is used, and in other similar instances; therefore, "it is simply non-hatred (*adoso*).
This is because in such passages as, "Monks, I allow going forth by means of the three goings for refuge," it is the refuge itself that is to be gone to.
If it is argued that the statement, “The word ‘refuge’ is for the purpose of showing the mode of going,” is not tenable, that is not incorrect.

Why? Because its meaning is indeed possible there as well. For even though it has not been explicitly applied, it should be understood as if it were applied, being exactly like what was stated previously. Otherwise, the very same fault mentioned before would necessarily follow.
Therefore, one should accept exactly as it has been instructed.
This is the explanation of what is to be understood.
The Analysis of Taking Refuge in the Dhamma and the Saṅgha.
Now, regarding what was stated—"The method for 'I go for refuge to the Dhamma,' etc., is considered to be the same for both"—it is here explained:

the method of commentary on the meaning that was set forth for the phrase "I go for refuge to the Buddha" should be understood as applying to these two phrases as well, namely, "I go for refuge to the Dhamma" and "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha. For in those cases too, [the meaning of] the Dhamma and the Saṅgha...
In terms of meaning and phrasing, there is only a slight difference; the rest is exactly as previously stated.
Therefore, that which is unique here is now explained: some maintain that the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna constitute "Dhamma.

This is because the Paths and Dispassion (virāga) alone sustain those who have cultivated the Path and realized Nibbāna by preventing them from falling into the lower realms and by providing the supreme consolation.
“Dhamma is our refuge,” so we maintain, and the *Aggappasāda Sutta* (The Discourse on Supreme Confidence) is the proof for this. It is said therein:
“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhammā*), the Noble Eightfold Path is declared to be their foremost,” and so forth.

Furthermore, the Saṅgha is the assembly of individuals who possess the fourfold Noble Path and whose mental continuities (*santāna*) of aggregates have been perfumed by the four fruits of recluseship (*sāmaññaphala*), because they are bound together by what is termed right view and virtue (*diṭṭhi-sīla*). And this was said by the Blessed One:
“What do you think, Ānanda? Regarding those teachings that have been taught to you by me through direct knowledge—
namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases for psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers,
the seven factors of awakening, and the noble eightfold path— do you see, Ānanda, any of these teachings?”
"Even two monks may hold different views.

For this ultimate Saṅgha is that which should be gone to for refuge. And in the Sutta it is said: "Worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Now, for one who has gone to this refuge...

Furthermore, whether toward another community of monks or a community of nuns, toward a Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, toward a Saṅgha of formal designation divided into groups of four or more, or even toward a single individual who has gone forth under the Blessed One, the act of going for refuge through such practices as paying homage is neither broken nor defiled;
this is the distinction here. As for the remainder that was mentioned:
The method for the analysis and non-analysis, etc., of the second going for refuge should be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
This concludes the commentary on the passage beginning with "He goes for refuge to the Dhamma," wherein it is said that "this method is considered to apply to both.
This is the exposition of the reason for the successive determination [of the refuges].
Now, regarding the phrase "and he shall clearly demonstrate the reason for the successive determination":
here, among these three words for refuge, the Buddha is mentioned first because he is the foremost of all beings; the Dhamma is mentioned next because it originates from him and is taught by him;
and the Saṅgha is mentioned last because they are the support for that Dhamma and because they practice it. Or alternatively, [it is in this order] for all beings...

One should also specify the reason for this sequential definition as follows: because he enjoins others to their welfare, the Buddha is mentioned first; because it originates from him and because it consists in the welfare of all beings, the Dhamma is mentioned immediately after;
and because they have practiced for the attainment of welfare and have attained that welfare, the Saṅgha is established as the refuge and explained last.
Thus, one should point out the reason for the sequential definition.
The Elucidation of the Similes:
Now, that which was stated—"And this Triple Refuge, one should elucidate by means of similes"—is also being explained here.
In this context, the Buddha is like the full moon; the Dhamma taught by him is like the mass of the moon's rays; and [the Sangha] is like one gratified by the production of the full moon's rays.

The Saṅgha is like the world. The Buddha is like the rising sun; the Dhamma of the aforementioned kind is like its web of rays, and the Saṅgha is like the world whose darkness has been dispelled by it. The Buddha is like a man who sets fire to a forest;

the Dhamma that burns away the forest of defilements is like the fire that consumes the forest. Because the forest has been burnt, the plot of ground becomes like a field; because the defilements have been burnt away, [the Saṅgha is likewise].
The Saṅgha is a field of merit. The Buddha is like a great rain cloud; the Dhamma is like the falling rain;

and the Saṅgha, with its dust of defilements stilled, is like the countryside when the dust has been settled by the falling rain. The Buddha is like a skilled charioteer; the Dhamma is like the method for training noble steeds;
and the Saṅgha is like a well-trained multitude of noble steeds. Because he extracts the arrows of all views, he is a surgeon.
The Buddha is like a physician; the Dhamma is like the method for extracting the arrow; and the Saṅgha, having extracted the arrow of views, is like a person from whom the arrow has been removed.
Or, because he tears away the film of delusion, the Buddha is like a surgeon; the Dhamma is like the method for tearing away the film;
and the Saṅgha, having torn away the film of delusion, with the eye of clear knowledge, is like a person whose film has been removed and whose eyes have become clear.
The Saṅgha. Or, because of its capacity to remove the diseases of the defilements along with their underlying tendencies (anusaya), the Buddha is like a skilled physician;

the Dhamma is like medicine properly administered; and the community of people whose diseases and underlying tendencies of defilement have been completely pacified through the application of that medicine is the Saṅgha.

Alternatively, the Buddha is like a skilled guide; the Dhamma is like the excellent path and like the land of safety; and the Saṅgha is like one who has set out on the path and reached the land of safety.
The Buddha is like a capable boatman; the Dhamma is like the ship; and the Saṅgha is like the people who have reached the further shore and attained their goal.
The Buddha is like the Himalayas; the Dhamma is like the medicinal herbs originating from them; and through the use of those medicinal herbs...

The Saṅgha is like people free from disease. The Buddha is like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), the Dhamma is like wealth, and the Saṅgha is like people who have properly acquired noble wealth after obtaining it according to their intention.
The Buddha is like one who points out a treasure, the Dhamma is like the treasure, and the Saṅgha is like people who have reached that treasure.

Furthermore, the Buddha is like a heroic man who grants fearlessness; the Dhamma is like that fearlessness itself; and the Saṅgha is like people who have attained that fearlessness, being entirely free from all fear.
The Buddha is like one who provides consolation; the Dhamma is like the consolation itself; and the Saṅgha is like people who have been consoled.
The Buddha is like a true friend; the Dhamma is like beneficial instruction; and the Saṅgha is like those who, through the application of that benefit, have attained their own welfare.
The Saṅgha is like the people. The Buddha is like a mine of wealth; the Dhamma is like the essence of wealth; the Saṅgha is like the enjoyment of that essential wealth.
The Buddha is like the one who bathes the prince; the Dhamma is like the water for washing the head;
the Saṅgha is like the group of princes well-bathed with the water of the True Dhamma. The Buddha is like the maker of ornaments; the Dhamma is like the ornament.
The Saṅgha is adorned with the True Dhamma, like a group of princes adorned with ornaments. The Buddha is like a sandalwood tree; the Dhamma is like its fragrance;
and the Saṅgha is like people whose feverish distress is stilled by the enjoyment of that sandalwood, through the enjoyment of the True Dhamma.
The Buddha is like a father who bestows an inheritance; the Dhamma is like the inheritance; and the assembly of disciples is like the sons who receive the inheritance.
The Saṅgha is like one who carries away the inheritance of the True Dhamma. The Buddha is like a blossomed lotus;
the Dhamma is like the honey produced from it; and the Saṅgha is like a swarm of bees enjoying that [honey]. Thus, this triad of refuges should be illustrated by means of these similes.

By this much, the outline for the commentary on the meaning—which was previously set forth in the four verses beginning with "By whom, where, when, and why were the three refuges spoken?"—has been explained according to its sense.
The commentary on the Three Refuges in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*, is concluded. 2.
Commentary on the Training Precepts (*Sikkhāpada*).
The Table of Contents for the Recitation of the Training Precepts (Sikkhāpadapāṭhamātikā):
Having thus shown the entry into the Dispensation by means of taking refuge,

this table of contents for the recitation of the training precepts is set forth in order to show those precepts in which a lay follower or one who has gone forth must first train once they have entered the Dispensation.
Now, for the purpose of commentary, this is the matrix (mātikā):
“By what means, where, when, and why these [terms] were spoken— having explained that method,
and having established the definitions according to their common and specific characteristics.”
“Having determined that which is faulty by way of nature and that which is faulty by way of designation,
and having done so according to the meaning of the words and their phrasing,
one should provide a common exposition for all those factors that are common.”
Now, regarding the five preceding sections, for the purpose of elucidating their specific distinctions:
[They differ] by way of the unity or diversity of killing living beings and so forth,
by way of the classification of the objects taken up, and likewise by way of the degree of blameworthiness.
“The exposition should be understood by way of the factors of application, the arising, the root-feeling, the action, the abstention,
and the fruit. Thereafter, what is appropriate should be joined even to the final five.”
"And the unique [qualities] should be stated, as well as the inferiority, etc., of what is to be known.
In this context, these ten training rules (sikkhāpada), beginning with "abstaining from taking life," were spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by disciples and others.
And they were spoken at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, to the Venerable...
Having ordained Rāhula, he arrived at Sāvatthī from Kapilavatthu for the purpose of establishing the training rules for the novices. For it is said:
"Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavatthu as long as he desired, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Wandering by stages, he eventually reached Sāvatthī. There, indeed, the Blessed One..."
He was staying at Sāvatthī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, it occurred to the novices: “How many training rules do we have, and where must we train?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One: “I allow, monks, [the recitation of] the training rules for the novices.”
The ten training rules (*sikkhāpada*), which the novices (*sāmaṇera*) must train in: abstaining from taking life... [and so on] ...abstaining from accepting gold and silver.

These should be understood as having been introduced into the path of recitation as follows: "I undertake the training rule of abstaining from taking life," in accordance with the Sutta passage, "He trains himself by undertaking the training rules," and in accordance with the text shown in the formulas for going for refuge.
Thus, first of all, having explained that method by which, where, when, and why these [precepts] were taught, that method is to be understood.
Regarding the determination of what is common and what is specific:
here, the first two and the fourth and fifth [precepts] are common to both lay followers (upāsakas) and novices (sāmaṇeras) by virtue of their being perpetual precepts.

Furthermore, regarding the lay followers (*upāsaka*), if one treats the seventh and eighth precepts as a single factor by way of the *uposatha* virtue, then all [the factors] except for the very last are shared with the novices (*sāmaṇera*).
However, the last one is a specific distinction belonging only to the novices. Thus, the classification should be made according to what is shared and what is specific.
Moreover, among these, the first five [factors] arise exclusively from unwholesome states of consciousness (*akusala-citta*).
Abstention from killing living beings and so forth is an offense by nature (*pakativajja*); the rest are offenses by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).
Thus, one should distinguish that which is an offense by nature and that which is an offense by rule.
This is the analysis of commonalities (*sādhāraṇavibhāvanā*).

And because in this context the phrases “I undertake the training precept of abstinence” (*veramaṇi-sikkhāpadaṃ samādiyāmi*) are common to all [the precepts], therefore this common exposition of these phrases should be understood both according to their literal form (*byañjana*) and their meaning (*attha*).

In that regard, first, according to the literal form: it “protects against enmity” (*veraṃ maṇati*), thus it is “abstinence” (*veramaṇī*). The meaning is that one abandons, dispels, eliminates, and brings to non-existence enmity.
Or else, by means of this [abstinence] acting as an instrument, a person abstains from enmity; thus it is a term for the modification [of the mind].
Having changed the *ve* into *ve-ra*, it becomes *veramaṇī*. For this very reason, they recite it here in two ways:

“the training precept of abstention (*veramaṇi-sikkhāpada*)” and “the training precept of refraining (*viramaṇi-sikkhāpada*)”. It is called *sikkhā* because it is to be trained in; it is called *pada* because one proceeds by means of it.
Thus, *sikkhāpada* is the basis for the training; the meaning is the means for attaining the training. Alternatively, it is stated that it is the root, the support, and the foundation.
It exists. "Abstention itself is the training precept" means *veramaṇīsikkhāpadaṃ*; or, according to the second method, it is *viramaṇīsikkhāpadaṃ*.

"I undertake correctly" (*sammā ādiyāmi*) means "I undertake properly"; that is to say, I undertake it with the intention of non-transgression, by way of practicing it unbrokenly, without gaps, and without flaws.
As for its meaning, however, *veramaṇī* (abstention) is the avoidance associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.

For one who abstains from the destruction of life, it is described in the *Vibhaṅga* by such a method as: "At that time, there is the refraining, the avoiding, the complete avoiding, the abstention, the non-doing, the non-performing, the non-transgression, the not overstepping the limit, and the destruction of the bridge, regarding the destruction of life. Granted, this is called *veramaṇī*.
There are also supramundane [abstinences], but because it is said here, "I undertake," they must be those that proceed by way of undertaking;
therefore, that [supramundane type] does not occur here, and thus it is stated as "the abstinence associated with wholesome sense-sphere consciousness.

Regarding the "trainings" (sikkhā), there are three trainings: the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). In this...
In this context, "training" (sikkhā) is intended to mean the virtue of abstinence from what is attained, mundane insight, the fine-material and immaterial jhānas, and the Noble Path.
As it is said:
"Which phenomena are training? At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy..."
Associated with knowledge... [as before] ...at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction; these states are the trainings. “Which states are the trainings?
At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states...
[as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first jhāna... [as before] ...up to the fifth jhāna... [as before].”
“Non-distraction occurs; these states are trainings. “What states are trainings?

At whatever time, for the attainment of the formless... [and so on] ... accompanied by the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception... non-distraction occurs; these states are trainings. “What states are trainings?
At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation... non-distraction occurs; these states are trainings.”
Among these trainings, a *sikkhāpada* is that which is a basis for any particular training, or else it is the root, the support, and the foundation.
For this has been said: "Relying on virtue, being established in virtue, one develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment," and so forth.
Thus, here the common terms are common both in their phrasing and in their meaning.
And the analytical exposition (vibhāvanā) should be made.
Regarding the commentary on the first five training rules (sikkhāpada), it was said:
"Now, concerning the five preceding [rules], for the purpose of elucidating their specific meaning... the detailed explanation (vinicchaya) is to be understood."

Regarding this, it is said as follows: First, concerning "the taking of life" (*pāṇātipāta*), here "life" (*pāṇa*) refers either to the continuity of the aggregates (*khandhasantati*) bound to the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), or to the "being" (*satta*) conceptually designated in dependence upon that [continuity].

Now, "taking of life" is the volition (*cetanā*) of killing—which arises through either the door of body or the door of speech—that originates from an undertaking intended to sever the life-faculty of that living being, while perceiving that living being as a living being. Regarding "taking what is not given" (*adinnādāna*): here...
"Stolen" (*adatta*) means what is possessed by another; that which another may take as they please without being subject to punishment or blame.

When one perceives such an object as belonging to another, the volition of theft—which originates from the undertaking of taking it and proceeds through either the door of body or speech—is "taking what is not given. "Unchastity" (*abrahmacariya*)...

Unwholesome conduct (*aseṭṭhacariya*) consists of engaging in sexual intercourse through the medium of the body by means of the union of two pairs; it is the volition that transgresses the occasion for practicing what is not the true Dharma (*asaddhamma*).
Regarding "false speech" (*musāvāda*): here, *musa* refers to a verbal or bodily exertion that destroys the truth for one whose primary intention is to deceive.
Furthermore, it is the mental state that originates the bodily and verbal exertions which, with the intent to deceive, cause another to be deceived.

False speech (*musāvāda*) is wrong volition proceeding through any one of the doors of body or speech. Regarding the phrase "the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants":

here, "fermented liquor" (*surā*) refers to five kinds of *surā*—namely, *piṭṭhasurā*, *pūvasurā*, *odanasurā*, that which has yeast added (*kiṇṇapakkhittā*), and that which is prepared from various ingredients (*sambhārasaṃyuttā*).

"Spirits" (*meraya*) likewise refers to five kinds: spirit distilled from flowers, spirit distilled from fruits, spirit distilled from molasses, spirit distilled from honey, and spirit prepared from various ingredients.
It is fivefold. Both of these are called *majja* (intoxicant) in the sense of being intoxicating;
or whatever else there may be that is intoxicating, by drinking which one becomes intoxicated and heedless—this is called *majja*.

It is a "basis for negligence" (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) because the volition (*cetanā*) by which one drinks and swallows it is a basis for negligence due to its being a cause for intoxication and heedlessness.

It is said that the volition of consuming fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, which proceeds through the door of the body with the intention of swallowing them, should be understood as "the basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants.
Thus, first, the analysis here is to be understood by means of killing living beings and so forth.
[Now follows] the analysis of unity, diversity, and so on.

Regarding the phrase "from unity and diversity, etc.," it is asked here: Is it the case that through the unity of the victim, the executioner, and the volition of the act, there is unity of the act of killing (*pāṇātipāta*) or of another [offense] such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), and through their diversity, there is diversity; or is it not so?
Why is this asked? If, first of all, unity results from unity, then when many executioners kill a single victim, [would there be only one offense?]

Either a single killer kills many who are to be executed, or many victims are killed by a single means of action such as direct physical contact, or a single volition initiates the process that severs the life-faculty of many victims;
in such cases, there must be only one act of taking life. However, if diversity arises from a diversity [of causes], then when a single killer—
One who performs a single application for the sake of one person kills many victims;
or many executioners, performing many applications for the sake of many people such as Devadatta, Yaññadatta, and Somadatta, kill only one—Devadatta, Yaññadatta, or Somadatta;
or a single victim is killed by many applications, such as those performed with one's own hand; or many volitions [arise] regarding a single victim.
If they were to initiate the effort that cuts off the life-faculty, then there would have to be many acts of killing.

But both of these [positions] are untenable. Now, if it is neither through the identity of the victims and so forth that there is identity, nor through their difference that there is difference, but rather identity and difference exist in some other way, then that must be stated regarding killing; and the same applies to the remaining [offenses].
It is said: In this context, regarding the taking of life, there is no unity based on the individual unity of the victim and the executioner, nor is there diversity based on their diversity;
rather, there is unity through the mutual conjunction of the victim and the executioner, while there is diversity through the diversity of both of them or of either one of them.
For instance, when there are many executioners and many means such as weapons, etc., [the act is accomplished].
Even when many victims are killed by a single means, such as digging a pitfall, there are many acts of taking life.
Even when many victims are killed by a single killer through one or many means, and by one or many volitions that originate those means, there are many acts of taking life.
And even when many killers kill many victims in the manner described above...
Even when many people kill a single person worthy of execution by means of many or a single effort, there are many acts of taking life (*pāṇātipāta*).
This same principle applies to taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and the other offenses as well. Thus, the analysis here should be understood through such aspects as unity and diversity.

Regarding the object (*ārammaṇa*): among these, taking life has the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) as its object; so too do taking what is not given, unchastity, and the occasion for negligence consisting of fermented and distilled liquors.

Among material phenomena, they have as their object any formation such as the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth. False speech has a being as its object because it proceeds by taking as its basis the person who speaks the falsehood. Some say that unchastity also has a being as its object.
And when theft involves a being who is to be carried away, then it has a being as its object; however, in this context, it has a being as its object only in the sense of a formation (*saṅkhāra*).
"Not by way of designation. Thus, in this context, the analysis should be understood also by way of the object (*ārammaṇa*).

By way of undertaking (*ādāna*): these training precepts, such as the abstention from taking life, are undertaken by a novice monk (*sāmaṇera*) only when they are undertaken in the presence of a bhikkhu;
however, they are undertaken by a lay follower (*upāsaka*) both when he undertakes them himself and when [they are undertaken] by another.
It is undertaken either by taking them all together or by undertaking them individually.
However, for one who undertakes them all at once, there is only a single abstinence and only a single volition;
yet, they are understood to be fivefold according to their respective functions. But for one who undertakes them individually, there are indeed five abstentions and five volitions.
It should be understood that they "exist. Thus, here the analysis should be known even from the perspective of undertaking [the precepts].
As for "by way of breach": here, among novices, when one is breached, all are breached as well;
for those rules are for them equivalent to the *pārājika* offenses, and by whatever one has transgressed, one becomes bound by that very act. But among householders, when one...
When [the precepts] are taken separately, if one is broken, only that single one is broken; for by the mere undertaking of those [individual precepts], the virtue again becomes fivefold.
However, others say: "When they have been undertaken separately, if one is broken, only that single one is broken;
but when they have been undertaken together, as in the case of [vowing], 'I undertake the virtue endowed with five factors,' if one..."

"When one [precept] is broken, all the remaining ones are also broken. Why? Because that which was undertaken has not been broken; one is bound by the kamma precisely through that which was transgressed.
Thus, in this context, the exposition should be understood even from the perspective of "breaking. Regarding "extreme blameworthiness":
among animals and other beings who lack virtuous qualities, the taking of life regarding a small creature is [less grave].

It is less blameworthy when the body is small, and more blameworthy when the body is large. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort (*payoga*). Even when the effort is equal, it is because of the greatness of the object (*vatthu*).
Furthermore, among humans and others who possess qualities, killing is less blameworthy when they have few qualities and more blameworthy when they have great qualities.

When there is equality in both body and qualities, however, it is less blameworthy due to the mildness of the defilements (*kilesa*) and the means employed (*upakkama*), and [more blameworthy] due to their intensity.

And its great blameworthiness should be understood. This same method applies to the remaining [offenses] as well. However, among these, only the occasion for negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants is greatly blameworthy, whereas killing living beings and so forth are not so. Why?
Because it leads even a human being to madness and thus creates an obstacle to the noble Dhamma. In this way, the analysis here should be understood by way of its great blameworthiness.

Regarding "the application" (*payoga*): here, for the taking of life, there are six modes of application—by one's own hand, by command, by relinquishing [an object], by immobility, by means of knowledge (*vijjā*), and by means of supernormal power (*iddhi*).
Among these, striking with the body or with something connected to the body is the application by one's own hand;
it is twofold, distinguished as "specified" (*uddissa*) and "unspecified" (*anuddissa*). Therein, in the case of the specified, that which one strikes having specified it—
One is bound by the karma through that very death. "Whosoever may die"—thus, by reason of a blow given without specification, one is bound by the karma through the death of anyone at all.

And in both cases—whether the person dies from the mere blow or later from that same illness—one is bound by the karma at the very moment of the blow. Furthermore, having given a blow with the intention of causing death, by that...
Furthermore, if another blow is dealt with a different mind while the victim is still alive, even if he dies later from the first blow alone, he is bound by the karma of that first blow.
If he dies from the second blow, there is no taking of life. Even if he dies from both blows, he is bound by the karma of the first blow alone;
if he does not die from either, there is no taking of life at all. This same principle applies.
Even when many people strike one person, the karmic bond belongs only to that one whose blow causes death.

However, instigating by giving an order is "instigation" (*āṇattika-payoga*). In that case as well, the karmic bond should be remembered according to the same method explained for the "personal" (*sāhatthika*) application. Furthermore, a sixfold restriction should be understood here:
"The object, the time, the place, the weapon, the posture;..."
"Specificity of action" refers to these six determinants of an instruction.
Therein, "the object" (*vatthu*) is the living being to be killed. "The time" (*kāla*) includes both times such as forenoon or evening, and times such as youth or old age.
"The place" (*okāsa*) refers to such things as a village, a town, a forest, a street, or a crossroads. "The weapon" (*āvudha*)...
"A sword, or an arrow, or a spear," and so forth. "Posture" refers to the standing or sitting position of both the one to be killed and the killer, and so forth.
"Specific action" refers to piercing, cutting, splitting, or decapitating with a conch-shell razor, and so forth.
For if, having deceived the target, one who is commanded with "Kill this person" kills someone else instead, there is no karmic bond for the commander.
But if he kills without deceiving the target, then both the commander—at the moment of commanding—and the commanded—at the moment of killing—are bound by the karma.
This same principle applies to time and other factors as well.

The preparatory effort (*payoga*) consisting of striking with the body or with something connected to the body for the purpose of killing is an act involving relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). That too is twofold, distinguished as being directed toward a specific person or not; and herein, the legal offense (*kammabaddha*) should be understood according to the method already explained.
The digging of a pit, the placing of a trap, or the application of medicine, poison, fire, and so forth, for the very purpose of killing, is a stationary preparatory effort (*thāvara-payoga*).
That too is twofold, distinguished as being directed toward a specific person or not; for in that case as well, it is according to the method already explained.
It should be understood that one is bound by the karma. This, however, is the distinction:

in the case of a pit or similar device, even if it was given to others for a price or for free, if someone dies because of it, the one who provided the means (the *mūlaṭṭha*) alone is bound by the karma.
And even if that person or another has since filled the pit and leveled it with the ground, those who are digging up the earth or taking the soil [are not the ones responsible].

Or, when root-diggers are digging for roots, they create a pit; or when it rains, mud forms there, and someone who falls into it or gets stuck in it dies—the karmic bond belongs to the owner of the roots alone.
But if the person by whom it was obtained, or another, makes it wider or deeper, then someone might [die] because of that very reason.
He dies; thus, both are bound by karma. Just as roots are interconnected by their own roots, so too, when that "dry land" is made, one is released.
In the same way, regarding the contemplations (apassena) and so forth, one should understand that as long as they continue to function, one remains bound by karma according to the circumstances.

However, the recitation of spells for the purpose of killing is an application consisting of supernatural knowledge (vijjāmayo payogo), just like the gnashing of fangs and so forth by those whose weapons are their fangs.

The employment consisting of psychic power (*iddhimaya-payoga*) refers to the exercise of psychic powers resulting from the ripening of kamma for the purpose of killing. As for taking what is not given, however, the modes of employment consist of theft, force, concealment, scheming, and the consumption of intoxicants;
their subdivisions should be understood according to the same principles already stated.
For all three—unchastity and so forth—only the mode of employment by one’s own hand (*sāhatthika*) is applicable. Thus, here the analysis should be understood also by way of the modes of employment.

Regarding "by way of factors": here, there are five factors for the destruction of life—there is a living being, one perceives it as a living being, the intention to kill is present, one makes an effort, and by that means, it dies.
For taking what is not given, there are likewise five—there is something possessed by another, one perceives it as possessed by another, and the intention to steal is present.
He exerts effort, and by that means the grasping that is to be taken up proceeds. Furthermore, there are four factors for unchaste conduct (*abrahmacariya*):
there is the basis for transgression, and the intention to indulge therein is present;
one undertakes the application on account of that indulgence, and one consents to it. It is the same for the other two as well.
In that regard, for false speech first of all, four factors should be understood: there must be a false matter; a mind intent on deceiving must be present;
there must be the corresponding effort; and there must be a communication that conveys the deception of another.
As for the basis of negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants, there must be one or another of these, such as fermented liquor and so forth.
The mind is intent on drinking intoxicants, it undertakes the corresponding effort, and it enters into the drinking—these are the four factors.
Thus, the analysis should be understood here by way of the factors (*aṅga*). By way of origination (*samuṭṭhāna*):
herein, killing, taking what is not given, and false speech originate from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

Thus, there are three origins [of offenses]. Unchastity (*abrahmacariya*) has only a single origin, namely by way of body and mind. The occasion for negligence through fermented and distilled liquors (*surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhāna*) has two origins:
by way of body and by way of body and mind. In this manner, the analysis here should be understood even by way of origin.
Regarding "by way of feeling": herein, killing living beings is associated only with painful feeling. Taking what is not given occurs in all three feelings.
One [of these] is associated with a specific feeling; likewise is false speech. The other two are associated either with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Thus, the analysis here should be understood by way of feeling. By way of root:

here, killing living beings has its roots in hatred and delusion. Taking what is not given and false speech have their roots in greed and delusion, or in hatred and delusion. The other two have their roots in greed and delusion. Thus, the analysis here should be understood by way of root.

Regarding "action" (*kamma*): here, killing, taking what is not given, and unchastity are exclusively bodily action, and they have reached the status of courses of action (*kammapatha*) only when they possess the specific characteristics;
false speech is exclusively verbal action. However, that which destroys the welfare [of others] has reached the status of a course of action;
the other is merely action. Intoxicants, spirits, and liquors that cause negligence are exclusively bodily action. Thus, the analysis should be understood here by way of action as well.
Regarding the term "abstaining" (*viramanto*) here, it is asked: "Abstaining from killing living beings and so forth, from what does one abstain? It is said:

First, one who abstains by way of formal undertaking (*samādāna*) abstains from unwholesome acts such as killing living beings—whether performed by oneself or others. From what does one begin? One begins from that very thing from which one abstains.

Furthermore, one who abstains by way of natural attainment (*sampatti*) abstains from the aforementioned types of unwholesomeness. From what does one begin? [One begins from that very thing from which one abstains.]
The objects for killing living beings and so forth are exactly as previously stated. However, some say:

"One abstains from the occasion for negligence through fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants by taking as the object those conditioned phenomena designated as 'fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants';

one abstains from taking what is not given and from false speech by taking as the object those conditioned phenomena which are to be stolen or destroyed; and one abstains from killing living beings by taking living beings themselves as the object."
And [the phrase] “and unchaste conduct. Then others, holding such a view as: “This being so, one might think of one thing while doing another;

one would not know what it is that one abandons,” and being unwilling [to accept this], say: “Whatever one abandons, one refrains from starting with that very unwholesome act of one’s own, such as the taking of life.
That is incorrect. Why? Because of its non-existence in the present and because of its existence outside [of oneself].
For instance, in the Vibhaṅga-pāṭha on the training rules (sikkhāpada), after asking, "Of the five training rules, how many are wholesome... pe ...how many are without conflict (araṇā)?

and when the reply proceeds thus, "They are indeed wholesome; they may be associated with pleasant feeling," it further states that they have "present objects" and "external objects. Thus, their state of having present and external objects is established.
What was stated—that it is not appropriate for one who abstains from unwholesome deeds such as taking life—is correct.
As for what was further stated: "One might think of one thing while doing another, and one might not even know what one is abandoning," to that it is replied:
It is not the case that one who acts by way of accomplishing a task is said to be "thinking of one thing while doing another," nor...
It is said that one does not know that which one abandons.
Having set out for the Deathless and abandoning all evil things,
the person who stands upon the Path is the illustration here.
In this way, the exposition should be understood even from the perspective of abstaining from these acts.
As for the fruit: all these [actions], beginning with the destruction of life, produce rebirth in the miserable destinies;

and even in the happy destinies, they produce undesirable, disagreeable, and unpleasant results; and in the future life, as well as in the present life, they produce fruits such as lack of self-confidence.

Furthermore, the analysis here should be understood from the perspective of its fruit according to such methods as: "The result of killing, which is the lightest of all, leads to a short lifespan for one who has become a human being.
Moreover, in this context, the analysis should also be understood from the standpoint of the origination, feeling, root, and karmic fruit of the abstentions from killing and so forth.
The analysis. Herein, this is the explanation:
all these abstinences originate from four sources—from body, from body-and-mind, from speech-and-mind, and from body-speech-and-mind.

And all of them are associated either with pleasant feeling or with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; they have either non-greed and non-hatred as their roots, or non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as their roots. All four are...

And herein, bodily action consists of abstaining from false speech; verbal action consists of abstaining from false speech; and at the moment of the Path, all these arise solely from the mind, thus they are all mental action.

Furthermore, through abstaining from the destruction of life, one attains perfection of limbs and members, perfection of height and proportion, perfection of speed, well-planted feet, beauty, softness, purity, gentleness, great strength, confidence in speech, and being dear to the world.

The fruits [of this] are such as: beauty of the neck, an inseparable retinue, fearlessness, being difficult to overcome by the attacks of others, immortality, an infinite following, handsome appearance, excellent physical proportions, freedom from illness, freedom from sorrow, non-separation from beloved and pleasing ones, and long life.
From abstaining from taking what is not given, there are such fruits as: great wealth, abundance of money and grain, infinite enjoyments, and the arising of unarisen wealth.
These include: the stability of wealth already arisen; the swift acquisition of desired riches; the non-commonality of one's wealth with kings, thieves, water, fire, or unwelcome heirs;
the acquisition of unique riches; superiority over the world; the absence of ignorance regarding non-existence;
and dwelling in happiness—such things as these.
Through abstaining from unchastity, one becomes free from adversaries, beloved by all people, a recipient of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and so forth;
one enjoys comfortable sleep and wakes up comfortably, is liberated from the fear of the states of misery (apāya), is incapable of attaining the state of a woman or the state of a neuter,
and possesses freedom from anger, directness of action, and an upright physical constitution.
Not having faces turned downwards; mutual affection between men and women; the perfection of the sense faculties;

the perfection of the physical marks; freedom from apprehension; lack of concern; dwelling in happiness; fearlessness from any quarter; and the absence of separation from loved ones—such things as these [result].
From abstaining from false speech come clear sense faculties, fluent and sweet speech, and teeth that are even, white, and pure.
Neither too stout, nor too thin, neither too tall, nor too short; pleasant to the touch, with a mouth smelling of lotus,
having a retinue that is eager to listen, with speech that is authoritative, with a tongue that is soft, red, and slender like a lotus or water-lily, being free from arrogance,
and free from fickleness— such qualities as these.
Through abstaining from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, there arises: quickness in acknowledging all duties and tasks—past, future, and present;
constant mindfulness; freedom from madness; possession of wisdom; lack of indolence; lack of dullness; lack of mental fog; lack of intoxication;
heedfulness; non-delusion; fearlessness; lack of agitation; lack of suspicion; and truthfulness in speech.

The fruits [of these virtues] are as follows: abstaining from malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter; being untiring by day and night; gratitude and thankfulness; freedom from stinginess and possessing generosity;
possession of virtue; uprightness; freedom from anger; modesty (*hiri*); conscientiousness (*ottappa*); straightness of view; great wisdom; intelligence; erudition;
and skill in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful—such are the fruits. Thus, herein [are the fruits] of the abstinences from killing living beings and so forth.
The analysis should also be understood by way of origin, feeling, root, and the fruit of kamma.
Now, as for what was stated—regarding the commentary on the last five training rules: [the following applies].
“From that, what is applicable should be joined, even to the final five;
the unique [factors] should also be stated, as well as the inferiority and so forth.
This is its commentary on the meaning: whatever is applicable from this commentary on the first five training rules, that [should be taken] from there.
This should also be applied to the final five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*). Herein, this is the application:

Just as, in the preceding training precepts, from the perspective of the object (*ārammaṇa*), liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence have as their object any of the formations such as the sense-base of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*), so too here is untimely eating.
By this method, the distinction of the objects for all [the precepts] should be understood. From the perspective of grasping (*ādāna*)...
And just as those previous precepts were undertaken by one becoming a novice or a lay follower, so too are these.
As for the factors (*aṅga*): just as the classification of factors for killing living beings and so forth was stated there, so here too there are four factors for eating at the wrong time:
the wrong time, what is suitable for the right time, swallowing, and being not insane. Following this same method...

The analysis of the factors for the remaining precepts should also be understood. Just as there, in the case of the offense involving fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness, it arises from two sources—namely, from the body and from both body and mind—so too is it here with eating at the improper time. By this method, the origin of all [the offenses] should be understood.
And just as there, in the case of taking what is not given, it occurs in relation to the three types of feeling; [so too should it be understood here].
It is associated with a particular feeling; likewise here, untimely eating [is associated with a particular feeling]. In this manner, the association with all feelings is to be understood.
And just as there, unchaste conduct has greed and delusion as its roots, so too here is untimely eating.
Furthermore, the distinction of the roots for all the others is to be understood by this same method. And just as there, killing living beings and so forth...
Just as bodily action [is defined there], so too here [are] eating at improper times and so forth.
However, the acceptance of gold and silver may be either bodily action or verbal action, by way of its occurrence through the doors of the body and so on;

it is not, however, by way of being a course of action (*kammapatha*). "Abstaining" means that, just as one abstaining there abstains from unwholesome states such as the taking of life—whether for oneself or for others—so too here.
In the same way here as well, [the precepts] range from unwholesome states such as eating at improper times to wholesome states, taken either individually or collectively.

And just as the first five abstinences (veramaṇī) arise from four origins—namely, from body, from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind—so too all of them are associated with pleasant feeling or associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
they have non-greed and non-hatred as their roots, or non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion as their roots; and all of them...
And just as [the previous factors] produce various kinds of desirable fruits, so it is here as well.
“From that, what is appropriate should be applied even to the last five;
the unique [characteristics] should also be stated, and the inferiority and so forth should be known.”—
Herein, "eating at the wrong time" refers to eating when the midday has passed. For this is eating when the permitted time has elapsed;
therefore it is called "eating at the wrong time," and [the precept is] from that eating at the wrong time. Regarding "dancing, singing, music, and witnessing performances":
here, "dancing" means any kind of dance; "singing" means any kind of song; "music" means any kind of instrumental performance.
“Visūkadassanaṃ” (the sight of performances) means the seeing of performances because they are a condition for the arising of defilements, thereby breaking the side of the wholesome;
or, the seeing that consists of performances is “visūkadassanaṃ. “Naccaṃ ca gītaṃ ca vāditaṃ ca visūkadassanañca” refers to dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the sight of performances.
And here, “visūkadassanaṃ” should be understood according to the method stated in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. For it is said there:
“Furthermore, there are certain venerable recluses and brahmins who, having eaten food given in faith, dwell devoted to such frivolous spectacles as these:
namely, dancing, singing, instrumental music, theatrical performances,
storytelling, hand-clapping, drum-beating, barrel-organs, puppet-shows, acrobatic feats, performances by outcasts, bamboo-pipe music, water-splashing, and elephant-fights.
“The ascetic Gotama abstains from such spectacles as elephant fights, buffalo fights, bull fights, goat fights, ram fights, cock fights, quail fights,
stick-fighting, boxing, wrestling, military parades, arraying of troops, and reviews of the army.”
Alternatively, according to the meaning already stated, dancing, singing, and instrumental music themselves are the "vanities" (visūka);

thus, "dancing, singing, and instrumental music vanities. The sight of these is "the sight of dancing, singing, and instrumental music vanities"; therefore, [the phrase is] "from the sight of dancing, singing, and instrumental music vanities.
Where it should have been said "sight and hearing," it is as in such expressions as: "And he is one of wrong view, of perverted vision," and so forth.
Even the apprehension of an object occurring through the door of the eye is called "seeing," and likewise, hearing is also termed "seeing.
In this context, an offense occurs only for one who approaches with the desire to see and then looks.

However, if one sees what has come into the range of vision while walking, or while standing, sitting, or lying down, there may be defilement, but no offense. This also applies when it is connected with the Dhamma.
In this context, singing is not permitted, but it should be understood that the Dhamma associated with song is permitted.
Wreaths and so forth should be applied respectively to wearing and so forth. Therein, "wreath" refers to any kind of flower.
"Ointment" refers to anything prepared by grinding for the purpose of anointing. All the rest, including perfumed powder, incense, and so on, is included.
"Kind of perfume" means fragrance. All of that is not permitted for the purpose of adornment and beautification; however, it is permitted for medicinal purposes.
Furthermore, for one who accepts what has been brought for the purpose of worship, it is not permitted by any means whatsoever.
"High bed" refers to that which exceeds the prescribed dimensions. "Large bed" refers to an unsuitable bed and an unsuitable bedding. Both of these [are prohibited].
It is not permissible in any way whatsoever to accept it. "Jātarūpa" means gold.

"Rajata" refers to the kahāpaṇa coin, as well as copper coins, wooden coins, resin coins, and so forth—whatever is known by those respective names in various places; both of these together constitute "jātarūpa-rajata.
Accepting them in any manner whatsoever is called "receiving" (paṭiggaha); that [is what is prohibited].
"In some way it is appropriate"—thus it should be stated as a unique [characteristic].
Furthermore, these ten training rules (sikkhāpada) are inferior when undertaken with inferior desire, consciousness, energy, or investigation;
they are middling with middling [factors], and superior with superior [factors]. Or, they are inferior when defiled by craving, views, and conceit.
The middling are those that are undefiled; the sublime are those supported here and there by wisdom.

Furthermore, the inferiority and so forth of the knowable should be understood as follows: those undertaken with a wholesome consciousness dissociated from knowledge are inferior; those undertaken with a wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge accompanied by effort are middling; and those undertaken with a wholesome consciousness associated with knowledge without effort are sublime.
Thus, the inferiority and other qualities of the knowable are to be known.

And to this extent, the matrix (mātikā) which was previously set forth for the purpose of explaining the recitation of the training rules (sikkhāpada) by means of the six verses beginning with "by whom, where, when, because of what," has been elucidated according to its meaning.
Thus ends the Explanation of the Training Rules in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
3. Explanation of the Thirty-two Aspects.
Explanation of the Connection of the Words:
Now, for that noble son who is thus established in virtue, whose application is purified by these ten training rules—

For the purpose of purifying the underlying tendencies and for the purpose of developing the mind—something that had never occurred before except upon the arising of a Buddha and was outside the scope of all other sectarians—it is stated in various discourses:
"Bhikkhus, one thing, when developed and cultivated, leads to great spiritual urgency; it leads to great benefit."
It leads to this: it leads to great security from bondage; it leads to great mindfulness and clear comprehension;
it leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision; it leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life; it leads to the realization of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation.
What is that one thing? It is mindfulness directed to the body. Monks, they do not partake of the Deathless.
“Those who do not consume mindfulness directed to the body, monks, do not consume the deathless; those who consume mindfulness directed to the body, monks, consume the deathless.
For those by whom mindfulness directed to the body has been undertaken, monks, the unconsumed has been consumed, the lost has not been lost, the missed has been attained.”
Having thus praised it in many ways, the Blessed One said:
“Monks, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it becomes very powerful and of great benefit? Here, monks, a monk, having gone to the forest...

and so forth, by way of the section on breathing (*ānāpāna*), the section on postures (*iriyāpatha*), the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension (*catusampajañña*), and the section on attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikūlamanasikāra*).

The meditation subject of mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*) has been explained by way of these fourteen sections: the section on the postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the nine sections on the charnel ground, along with the section on attention to the elements. The exposition of its cultivation now follows.

In this regard, since the three sections—the section on the postures, the section on the four kinds of clear comprehension, and the section on attention to the elements—are by way of insight (*vipassanā*), [the following applies].

These have been explained. The nine sections on the charnel ground are taught specifically within the context of the knowledges of insight (*vipassanā-ñāṇa*) by way of the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*).
