Furthermore, whatever development of concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā*) one might desire regarding the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and the others, that has already been set forth in detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition on the development of foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā-niddesa*).
As for the section on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-pabba*) and the section on attention to repulsiveness (*paṭikūla-manasikāra-pabba*), [they are treated elsewhere].

These two [sections] here are spoken of by way of concentration (*samādhi*). Among them, the section on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānapabba*) is a distinct meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in its own right by way of mindfulness of breathing. As for this [other section]:
"Furthermore, monks, a monk, with regard to this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards..."
He reviews it as full of various kinds of impurity, bounded by the skin, [thinking]: “In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs... down to... urine.

Thus has been undertaken the meditation on the thirty-two-fold subject of kammaṭṭhāna, which is a method for developing the mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati) taught by grouping the brain together with the bone-marrow in each respective place. This is its commentary on the meaning:

therein, “there are” (atthi) means they are found. “In this” (imasmiṃ) refers to that which extends from the soles of the feet upwards, from the hair of the head downwards, and is bounded by the skin.
"Pūra" means full of various kinds of impurity; [this refers to] "in that. "Kāya" means in the body.

For the body is called "kāya" because it is a collection (*sañcaya*) of impurities, or because it is the source (*āya*) of the loathsome things such as head-hairs and so forth, as well as the hundreds of diseases such as eye-disease and so forth.
"Head-hairs... urine"—these are the thirty-two aspects beginning with head-hairs; therein: "In this body there are head-hairs... etc.
The connection should be understood as “down to the body hairs. What is stated by this?

Even if one were to search in every possible way within this fathom-long carcass—from the soles of the feet upwards, from the top of the head downwards, and from the skin outwards—one would not find anything at all, whether gold, silver, pearl, beryl, aloeswood, or sandalwood.
If one sees even the slightest degree of purity— whether it be saffron, camphor, or perfumed powder—
one instead sees only various kinds of impurity, such as the hair of the head and body, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and unsightly to behold. This, then,
is the explanation according to the connection of the words here.
Now, the exposition of the development of foulness (*asubha-bhāvanā*) should be understood in this way: by means of the development of foulness, a clansman who is a beginner,
pure in his conduct and established in such virtue as the training precept of abstaining from taking life, should— for the sake of attaining purity of intention— [apply himself].
For one who wishes to apply himself to the development of the meditation subject consisting of the thirty-two aspects, there are first ten impediments:
namely, the impediments of dwelling, family, gain, community, business, relatives, books, illness, psychic power, and fame.
Then, by abandoning attachment to dwelling, family, gain, community, and fame; by non-involvement in business and books; and by treating illness—thus these ten [impediments are removed].
The obstacles must be severed. Then, by one who has severed the obstacles but whose desire for renunciation has not yet been severed,
having embraced a life of extreme austerity that has reached its pinnacle, and without abandoning even the minor and lesser rules of discipline,
there should be a teacher endowed with mastery of the scriptures or endowed with some other factor who provides the meditation subject.
He should approach him according to the proper method suited to the Vinaya; and when the teacher’s mind has been won over by his perfection in conduct, he should announce his own purpose.
Having understood the distinctions of that person’s physical signs, inclinations, temperament, and disposition, [the teacher] should consider whether this meditation subject is suitable for him.
Then, if the student lives in the same monastery where the teacher himself resides, [he should ask: "If it is in that very place..."
If he wishes to dwell there, then the meditation subject should be given to him in brief.

But if he wishes to dwell elsewhere, then it should be explained in detail, including its preliminary tasks by way of what is to be abandoned and what is to be undertaken, and its classifications by way of the discourse suitable for one of lustful temperament and so forth.
By that means, that meditation subject—complete with its preliminary tasks and its classifications—[should be understood].
Having mastered it and having requested permission from the teacher, [he should recite:
“The Great Abode, the New Abode, the Old Abode, and the Roadside;
The Thicket, the Leaf, the Flower, the Fruit, and the Desired.”
“A city, a field of timber, a port with dissimilar inhabitants,
a frontier borderland, or a place where no friend is found—
these eighteen places, having understood them thus, the wise man [should avoid].”
“One should avoid from afar, just as one would a dangerous path.
Thus it is said that eighteen types of lodgings are to be avoided. Having avoided those, [it is asked]:
“And how, bhikkhus, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a lodging…”

It is not too far away, nor too close; it is well-suited for coming and going; it is not crowded by day, and at night it is quiet, with little noise, and free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping creatures.
Furthermore, for one dwelling in such a lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick arise without difficulty.
Now, in that monastery there dwell elder bhikkhus who are learned, masters of the tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā.
From time to time he approaches them and questions and inquires:
"Venerable sirs, what is this? What is the meaning of this? Then those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed and clarify what has not been made clear.
They clarify what is obscure and dispel doubt regarding various matters that give rise to uncertainty.
In this way, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors. Having approached such a lodging and having performed all necessary duties—
Having reflected upon the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation,
and having gladdened the mind by recollecting the Buddha’s perfect Buddhahood, the Dhamma’s perfect Dhamma-nature, and the Saṅgha’s perfect practice,
[one should recite]: “By word and by mind, by color and by shape, by direction;”
"From the perspective of occasion, the wise know the sevenfold grasping.

Thus is the sevenfold skill in grasping: by way of successive order, not too quickly, not too slowly, warding off distraction, transcending the designation, successive relinquishing, absorption, and the three discourses—thus it is tenfold.
Skill in attention has also been taught. One who does not abandon that [skill] should undertake the development of the thirty-two aspects.
For one who undertakes it in this way, the development of the thirty-two aspects succeeds in every respect, but not otherwise.
In that regard, first taking up the fivefold skin-group according to the method beginning with "head-hairs, body-hairs," and so forth, as stated in the Tipiṭaka—
When that has become familiar, one should proceed in reverse order by way of "skin, teeth," and so forth; when that too has become familiar,

for half a month one should practice both in forward and reverse order— both by means of speech for the purpose of severing outwardly wandering thoughts and for the purpose of becoming familiar with the text,
and by means of the mind for the purpose of discerning the individual characteristics of the parts.
It should be developed. For verbal development serves as a condition for cutting off discursive thoughts that have strayed outward and for the mastery of the text through mental development;
while mental development consists of the discernment of the foul, the beautiful, or the characteristic [of impermanence, suffering, and non-self] by way of one or another of these.
Then, by that same method, one develops the fivefold group of bones for half a month, and thereafter both together for half a month.
Then, for half a month, the fivefold lungs; then, for another half-month, those three fivefold sets as well;

then, at the end, although not explicitly mentioned, the brain is included here along with the earth element and its aspects for the purpose of unified meditation, and for half a month, the fivefold brain;
then, for half a month, that fourfold set of five; then, for half a month, the sixfold fat; then, with the sixfold fat...

Together with the fivefold and fourfold sets for half a month, then the pearl-like sixfold set for half a month, and after that, the entire thirty-two-fold aspect for half a month—in this way, it should be developed by defining [the body] according to its color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation for six months.

This was said with reference to a person of medium intelligence; however, one of dull intelligence must develop it for as long as life lasts, while one of sharp intelligence [may do so] for a shorter time.
"Development is accomplished before long.
Here it is asked: "But how does he define these thirty-two aspects by way of color and so forth?
For he develops the thirty-two aspects by means of the classification into the five groups beginning with skin, according to the method starting with, "In this body there are head-hairs," and so on.
First, one defines the hair by color as "black," or as it appears to him when seen. By way of shape, one defines it as "long and cylindrical, like the beam of a scale.
As for direction, since in this body the region above the navel is called the upper direction and the region below is called the lower, therefore [it is defined] in the upper direction of this body.
He defines them by way of their origin: they are originated on the skin of the head, which is demarcated by the forehead, the ears, the crown of the head, and the nape of the neck.

In this regard, just as the tufts of grass growing on the top of an anthill do not know, "We are grown on the top of an anthill," nor does the top of the anthill know, "Tufts of grass are grown upon me"; even so, the hairs [do not know...].
They know, "We are born upon the head-skin," but the head-skin does not know, "Hair is born upon me. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application and reflection;
they are insentient, indeterminate, empty, supremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive. One defines them as neither a being nor a person.
As for delimitation, there are two kinds of delimitation: by way of the homogeneous and the heterogeneous.
In this context, the head hairs are delimited by their own root-bases—which enter the surface of the skin established below them to the extent of a grain of rice—and by the space above;
they are thus delimited by the similar (sabhāga) [delimitation].
Therefore, the head hairs are not the remaining thirty-one aspects. The remaining thirty-one are not the head hairs; thus they are delimited by the dissimilar (visabhāga).
And he defines it. Thus, first of all, he defines the head-hairs by way of color and so forth.
As for the remaining parts, he defines the body-hairs by way of color as being mostly blue-colored, or whatever kind he has seen them to be.
By way of shape, they are the shape of a bent bow, or the shape of a curved palm-leaf stalk. By way of direction, they are in two directions.
They are born in various directions; spatially, with the exception of the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet, they are mostly born on the skin of the rest of the body.

In this regard, just as the *dabba* grasses growing on the site of an old village do not know, "We are grown on the site of an old village," nor does the site of the old village know, "The *dabba* grasses are grown upon me," even so, it is not...
The body hairs know, "We have grown on the skin of the body," yet the skin of the body does not know, "Body hairs have grown on me.
For these phenomena (dhammas) are devoid of mental effort and reflection; they are insentient, indeterminate, empty, supremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and repulsive.
One defines them as neither a being nor a person. As for their delimitation: [they are bounded] below by the surface of the skin upon which they rest.
Having entered [the body] by the measure of a hair’s tip and established himself there, he defines it as being delimited above by space and across by one another through his own base.
This is their delimitation by the similar; however, the delimitation by the dissimilar is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines the body-hairs by color and so forth.
Beyond that, he defines those whose nails are complete as being twenty.

He defines them all by color as white in the parts where they are detached from the flesh, and copper-colored where they are connected to the flesh. By shape, he defines them as having the shape of their respective positions;
for the most part, they have the shape of the seeds of the *madhuka* fruit, or the shape of fish scales.
"By direction, they are produced in two directions; by location, they are established at the tips of the fingers.
In this regard, it is just as when village children place the seeds of *madhuka* fruit on the ends of sticks:
the seeds do not know, "We have been placed on the ends of sticks," nor do the sticks know, "Seeds of *madhuka* fruit have been placed upon us."
In the same way, the nails do not know, "We are fixed on the tips of the fingers," nor do the fingers know, "Nails are fixed on our tips.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental effort and reflection; they are insentient... [and so forth] ...one defines them as "not a person.
By way of delimitation: below and at the root, they are delimited by the flesh of the fingers, and there, by the surface upon which they rest.
Or, one defines it as being bounded above and at the tip by space, and on both sides by the skin at the two ends of the fingers.
This is their common delimitation; however, their uncommon delimitation is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines the nails by way of color and so forth.
Beyond that, he defines those for whom the teeth are complete as having thirty-two. He determines that all of them are white in color.
Those whose teeth are evenly set appear like a layer of conch shells cut by a coarse saw, or like a garland of white flower buds strung together evenly.
Those whose teeth are unevenly set appear like a row of old chairs and benches in a dilapidated assembly hall.
"Of various shapes": he defines them by way of their shape.
For at the ends of both rows of teeth, two each below and two each above—making eight teeth in total—are four-cornered and four-rooted, shaped like a stool (*āsandi*).
On the inner side of those, arranged in that same sequence, are eight teeth that are three-cornered and three-rooted, shaped like a crossroads (*siṅghāṭaka*).
Within those [tusks], arranged in that same sequence from bottom to top, are four teeth with two points and two roots, shaped like the pillars of a carriage well.
Within those as well, arranged in that same sequence, are four fang-teeth with one point and one root, shaped like jasmine buds. Then, in the middle of both rows of teeth...
Having placed four below and four above, there are eight teeth, each with a single point and a single root, shaped like the seed of a gourd.

As for their direction, they are born in the upper direction. As for their location, the upper ones are fixed upon the upper jawbone with their points facing downward, and the lower ones are fixed upon the lower jawbone with their points facing upward.
In this regard, just as the pillars set by a mason— fixed at the lower stone surface and inserted into the upper surface—

do not know, "We have been fixed at the lower stone surface and inserted into the upper surface," nor does the lower stone surface know, "The pillars have been fixed upon me," nor does the upper surface know, "Upon me..."

“the pillars have entered”; even so, the teeth do not know, “We are established upon the lower jawbone and have entered into the upper jawbone,” nor does the lower jawbone know, “The teeth are established upon me,” nor does the upper jawbone know, “The teeth have entered into me. They are devoid of mental application and reflection.

For these are merely phenomena... [as before] ...not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines them as delimited below by the surface of their own roots which enter and rest within the socket of the jawbone; above, by space; and across, by each other.
This is their delimitation by way of similar parts; however, their delimitation by way of dissimilar parts is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines the tooth by its color and other characteristics.
Thereafter, he defines the skin within the body—which conceals the accumulation of various kinds of filth—by its color as "white.
For although that skin appears to have various colors, such as black or white, due to being tinted by the color of the underlying flesh;
Nevertheless, it is white by virtue of its similar color. Moreover, this whiteness of his becomes evident when the skin has been destroyed by the impact of flames, blows from weapons, and so forth.
As for its shape, in brief it is the shape of a sheath; in detail, it is of various shapes.
For instance, the skin of the toes is the shape of a weaver’s shuttle-case; the skin of the back of the foot is the shape of a pair of leather sandals with a top.
The skin of the calves is shaped like a palm leaf used as a food container; the skin of the thighs is shaped like a long bag filled with rice;
the skin of the buttocks is shaped like a water-strainer made of cloth filled with water; the skin of the back is shaped like leather stretched over a wooden board;
the skin of the belly is shaped like leather stretched over the hollow body of a lute; and the skin of the chest is for the most part square-shaped.
The skin of the two forearms is shaped like a quiver-bound leather case; the skin of the back of the hand is shaped like a sheath for a razor or like a case for a comb;
the skin of the fingers is shaped like a key-case; the skin of the neck is shaped like a neck-cloth;
the skin of the face is shaped like a hollowed-out nest of crickets with many holes; and the skin of the head is shaped like a leaf-bag.

And the yogāvacara who is practicing the contemplation of the skin should first define the skin of the face by directing his mind between the skin and the flesh starting from the upper lip; then the skin of the head; then the skin of the exterior neck;
then, in both forward and reverse order, the skin of the right hand. Then, in that same sequence, the skin of the left hand.
Then the skin of the back, then the skin of the anus; then, in both forward and reverse order, the skin of the right foot, then the skin of the left foot;
then the skin of the bladder, the belly, the heart, and the inner neck; then the skin of the lower jaw, then the skin of the lower lip.
Thus, continuing upward again until the skin of the upper lip. As for its direction, it is produced in two directions.
In terms of location, it stands enveloping the entire body.
In this regard, just as a chest covered with wet hide does not know, "The chest is enveloped by me," nor does the chest know, "I am enveloped by wet hide"; even so, the skin does not know, "By me..."
And this body composed of the four great elements is bound [by skin], yet this body composed of the four great elements does not know, "I am bound by skin.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental application and reflection... [as before] ...they are not a person.
But merely— "Covered with raw hide, a great wound with nine openings;..."
"It trickles out from all sides, with impure and putrid odors.
As for its delimitation, one defines it as being bounded below by the flesh or by the surface resting upon that flesh, and above by the skin.
This is its delimitation by way of similar parts; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilar parts is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines that element by its color and other characteristics.
Thereafter, one defines the flesh within the body—which is divided into nine hundred muscles—by its color as "red, resembling the *pālibhaddaka* flower.
By its shape, it is "of various shapes"; for instance, among them, the flesh of the calves is shaped like rice placed in a palm-leaf basket.
Some say it has the shape of an unblown ketaki bud. The flesh of the thighs is shaped like a small pot for grinding lime;
the flesh of the buttocks is shaped like the edge of a hearth; the flesh of the back is shaped like a layer of palm sugar;

the flesh of the two sides is shaped like a thin coating of clay applied to the interior of a bamboo granary; and the flesh of the breasts is shaped like lumps of half-baked clay that have been rounded and cast aside.
The flesh of the two upper arms is like a large rat placed there with its skin removed;
some say it is shaped like a meat-sausage. The flesh of the cheeks is shaped like a *karañja* seed placed on the cheek region;
some say it is shaped like a frog. The flesh of the tongue is shaped like a *nuhī* leaf; the flesh of the nose is shaped like a leaf-sheath placed inside the mouth.
The flesh of the eye-socket is shaped like half-ripened udumbara fruit; the flesh of the head is shaped like the coating on the surface of a vessel being cooked over a fire.
And by the practitioner who examines the flesh, these very gross pieces of flesh must be defined according to their shape.
For when he defines them in this way, the subtle pieces of flesh come within the range of his knowledge. As for direction, they are in two [directions].
It is produced in various directions. By way of location, it stands anointing more than three hundred bones.

In this regard, just as when a wall is plastered with thick clay, the thick clay does not know, "I have plastered the wall," nor does the wall know, "I am plastered with thick clay," even so, [the body] consisting of nine hundred varieties of skin...

The flesh knows, "I am smeared over by three hundred bones," nor does the three hundred bones know, "I am smeared over by flesh divided into nine hundred muscles. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality and reflection...
[and so on] ...they are not a person. But merely—
“Nine hundred muscles, smeared over the carcass, Are strewn with various kinds of worms, like a putrid place of filth.
As for its delimitation: below, it is bounded by the collection of bones or by the surface resting upon them; above, by the skin; and across, by—
He defines it as "delimited by one another. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
however, the delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that for the head-hairs. In this way, he defines the flesh by way of color and so forth.
Following that, he defines the nine hundred types of sinews in the body by way of color as "white," or even as "honey-colored."
Some say they are of various shapes according to their configuration. For instance, among them, the very large sinews are shaped like the stalks of a *kandala* flower bud;
those finer than these are shaped like the strings of a boar-trap net; those finer still are shaped like rotting creepers;
those finer still are shaped like the strings of a Sinhalese *mahāvīṇā* lute; and those finer still are shaped like coarse threads, [found] on the backs of the hands and the backs of the feet.
The sinews are shaped like the feet of a bird; the sinews on the head are shaped like the sparse strands of fine *dukūla* cloth placed upon the heads of village children;

the sinews on the back are shaped like a fish-net spread out in the sun after being soaked; and the remaining sinews following various limbs and members of this body are shaped like a netted suit worn upon the body.
As for their direction, they arise in two directions; and among those, from the tip of the right ear—
Starting from the front, five great sinews named Kaṇḍara, binding both front and back, extend to the left side;
starting from the tip of the left ear, five [sinews], binding both front and back, extend to the right side;
and starting from the right throat-junction, five [sinews], binding both front and back, extend to the left side.
Having gone from the left side of the neck, five [tendons] bind forward and five backward, and having gone to the right side, they bind the right hand;
thus ten great sinews named *kaṇḍara* have ascended, five each forward and backward.
Likewise for the left hand, the right foot, and the left foot—thus these sixty.

He also defines the great sinews as those that support the body and control the body. By way of location, they exist throughout the entire body, binding the bones together between the skin and the bones.
In this regard, just as the creepers do not know, "By us the wall-beams are bound," when the wall-beams are bound by a succession of creepers...
“...are bound together,” nor do the wooden beams know, “We are bound together by creepers.
In the same way, the sinews do not know, “The three hundred bones are bound together by us,” nor do the three hundred bones know, “We are bound together by sinews.
For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality and reflection... [and so on] ...they are not a person. But rather—
“There are nine hundred sinews in this body, a fathom in length;
they bind together the framework of bones as creepers bind a house.
As for its delimitation: it is bounded below by the three hundred bones that form its foundation, and above by the skin and flesh.
He defines them as being "delimited from one another horizontally. This is their delimitation by way of similarity;
however, their delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this manner, he defines the sinews by way of color and so forth.
Following that, since the thirty-two teeth-bones have been taken separately in the body, there remain sixty-four hand-bones.
There are sixty-four bones of the feet, sixty-four soft bones supported by flesh, two heel bones;
in each foot there are two ankle bones, two shin bones, one knee bone, and one thigh bone;
and there are two hip bones, eighteen vertebrae, twenty-four ribs, and fourteen [ribs].

There are thirty-two bones: one breast bone, two heart bones, two collar bones, two shoulder-blade bones, two upper-arm bones, two pairs of forearm bones, seven neck bones, two jawbones, one nose bone, two eye bones, two ear bones, one forehead bone, one skull bone, and nine cranial plates; such is the enumeration.
By means of this method, one defines all the bones according to their classification as white in color.

As for their shape, they are of various shapes; for instance, among them, the bones of the toes of the feet are shaped like *kataka* seeds, the middle phalanges of the fingers immediately following those are shaped like incomplete jackfruit stones, and the base phalanges...
Some say they are shaped like small drums (paṇava) or like peacock feathers. The bones of the back of the foot are shaped like crushed kanda-lotus roots;
the bones of the heel are shaped like a single stone seed of a palmyra fruit; the ankle bones are shaped like a ball tied at one end for playing with;
among the shin bones, the smaller one is shaped like a bow-staff, while the larger one is shaped like the back of a vein withered by hunger and thirst.
The place where the shin bone rests upon the ankle bones is shaped like the core of a peeled date palm;
the place where the shin bone rests upon the knee bone is shaped like the top of a *mudiṅga* drum;
the knee bone is shaped like foam struck on one side; and the thigh bones are shaped like badly planed handles for axes or adzes.
The place where the thigh bone rests upon the hip bone has the shape of a goldsmith’s cluster of heating tongs;

the area where it is supported has the shape of a *punnāga* fruit with its tip cut off. The two hip bones are joined together in the shape of a potter’s kiln, though some say they have the shape of an ascetic’s water-strainer. The buttock bones...
The eighteen vertebrae of the spinal column are shaped like the upturned hoods of snakes with their mouths facing downward;
they are perforated in seven or eight places and, internally, are shaped like copper-plate headbands placed one upon another, while externally they are shaped like rows of circles.
Between each of these, there are two or three thorns resembling the teeth of a saw.
Among the twenty-four comfortable bones, those that are complete have the shape of a full Sinhalese tooth, while those that are incomplete have the shape of an incomplete Sinhalese tooth;
some say they all have the shape of the two outspread wings of a white cock.
The fourteen breast-bones have the shape of a row of planks on an old chariot; the heart-bone has the shape of the blade of a spear.
The collarbones are shaped like small iron hoe-handles; beneath them is a bone shaped like a half-moon.
The shoulder-blade bones are shaped like the handles of axes, though some say they are shaped like half-cut Sinhalese hoes.
The upper arm bones are shaped like mirror-sticks, though some say they are shaped like large hoe-handles. The forearm bones—
The bones of the wrist-joints are shaped like *yamaka* lotus bulbs; the bones of the forearm are shaped like a leaden bandage wrapped around a joint;
the bones of the back of the hand are shaped like crushed kanda tubers; the bones of the proximal joints of the fingers are shaped like small drums (*paṇava*);
the bones of the middle joints are shaped like incomplete jackfruit seeds; and the bones of the distal joints—
The vertebrae are shaped like *kataka* seeds; the seven cervical vertebrae are shaped like sections of bamboo stalks placed one after another, pierced through by a rod;
the lower jawbone is shaped like blacksmiths’ iron hammers joined by a cord; the upper jawbone is shaped like a scraping knife;
the bones of the eye-sockets and nostrils are shaped like young palm kernels with the pulp removed; and the frontal bone is shaped like a broken conch shell placed face down.

The bones of the ear-lobes are shaped like the leather cases used by barbers for razors; the bone above the forehead and the ear-lobes, in the place where a cloth bandage would be tied, is shaped like a thick-boned jar filled with cloth rags; the skull bone is shaped like a curved coconut with its top cut off;
and the bones of the head, when sewn together, are shaped like a worn-out gourd bowl set upright. As for direction, they are produced in two directions.
In terms of location, they reside without distinction throughout the entire body; however, specifically, the bones of the head rest upon the neck-bones;
the neck-bones rest upon the vertebrae of the spine; the vertebrae of the spine rest upon the hip-bones;
the hip-bones rest upon the thigh-bones; the thigh-bones [rest] upon the knee-bones; and the knee-bones [rest] upon the shin-bones.
The shin bones rest upon the ankle bones; the ankle bones rest upon the heel bones;
and the heel bones stand supporting the ankle bones. The ankle bones [support] the shin bones... and so on, up to:
the neck bones stand supporting the head bone. Following this sequence, the remaining bones should also be understood.

In this regard, just as among the bricks, rafters, and so forth of a building, the upper bricks do not know, "We are supported by those below," nor do the lower ones know, "We stand having lifted up those above";
even so, the bones of the head do not know, "We are supported by the bones of the neck"... and so on... down to the bones of the ankles.

They do not know, "We are supported by the ankle-bones," nor do the ankle-bones know, "We are standing having lifted up the shin-bones. For these phenomena are devoid of mental effort (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)...
[and so on] ...they are not a person. However, these three hundred and more bones, together with nine hundred sinews and nine hundred...
And [the body] is bound and smeared with hundreds of pieces of flesh, entirely enveloped by a single solid layer of skin, moistened by the fat that follows along the seventeen thousand channels,
with sweat and grime trickling from ninety-nine thousand pores, and swarming with eighty families of worms;
when a practitioner of yoga examines it according to its true nature, he sees nothing at all worth grasping— only...
But he sees only the heap of bones, connected by sinews and strewn with various corpses; seeing which, he attains the state of being a son of the One of Ten Powers. As it is said:
"The bones stand in succession, reaching to the very end..."
Passing through many births,
it is not bound by anyone; impelled by old age,
it is without consciousness, like a wooden puppet.
“Born from a corpse, in a corpse, in the impure and putrid;
foul-smelling in the foul-smelling, and subject to decay in that which is destined to break apart.
Born within the shell of bones, he has arisen in a putrid body that is itself putrid.”
"And direct your desire toward that; you shall become sons of the One Possessed of Ten Powers.
As for their delimitation: one defines them as being delimited internally by the marrow, externally by the flesh, and at the top and bottom by each other.
This is their delimitation by way of similar factors (*sabhāga-pariccheda*); however, their delimitation by way of dissimilar factors (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines the bones by color and so forth.
Thereafter, he defines the bone-marrow located within the bones of the body—which have been described with their various classifications—by color as "white.
By shape, he defines it as having the shape of its own location. For example, in the case of the very large [bones]...
Having been steamed and rounded inside the bones, it has the shape of a large bamboo shoot placed inside the hollows of large bamboo or reed stalks;
having been steamed and rounded inside the smaller and minute bones, it has the shape of a thin bamboo shoot placed inside the hollows of small and minute bamboo or reed stalks.
As for its direction, it is located in two directions. As for its location, it is established within the interior of the bones.
In this regard, just as curds and molasses contained within bamboo or reeds do not know,
"We are contained within bamboo or reeds," nor do the bamboo and reeds know, "Curds and molasses are contained within us";
even so, the marrow does not know, "I am contained within the bones," nor do the bones know, "Marrow..."
"...is included within us. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (ābhoga) and reflective review (paccavekkhaṇa)... [as before] ...they are not a person.
By way of delimitation, one defines them as delimited by the inner surfaces of the bones and by the portion consisting of the bone-marrow.
This is its delimitation by way of similar things; however, the delimitation by way of dissimilar things is the same as that of the head-hairs. Thus [one defines] the bone-marrow.
He defines it by way of color and so forth.

Thereafter, he defines the kidneys—which are of two types, including the "ball-like" (dvigoḷaka) variety—within the interior of the body, as being pale red in color, like the color of *pālibhaddaka* seeds.
As for their shape, they are shaped like the balls used for string games by village children, or like two mangoes joined at a single stalk.
Some say: "It is born in the upper direction. As for its location: having emerged from the throat-passage, it travels a short distance on a single stalk that then splits into two;
thus bound by thick sinews, it stands surrounding the heart-flesh.
In this regard, just as a pair of mango fruits attached to a single stalk does not know, "I am bound by a stalk," [so too the lungs do not know they are so bound].
Nor does the stalk know, "I have bound together two mango fruits";
even so, the kidney does not know, "I am bound together by the thick sinew," nor does the thick sinew know, "I have bound together the kidney.

For these phenomena are devoid of intention (ābhoga) and reflection (paccavekkhaṇa)... [as before] ...they are not a person. By way of delimitation, the kidney is delimited by its own portion as kidney.
"One delimits" means one defines it. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
as for the delimitation by way of dissimilarity, it is just like that of the head-hairs. In this way, one defines the kidney by color and so forth.
Following that, within the interior of the body, one defines the heart by color as "red, with the color of the back of a red lotus petal."
He defines it by its shape: setting aside the outer petals, it has the shape of a lotus bud placed face down;
and that [bud] has one side opened like a *punnāga* fruit with its tip cut off, smooth on the outside, and inside resembling the interior of a *kosātakī* fruit.
For those of great wisdom, it is slightly blossomed; for those of dull wisdom, it remains merely a bud. That which...

The mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element proceed depending upon the physical form; setting that aside, within the heart—which is reckoned as a lump of flesh—the blood remains in the measure of half a *pasata*.

That blood is red in one of lustful temperament, blackish in one of hating temperament, like water used for washing meat in one of deluded temperament, the color of horse-gram soup in one of discursive-thought temperament, and [clear] in one of faithful temperament.
It has the color of a *kaṇikāra* flower; for one whose conduct is characterized by wisdom, it appears clear, serene, and undisturbed, radiant like a well-polished natural gem.
As for its direction, it is born in the upper direction. As for its location, it is established within the body between the two breasts.
In this regard, just as a doorpost standing between two window-panels does not know,
"I am standing between two window-panels," nor do the window-panels know,
"A doorpost is standing between us"; even so, the heart does not know, "I [am between] two..."
Nor do the breasts know, "The heart is situated between us. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (ābhoga) and reflection...
[as before] ...they are not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines the heart as being delimited by its own heart-portion.
This is its delimitation by way of the similar; the delimitation by way of the dissimilar is as follows:
But it is exactly like hair; thus one defines the heart by way of its color and other characteristics.
Following that, within the body, one defines the twin mass of flesh known as the liver (*yakana*) by its color as red, with the color of the back of the petals of a red water-lily (*raktakumuda*).
As for its shape, having a single root, it is twin at the top and shaped like a *koviḷāra* leaf; and that—
For those who are dull-witted, there is only one large [flesh-mass]; for those possessed of wisdom, there are two or three small ones.
As for its direction, it is born in the upper direction. As for its location, it stands within the space between the two breasts, supported by the right side.
In this regard, just as a piece of meat clinging to the side of a cooking pot does not know, "I am clinging to the side of a cooking pot," so too...
Nor does the side of the pot know, "A piece of meat is stuck to me.
In the same way, the liver does not know, "I am situated on the right side within the two breasts," nor does the right side within the breasts know, "The liver is situated depending on me.
They are devoid of mental engagement (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*).
For these phenomena... [as before] ...are not a person. Furthermore, by way of delimitation, one defines it as: "The liver is delimited by its own portion as liver.
This is its delimitation by way of its own class; however, its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar is the same as that of the head-hairs and so forth.
In this way, one defines the liver by way of color and the other characteristics.

Beyond that, he defines the *kilomaka* (spleen), which is twofold according to the distinction between that which is concealed and that which is unconcealed within the body. As to color, it is white, the color of a piece of *dukūla* cloth.
As to shape, it has the shape of its own location. As to direction, it is situated in two directions.
As to location, the concealed *kilomaka* surrounds the heart and the kidneys, while the unconcealed *kilomaka* [is located]...
It stands enveloping the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body.

In this regard, just as when meat is wrapped in a cloth, the cloth does not know, "I have wrapped the meat," nor does the meat know, "I am wrapped in cloth"; even so, the *kilomaka* (spleen) does not know [this].
“[I think,] ‘The heart and kidneys, and the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body, are enveloped by the fat.
Yet neither the heart and kidneys nor the flesh throughout the entire body knows, ‘I am enveloped by the fat. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality and reflection...
[as before] ...they are not a person. By way of delimitation: below by the flesh, above by the skin, and across...
One defines and delimits it as being limited by a portion of a kilo. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this way, one defines the *kilomaka* (mesentery) by way of color and so forth.
Following that, within the interior of the body, one defines the *pihaka* (spleen) by way of color as being blue, the color of a withered *nigguṇḍī* flower.
One defines it by way of shape: for the most part, it measures seven finger-breadths, is without attachment, and has the shape of a black goat’s tongue.
By way of direction, it is born in the upper direction. By way of location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, resting against the upper surface of the abdominal membrane;
when struck by a blow from a weapon, the life of beings passes away because of its exit to the outside.
In this regard, just as a lump of cow dung standing against the upper wall of a storehouse does not know,
"I am standing against the upper wall of the storehouse," nor does the upper wall of the storehouse know, "A lump of cow dung is standing against me";
even so, the spleen does not know, "I am standing against the upper wall of the stomach lining."
Nor does the surface of the stomach know, "I am situated in dependence upon the liver. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection;
they are not a person (*puggala*). By way of delimitation, one defines the liver as being delimited by its own liver-portion.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*); however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines the spleen by its color and other characteristics.
Thereafter, one defines the lungs—which consist of thirty-two distinct portions of flesh within the body—by their color as being red, like the color of a slightly ripened *udumbara* fruit;
and by their shape as having the form of unevenly cut cakes.
Some say its shape is like a heap of broken, withered husks.

This [organ] is tasteless and lacks nutritive essence because it is struck by the heat of the kamma-born fire that has risen up due to the absence of food, drink, and so forth within it; it is like a lump of chewed straw.
In terms of direction, it is born in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is inside the body, between the two breasts.
It stands hanging down, covering the heart and the liver from above.
In this regard, just as a bird’s nest hanging inside an old tower does not know,
"I am standing hanging inside an old tower," nor does the interior of the old tower know, "A bird’s nest is hanging on me."

"stands"; even so, the lungs do not know, "I am standing hanging inside the body between the two breasts," nor does that which is inside the body between the two breasts know, "The lungs are standing hanging in me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)... [and so on]... they do not.
"Person": By way of delimitation, he defines the lungs as being delimited by the portion that is lung.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this way, he defines the lungs by color and so forth.
Following that, within the body of a man, [the space] is thirty-two cubits, and for a woman, twenty-eight cubits; in one who is... twenty-one... [cubits].
In terms of location, one defines it as being sunken in certain places, and in terms of color, as white, with the hue of lime or gravel.

In terms of shape, it has the form of a dhamma-stone (judicial stone) that has been cut off at the top and placed after being rolled around in a trough of blood. In terms of direction, it is situated in two directions.
In terms of location, because it is bound above by the throat-passage and below by the path of excrement, its boundaries are the throat-passage and the path of excrement.
"Situated within the body.
In this regard, just as a severed head— a mere heap of bones— placed in a bowl of blood does not know,
"I am situated in a bowl of blood," nor does the bowl of blood know, "In me is a severed head— a mere heap of bones..."
"Stationed"; even so, it does not know "I am stationed within the body," nor does it know the interior of the body as "the end is stationed within me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)... [as before] ...it is not a person (*puggala*).
By way of delimitation, one defines the end as being delimited by its own internal portion. This is its delimitation by way of commonality (*sabhāga-pariccheda*).
The delimitation by way of what is dissimilar is just like that of the head-hairs; thus he defines the end by way of color and so forth.
Thereafter, within the body, between the ends, he defines the entrail (antaguṇa) by way of color as white, with the color of the root of the *dakasītalikā* plant.
By way of shape, it is shaped exactly like the root of the *dakasītalikā*; some say its shape is like cow's urine.
By direction, it is that which has arisen in two directions.

By location, it stands between the twenty-one intestinal coils, like a cord situated between the rings of a foot-wiping rope; for when those performing work with spades, axes, and so forth pull on a machine, the wooden planks of the machine are bound together at one end by the inner coils, just as the cords are sewn together within the ring of a foot-wiping rope.
In this regard, just as the string used for sewing a foot-wiping cloth does not know,
"I have sewn this foot-wiping cloth," nor does the foot-wiping cloth know, "The string has sewn me together," even so,
the small intestine does not know, "I am situated having bound the large intestine within twenty-one coils."
Nor does it know its own end, thinking, "I am standing bound by the inner cord. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality (ābhoga) and reflection;
... [as before] ... they are not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines them as being delimited by the portion that constitutes the inner cord.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity; however, their delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines the internal entrails by color and so forth.
Thereafter, one defines the undigested food (udariya) within the body by color as being the color of the food that has been swallowed.
By shape, it has the shape of rice grains loosely bound in a strainer. By direction, it is located in the upper direction. By location, [it is found]...
"Situated in the belly. The belly is the intestinal membrane that resembles a blister formed in the middle of a wet cloth when it is squeezed from both sides;
it is smooth on the outside and wrapped in a layer of flesh on the inside, resembling a soiled *pāvāra* flower, and according to some, like the interior of a rotting jackfruit.
Within it dwell the *takkolaka*, *gaṇḍuppādaka*, *tālahīraka*, *sūcimukhaka*, and *paṭatantusuttaka* worms.
In this way, thirty-two species of worms dwell there, crowded and swarming together, moving in dense throngs.
When food, drink, and so forth are not present, they leap up and, crying out, pierce the heart-flesh.
And at the time of swallowing food, drink, and so forth, they turn their faces upward and rush in great haste toward the first two or three morsels that have been swallowed.
They devour it. That which is the birthplace of these worms— the privy, the latrine, the infirmary, and the charnel ground—
is like a cesspool at the gate of a village of outcasts, where, during the autumn season when the sky rains down thick drops,
various kinds of filth such as urine, feces, skin, bones, pieces of flesh, sinews, spittle, snot, blood, and so forth, are swept away by the water.
Having fallen, it becomes churned by mud and water, swarming with a multitude of worms;

after two or three days have passed, heated by the force of the sun’s heat, emitting froth and bubbles on top, deep blue in color, and becoming extremely foul-smelling and loathsome, it reaches a state where it is unfit even to approach or look upon, let alone to smell or taste. Even so...

Various kinds of food and drink, crushed by the pestle-like teeth, turned over by the hand of the tongue, smeared with saliva and spittle, having at that moment lost its excellence of color, fragrance, and taste—
resembling the refuse of a *koliya* grove or the vomit of a dog— falling down and becoming enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind,
is heated by the force of the heat of the stomach-fire and becomes teeming with swarms of worms, one upon another.
It remains emitting froth and bubbles, having reached a state of extreme stench, foulness, and loathsomeness;
hearing of which, even in regard to food and drink, a sense of repulsiveness arises, let alone after one has looked at it with the eye of wisdom.
And wherever that food and drink falls, it undergoes a fivefold separation: one portion is eaten by living creatures,
One portion is consumed by the digestive fire; one portion becomes urine; one portion becomes feces;
and one portion, having attained the state of nutritional essence (*rasa*), nourishes the blood, flesh, and other bodily constituents.
In this regard, just as dog-vomit situated in an utterly loathsome dog-tub does not know, "I am in a dog-tub..."

“...is situated”; nor does the dog’s trough know, “The dog’s vomit is situated in me. In the same way, the undigested food in the stomach (*udariya*) does not know, “I am situated in this most foul-smelling and loathsome belly”; nor does the belly know, “The undigested food is situated in me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental effort (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)... [and so on] ...they are not a person.
By way of delimitation, one defines the stomach contents (*udariya*) as being delimited by its own portion of stomach contents. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs (*kesa*). In this manner, one defines the stomach contents by way of color and so forth.
Following that, one defines the excrement (*karīsa*) within the body by way of color as being, for the most part, the color of the food that has been swallowed.
As to shape, it has the shape of a space; as to direction, it is born in the downward direction; as to location, it is situated in the receptacle for digested food (pakvāśaya).

The "receptacle for digested food" is a region eight finger-breadths in height, located below between the navel and the base of the spinal column at the end of the intestines, resembling the interior of a bamboo tube;
therein, just as if something had fallen on the upper floor of a building...
Just as rainwater, having flowed down, remains filling the lower ground, even so whatever food, drink,

and so forth has fallen into the stomach is cooked by the digestive fire until it becomes like a mass of foam; then, being repeatedly cooked, it attains a state of smoothness like flour ground on a millstone,
and flowing down through the interior of the intestines, it is pressed together like yellow clay placed inside a bamboo tube.
It remains there having become accumulated as it were.

In this regard, just as yellow clay pressed and placed inside a bamboo tube does not know, "I am situated in a bamboo tube," nor does the bamboo tube know, "Yellow clay is situated in me"; even so, the dung [does not know].
It knows, "I am situated in the receptacle for digested food," but the receptacle for digested food does not know, "Feces are situated in me.

For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection; ... [as before] ... it is not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines feces as being delimited by its own nature as feces.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity (*sabhāga-pariccheda*); the delimitation by way of dissimilarity (*visabhāga-pariccheda*) is as follows:
"But it is just like hair"—in this way he defines the excrement by its color and other characteristics.
Thereafter, he defines the brain inside the skull of the body by its color as white, with the color of a cluster of *ahichattaka* mushrooms;
some say it has the color of boiled milk. By way of shape, it has the shape of its location. By way of direction, it belongs to the upper [direction].

As for its location: within the skull, it is situated in a massed heap, supported by the four sutures of the cranium like four lumps of dough placed together; it exists as a division of four types of brain-matter.
In this regard, just as a lump of dough placed inside an old gourd shell, or boiled milk, does not know [its container], so too [the brain does not know the head].
Just as a lump of dough or boiled milk does not know, "I am situated in an old gourd-shell," nor does the old gourd-shell know, "A lump of dough or boiled milk is situated within me";
even so, the brain does not know, "I am situated inside the skull," nor does the interior of the skull know, "Brain is situated within me. They are devoid of intentionality and reflective awareness.
For these are phenomena... [as before] ... not a person. By way of delimitation, he defines it thus: "The brain is delimited by its own brain-portion.
This is its delimitation by the similar; however, its delimitation by the dissimilar is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines the brain by way of color and so forth.
Beyond that, one defines bile—which is twofold, distinguished by being bound or unbound within the body—in terms of color as having the color of thick madhuka oil.
Some say that unbound bile has the color of a withered bakula flower. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location.
In terms of direction, it is produced in two directions. In terms of location, unbound bile is found in the places where the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth are detached from the flesh.
Avoiding the stiff, dry skin, it remains pervading the rest of the body like a drop of oil on water;
when it is disturbed, the eyes become yellow and roll, and the limbs tremble and itch.
As for the "bound bile" (*baddhapitta*), it is situated between the heart and the lungs, supported by the liver, resembling the pod of a large *kosātaki* creeper.

It resides in the gall-bladder; when it becomes disturbed, beings become insane, their minds deranged, and having abandoned shame and dread of blame, they do what should not be done, say what should not be said, and think what should not be thought.
In this regard, just as oil spread over water does not know, "I am spread over water," so too [the bile does not know its own state].
Nor does the water know, "Oil has pervaded me and is staying here.
In the same way, the free-floating bile (*abaddhapitta*) does not know, "I am staying having pervaded the body," nor does the body know, "Free-floating bile has pervaded me and is staying here.
And just as rainwater staying in the hollow of a *kosātaki* gourd does not know, "I am in the hollow of a *kosātaki* gourd..."
“‘It is stored’: nor does the sheath of the *kosātaki* gourd know, ‘Rainwater is stored within me.
In the same way, the bound bile does not know, ‘I am stored in the gall-bladder,’ nor does the gall-bladder know, ‘Bound bile is stored within me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection; ... [as before] ... they are not a person. By way of delimitation, bile is delimited by its own nature as bile.
He defines it as "delimited. This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this manner, he defines bile according to its color and other characteristics.
Following that, he defines phlegm within the interior of the body—measuring about one bowlful—as being white in color, like the juice of the *kacchaka* leaf.
He defines it by shape as having the shape of its location; by direction as being born in the upper direction; and by location as situated on the surface of the belly.

Just as when food, drink, and so forth are swallowed, it remains covering [the stomach] just like duckweed or moss in water—splitting in two when a piece of wood or a stone falls into it, and then covering it over again—in the same way...
It falls upon the food, drink, and so forth; having split into two, it remains covering them.
And when that [fire] has subsided, the lining of the stomach becomes like a ripe boil or a rotten hen’s egg, possessing the utterly loathsome stench of a corpse.
Furthermore, from the odor rising up from it, both the eructation and the mouth become foul-smelling, resembling a putrid corpse.
And that person becomes subject to being told, "Go away, you foul-smelling crow!
for within the very membrane of the belly, he remains suppressing the stench of corpses— just like the inner lining of a cesspool—
which has increased and become thickened.
In this regard, just as the layer of froth on top of a cesspool does not know, "I am situated upon a cesspool," nor does the cesspool know, "A layer of froth is situated upon me";

even so, the phlegm does not know, "I am situated on the surface of the stomach," nor does the surface of the stomach know, "Phlegm is situated within me. They are devoid of mental application and reflection.
For these phenomena... [as before] ...are not a person. By way of delimitation, he defines phlegm as being delimited by its own portion of phlegm.

This is its delimitation by way of its own nature; however, its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar is the same as that of head-hair. In this way, he defines phlegm by way of color and so forth.
Beyond that, one defines pus in the body by way of color as "the color of a withered leaf. By way of shape, it is the shape of its location.
By way of direction, it is born in two directions. By way of location, there is no fixed place for pus called its "location" where it might remain accumulated;
rather, wherever a part of the body is struck by stumps, thorns, weapons, flames, and so forth, [there it arises].
The blood coagulates and cooks, or boils erupt such as abscesses and pustules, and it remains here and there. In this regard,
just as the resin that has flowed out and settled in various places on a tree where it was struck by the edge of an axe or other tools does not know,
"I am situated in the struck places of the tree," nor does the struck place of the tree [know this].
Just as pus does not know, "I am situated here and there in the body on places struck by stumps,
thorns, and so forth, or on places where boils, pustules, and the like have arisen," nor does that part of the body know, "Pus is situated in me"—
for these phenomena are devoid of mental engagement (*ābhoga*) and reflection... [and so on].
"It is not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines it thus: "The pus is delimited by what precedes it.

This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this manner, one defines the pus by way of color and so forth.
Following that, regarding the two kinds of blood in the body—namely, stored blood and circulating blood—one [first] takes the stored blood.
First, by way of color, one defines it as follows: the stored blood is the color of thick, boiled lac juice, while the circulating blood is the color of clear lac juice.
By way of shape, all of it has the shape of its own respective location. By way of direction, the stored blood is located in the upper direction, whereas the circulating blood is in both directions.
By way of location, the circulating blood is found in the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth.
Excluding both the places where the flesh is absent and the stiff, dry skin, it remains pervading the entire acquired body by following the network of veins.
As for the accumulated blood, it fills the lower part of the liver;
measuring about one bowlful, it falls drop by drop upon the kidneys, heart, and lungs, moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs.
It wets what it stands upon; while standing there, it wets the kidneys, heart, and so forth, causing sentient beings to become thirsty.

In this regard, just as water standing in a worn-out pot does not know, "I am standing in a worn-out pot and am wetting the clods of earth and other things below," nor does the worn-out pot [know this].
Just as those below, such as clods of earth and the like, know, "Water is standing upon me," or "It is standing there soaking us," even so the blood does not know,
"I am standing beneath the liver, soaking the kidneys, heart, and so forth," nor do the region beneath the liver or the kidneys, heart, and so forth, know, "Blood is standing upon me."
"Or us, while we stand [watching] him deceiving. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality and retrospective reflection... [and so on] ...they are not a person.
By way of delimitation, one defines blood as "delimited by its own blood-portion. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of head-hair. In this manner, one defines blood by way of color and so forth.
Thereafter, one defines sweat in the body by way of color as having the color of clear sesame oil. By way of shape, it has the shape of its location.
By way of direction, it arises in two directions. By way of location, there is no fixed location for sweat where it might always remain like blood;
rather, whenever [it arises] due to the heat of a fire, the heat of the sun, seasonal changes, and so forth—

The body heats up, and then it trickles out from all the openings of the pores of the head-hair and body-hair like a mass of water that has just been drawn from a pond, or like a cluster of unevenly cut lotus stalks, water-lilies, and lotus stems. Therefore, by way of those openings of the head-hair and body-hair pores, he defines it according to its shape.
And the meditator who is examining the sweat should [visualize] it as filling the openings of the head-hair and body-hair pores.
"The sweat should be brought to mind by way of its persistence alone," so it was said by the ancient teachers.
In this regard, just as water trickling out through the openings of a cluster of lotus roots or stalks does not know,
"I am trickling out through the openings of a cluster of lotus roots or stalks," nor do the openings of the cluster of lotus roots or stalks [know this].

They know, "Water is trickling from us. In the same way, sweat does not know, "I am trickling from the pores of the head hairs and body hairs," nor do the pores of the head hairs and body hairs know, "Sweat is trickling from us. For these phenomena are devoid of mental effort and reflection...
[as before] ...there is no person. By way of delimitation, he defines sweat as being delimited by its own nature as sweat.
"This is its delimitation by way of similarity; as for its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, it is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this way, one defines sweat by way of color and so forth.
Thereafter, one defines fat—which lies between the skin and the flesh in the body—by way of color as being like the color of split turmeric.
As to shape, it has the shape of a space. For in one who is happy and of a stout body, it is spread out between the skin and the flesh, having the shape of turmeric-dyed dukūla rags;

whereas in one of a lean body, it is coiled up, resting against the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the flesh of the spine supported by the spinal vertebrae, and the flesh of the belly-wall, having the shape of a piece of turmeric-dyed dukūla rag. As to direction, it is in two directions.
It is produced in the various directions. In terms of location, it pervades the entire body of one with a stout physique;

in those who are thin, it rests upon the flesh of the shanks and so forth. Although it consists of oily matter, because it is supremely loathsome, it is not collected for the purpose of head-oil, nor for mouth-rinse oil, nor for lighting lamps.
In this regard, just as a piece of yellow-dyed fine cotton rag placed upon a heap of flesh does not know,
"I am placed upon a heap of flesh," nor does the heap of flesh know, "A piece of yellow-dyed fine cotton rag is placed upon me";
even so, fat does not know, "I [am] in the entire body or on the flesh of the calves and so forth."
Nor does it know the entire body, nor the flesh in the calves and so forth, thinking, "Fat is situated supported by me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)... [as before] ...they are not a person.
By way of delimitation, one defines fat as delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and all around by its own portions of fat.
"This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines fat by color and so forth.
Following that, one defines tears in the body by color as being the color of clear sesame oil. By shape, they have the shape of their location.
By direction, it is born in the upper direction. By location, it resides in the eye sockets.
And this does not remain constantly accumulated in the eye sockets like bile in the gall-bladder;
rather, it occurs when beings born of joy laugh with loud laughter, or when beings born of grief weep and lament, or when they consume such unwholesome food.

Or they carry it away; and when their eyes are struck by smoke, dust, sand, and so forth, then tears arise from these factors such as joy, grief, and irregular diet, and remain filling the eye sockets or flow out.
"The meditator who is grasping the tears should attend to them precisely by way of their remaining filling the eye sockets," so the ancient teachers explain.
In this regard, just as water standing in hollows made by cutting off the tops of young palm trees does not know,
"I am standing in hollows made by cutting off the tops of young palm trees," nor do those hollows made by cutting off the tops of young palm trees know,
"Water is standing in us"; even so, the tears do not know, "I am standing in the eye-hollows."
Nor do the eye-sockets know, "Tears are situated within us. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection...
[as before] ...nor is it a person. By way of delimitation, one defines tears as being delimited by what is similar to tears.
This is their delimitation by way of similarity; however, their delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of head-hairs. Thus [one defines] tears.
One defines it by way of color and so forth.
Thereafter, one defines *vasā*—which is the grease dissolved within the body—by way of color as being the color of oil poured into gruel.

By way of shape, it has the shape of its respective locations. By way of direction, it is found in two directions. By way of location, it is found on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the tops of the shoulders.
"Abiding": This does not mean that it remains permanently dissolved in these locations;
rather, when those places become heated by fire, by the heat of the sun, or by an imbalance of temperature or elements, it then flows there as if melted, like frost over clear waters in a spring.
Just as the frost covering a spring does not know, "I am [over] the springs," so too...
...standing after having overspread it; nor do the water-pools know, "The frost stands having overspread us.

In the same way, the fat does not know, "I stand having overspread the palms of the hands and so forth," nor do the palms of the hands and so forth know, "Fat stands having overspread us. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality and reflection... [and so on].
"It is not a person. By way of delimitation, he defines it as being delimited by its own portion, which is fat.
This is its delimitation by way of its own class; however, its delimitation by way of what is dissimilar is the same as that of the head-hairs. Thus he defines fat by way of color and so forth.
Following that, within the body, inside the mouth, he defines saliva by way of color as white, with the color of foam.
As to its shape, it has the shape of a space; some say it has the shape of sea-foam. As to direction, it is born in the upper direction.
As to location, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, it rests upon the tongue. And this does not remain here always accumulated;
rather, when beings see or remember such food as is hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour, [it arises].
Or they place something in their mouth. And when their heart becomes weary, or when a sense of disgust arises toward something, then saliva is produced;
having emerged from both sides of the cheeks, it settles upon the tongue.
This saliva is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue, as is the grain placed in the mouth.
Whether it be rice, or something else to be chewed, it is always capable of digesting it without ever reaching exhaustion, just as water in a well dug on a riverbank never runs dry. In this regard,
just as the water standing at the bottom of a well dug on a riverbank does not know, "I am standing at the bottom of a well," [so too is the digestive fire].
Nor does the bottom of the well know, "Water is resting within me.

In the same way, the saliva does not know, "I have descended from both sides of the cheeks and am established upon the surface of the tongue," nor does the surface of the tongue know, "Saliva has descended from both sides of the cheeks and is established upon me.
For these phenomena are devoid of mental effort and reflection... [and so forth].
"It is not a person. By way of delimitation, he defines it thus: "Saliva is delimited by its own portion of saliva. This is its delimitation by way of similarity;
as for its delimitation by way of dissimilarity, it is the same as that of the head-hairs. In this way, he defines saliva by its color and so forth.
Following that, he defines the snot in the body by its color as white, with the color of the pith of a young palmyra fruit. By way of shape...
Some say its shape is that of the space [within the nostrils], while others say it has the shape of bamboo sprouts inserted continuously into the nostrils after being repeatedly steamed.
As for its direction, it is born in the upper direction. As for its location, it stands filling the nostrils.
Furthermore, this does not remain here always accumulated; rather, it is just as if a man were to place curd in a lotus leaf.
Suppose one were to tie a lotus leaf underneath and pierce it with a thorn;

then, through that opening, a lump of curd would drip out and fall away. In the same way, when beings weep, or when their elements become disturbed due to incompatible food or climate, the brain—which has reached a state of putrid phlegm—drips from within the head and passes through the opening between the palate and the upper jaw.
Having descended, it fills the nostrils and remains there.

In this regard, just as putrid curd placed in a leather bag does not know, "I am staying in a leather bag," nor does the leather bag know, "Putrid curd is staying in me"; even so, the snot does not know, "I..."
“Snot is situated in the nostrils,” nor do the nostrils know, “Snot is situated in us. For these phenomena are devoid of intentionality (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)...
[as before] ...they are not a person. By way of delimitation, one defines snot as delimited by its own portion of snot.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, one defines the nasal mucus by its color and other characteristics.
Following that, regarding the synovial fluid (*lasikā*) within the body—the slimy, putrid substance inside the joints—one defines it as being, by color, the color of *kaṇikāra* resin.
By shape, it has the shape of its location. By direction, it is in two directions.
As for its location: it is situated within the eighty-one hundred joints, performing the function of lubricating the articulations of the bones.
And in one whose [marrow] is deficient, when that person stands up, sits down, approaches, retreats, bends, or stretches, the bones creak and produce a sound like snapping fingers.
He wanders about as if he were doing so; even when he has traveled a distance of only one or two *yojanas*, his air element becomes disturbed and his limbs ache.

However, for one in whom this [meditation] is abundant, his bones do not creak when standing or sitting, and even after traveling a long distance, his air element does not become disturbed nor do his limbs ache.
In this regard, just as the lubricating oil does not know, "I stand having lubricated the axle," nor does the axle know,
"The oil stands having lubricated me"; even so, the synovial fluid does not know,
"I stand having lubricated the eighty joints," nor do the eighty joints know, "The synovial fluid stands having lubricated us."

For these states are devoid of mental application and reflection... [and so on] ...they are not a person. By way of delimitation, he defines it thus: "The synovial fluid is delimited by its own portion of synovial fluid.
This is its delimitation by way of similar things; as for its delimitation by way of dissimilar things, however, it is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines the synovial fluid by way of color and the other characteristics.
Thereafter, one defines the urine within the body by color as being the color of bean-brine water.
By shape, it has the shape of the water inside a water-pot placed upside down and filled with water. By direction, it is located in the lower direction.
By location, it is situated within the bladder (*vatthi*). The "bladder" (*vatthi*) refers to the bladder-sac.
Just as when a mouthless wooden box is placed upon a cesspool, the liquid from the cesspool enters it, yet no path of entry is perceived;
even so, urine enters through the body, yet no path of entry is perceived, while the path of exit alone is manifest. And when the bladder is filled with urine, one knows: "Urine."

The accumulation of beings occurs with the thought, "I shall do [it]. In this regard, just as the liquid from a cesspool does not know when it has been poured into a mouthless wooden barrel, "I am situated in a mouthless wooden barrel," nor does the wooden barrel know, "The liquid from a cesspool is situated in me";
even so, the urine does not know, "I am situated in the bladder."
Nor does the bladder know, "urine is contained within me. For these phenomena are devoid of mental application (*ābhoga*) and reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa*)...
[as before] ...it is not a person. As to delimitation, one defines it as delimited by the interior of the bladder and by the portion of the urine.
This is its delimitation by way of similarity; however, its delimitation by way of dissimilarity is the same as that of the head-hairs.
In this way, he defines excrement by way of its color and so forth. Thus, he defines these thirty-two aspects by way of their color and so forth.

As he thus defines these thirty-two aspects by way of color and the rest, through his application to that respective meditation, the head-hairs and other parts become familiar and appear as distinct components. From that time on, just as...

Just as when a man with good eyesight looks at a garland of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread, all the flowers become clearly manifest to him as if they were neither before nor after one another;

even so, for one who observes this body with mindfulness, thinking "In this body there are head-hairs," all those phenomena become clearly manifest as if they were neither before nor after one another. Regarding the head-hairs:
When [the mind] is directed toward them, mindfulness proceeds uninterruptedly until they are excreted.
From that point on, humans, animals, and other beings as they wander about appear to him having abandoned their sentient form, appearing merely as heaps of constituent parts.
And the food, drink, and so forth being swallowed by them appear as if they were being thrown into those heaps of constituent parts.
Here it is asked: "What then should be done by him after that? It is said in reply:
That very sign (nimitta) should be cultivated, developed, practiced frequently, and well-defined.
But how does he cultivate, develop, practice frequently, and well-define that sign? For he [perceives] it as the constituent parts of hair and so forth.
He cultivates the sign of presence; he adheres to, frequents, and approaches mindfulness, causing it to take root within him.
Therein, by increasing the mindfulness already attained, he is said to "develop" it.
He "cultivates it repeatedly" means that he makes it associated with mindfulness again and again, struck by applied thought and sustained thought. He "defines it well-defined" means that, as follows:
It becomes well-defined and does not disappear again; in that way, one defines it with mindfulness, sustains it, and anchors it.

Alternatively, [one defines it] by means of what was previously mentioned: in successive order, not too quickly, not too slowly, through the abandoning of distraction, and through the transcending of the conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti*).
Skill in attention is said to be tenfold: by way of gradual release, by way of characteristics, and by way of the three discourses.
