In this context, one who attends gradually "cultivates" [the meditation]; one who attends neither too quickly nor too slowly "develops" it;
one who attends with the abandoning of distraction "repeatedly practices" it; and one who attends by way of surmounting designations...
It should be understood that while attending [to them], he defines them as well-defined.
Here it is asked: "But how does he attend to these phenomena by way of successive order and so forth? It is said:
For having attended to the head-hairs, he next attends to the body-hairs, not to the nails. Likewise, having attended to the body-hairs...
Having done that, he next brings the nails to mind, not the teeth. This method applies everywhere.

Why? Because one who attends to them out of sequence is like an unskilled man who, climbing a thirty-two-rung ladder out of order, becomes exhausted and falls from the ladder rather than completing his ascent; even so, by way of the failure to achieve success in meditation...
Because he does not attain the gratification that ought to be attained, his mind becomes weary and he falls away from the development of the thirty-two aspects;
he does not bring the development to completion.
Even when attending to them in successive order, he attends to "head-hairs, body-hairs" and so forth without being too rapid. [If] too rapidly...
For just as a man traveling along a road who is unable to observe the signs of the path— such as level and uneven ground, trees, open spaces, depressions, and forked paths—
is consequently unskilled in the way and fails to reach the end of his journey;
even so, one who is unable to observe the signs of the thirty-two aspects, such as color and shape, is likewise [unskilled].
He is not skilled in the thirty-two aspects, and he brings the meditation subject to exhaustion.
And just as he does not attend too quickly, so he attends not too slowly either.
For by attending too slowly, it is just as if a man traveling on a long journey were to spend time among trees, mountains, ponds, and so forth along the way.
Just as one who delays and fails to reach his desired destination meets with ruin and disaster at the hands of lions, tigers,

and other predators along the way, even so, one who fails to attain the perfection of the thirty-two aspects of meditation meets with ruin and disaster through sensual thoughts and the like due to the interruption of that meditation before reaching its goal.
He attends to it neither too quickly nor too slowly, and he attends to it for the purpose of abandoning distraction.
"Abandoning distraction" means that he attends in such a way that his mind does not become distracted by other things, such as building works and the like.
For one whose mind is distracted externally, with thoughts directed toward the hair and so forth, fails to reach perfection in meditation because the mind is not concentrated.
If he is distracted, he encounters misfortune and ruin along the way, like the companions of the Bodhisatta on his journey to Takkasilā.

But one whose mind is undistracted, whose thoughts are concentrated precisely upon the hair and so forth, reaches perfection in development, just as the Bodhisatta reached the perfection of sovereignty over Takkasilā.
As he thus abandons distraction and attends to these phenomena by way of his specific function, practice, and inclination...
They appear either as foul, or as beautiful, or as empty.
Then he attends to those phenomena by transcending the conceptual designation (*paṇṇatti*).

"Transcending the conceptual designation" means that having transcended and relinquished such conventional expressions as "head-hairs," "body-hairs," and so forth, he attends only to the foulness and the rest exactly as they have appeared.

He attends by way of this. How? Just as people who have gone to live in the forest, because they are unfamiliar with the terrain, make a sign such as a broken branch in order to recognize the location of water, and having followed it, they enjoy the water;
but when they become familiar with the terrain, they then discard that sign.
Just as people, without giving it any further attention, approach a body of water and make use of the water,

even so this person first attends to those phenomena by way of their respective conventional designations, such as "head-hairs" and "body-hairs. When those phenomena appear to him through one of the modes such as foulness (*asubha*),
he transcends and relinquishes that conventional designation and attends only to the foulness and so forth.
Here it may be asked: "In what way do these phenomena appear to him as foul and so forth;
how as beautiful, or how as empty? And how does he attend to them as foul, how as beautiful, or how as empty?
First of all, the head-hairs appear to him as foul in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, location, and habitat.
In five ways he attends to these [parts] as foul. That is to say: these hairs of the head are foul by way of color, being extremely repulsive and loathsome.

For instance, when people see a hair-colored straw or thread fallen into their food and drink during the day, they discard even that delicious food and drink because of the perception of "hair," or they feel loathing.

It is also foul by way of shape. For instance, at night, having touched hair, wool, or thread fallen into food or drink, people either discard even delicious food and drink with the perception of hair, or they feel disgust.
It is also foul by way of smell. For instance, [this is evident] in the case of hair that is devoid of the preparations such as oil-anointing, flowers, and incense.
The smell is supremely loathsome; having smelled the odor of hair cast into fires, beings close their nostrils and even distort their faces.

It is also unattractive by its very location, for it is heaped up and grows there by the outflow of various kinds of human impurities—bile, phlegm, pus, and blood—just as weeds grow in a rubbish heap by the outflow of various kinds of human filth.
"It has been brought to growth and abundance. Thus, the foulness exists even by way of its location;

for just as *taṇḍuleyyaka* weeds grow in a rubbish heap, so too these thirty-one kinds of parts beginning with body hair have grown upon the surface of a mass of filth, on the moist skin that envelops the heads of human beings.
This same method applies to the body hairs and the rest. In this way, first of all, when these phenomena appear as foul, he attends to them as foul.
If, however, they appear to him by way of color, then the head-hairs appear by way of the blue kasiṇa;
likewise, the body-hairs and teeth appear by way of the white kasiṇa. This method applies everywhere.

He attends to these [parts] precisely by way of their respective kasiṇas; thus, when they appear by way of color, he attends to them by way of color. If, however, for him they appear by way of emptiness...
When they appear, then the head hairs appear by way of the resolution of their dense massification, as a collection of groups consisting of eight units of nutritive essence (*ojas*).
So too with body hairs and the rest, according to how they appear. In this way, he attends to them exactly as they are. Thus, when they appear as empty, he attends to them as empty.
One who attends in this way attends by means of successive relinquishing.
"By means of successive relinquishing" means that when one of the [meditation subjects] such as the foul has appeared, having relinquished the head-hairs while attending to the body-hairs,
one proceeds just as a leech, while still attached to the place it has grasped with its tail, grasps another place with its mouth.

And when that has been grasped, he lets go of the other; even so, while still being concerned with the head hairs, he gives attention to the body hairs, and when his attention is established upon the body hairs, he lets go of the head hairs. This method applies everywhere.
For as he gives attention in this way by letting go successively, those phenomena—whether through the aspect of foulness or any other—appear to him completely and without remainder.
And they appear in a more manifest form.
Then, for one to whom those phenomena appear as foul and stand out in a more manifest form,
it is just as if a monkey, being pursued by a hunter through a palm grove of thirty-two palm trees, could not settle even on a single tree.
When the monkey has run about and returns exhausted, it then stands leaning against a single palm-spike wrapped in thick palm leaves;
in the same way, when the mind-monkey, being driven by that very yogi through the thirty-two parts of this body,
does not settle even in a single part and runs about until its wandering among manifold objects—

Due to the absence of desire, he turns back and becomes weary. Then, relying on that phenomenon among the head hairs and so forth which is more familiar to him or more suited to his temperament, or on that wherein he has previously performed spiritual work, he remains by way of access concentration.
Then, having repeatedly struck that very sign with thought and reflection, he successively gives rise to the first jhāna.
Established therein, one undertakes insight (vipassanā) and reaches the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).
However, for one to whom those phenomena appear according to their specific characteristics (vaṇṇato), it is just as, for example, with a monkey...

[as previously described] ... Now, whichever phenomenon among the head-hairs and so forth is more familiar to him, or more in accordance with his temperament (carita), or that toward which he has previously performed spiritual exertion—
Having arisen, it remains by way of access concentration supported by that [object].
Then, by repeatedly striking that very sign with thought and applied thought, he successively produces all five fine-material-sphere jhānas by way of the blue kasiṇa or the yellow kasiṇa.
And having established himself in any one of these, he initiates insight and reaches the plane of the Noble Ones.
However, for one to whom those phenomena appear as empty, he attends to them by way of their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*).
While attending to them by way of their characteristics, he attains access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) therein through the analysis of the four elements.
Then, while attending to them, he attends to those phenomena by way of the three suttas on impermanence, suffering, and non-self. This is his method of insight (*vipassanā-naya*).
Thus, having begun this insight and practicing in due order, one reaches the plane of the Noble Ones.
At this point, that which was asked—“But how does he attend to these states in the manner of a gradual sequence, etc.?”—has been explained.
And as for what was said—“But its description should be understood by way of development”—[that too has been provided].
Thus its meaning has been explained.
Now, in this very section on the thirty-two aspects, this miscellaneous method (pakiṇṇakanaya) should be understood for the sake of proficiency in the commentary.
“By way of sign, by way of characteristic, by way of element, and also by way of emptiness;
and by way of the aggregates and so forth—the determination of the thirty-two aspects is to be understood.
Herein, “by way of sign”: in these thirty-two aspects thus described, there are one hundred and sixty signs.
These are the factors by means of which the practitioner grasps the thirty-two aspects by way of their constituent parts. Namely:
for the head-hair there are five signs—the sign of color, the sign of shape, the sign of direction, the sign of location, and the sign of delimitation.
It is the same for body-hair and the rest.

As to characteristics: there are one hundred and twenty-eight characteristics in the thirty-two aspects, by means of which the practitioner attends to the thirty-two aspects according to their characteristics. Namely, for the head-hair there are four characteristics:
the characteristic of hardness, the characteristic of binding, the characteristic of heat, and the characteristic of motion. It is the same for body-hair and the rest.
“By way of elements”: in the thirty-two-fold aspect, there are one hundred and twenty-eight elements among those stated in the passage, “Bhikkhus, this person consists of six elements.
It is by means of these that the practitioner comprehends the thirty-two-fold aspect by way of elements.
Namely: whatever rigidity there is in the head-hairs, that is the earth element; whatever cohesion there is, that is...
The water element; that which is ripening is the fire element; that which is distending is the air element—thus there are four elements.
It is the same with the body hairs and so forth.
Regarding emptiness: within the thirty-two aspects, there are one hundred and twenty-eight kinds of emptiness, by means of which the practitioner [contemplates] the thirty-two aspects.
He sees it as empty. For example: first, the head hairs are empty of the earth element, the water element, and so forth;
likewise, the water element and the others are empty of the earth element and so forth. Thus there are four kinds of emptiness. It is the same with body hairs and the rest.

Regarding the "aggregates and so forth": when the thirty-two parts, beginning with head hairs, are subsumed under the categories of aggregates and so on, one considers, "How many aggregates are the head hairs? etc.
The analysis should be understood according to such methods as: "How many aggregates are there? How many bases? How many elements? How many truths? How many foundations of mindfulness?
When he understands in this way, the body appears to him like a heap of grass and sticks.
As it is said: "There is no being, no man, no person; no individual is to be found."
“This body is empty, like a heap of grass and sticks.
Then, for him who had entered an empty house, whose mind was peaceful, and who was such a one:
“Supernatural delight arises for one who clearly sees the Dhamma with right insight.
Thus, supernatural delight has been described; that is not very far off. Then there is this:
“From whatever [aspect] one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates...”
"One who understands that attains rapture and gladness, which is the Deathless.

Thus, the rapture and gladness consisting of insight have been described. Experiencing that, one before long realizes the Deathless Nibbāna, which is served by the Noble Ones and is free from aging and death.
[From] the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
The commentary on the Thirty-two Marks is finished. 4.
Commentary on the Questions of the Prince:
The Origin of the Occasion.

Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the meaning of the "Questions of the Boy" (*Kumārapañha*), beginning with the verse "What is called 'one'? (*ekaṃ nāma kiṃ*). Having stated their origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*) and the purpose for their inclusion here, we shall provide the exposition.
First, as for their origin: there was a great disciple of the Blessed One named Sopāka.

By that venerable one, full knowledge (*aññā*) was attained at the age of only seven years. The Blessed One, desiring to grant him full ordination (*upasampadā*) by means of answering his questions, [spoke these verses].
Seeing his own capacity to answer questions concerning the intended meanings, he asked the question beginning with, "What is called 'one'?
The Blessed One answered it. By that answer, he pleased the Blessed One's mind;
that itself was the venerable one’s full ordination (*upasampadā*).
This is the origin of those [precepts].
As for the purpose of their presentation:
by means of going for refuge, there is the cultivation of the mind through the recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha; and by means of the training rules...

The development of virtue and the development of the body by way of the thirty-two aspects have been explained. Therefore, these questions and answers are now set forth here for the purpose of showing the various ways of developing wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*).
Or, because concentration has virtue as its proximate cause (*padatthāna*), and wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause—as it is said:
"A wise man, established in virtue, develops his mind and wisdom"—therefore...

It should be understood that these [trainings] have been set forth here for the purpose of showing, by means of the thirty-two aspects of virtue (sīla) through the training rules (sikkhāpada), both that virtue and the concentration (samādhi) which has it as its object;
and then, for one whose mind is concentrated, for the purpose of demonstrating the various divisions of wisdom (paññā) which is the equipment for the manifold states of Dhamma.
This is their purpose for being set forth here.
Commentary on the Questions.
Regarding the question "What is one?":
Now follows the commentary on their meaning—"What is one?"—wherein the Blessed One [taught] that single dharma in which a bhikkhu...
"One who becomes rightly disenchanted gradually makes an end of suffering.
It is with reference to that Dhamma which this venerable one, becoming disenchanted with, has gradually made an end of suffering, that he asks the question.
"All beings subsist by nutriment," the Elder replies, answering by means of a teaching directed toward the person (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*). "And what, bhikkhus, [is that nutriment]?"
"Right mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body," and so forth—these are the suttas that serve as proof here, given that such a method of answering is possible.

In this context, the nutriment by which all beings are said to be "subsisting on nutriment"—that nutriment, or their state of subsisting on nutriment—is what was asked about when the Elder was questioned, "What is 'one'?"

It should be understood as "pointed out. For that was intended by the Blessed One here as "the one," not stated to inform [us] that there is no other "one" whatsoever in the Dispensation or in the world. Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with one thing, completely dispassionate toward it, and completely liberated from it..."
Seeing the limit rightly and having fully realized rightness, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
What is that one thing? All beings subsist by nutriment. It is by becoming completely disenchanted with this one thing, monks, that a bhikkhu...
[as before] ...makes an end of suffering. "One question, one summary, one..."
"Regarding the phrase 'explanation,' it was said with reference to this.
Furthermore, in the context of "subsistence by nutriment," just as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, there is the sign of the beautiful.
Therein, frequent improper attention is the nutriment for the arising of unarisen sensual desire," a condition is called "nutriment."
Thus, having taken "condition" in the sense of "nutriment," those things that exist by way of conditions are called "subsisting by nutriment.
However, if one were to say "subsisting by nutriment" with reference only to the four nutriments, then because of the statement, "The gods who are non-percipient beings are rootless,
without nutriment, without contact, and without feeling," the word "all" would be inappropriate.
In this regard, it might be argued: "Even if it is stated thus, since it is said—'Which phenomena are conditioned? The five aggregates: the aggregate of form... [and so on]...
the aggregate of consciousness'—it would be logical that only the aggregates possess the state of being established through conditions;
however, this statement regarding sentient beings would be entirely illogical. But this should not be viewed in such a way. Why? Because with respect to sentient beings...

Because of the established application of the term "aggregate" [to beings]. For the application of the term "aggregate" to sentient beings is established. Why? Because it must be designated by depending upon the aggregates.
How so? Just as there is the application of the term "village" to a house.

For just as the term "village" must be designated by depending upon houses, so that even when only one, two, or three houses have been burnt, one says, "The village has been burnt"—thus the application of the term "village" to a house is established.
In the same way, it should be understood that this figurative usage— that "beings subsist by nutriment"—
is established with respect to the aggregates in the sense of being conditioned by nutriment. And from the perspective of ultimate reality,
when the aggregates are being born, aging, and dying, the Blessed One, in saying to the bhikkhu, "Moment by moment, bhikkhu, you are born, you age, and you die," [referred] to them...
It should be understood that it has thus been shown that the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of "aggregates" (*khandha*) for sentient beings is established.

Therefore, one should understand that the nutriment by which all beings subsist—being called "condition"—is either that very nutriment or their state of subsistence through nutriment as a single entity.
For nutriment, or the state of subsistence through nutriment, is a basis for disenchantment because it is a cause of impermanence. Now, regarding those [beings] designated as "all sentient beings":
By seeing impermanence in formations, one becomes disenchanted and gradually makes an end of suffering, attaining ultimate purification. As it is said:
"When one sees with wisdom that all formations are impermanent, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification."
And here, there are two readings: “ekaṃ nāma kiṃ” and “kiṃhā. Among these, the reading for the Sinhalese is “kiṃhā.
For they say “kiṃhā” when it should be said as “kiṃ. Some say that “ha” is a particle, and that this is indeed the reading even among the Theravādins;
however, in both cases the meaning is the same. One may read it in whichever way one prefers.
Just as in such passages as, "Touched by pleasure or by pain,
one experiences pain and mental grief," where sometimes it is called *dukkhaṃ* and sometimes *dukkhaṃ*, so too in some places it is called *ekaṃ* and in others *ekkaṃ*.
However, in this context, the reading is simply *ekaṃ nāma*.
The Explanation of the Question on "Two":
Thus, with his mind thus aroused by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question in the same manner as before:
"What are the two called? The Elder, having repeated the word "two," answers, "Name and form," thereby establishing the teaching from the perspective of phenomena (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*).
It is explained by way of teaching. In that context, all that is formless is called "name" (nāma) because it bends toward its object and because it is the cause of the mind's bending.
However, here, only those phenomena associated with the taints (sāsava-dhamma) are intended as the cause of disenchantment.
Furthermore, the four great elements in the sense of being subject to transformation (ruppana), and all matter derived from them that arises, is called "form" (rūpa). That—
All of this is intended here. And it is by way of intention alone that it is said here, “Two indeed: name and form,” not because of the non-existence of other pairs. As it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with two things... [omitted] ...he makes an end of suffering.”
"In which two? In name and in form. It is, monks, by becoming completely disenchanted with these two things...
[as before] ...that a bhikkhu makes an end of suffering. That which was said—'Two questions, two summaries, two explanations'—it was with reference to this that it was said."

And herein, it should be understood that by seeing mere name-and-form, one abandons the view of self; then, through the very gateway of contemplation on non-self, becoming disenchanted, one gradually makes an end of suffering and attains ultimate purification. As it is said:
"When one sees with wisdom that all phenomena are non-self, then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification."
The Explanation of the Question "What Are the Three?
Now, with his mind aroused by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question in the same manner as before:
"What are the three? The Elder, having repeated the word "three," [proceeds] to the meaning that is to be explained.
Showing the number in accordance with the gender, he answers, “three feelings. Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as follows:
he speaks thus showing that, “Regarding those which were spoken of by the Blessed One as ‘three feelings,’ I understand their meaning to be three.
For the teaching of those who have attained mastery in the elegance of instruction is manifold, being distinguished by the various modes of the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
However, some say: "The word 'three' here is redundant. And in this context, it is stated as "three feelings" according to the same method as before;
it is not because of the absence of other triads. As it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with three things... [and so on] ...he makes an end of suffering."
“In which three? In the three kinds of feeling. It is, monks, with regard to these three things that it was said:
‘Three questions, three summaries, three explanations. Thus was it said.
This is what it refers to.
And here, it is either according to the sutta stated thus: “Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering,” or according to:
“He who saw pleasure as suffering, and saw suffering as a dart, and saw the peaceful state that is neither-suffering-nor-pleasure as impermanent.”

Thus, by following the sequence of the suffering of suffering (*dukkhadukkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmadukkhatā*), and the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāradukkhatā*), or by seeing the painful nature of the three feelings, one abandons the perception of pleasure.

Becoming disenchanted through the gateway of contemplation on suffering, one gradually brings an end to suffering and attains ultimate purification; this is how it should be understood. As it has been said:
“When one sees with wisdom that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering,’ then one becomes disenchanted with suffering; this is the path to purification.
This concludes the commentary on the four questions beginning with *kiṃ*.
Thus, with his mind thus aroused by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question in the same manner as before:
"What are the four called? In this context, regarding the side of answering this question, in some places the four nutriments (āhāra) are intended in the same manner as before. As it has been said:
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with four things... [as before] ...he makes an end of suffering.
With which four? With the four nutriments. It is with these four things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu, becoming completely disenchanted...
[as before] ...makes an end of suffering. ‘Four questions, four summaries, four explanations.’”
Thus, regarding that which was said, this was said with reference to this.
In some instances, those in which one whose mind is well-developed gradually makes an end of suffering are the four foundations of mindfulness. As the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalā said:
"Friends, when a bhikkhu has his mind well-developed in four things, seeing their limit rightly, [he attains] rightness..."
Having realized it, one makes an end of suffering in this very life. In which four? In the four foundations of mindfulness.
It is by having rightly developed the mind in these four things, friends, that a bhikkhu... [as before] ...makes an end of suffering.
This is what was said by the Blessed One: “Four questions, four summaries, four explanations. Thus it was spoken.
"This was said with reference to this.
Here, however, those four noble truths are intended, through the awakening to and penetration of which there is the cutting off of craving for existence;
or rather, because it has been explained in this manner, it is indeed well-explained.
Therefore, having recited "four" as the response, the Elder answers with "Noble Truths. In this context, "four" is a limitation by way of number.
"Noble Truths" means truths that are noble; the meaning is that they are non-false and non-deceptive.
As it has been said: "These, monks, are the four Noble Truths; they are such, non-false, and not otherwise. Therefore, they are called 'Noble Truths.'"

Or alternatively, because they are to be sought after and approached by the world together with its devas— this being what is meant— or because they proceed toward the "ay" (the goal) known as the place where effort must be exerted,
or do not proceed toward the "an-ay" (the non-goal), or because they are associated with the thirty-seven noble qualities conducive to enlightenment,
these are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*), for it is the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples of the Buddha who are honored as "noble" (*ariya*) that penetrate them. As it has been said:
“Monks, there are these four noble truths... [as above] ...These, monks, are the four noble truths; the Noble Ones penetrate them, therefore they are called ‘noble truths.
Furthermore, they are the noble truths because they are the truths of the Noble One, the Blessed One.
As it is said: “Monks, among the world with its devas... [as above] ...among the generation with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the Noble One; therefore they are called ‘noble truths.’”
Alternatively, they are called "Noble Truths" (ariyasacca) because the noble state is established through their full awakening. As it is said:
“Monks, it is because he has fully awakened to these four Noble Truths as they really are that the Tathāgata is called the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
This is the meaning of the term. Furthermore, through the awakening to and penetration of these Noble Truths, craving for existence is severed. As it is said:

“Bhikkhus, that noble truth of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated... [and so on] ...that noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering has been awakened to and penetrated;
craving for existence has been cut off, the conduit to existence has been exhausted, and now there is no further becoming.
This concludes the commentary on the five questions beginning with “What? (Kinti-pañha).
With this answer to the question, the Teacher, his mind being thus aroused, asked a further question in the same manner as before:
"What are the five called? The Elder, having repeated "The five," answered:

"The aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhā). In that context, "five" is a numerical delimitation. The aggregates produced by clinging, or those which produce clinging, are the aggregates of clinging.
Whatever form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are accompanied by taints and subject to clinging—this is a designation for these.
And here, they are called the "five aggregates of clinging" according to the previous method, not because there are no other five. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with five things... [he] makes an end of suffering."
“In which five? In the five aggregates of clinging. It is, monks, regarding these five things that a monk, becoming completely disenchanted...
[as before] ...becomes one who makes an end of suffering. ‘Five questions, five summaries, five explanations’—it was with reference to this that it was said.”
And here, by comprehending the five aggregates through their arising and passing away, one attains the deathless state of insight and gradually realizes the deathless state of Nibbāna. As it is said:
"From whatever point one comprehends the arising and passing away of the aggregates, one finds rapture and gladness; that is the deathless for one who understands."
The Explanation of the Question on the Six:
Thus, with his mind thus aroused by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question in the same manner as before:
"What are the six? The Elder, having repeated "The six," answers: "The internal sense bases."
In this context, "six" (*cha*) is a numerical delimitation. "Internal" (*ajjhattika*) means those things connected to the internal, or those that occur with reference to the self (*attā*).
They are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because they extend the life-continuum (*āya*), or because they stretch out (*tanana*), or because they lead (*nayana*) to the suffering of saṃsāra.
This is a designation for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. And here, according to the previous method, "six..."
"the internal sense bases," it is said, not because of the absence of other six [external ones]. As it was said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with six things... he makes an end of suffering. With which six?
With the six internal sense bases. It is with these six things, bhikkhus..."

“A bhikkhu who becomes completely disenchanted... [as before] ...is one who makes an end of suffering. It was with reference to this that it was said: ‘Six questions, six summaries, and six explanations.
And herein, the six internal sense bases are referred to as “the empty village,” O bhikkhus. These six internal sense bases...
Because of the statement, "It is a designation for the sense bases," one should contemplate them as empty, as lacking long duration like bubbles or a mirage, and as hollow and deceptive;
becoming disenchanted through such contemplation, one gradually brings an end to suffering and reaches the point where King Death is no longer seen. As it has been said:
“As one would look upon a bubble, as one would look upon a mirage;
so for one who contemplates the world in this way, the King of Death does not see him.
This concludes the commentary on the question beginning with “What indeed is a being? (*Satta*).
With this answer to the question, the Teacher’s mind was satisfied, and he asked a further question:

"What is meant by 'seven'? Although the Elder had already mentioned the seven stations of consciousness (*viññāṇaṭṭhiti*) in his answer to the great question, he nevertheless replied, "The seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*)," pointing out those qualities in which a bhikkhu whose mind is well-developed brings an end to suffering.
She answers it. This matter has indeed been approved by the Blessed One. As he said:
"Householders, the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā is wise; householders, the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā is of great wisdom.
Householders, even if you had approached me and asked about this matter, I too would have answered exactly as she has."
“I would answer exactly as the bhikkhunī Kajaṅgalikā has answered.
And she had answered thus:
“Friends, when a bhikkhu’s mind is rightly well-developed in seven things... he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.”
"In which seven? In the seven factors of enlightenment. It is, friends, when a bhikkhu has rightly and well developed his mind in these seven things...
that he becomes an ender of suffering. That which was said by the Blessed One, 'Seven questions, seven summaries, seven explanations,' this was said with reference to this."
Thus it should be understood that this meaning has been approved by the Blessed One.

In this context, "seven" (*satta*) is a numerical delimitation intended to exclude fewer or more [factors]. "Factors of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) is a designation for the states beginning with mindfulness.

Herein, the word-meaning is as follows: when these [states] arise at the moment of the mundane or supramundane path, they counteract sloth-and-torpor, agitation, the basis for stagnation, the accumulation [of defilements], devotion to sensual pleasure, devotion to self-mortification, adherence to annihilationism, adherence to eternalism, and so forth.
Because the noble disciple awakens by means of the harmony of qualities— consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—
which serves as the antidote to manifold calamities, it is called "awakening" (bodhi). It is said that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements,
or penetrates the four noble truths, or realizes Nibbāna itself.
As it is said: “Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he has fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Alternatively, because he awakens by means of this harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggi*) of the kind already described, the noble disciple is also called “enlightenment” (*bodhi*).

Thus, because they are constituent parts of that enlightenment—which is defined as the harmony of states—the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅgā*) are so named, just like the factors of absorption (*jhānaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*maggaṅga*); or else, because they belong to him who is designated by the conventional term “enlightenment,” they are called factors of enlightenment.
The factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are so called because they constitute the limbs of the noble disciple, just as the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot do.
Furthermore: "In what sense are they 'factors of enlightenment'? They are factors of enlightenment because they conduce to enlightenment;

they are factors of enlightenment because they awaken; they are factors of enlightenment because they cause one to awaken; they are factors of enlightenment because they cause one to awaken thoroughly; they are factors of enlightenment because they cause one to awaken fully."
By this same method set forth in the *Paṭisambhidā*, the meaning of the enlightenment factors as "enlightenment factors" is to be understood.
Thus, one who develops and cultivates these seven enlightenment factors does not long before become a recipient of the qualities beginning with absolute disenchantment;
therefore, it is said that he makes an end of suffering in this very life. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, lead to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna.
Thus, with his mind thus inclined by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question: “What eight? This is the commentary on the question beginning with “eight.”

How so? Although the eight worldly conditions (*lokadhammā*) were mentioned in the explanation of the Great Question, nevertheless, in order to show those qualities through which a bhikkhu whose mind is well-developed brings about the end of suffering, the Elder did not say "the eight noble path-factors" (*ariyāni aṭṭha maggaṅgānī*);
for there is no such thing as a path separate from the eight factors—it is merely the eight factors themselves.
But since that is the path, therefore, in order to establish that meaning, he provides the answer through his skill in teaching: "The Noble Eightfold Path.
This purpose and method of teaching were indeed approved by the Blessed One himself. As he said:
"Wise, householders, is the nun Kajaṅgalikā... I too would explain it in exactly the same way as it has been explained by the nun Kajaṅgalikā."
And she replied thus:
"Friend, when a bhikkhu has well cultivated his mind in eight things... [as above] ...he becomes one who makes an end of suffering.
Regarding that which was said by the Blessed One: 'Eight questions, eight summaries, eight explanations.'"
"This was said with reference to this"—thus it should be understood that both this meaning and the method of teaching were approved by the Blessed One.

In this context, "noble" (ariya) means that which is to be approached by those seeking Nibbāna; furthermore, it is so called because it proceeds far away from the defilements (kilesa) and because it brings about the state of nobility (ariyabhāva).
And one should be understood as "noble" (ariya) because of the attainment of the noble fruit (ariyaphala). It is "eightfold" (aṭṭhaṅgika) because it possesses eight factors (aṅga).

This [path] should be understood as consisting of mere factors, because—just like a fourfold army or a fivefold musical ensemble—it cannot be apprehended as a distinct entity apart from its constituent parts.
One travels to Nibbāna by means of this, or it itself travels [toward it], while destroying the defilements (kilesa).
Or, it is called the "path" (*magga*) because one goes by means of it.
Thus, a bhikkhu who develops this eightfold path with its eight divisions shatters ignorance, arouses true knowledge, and realizes *nibbāna*;
therefore, he is said to be "one who makes an end of suffering in this very life. For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, just as it is possible that a rice husk or a barley husk, when properly placed, might—when stepped upon by hand or foot—break the hand or foot and draw blood;
for what reason? Because of the proper placement of the husk, bhikkhus, even so, bhikkhus, he...”
"It is possible, monks, that a bhikkhu, through rightly directed view and through the development of the path rightly directed, will pierce ignorance, arouse true knowledge, and realize Nibbāna.
This concludes the commentary on the ninth question, "What indeed? (Kinti-pañha).
With this answer to the question, the Teacher, his mind being thus aroused, asks a further question:
"What are the nine? The Elder, having repeated the word "nine," answers: "The abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*). Therein, "nine" is a numerical limit.
"Beings" (*satta*) refers to living creatures designated by way of the aggregates bound to the life-faculty, or it is a designation (*paññatti*). "Abodes" (*āvāsā*)...
They dwell in these, thus they are "abodes" (*āvāsā*); the abodes of beings are "beings' abodes" (*sattāvāsā*). This is the path of the teaching;
in terms of meaning, however, this is a designation for nine kinds of beings. As it is said:
"There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans and some gods... [and so forth].

and those in states of deprivation—this is the first abode of beings. There are, friends, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of Brahma’s company who were first reborn there; this is the second abode of beings.
There are, friends, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods; this is the third abode of beings.
"Friends, there are beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the Subhakiṇha devas; this is the fourth abode of beings.
Friends, there are beings who are non-percipient and devoid of sensation, such as the Asaññasatta devas;
this is the fifth abode of beings. Friends, there are beings who, having completely transcended perceptions of form... [and so on] ...have attained rebirth in the sphere of infinite space."
This is the sixth abode of beings. There are, friends, beings... [as before] ...who have reached the base of infinite consciousness; this is the seventh abode of beings. There are, friends, beings...
[as before] ...who have reached the base of nothingness; this is the eighth abode of beings. There are, friends, beings...
[as before] ...who have reached the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the ninth abode of beings.”
And here, the phrase "nine abodes of beings" is stated in the same manner as before; it is not because there is an absence of other nine [categories]. As it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with nine things...
he makes an end of suffering. With which nine? With the nine abodes of beings. It is with these nine things, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu..."

“Becoming rightly disenchanted... [as before] ...he makes an end of suffering. As for what was said—‘Nine questions, nine summaries, nine explanations’—it was said with reference to this. And here, from the statement:
“Nine things are to be fully understood. Which nine? The nine abodes of beings,” regarding these nine...

Having abandoned the perception of stability, beauty, pleasure, and selfhood regarding the abodes of beings through the full understanding of the known (*ñāta-pariññā*), he becomes disenchanted by seeing them as merely a heap of pure formations (*saṅkhāra-puñja*).
Through the full understanding of scrutiny (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), he becomes dispassionate by contemplating impermanence; he becomes liberated by contemplating suffering;
and by contemplating non-self, he correctly perceives the limit [of existence]. Having fully realized rightness through the full understanding of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*), even here and now...
One makes an end of suffering in this very life. Therefore it was said:
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with nine things... he makes an end of suffering in this very life. With which nine? With the nine abodes of beings.
This concludes the commentary on the ten questions beginning with “What? (Kinti-pañha).
Thus, with his mind thus aroused by this answer to the question, the Teacher asks a further question: "What are the ten?
In this regard, although in other discourses this question has been answered as referring to the ten unwholesome courses of action—as it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with ten things... he makes an end of suffering"—it is here [answered differently].
“In which ten? In the ten courses of unwholesome action. It is, monks, by becoming completely disenchanted with these ten things...
[as before] ...that a monk makes an end of suffering. ‘Ten questions, ten summaries, ten explanations’—it was with reference to this that it was said.”

But here, because this venerable one, not referring to himself, desires to declare another [state], or because what has been declared by him through this method is indeed well-declared, he therefore illuminates the attainment of those ten factors by which one is called an "Arahant";
thus, with reference to the person, it is said: "One who is endowed with ten factors is called an Arahant."

He answers by way of the teaching. Therefore, it should be understood that those ten factors by which one is endowed with which one is called "an Arahant" were pointed out by the Elder when he was asked, "What are the ten? And those ten are as follows:
"Venerable sir, 'one beyond training, one beyond training' is said; in what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one beyond training?"
Here, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of the right view of one beyond training; he is possessed of the right intention of one beyond training;
he is possessed of the right speech of one beyond training; he is possessed of the right action of one beyond training;
he is possessed of the right livelihood of one beyond training; he is possessed of the right effort of one beyond training.
He is possessed of right mindfulness of one beyond training; he is possessed of right concentration of one beyond training;
he is possessed of right knowledge of one beyond training; he is possessed of right liberation of one beyond training.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one beyond training.”
These [passages] are to be understood according to the method explained in such suttas as these.
Thus ends the commentary on the "Questions of the Boy" in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
5. Commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta:
The Purpose of its Introduction.
Now, following the Questions of the Prince, the turn has come for the commentary on the meaning of the Maṅgala Sutta, which was introduced immediately after them.
Having stated the purpose for its placement here, we shall now provide a commentary on its meaning. To explain:

although this discourse was not spoken by the Blessed One in this specific sequence, it nevertheless demonstrates—through the refuge formula, the thirty-two aspects of the training rules, and the questions of the young man Kumāra—the method consisting of the divisions of virtue, concentration, and wisdom by which one enters the Dispensation. All of this is the supreme blessing; therefore, it is for one who seeks blessings...
This is stated for the purpose of showing that application should be made right here, and that its status as an auspicious factor (maṅgalabhāva) is to be understood according to this sutta.
This is its purpose for being placed here.
The Account of the First Great Council.
Now, for the purpose of explaining the meaning of this [text] thus set forth, here is the table of contents:
"By whom, when, and why it was spoken— having stated this method,
the meaning of the passage beginning with 'Thus' (evam) and so forth will be explained in its various aspects."
“Describing the origin, having stated what constitutes an auspicious occasion (maṅgala) wherever it may be,
and having defined that for each case, one should clarify its nature as an auspicious occasion.
Regarding this, first, the half-verse beginning with “Having stated by whom, when, and why this method was taught” is as follows:
This was said with reference to the statement: “Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One... [pe] ...addressed the Blessed One in verse. For this was spoken by way of oral tradition;
and that Blessed One was self-become (*sayambhū*) and teacherless (*anācariyaka*).
Therefore, this is not the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*). Consequently, it should be stated as follows:

“By whom was this statement spoken? When and for what reason was it spoken? It is replied: It was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, and that was at the time of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
This First Great Council should be understood from the very beginning as follows, for the sake of proficiency regarding the origins of all the Suttas.
From the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma as the beginning, until the taming of the wanderer Subhadda—

when the Buddha’s duties were completed and the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, had attained final Nibbāna by the element of Nibbāna without residue at the time of dawn on the full moon of Visākha, between the twin Sāla trees in the Mallans’ Sal Grove at Upavattana in Kusinārā— the [story] of the Blessed One...

When seven hundred thousand bhikkhus had assembled for the Parinibbāna, the Elder of the Saṅgha, the Venerable Mahākassapa, while the Blessed One had been Parinibbānized for seven days, [encountered] Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, saying: "Enough, friends, do not grieve, do not lament;
we are well rid of that Great Ascetic, under whom we were troubled by [the thought]: 'This is permitted for you...'"
"This is not allowable for you," [he said]. But now, remembering the words spoken [by the Buddha], "We shall do whatever we wish and we shall not do what we do not wish," he thought:
"It is indeed possible that wicked bhikkhus, imagining the teaching to be 'one whose Teacher has passed away,' might gain a following and before long cause the true Dhamma to disappear."
As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure, so long does this teaching remain one whose Teacher has not passed away. As the Blessed One said:
“Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya which have been taught and laid down by me to you shall be your teacher after my passing. [He thought:
“What if I were to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya together, so that this Dispensation might be enduring and long-lasting?”
And when the Blessed One said to me, "Kassapa, will you accept from me these worn-out hempen rag-robes?
and [shared] with me the common use of robes—[saying], "Monks, as long as I desire, secluded from sensual pleasures... [attaining] the first jhāna..."

“Monks, Kassapa too, as long as he wishes, dwells, secluded from sensual pleasures... [and so on] ...having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein”— in this manner, by means of these and other such passages,
[the Buddha spoke] of the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) distinguished by the nine successive dwellings and the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā), which he had realized for himself.
And since I have been favored by this bestowing of equality upon equals,
what other debtlessness could there be for me? "Did not the Blessed One, like a king who establishes his own lineage through the granting of armor and sovereignty,
consider me— thinking 'this one shall be the establisher of my lineage of the True Dhamma'— and favor me with this extraordinary favor?"
Reflecting thus, "He has favored me," he inspired the bhikkhus for the purpose of compiling the Dhamma and Vinaya.
As it is said: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
'Friends, on one occasion I was traveling along the highway from Pāvā to Kusinārā together with a great Saṅgha of bhikkhus, numbering about five hundred.'"
The entire Subhadda Chapter should be recited in detail.
Following that, he said:
"Come now, friends, let us recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, before un-Dhamma shines forth and the Dhamma..."
“The non-Dhamma is being upheld, the non-Vinaya is being displayed, the Vinaya is being set aside;
those who speak what is not Dhamma are strong, while those who speak the Dhamma are weak; those who speak what is not Vinaya are strong, while those who speak the Vinaya are weak.

The monks said, “In that case, venerable sir, let the Elder select monks. The Elder [selected] those who had mastered the study of the Teacher’s entire dispensation consisting of the ninefold division.
Having set aside many hundreds and thousands of ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*),
dry-insight practitioners (*sukkhavipassaka*), and bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), he selected four hundred and ninety-nine bhikkhus whose taints were destroyed—

those who possessed the various divisions of the entire scriptural tradition of the Tipiṭaka, had attained the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), were of great power, and were for the most part designated by the Blessed One as "foremost" (*etadagga*) in categories such as the "threefold knowledge" (*tevijja*).
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected four hundred and ninety-nine arahants.
But why did the Elder omit one? It was for the sake of making room for the Venerable Ānanda.
For it is not possible to hold the Dhamma Council either together with or without that Venerable; he is still a trainee (sekha) who has duties yet to perform.

Therefore, it was not possible for him to do so together with others; yet, because there was nothing taught by the One of Ten Powers—such as the Suttas, Geyyas, and so forth—that he had received from the Blessed One in the Blessed One’s absence, it was also not possible for him to do so alone.

If this is so, and since he was still a learner (*sekha*), why was he not selected by the Elder for the Dhamma Council, given that he would have been of great assistance? [The answer is: Because he wished to avoid the censure of others.

For the Elder was exceedingly confident in the Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, even when grey hairs had grown upon his head, he would exhort him with the address "boy," saying, "This boy does not know his measure.

Moreover, this Venerable One was born into the Sakyan clan, being the Tathāgata’s brother and the son of his paternal uncle; thus, for the monks there, it was as if they were acting out of favoritism toward him.

Thinking that [the Elder] had selected the Elder Ānanda—who had attained the analytical knowledges of one still in training—while setting aside many bhikkhus who had attained the analytical knowledges of those beyond training, they might criticize him, saying: "The Elder chose [him] while excluding [others]. To avoid such criticism from others, he did not select him, thinking:
"It is impossible to hold the council without Ānanda; I shall include him with the consent of the bhikkhus themselves."
Then the monks themselves requested the Elder on behalf of Ānanda. As it is said:

“The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: ‘Venerable sir, although this Venerable Ānanda is still a learner (*sekha*), he is incapable of going astray through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear; moreover, he has spent much time in the presence of the Blessed One.’”
“The Dhamma and the Vinaya have been mastered; therefore, venerable sir, let the Elder choose Venerable Ānanda as well.
Then Venerable Mahākassapa chose Venerable Ānanda too.
Thus, together with that Venerable who had been chosen with the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders.
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Where indeed should we recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?
Then it occurred to the elder bhikkhus: "Rājagaha has a great alms-resort and abundant lodgings;
what if we were to spend the rains retreat at Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?"
"Let no other bhikkhus enter the rains residence at Rājagaha. But why did they think this? [They thought:
"This is our secure undertaking; perhaps some person of a different character might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and reopen the matter.

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa announced it by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*). This should be understood according to the method stated in the *Saṅgītikkhandhaka*.
Then, after seven days of celebratory festivities following the Tathāgata’s parinibbāna and seven days of relic worship had passed,
the Elder Mahākassapa— considering that "half a month has elapsed, now only one and a half months of the summer remain, and the time for entering the rains retreat is drawing near"— said, "Friends,
let us go to Rājagaha," and taking half of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with him, departed.
[The Buddha] set out on one path. The Elder Anuruddha also took [the other half] and set out on one path;

however, the Elder Ānanda, taking the Blessed One’s bowl and robes and surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, went to Sāvatthī and then set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī, desiring to go to Rājagaha. Wherever the Elder Ānanda went, there was great lamentation.
“Venerable Ānanda, where have you come from, having left the Teacher behind?
When the Elder had gradually arrived at Sāvatthī, there was a great lamentation, as if at the time of the Blessed One’s final passing away.
There, the Venerable Ānanda [comforted] that great multitude with a discourse on the Dhamma concerning impermanence and other such themes.
Having consoled him, he entered the Jeta Grove, opened the door of the Fragrant Chamber where the One of Ten Powers had resided,
removed the bed and chair, shook them out, swept the Fragrant Chamber, discarded the withered garland debris,
brought the bed and chair back inside, and placed them again in their original positions; thus he performed every duty and service that was to be done when the Blessed One was present.
Then the Elder, because he had spent much time standing and sitting since the Blessed One’s final passing away,
drank a milk-purgative on the following day to settle his body which was disturbed by the humors, and sat down right there in the monastery;
it was with reference to this that he spoke thus to the young man sent by the youth Subha:
“It is not the right time, young man; I have drunk my dose of medicine today. Perhaps we may come again tomorrow.
On the second day, having gone with the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, he was questioned by the young man Subha and preached the tenth sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya, known as the Subha Sutta.
Then the Elder, having overseen the repair of dilapidated parts in the Jetavana monastery, when the time had nearly arrived—
At the commencement of the rainy season, he went to Rājagaha. Likewise, the Elder Mahākassapa and the Elder Anuruddha, taking the entire Saṅgha of bhikkhus with them, also went to Rājagaha.
Now at that time, there were eighteen great monasteries in Rājagaha; all of them were abandoned, fallen into ruin, and dilapidated.
They were thus. For at the time of the Blessed One’s Parinibbāna, all the bhikkhus, having taken their own bowls and robes, departed after abandoning the monasteries and the cells.
Thereupon, the elders, for the sake of honoring the word of the Blessed One and for the sake of refuting the doctrines of the sectarians, said:
"Let us perform the restoration of broken and dilapidated parts during the first month."

They reflected thus: "For the followers of other sects might say, 'The disciples of the ascetic Gotama tended to the monasteries only while the Teacher was still alive, but once he had attained final Nibbāna, they abandoned them. It was for the purpose of refuting such a claim that they reflected," so it is said. And this has also been stated:
Then it occurred to those elder bhikkhus: “Friends, the Blessed One has praised the repair of what is broken and dilapidated.
Come, friends, let us perform the repair of what is broken and dilapidated during the first month;
then, having assembled during the middle month, we shall recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.”
On the second day, they went and stood at the king’s gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid his respects, and invited them, asking, "Venerable sirs, what shall I do?
What is your need? The elders informed him that they required manual labor for the restoration of the eighteen great monasteries.
"Excellent, venerable sirs," the king replied, and he provided the men to perform the manual work.
The Elders first had all the monasteries repaired during the first month.
Then they informed the King: "Great King, the repairs to the monasteries are finished; now let us perform the compilation of the Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Very well, venerable sirs, do so with confidence. My wheel is the wheel of authority, while yours is the wheel of the Dhamma."
“Let it be so. Command me, venerable sir; what shall I do? “A place for the monks who are compiling the Dhamma to sit together, Great King.
“Where shall I build it, venerable sir? “It is fitting, Great King, to build it on the slope of Mount Vebhāra, at the entrance to the Sattapaṇṇi Cave.
“Very well, venerable sir,” said King Ajātasattu, and he had a hall constructed that was like one fashioned by Vissakamma.
Having had a great pavilion constructed with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and stairs, adorned with various kinds of floral and creeper carvings;
having decorated it so that it resembled the celestial palace of Brahmā— its floor like a mosaic of various gems and jewels, its ground-work perfectly finished,
and its beautiful canopy hanging down from suspended garlands of diverse flowers, variegated with offerings of many kinds of blossoms.
In that great pavilion, having prepared five hundred priceless, allowable rugs for five hundred bhikkhus,
he arranged the seat of the Elder facing north, supported by the southern side; and in the center of the pavilion,
he prepared a Dhamma-seat worthy of the Blessed Buddha, facing east, where there was a fan inlaid with ivory and decorated with paintings.
Setting him aside, he had it announced to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus: "Venerable sirs, the task is finished.
The bhikkhus said to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, there is a gathering of the Saṅgha tomorrow;
and since you are still a trainee with work yet to be done, it is not fitting for you to go to that gathering. Be diligent! Then the Venerable...
Ānanda thought, “There is an assembly tomorrow; yet it is not fitting that I, being still a learner (*śaikṣa*), should go to the assembly.

Having spent much of the night contemplating the body with mindfulness (*kāyagatā smṛtiḥ*), at the time of dawn he descended from his walking-path (*caṅkrama*), entered his dwelling, and intending to lie down, he directed his attention toward his body. His two feet [were still] upon the ground...
His head had not yet reached the pillow when, in that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
For this venerable one, having spent much time outside walking back and forth, being unable to achieve further distinction, thought:
"Did not the Blessed One say this to me: 'You have performed merit, Ānanda; apply yourself to striving, and you will soon become...'"

“...is free from taints. Now, there is no fault in the speech of the Buddhas; however, my energy was excessive, and because of that, my mind led to restlessness. “Well then, I shall apply myself to evenness of energy.
Having descended from his walking path, he stood at the place for washing his feet, washed his feet, entered the vihāra, sat down on the couch, and [thought] “a little...”
Thinking, "I shall rest," he raised his body onto the couch. His two feet were lifted from the ground, yet his head had not yet reached the pillow;
in that interval, through non-clinging, his mind was liberated from the taints. The Elder attained Arahantship while devoid of the four postures.
Therefore, [the Buddha asked]: "In this Teaching, what monk is there who has not sat, not lain down, not stood, and not walked?"
When it was said, "He has attained Arahatship," it was appropriate to say, "The Elder Ānanda.
Then, on the following day, after the elder monks had finished their meal duties and put away their bowls and robes, they assembled in the Dhamma Hall.
However, the Elder Ānanda, desiring to make known his own attainment of Arahatship, [went] together with the monks...
He had not gone. As the bhikkhus were sitting down on their respective seats according to seniority, they left empty the seat of the Elder Ānanda and sat down.
There, when some asked, "Whose seat is this?", they replied, "It is Ānanda's. But [others asked], "Where has Ānanda gone?
At that moment, the Elder thought, "Now it is time for me to go. Then, his own...
Displaying his supernormal power, he sank into the earth and showed himself at his own seat; some say that he came through the air and sat down.
When the Venerable One was thus seated, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks:
"Friends, which shall we recite first, the Dhamma or the Vinaya? The monks replied, "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is indeed the lifeblood of the Buddha’s Dispensation."
“Venerable Āyusman, when the Vinaya is established, the Teaching is established; therefore, let us first recite the Vinaya.
“With whom as our leader should the Vinaya be recited? “With the Venerable Upāli. “Is the Venerable Ānanda not capable? “He is not incapable;
however, while the Perfectly Enlightened One was still living, [the Venerable Upāli] relied upon the mastery of the Vinaya.”
He placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position, saying: “Monks, this is the foremost among my disciples, the monks who are masters of the Vinaya, namely Upāli.
Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya after consulting the Elder Upāli.
Then the Elder, for the purpose of being questioned on the Vinaya, appointed himself by himself. And the Elder Upāli, for the purpose of answering, [appointed himself].
He was thus authorized. Herein is the canonical text:
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa made a formal announcement to the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, I would question Upāli on the Vinaya."
The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, when questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa on the Vinaya, I shall provide the answer.
Having thus authorized himself by himself, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, and—
There, having paid homage to the monks, he sat upon the Dharma-seat, taking up a fan inlaid with ivory.
Then the Elder Mahākassapa questioned the Elder Upāli on the entire Vinaya, beginning with the first Pārājika offense; the Elder Upāli answered him.
All five hundred monks, including the introductory narrative, performed the communal recitation (*gaṇasajjhāya*) of the first Pārājika training rule together as one.
In this same way, all the remaining sections should be understood according to the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*.
Following this method, after the Elder Upāli had recited the entire *Vinaya Piṭaka*, including the *Saubhatovibhaṅga*, the *Khandhaka*, and the *Parivāra*,
he set aside his ivory-inlaid fan, descended from the Dharma-seat, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat down on his own seat.
Having recited the Vinaya, the Venerable Elder Mahākassapa, desiring to recite the Dhamma, asked the bhikkhus:
"When reciting the Dhamma, upon whom as the authority should the Dhamma be recited?
The bhikkhus replied: "Upon the Elder Ānanda as the authority."
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, I would question Ānanda regarding the Dhamma.
Then the Venerable Ānanda informed the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: if it is timely for the Saṅgha, I shall answer when questioned on the Dhamma by the Venerable Mahākassapa.

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder bhikkhus, and sat down on the Dhamma-seat, taking up a fan inlaid with ivory. Then the Elder Mahākassapa [questioned] the Elder Ānanda on the Dhamma.
He asked: “Friend Ānanda, where was the *Brahmajāla Sutta* spoken?
“Between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā, at Ambalaṭṭhikā in the royal rest-house, venerable sir. “With reference to whom? “With reference to the wanderer Suppiya and the young Brahmin Brahmadatta.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa [addressed] the Venerable Ānanda regarding the *Brahmajāla*.
He asked about the occasion and he asked about the person: "But, friend Ānanda, where was the *Sāmaññaphala* spoken?
"At Rājagaha, venerable sir, in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. "With whom? "With Ajātasattu, the son of Vedehiputta.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa [asked] the Venerable Ānanda about the occasion of the *Sāmaññaphala*.
He asked about the Dhamma, and he also asked about the Puggala-paññatti. By this very method, he questioned all five Nikāyas, and each time he was questioned, the Venerable Ānanda gave the answer.
This First Great Council (Mahāsaṅgīti) was performed by five hundred elders:
"Because it was performed by five hundred, it is therefore called 'the Five Hundred';"
“And because she performed that very act, she is called ‘Therikā’ (the Elder Nun).

While this First Great Council was taking place, the Venerable Mahākassapa, having inquired about the entire Dīgha Nikāya, the Majjhima Nikāya, and so forth, and gradually inquiring about the Khuddaka Nikāya, said: “Friend, the Maṅgala Sutta...”
At the conclusion of such words as, "Ānanda, where was it spoken?", [the Blessed One] asked about the *nidāna* (the setting) and asked about the *puggala* (the person).
Here, when the *nidāna* was asked, one who wishes to explain all of it— having detailed that *nidāna*, as well as how it was spoken,
by whom it was heard, when it was heard, by whom it was spoken, where it was spoken, and for whom it was spoken— [should speak].

By showing the meaning as follows: “Thus it was spoken by me; it was heard by me at one time; it was spoken by the Blessed One; it was spoken at Sāvatthī; it was spoken by a deity,” the Venerable Ānanda said:
“Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery... [pe] ...to the Blessed One.”
“...addressed him with a verse. Thus it was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda; furthermore, it should be understood that this was spoken at the time of the First Great Council (Paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti).
Now, as for the question “Why was it spoken?”—it is said here: because this Venerable [Ānanda] was the source (nidāna) for the Elder Mahākassapa.
Being questioned, he therefore spoke to explain that origin in detail from the beginning.
Or rather, because some deities, seeing Ānanda seated on the Dhamma-seat surrounded by a host of masters, had a thought arise:
"This venerable one, the sage of Videha, is by nature a descendant of the Sakyan clan, an heir of the Blessed One; and by the Blessed One as well, five times..."
"He has been designated as foremost in this; he is endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities and is dear and pleasing to the four assemblies;
now, I think, having received the inheritance of the Dharma-kingdom from the Blessed One, he has become a Buddha.
Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those deities, [perceived] that praise for unattained qualities.
Unable to endure it, and wishing to demonstrate his own status as a disciple, he said: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One...
[and so on] ...addressed [them]. In the meantime, five hundred arahants and many thousands of deities applauded the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Excellent! Excellent!
A great earthquake occurred, and a rain of various kinds of flowers fell.
He fell from the sky, and many other wonders appeared;
and a sense of spiritual urgency arose in many deities, thinking, "That which we heard in the presence of the Blessed One has now become something out of our sight.
Thus, this was also stated by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council for this very reason.
This is how it should be understood. At this point, the meaning of the half-verse, "By whom, when, and for what reason it was spoken—having stated this procedure," has been elucidated.
This concludes the commentary on the passage beginning with "evam" (thus).

1. Now, for the purpose of explaining the various meanings of the passage beginning with "evam" (thus), which is included in the summary matrix (*mātikā*) starting with "the meaning of the passage beginning with 'evam' in its various modes," it is said: this word *evaṃ* (thus) should be understood in such senses as comparison, instruction, praise, censure, acceptance, manner, indication, restriction, and so forth.
For instance, it is used in such passages as: "By a mortal born in this way, much wholesome merit should be performed."
It is seen as a simile, as in: “In this way you should advance; in this way you should retreat,” and so forth. It is used in instruction, as in:
“So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata,” and so forth. It is used in encouragement, as in:
“So indeed it is, O outcaste woman, that you speak praise of that shaveling ascetic, whoever he may be,” and so forth. It is used in censure, as in: “So indeed it is... and so forth.
In such cases as, “‘So it is, venerable sir,’ those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One,” it refers to the acceptance of speech.
In such cases as, “‘Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One,’” it refers to a manner of understanding.
In such cases as, “‘Come, young man, approach the ascetic Ānanda; having approached him, in my name... it refers to an instruction.
Ask the ascetic Ānanda whether he is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort.
Say: “The young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether the venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort,” and say this:
“It would be well indeed if the venerable Ānanda were to go to where the young brahmin Subha, son of Todeyya, is.”
“...the dwelling; let him approach out of compassion”—in such instances as these, it serves as an illustration.
“What do you think, Kālāmas: Are these states wholesome or unwholesome? “Unwholesome, venerable sir. “Are they blameworthy or blameless?
“Blameworthy, venerable sir. “Are they censured by the wise or praised by the wise? “Censured by the wise, venerable sir. “Accepted...”
"Are the things undertaken conducive to harm and suffering, or not? What is your view in this matter?
"Venerable sir, those things undertaken and observed lead to harm and suffering; such is our view in this matter. In such passages, it is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
However, here it should be understood as indicating a manner (*ākāra*), an illustration (*nidassana*), and an emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

Therein, by the word *evaṃ* in the sense of "manner," he illuminates this meaning: the speech of that Blessed One— in every respect— is endowed with various methods, skillful, arising from many underlying intentions,
perfect in both meaning and phrasing, possessing manifold wonders, profound in its penetration of the Dhamma, the meaning, the teaching, and realization,
and reaching the range of hearing for all beings according to each one's own language.
Who is capable of knowing [this]? Nevertheless, having generated a desire to hear with all one's might, one says, "Thus have I heard;
it was heard by me in this manner.

By way of illustration, in order to exempt himself [from the charge of being an omniscient self-arisen one], saying, "I am not a self-arisen one (sayambhū), nor has this been realized by me," he indicates the entire discourse that is now to be spoken with the words, "Thus have I heard; it was heard thus by me."

By way of emphasis, demonstrating his own power of retention in accordance with the state of being praised by the Blessed One thus: "Bhikkhus, among my disciples, bhikkhus, this Ānanda is the foremost of those who are learned;
this Ānanda is the foremost of those who possess understanding, mindfulness, fortitude, and attendants," he [arouses] the desire of beings to hear.
He generates [the thought]: “Thus have I heard; and that indeed, whether in meaning or in phrasing, is neither deficient nor redundant;
it is exactly so and should not be viewed otherwise.
The word *me* (by me) is seen in three senses. For instance, in such passages as “Food sung to with verses is not for me to eat,” and so forth.
The meaning is "by me. In such passages as, "It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief," the meaning is "to me.
In such passages as, "Be my heirs to the Dhamma, monks," the meaning is "my.
But here, both of the two possible meanings—"heard by me" and "heard from me"—are appropriate.

Regarding the word *suta*: this term *suta*, whether with or without a prefix, has many distinct meanings, such as "going," "renowned," "overcome by lust," "accumulated," "devoted to," "perceivable by the ear," and "cognized by the door of the ear.

For instance, in phrases such as "gone forth with the army" (*senāya pasuto*), the meaning is "going. In phrases such as "of one who has heard the Dhamma and sees it" (*sutadhammassa passato*), the meaning is "one whose Dhamma is renowned.
In phrases such as "the lustful toward the lustful" (*avassutā avassutassa*), the meaning is "overcome by lust" (*rāgābhibhūtā*).
The meaning is "one overcome by lust. In such passages as "By you, merit has been accumulated, not small," the meaning is "accumulated.
In such passages as "Those wise ones intent on meditation," the meaning is "devoted to meditation. In such passages as "Seen, heard, and sensed," the meaning is "to be cognized by the ear.
In such passages as "One who retains what is heard, one who stores what is heard," the meaning is "one who retains what is known through the pursuit of the ear-door."

The meaning is as follows: here, however, "heard" (*suta*) means either that it has been apprehended by the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) preceded by ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*), or the act of apprehending.

In that context, when the word *me* has the sense of "by me," then it is appropriate to say: "Thus have I heard, [meaning] it was apprehended by the cognitive process preceded by ear-consciousness.
