When the word *me* has the sense of "my," [it is appropriate to say]: "Thus have I heard, [meaning] it was apprehended by the cognitive process preceded by ear-consciousness belonging to me."

In that case, it is appropriate [to say]: "Thus was it heard by me" (*evaṃ me sutaṃ*), which refers to the retention [of the teaching] through the cognitive process (*viññāṇavīthi*) preceded by auditory consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa*).
Thus, among these three terms: *evaṃ* indicates the function of auditory consciousness; *me* indicates the person possessing the aforementioned consciousness;
and *sutaṃ* indicates the apprehension that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor erroneous, by way of negating the state of not having heard. Likewise, *evaṃ*.
This is a demonstration of the various ways in which the mind, beginning with the thought of hearing [the Dhamma], proceeds toward its object. "Me" (meti) is a demonstrative of oneself.
"Sutaṃ" (sutanti) is a demonstrative of the Dhamma.
"Tathā evaṃ" (tathā evanti) is a demonstrative of the Dhamma that is to be demonstrated. "Me" (meti) is a demonstrative of the person. "Sutaṃ" (sutanti) is a demonstrative of the person's activity.

"Thus" (*tathā*) and "so" (*evaṃ*): this is a description of the various modes by way of the designation of the aspect (*ākāra-paññatti*) of the process-thoughts (*vīthi-citta*). "Me" (*me*): this is a description of the agent. "Heard" (*sutaṃ*): this is a description of the object. "Thus" (*tathā*) and "so" (*evaṃ*):

this is a description of the person's activity. "Heard" (*sutaṃ*): this is a description of the activity of consciousness. "Me" (*me*): this is a description of the person endowed with both activities.
"Thus" (*tathā*) and "so" (*evaṃ*): this is a description of the state (*bhāva*). "Me" (*me*): this is a description of the person. "Heard" (*sutaṃ*): this is a description of that person's activity.
In this context, "thus" (*evaṃ*) and "mine" (*me*) are designations of what does not exist in terms of the directly realized ultimate sense (*sacchikaṭṭha-paramattha*).
"Hearing" (*suta*) is a designation of what exists. Likewise, "thus" and "mine" are dependent designations (*upādāpaññatti*), because they are spoken in dependence upon this or that [object].
"Hearing" is a comparative designation (*upanidhāpaññatti*), because it is spoken in comparison with what has been seen and so forth.
And here, by the word "thus" (evaṃ), he illustrates non-delusion; by the word "heard" (suta), he illustrates the non-forgetting of what has been heard.
Likewise, by the word "thus," he illustrates wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), because for one who attends unwisely, there is no penetration in its various modes.
By the word "heard," he illustrates non-distraction, because there is no hearing for one whose mind is distracted. For indeed, one whose mind is distracted...
Even when told of every possible attainment, a person says, "I have not heard this; say it again.

Here, through wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), one accomplishes right self-application and previously performed merit; and through non-distraction, one accomplishes hearing the true Dhamma and reliance upon a superior person (*sappurisūpanissaya*).
And thus, by means of this auspicious manner, one fulfills the excellence of the latter two wheels.
He illuminates his own [attainment]: by the phrase "it has been heard" (*suta*), he demonstrates the excellence of the first two wheels through the application of hearing.

Likewise, he demonstrates the purity of his disposition (*āsaya*) and the purity of his practice (*payoga*); and by that purity of disposition, the excellence of his realization (*adhigama*), and by the purity of practice, the excellence of his scriptural knowledge (*āgama*).

Furthermore, by this statement which illustrates various modes of penetration (*paṭivedha*), he demonstrates his own perfection in the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) of meaning (*attha*) and ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*).

It illuminates. By the word "heard" (*suta*), which illuminates the penetration of the various things to be heard, he demonstrates his perfection in the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma and its terminology (*dhammaniruttipaṭisambhidā*).
And by speaking this statement "thus" (*evaṃ*), which illuminates systematic attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), he makes it known:
"These phenomena have been examined by me with the mind and well-penetrated through vision. "Heard" (*suta*) is this statement that illuminates the application of hearing.

By saying, "Many teachings have been heard, retained, and mastered by me through speech," he makes this known. By both of these [statements], while demonstrating the perfection of both the meaning and the phrasing, he generates respect for hearing [the Dhamma].
Furthermore, by this entire expression, "Thus have I heard," the Venerable Ānanda [indicates] that which has been proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
By not withholding the Dhamma from himself, he transcends the plane of the unworthy person; by professing discipleship, he enters the plane of the worthy person.
Likewise, he draws the mind away from what is not the true Dhamma and establishes the mind in the true Dhamma.
And demonstrating, "This has been heard by me in its entirety; it is the word of that very Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
He liberates himself, points to the Teacher as his authority, applies himself to the word of the Victor, and establishes the guide of the Dhamma.
Furthermore, by saying "Thus have I heard," he does not claim the state of having produced [the teaching] himself; rather, disclosing his prior hearing, he shows:
"This was received directly by me from that Blessed One, who is confident in the four grounds of self-confidence and who possesses the ten powers."

“Of the one who stands in the place of the bull, the roarer of the lion’s roar, the supreme among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Island of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, the Wheel-turner of the sublime True Dhamma— the Perfectly Enlightened One. Herein,
no doubt or uncertainty should be made regarding the meaning, the Dhamma, the phrases, or the syllables,” [he said] to all gods and humans.
It should be understood that this Dhamma destroys lack of faith and generates perfection of faith. And on this point there is this verse:
"It destroys lack of faith and increases faith in the Teaching;
Thus saying 'Thus have I heard,' the disciple of Gotama speaks."
This is the exposition of the delimitation by number. "At one time" (ekasmiṃ samaye) is an exposition of the delimited. "At one time" (ekaṃ samayaṃ) is an indication of the unspecified.
In this context, the word *samaya* is seen to apply to: assembly, moment, time, collection, cause, view, acquisition, abandoning, and penetration.
For instance, in such passages as, “Perhaps tomorrow we might approach him, taking into account the time and the occasion,” the meaning is *samavāya* (conjunction).
In such passages as, “Bhikkhus, there is indeed but one moment and one occasion for living the holy life,” the meaning is *khaṇa* (moment).
In such passages as, “The time of heat, the time of fever,” the meaning is *kāla* (time). In such passages as, “A great assembly in the forest,” the meaning is... [assembly].
A collection. [In such passages as: “Bhaddāli, you also did not penetrate this circumstance: ‘The Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī;
he too will know me as a monk named Bhaddāli who does not fulfill the training in the Teacher’s dispensation.
This circumstance also, Bhaddāli, was not penetrated by you”—in these cases it is a cause. Furthermore, by that...

The view [found] in such passages as: "At one time the wanderer Uggāhamāna, son of Samaṇa Muṇḍikā, was staying at Mallikā’s Park, in the Tindukācīra grove of the Single-Sālaka tree, among those who propound doctrines for specific occasions. And:
"Whatever benefit there is in this visible world, and whatever benefit there is in the future world..."
In such passages as, “The steadfast one who has realized the goal is called wise,” it refers to acquisition (*paṭilābha*).
In such passages as, “Through the realization of conceit rightly, he made an end of suffering,” it refers to abandoning (*pahāna*).

In such passages as, “The meaning of suffering is oppression, the meaning of being conditioned, the meaning of burning, the meaning of change, and the meaning of realization (*abhisamaya*),” it refers to [realization].

*Paṭivedha*. Here, however, the meaning is "time. By this, "at one time" (*ekaṃ samayaṃ*) indicates one among those times designated as "time" (*kāla*), such as a year, a season, a month, half a month, a day and night, the morning, midday, evening, the first watch, middle watch, or last watch of the night, or the moments [of the day], and so forth.
Or else, it refers to these: the time of descent into the womb, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency, the time of the Great Renunciation, and the time of practicing austerities.

The time of the victory over Māra, the time of full enlightenment, the time of dwelling in happiness in this very life, the time of teaching, and the time of final Nibbāna—such times as these were exceedingly well-known among gods and humans for the Blessed One, occurring indeed at many different times.
Among those times, it is said that "at one time" refers specifically to the time of teaching. And as for this [expression] regarding the times of his duties of wisdom and compassion:
The occasion for the function of compassion; the occasion for the practice of the welfare of others among the two occasions of practicing for one's own welfare and the welfare of others;
the occasion for a discourse on the Dhamma among the two things to be done by those who have assembled;
and the occasion for teaching among the two occasions of teaching and practice—it is with reference to any such occasion that the expression "at one time" is used.
Here it is asked: Why is it that, unlike the description made by means of the locative case in the Abhidhamma— such as "at whatever time, pertaining to the sense-sphere"—
and in other Sutta passages such as "at whatever time, monks, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures," and unlike the instrumental case used in the Vinaya—
"at that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One"— it is not done in that same way here?
Here, the expression "at one time" (*ekam samayam*) is given as an accusative case designation.

This is because the meaning is possible both there [in the Abhidhamma] and here [in the Sutta], though in different ways. For in that context—the Abhidhamma—and in other Sutta passages besides this, the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the sense of characterizing a state by means of another state (*bhāvena bhāva-lakkhaṇa*) are possible.
For "time" (*samaya*) has the sense of a locus as well as the sense of a collection; and in that [locus], the phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth are spoken of.
Furthermore, their state is characterized by the state of "time" (samaya), which is defined as the causal concurrence of moments;
therefore, the locative case is employed there in order to indicate that meaning.

In the Vinaya, both the sense of cause and the sense of instrument are possible. For that time at which the formulation of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) occurred was [known] even to Sāriputta and others.

Difficult to understand; at that time, the Blessed One dwelt here and there while enacting the training rules (sikkhāpada) by means of them as causes and instruments, and while taking into account the reasons for the enactment of those training rules.
Therefore, the instrumental case is employed there to illustrate that meaning.
However, in this and other similar Sutta passages, the sense of absolute connection (accantasaṃyoga) is possible. For that which...
On that occasion, whether the Blessed One taught this sutta or another, he dwelt exclusively in the abiding of compassion.
Therefore, it should be understood that the use of the locative case is employed here for the purpose of illustrating that meaning.
And there is a verse on this point: “Depending upon various meanings, by means of the locative and the instrumental;”
"The exception to the rule has been stated; here it is by way of application.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for one who is honored with reverence for being the supreme among beings distinguished by special qualities. As it is said:
"The word 'Bhagavā' is the best; the word 'Bhagavā' is the most excellent."
“Because he is possessed of such reverence, the Blessed One is so called.
For names are indeed of four kinds: situational (*āvatthika*), indicative (*liṅgika*), causal (*nemittaka*), and accidental (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
An accidental name is what is called “arbitrary. Among these, names such as “calf,” “ox,” or “bull” are situational.

Expressions such as "the staff-bearer," "the umbrella-holder," or "the one with a topknot" are based on physical marks (*liṅgika*). Expressions such as "one possessing the three knowledges" or "one possessing the six superknowledges" are based on signs (*nemittaka*).
Expressions such as "Sirivaḍḍhaka" (Fortune-increaser) or "Dhanavaḍḍhaka" (Wealth-increaser), which occur without regard for the actual meaning of the words, are adventitious (*adhiccasamuppanna*).
However, this name "Bhagavā" is based on qualities (*guṇanemittaka*); it was not given by Mahāmāyā, nor by King Suddhodana.
This was not made by eighty thousand kinsmen, nor by distinguished deities such as Sakka and Santusita.
As the Venerable Sāriputta Thera said: "‘Bhagavā’—this name was not given by his mother... [and so on] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely ‘the Blessed One’ (Bhagavā).
Since this name is derived from his qualities (*guṇa*), they recite this verse in order to explain those qualities:
“He is a possessor, a partaker, a sharer, and a distributor;
he has broken [defilements], he is venerable, and he is fortunate.
By many methods, he has well-cultivated himself.”
“He is called the Blessed One because he has gone to the end of existence.
Its meaning should be understood according to the method stated in the Niddesa and other such texts.
However, there is this other way of explanation:
“He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), he has overcome (bhaggavā), he is endowed with (yutto), he is distinguished by excellences (bhagehi ca vibhattavā);
he has enjoyed (bhattavā) and has gone beyond (vantagamano) states of existence (bhavesu)—therefore he is the Blessed One (bhagavā).

In this regard, having taken the characteristic of etymology (niruttilakkhaṇa) as “the addition of a syllable (vaṇṇāgamo) and the substitution of a syllable (vaṇṇavipariyāyo),” or according to the method of grammar (saddanayena):

Having taken the characteristic of being filled with the "pisodara" (the belly) and so forth, it should be understood that because he possesses the fortune (*bhāgya*)— reaching the further shore of giving, virtue, and so on— which produces mundane and supramundane happiness,
he is called "Bhagavā" when he ought to be called "Bhāgyavā. Furthermore, because [he has abandoned] greed,

hatred, delusion, distorted attention, lack of shame, lack of dread, anger, resentment, spite, malice, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, stubbornness, impetuosity, conceit, arrogance, pride, intoxication, negligence, craving, ignorance, the various unwholesome roots, and misconduct...
The hundreds of thousands of defilements consisting of: the stains of corruption; the fourfold diversity of perceptions, thoughts, and conceptual proliferations;

the fourfold perversions; the taints, fetters, floods, yokes, and underlying tendencies; the cravings and clingings; the five mental barrennesses, bondages, hindrances, and relishings; the six roots of dispute; the seven latent tendencies of craving; the eight wrong views; the nine root-cravings; the ten unwholesome courses of action; the sixty-two types of speculative views;
and the eighty-four thousand varieties of distress, fever, and defilement—briefly stated.

Or, because he has shattered the five aggregates of defilement, the formative forces, Māra the Death, and Māra the Son of the Deva, he is called the Blessed One (*bhagavā*) because these perils have been shattered (*bhagga*); for it is said therein:
"He whose lust is shattered, whose hatred is shattered, whose delusion is shattered, and who is free from taints."
“Evil states have been shattered by him; therefore he is called the Blessed One (Bhagavā).

By this, his excellence of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is illustrated through his possession of fortune—bearing the hundred marks of merit—and his excellence of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*) through his destruction of faults.
Likewise, it shows the state of great esteem from those in the world who are his peers, as well as from householders and renunciants.

It is the state of being approachable. Furthermore, it is shown that for those who have approached him, he is capable of removing their physical and mental suffering, that he is a benefactor through the giving of material goods and the giving of the Dhamma, and that he is able to unite them with both mundane and supramundane happiness.
And because the word *bhaga* is used in the world to denote six qualities—sovereignty, virtue, fame, glory, beauty, and effort—[the Buddha is called Bhagavā].
Furthermore, he possesses supreme mastery over his own mind, including the mundane powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and *laghimā* (lightness), which are fully perfected in every aspect;
likewise, there is the supramundane Dhamma, and a fame that pervades the three worlds, attained through qualities as they truly are and exceedingly pure;
and [he possesses] a form-body that is fully perfected in every aspect and capable of producing serene confidence in the eyes and minds of those people intent on beholding it.

Because he possesses all the splendor of every limb and member, and because whatever he desires or aspires to—whether for his own benefit or the benefit of others—is accomplished exactly as intended, there is in him the "desire" (kāma) known as the fulfillment of desired aims;
and there is also the "effort" (payatta), consisting of right exertion, which is the cause for attaining a state of being honored by the whole world.
Therefore, because he is endowed with these "blessings" (bhaga), it is said that "he has blessings" (bhagavā).
In this sense, he is called the "Bhagavā.

Furthermore, because he has understood all phenomena—whether classified as wholesome and so forth, or as the aggregates, bases, elements, truths, faculties, dependent origination, and so on—or because he has understood the noble truth of suffering in the sense of oppression, being conditioned, burning, and changeability, or in the sense of accumulation, source, bondage, and obstruction; [he is thus called the Bhagavā].
Having analyzed— meaning having analyzed, opened up, and taught— the origin [of suffering], the cessation in the sense of escape, seclusion, the unconditioned, and the deathless,
and the path in the sense of being a leading-out cause, vision, and predominance; therefore, although he should be called "the analyzer" (*vibhattavā*),
he is called "the Blessed One" (*bhagavā*).
And because he cultivated, frequented, and practiced extensively the divine, brahma, and noble abidings; the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites;

the liberations of emptiness, the wishless, and the signless; and other mundane and supramundane superhuman states, therefore—though he should be called "one who possesses food" (bhattava)—he is called "Bhagavā."
However, because he has vomited out (*vanta*) the going (*gamana*)—which is to say, craving (*taṇhā*)—within the three realms of existence (*bhava*), he is called "Bhagavā.

While he should be called "one who has vomited the going in existences" (*bhavesu vantagamana*), by taking the letter *bha* from the word *bhava*, the letter *ga* from the word *gamana*, and the letter *va* from the word *vanta* (lengthening it), he is thus termed "Bhagavā.
This is just as in the world, where one should say "a garland for the privy" (*mehanassa khassa mālā*), yet it is called "mekhalā" [a girdle].
To this extent, by the words "Thus have I heard," he reveals the Dhamma-body of the Blessed One by making it manifest as he teaches the Dhamma exactly as it was heard and mastered;
thereby, he consoles those people who are distressed by not seeing the Blessed One, showing them: "This teaching is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this is your Teacher."
By the phrase "at one time the Blessed One," he shows that at that time the Blessed One was no longer present, thereby demonstrating the parinibbāna of the physical body (rūpakāya).

By this, [the author] implies: "Even the Blessed One who possessed the ten powers and a body like a diamond-mace, the teacher of such noble Dhamma as this, has passed away; in that case, what other hope for life should one conceive?"
He arouses a sense of spiritual urgency in people intoxicated by the pride of life, and he generates enthusiasm for the True Dhamma.

By saying "Thus," he indicates the excellence of the teaching; by "heard by me," the excellence of the disciple; by "at one time," the excellence of the time; and by "the Blessed One," the excellence of the teacher.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling at Sāvatthī": here, "Sāvatthī" refers to the city that served as the residence of the sage Savattha.
Just as *Kākandī* is called *Mākandī*, so too, according to its feminine gender, it is called *Sāvatthī*; such is the view of the grammarians (*akkharacintaka*).
However, the masters of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariya*) say: "Whatever is a requisite for human enjoyment or use, all that exists here," thus it is *Sāvatthī*.
Furthermore, in the *Satthasamāyoga*, when asked, "What goods are there?", the reply is, "Everything is there."
“Based on its speech, it is Sāvatthī.
‘All requisites at all times are gathered in Sāvatthī;
therefore, based on everything, it is called Sāvatthī.’”
“The lovely city of the Kosalans is beautiful to behold and delightful;
it is never devoid of ten kinds of sounds and is well-supplied with food and drink.
It has reached growth and abundance, prosperous, flourishing, and enchanting.”
"Āḷakamandā for the gods, Sāvatthī the supreme city.
In this context, the locative case in "Sāvatthiyaṃ" expresses proximity.
"Viharati" (dwells) is a general term indicating that he is endowed with any one of the various modes of dwelling: the postures, the divine dwellings, the brahma-dwellings, or the noble dwellings.
Furthermore, here there is an indication of association with one or another of the postures—divided into standing, walking, sitting, and lying down;
by this it should be understood that the Blessed One dwells even when standing, walking, sitting, or lying down.
For he, having interrupted the oppression of one posture by means of another, maintains his person from falling [into exhaustion].
It carries away and causes to proceed; therefore, it is called "dwelling" (*viharati*).
Regarding the word "Jeta’s Grove" (*Jetavana*): here, one who conquers his own enemies is *Jeta*; or, it is *Jeta* because it was produced when the King had conquered his own enemies;
or, out of a desire for auspiciousness, he himself gave it that name—thus it is *Jeta*. He causes to grow (*vanayati*)...
*Vanaṃ*: it causes beings to feel devotion toward self-perfection; the meaning is that it arouses affection for itself. Or, *vanaṃ* means "it entreats" (*vanute*);

the meaning is that, through the warbling of birds such as intoxicated cuckoos delighted by the fragrance of various flowers, and through the branches, twigs, blossoms, fruits, shoots, and foliage of trees swayed by gentle breezes, it is as if it were requesting living beings, saying, "Come, enjoy me. *Jetassa vanaṃ* is *jetavanaṃ*.
For that [grove] was planted, nurtured, and protected by Prince Jeta, and he was its owner;
therefore it is called "Jeta’s Grove" (*Jetavana*). In that Jeta’s Grove.
Regarding the phrase "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery," that householder was named Sudatta according to the name given by his parents.
Because he constantly gave alms to the destitute, being free from the stain of stinginess and endowed with qualities such as compassion for the sake of fulfilling all desires,
he became known by the name Anāthapiṇḍika. It is called an *ārāma* because living beings—

especially those who have gone forth— find delight therein, owing to its beauty of flowers, fruits, and foliage, and its possession of the five factors of a suitable dwelling site, such as being neither too far nor too near.
The meaning is that having come from here and there, they delight, take pleasure, and dwell without longing.
Alternatively, it is called an *ārāma* because, even when one has gone to various places, one brings oneself back within [the reach of] such excellences as those described and finds delight therein.
For that [garden] was acquired by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from Prince Jeta through the covering of it with eighteen crores of gold.

Having purchased it for eighteen crores of gold and had dwellings constructed, and having completed the festival of the monastery with another eighteen crores of gold, he thus dedicated it to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha at a cost of fifty-four crores of gold;
therefore, it is called "Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. In that Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
And here, the mention of "in Jeta’s Grove" is the description of the former owner, while "in Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery" is the description of the latter owner.
What is the purpose of these descriptions? It is said: first, by way of context, it serves to determine the answer to the question "Where was it spoken?
and to induce others who desire merit to follow the example of those [who made the offerings].

And there is the application [of the discourse]. For in that context, when the gate-tower and palace were being built, the eighteen crores of gold obtained from the sale of the land and the trees worth many crores were the gift of Jeta, while fifty-four crores were Anāthapiṇḍika’s.
Therefore, by praising those two, the Venerable Ānanda showed: "In this way, those desiring merit perform meritorious deeds."

He also enjoins others who desire merit to follow in their footsteps. Thus, it should be understood that the purpose here is the enjoining of those desiring merit to follow in the footsteps of these [disciples].
Here it is asked: "If the Blessed One is staying at Sāvatthī, why does he say, 'In Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery'?"
"It should not be said. If he dwells there, it should not be said that he is 'in Sāvatthī. For it is not possible to dwell in both places at one and the same time.
It is replied: Has it not been stated that "the locative case is used in the sense of proximity"?
Therefore, just as herds of cattle grazing near the Ganges or the Yamunā are said to be "grazing on the Ganges" or "on the Yamunā,"...

Just as those who move about are said to be "dwelling," so too here it should be understood that when he is staying at Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery near Sāvatthī, he is said to be "dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

For the word "Sāvatthī" is used for the purpose of indicating the village of his alms-round, while the remaining words are used for the purpose of indicating a dwelling place suitable for one who has gone forth.

In this context, by the mention of Sāvatthī, he shows the Blessed One’s provision of support for householders; by the mention of Jetavana and so forth, he shows his provision of support for those who have gone forth.
Likewise, by the former, through the acceptance of the [four] requisites, there is the avoidance of devotion to self-mortification;
by the latter, through the abandoning of sensual objects, there is the demonstration of the means for avoiding devotion to sensual pleasure. By the former...
And by the former [verse], the application to teaching the Dhamma; by the latter, the inclination toward seclusion.
By the former, the approach through compassion; by the latter, the withdrawal through wisdom. By the former, the inclination toward accomplishing the welfare and happiness of beings;
by the latter, the state of being untainted while performing the welfare and happiness of others. By the former, the cause for not abandoning righteous happiness.
The former [is for] dwelling in comfort, while the latter is for the purpose of application to superhuman states. By the former, there is great benefit to human beings;
by the latter, to devas. By the former, there is the state of being born in the world and having grown up in the world;
by the latter, there is non-defilement by the world—and so forth.
Now, *atha* has the sense of non-interruption (*aviccheda*), while *kho* is a particle used to indicate a change of subject (*adhikārantara*).
By this, he shows that even within that uninterrupted sequence, this new subject arose while the Blessed One was dwelling there. What is that subject?
It is "a certain deity," and so forth. In that context, *aññatarā* (a certain) is an indefinite designation; for she was not known by name or clan, and therefore—

"A certain one" is what was said. A *devatā* is simply a deity (*deva*); this term is common to both male and female. However, in this context, it refers specifically to a male, a son of the gods; yet, by way of a common designation, he is called a "deity.
Regarding the phrase "when the night had advanced," here the word *abhikkanta* [is used] in the senses of passing away, beautiful, handsome, or expressing approval, and so forth.
It is seen [in various senses]. Therein, in such passages as, "Venerable sir, the night has passed; the first watch has ended; the community of bhikkhus has been sitting for a long time;
let the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus," it is seen in the sense of *destruction* (*khaya*).
In such passages as, "This person is more excellent and more sublime than these four persons," it is seen in the sense of *beautiful* (*sundara*).
“Who is it that worships my feet, shining with supernatural power and glory, illuminating all directions with a most excellent complexion?”—in such passages as these, *abhikkanta* means beautiful.

In such passages as “Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama! it means to express great appreciation (*abbhanumodana*). But here, it means destruction (*khaya*). Therefore, by the phrase “when the night was *abhikkanta*,” it is meant that the night had been completely exhausted.

Regarding the phrase *abhikkantavaṇṇā*: here the word *abhikkanta* means "excellent" (*abhirūpa*), while the word *vaṇṇa* is seen used in reference to the skin, praise, lineage, group, cause, shape, measure, the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), and so forth.
Among these, in such passages as "The Blessed One is golden-colored," it refers to the skin.
In such passages as "Householder, when were these 'excellences' (*vaṇṇā*) of the ascetic Gotama acquired? it refers to praise. [In the passage: "These four, sir... [it refers to lineage].
In such passages as "the castes of Gotama," it refers to a clan. In such passages as "Now by what quality is one called a thief of fragrance?
it refers to a cause. In such passages as "having manifested the form of a great king of elephants," it refers to shape.
In such passages as "there are three qualities of a bowl," it refers to measure. In such passages as "color, fragrance, taste, and nutritive essence," it refers to the sense-sphere of visible form.
Thus, here it should be understood as referring to the skin. By the phrase "excellent complexion" (*abhikkanta-vaṇṇa*), what is meant is "beautiful skin. Regarding the term *kevalakappa*:
here the word *kevala* has many meanings, such as "without remainder," "for the most part," "unmixed," "extraordinary," "firm," "separation," and so forth.
For instance, in such passages as "the holy life (*brahmacariya*) that is complete, perfect, and pure," it carries the sense of being "without remainder."
The meaning [of *kevala*] is as follows: in such passages as, “They will approach, bringing abundant food and drink from the whole of Aṅga and Magadha,” it means the majority.
In such passages as, “There is the arising of the entire mass of suffering,” it means unmixed.
In such passages as, “Surely this venerable one has only mere faith,” it means no more than that. “Venerable sir, of the venerable one...”
In such passages as, "Anuruddha’s co-resident named Bāhiya stood intent upon the schism of the entire Saṅgha," the meaning is firmness.
In such passages as, "The Perfect One (kevalī), having lived [the holy life], is called the Supreme Person," the meaning is disjunction.
But here, its intended meaning is the state of being without remainder.

This word *kappa*, however, has many meanings, such as: conviction (*abhisaddahana*), conventional usage (*vohāra*), time (*kāla*), designation (*paññatti*), cutting off (*chedana*), alternative (*vikappa*), a trace (*leśa*), and all-encompassing state (*samantabhāva*).
For instance, in such passages as, "This is to be accepted by the venerable Gotama, as it is for an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One," its meaning is conviction (*abhisaddahana*).
Likewise, in the passage, "I allow you, monks, five kinds of fruits according to the monastic convention (*samaṇakappa*)," [its meaning is conventional usage].
In such expressions as "to enjoy," it refers to usage (*vohāra*). In such expressions as "by which indeed I dwell for all time," it refers to time (*kāla*).
In such expressions as "Thus said the Venerable Kappa," it refers to a designation (*paññatti*). In such expressions as "adorned, with hair and beard trimmed," it refers to cutting (*chedana*).

In such expressions as "the two-finger-breadth allowance is permitted" (*kappati dvaṅgulakappo*), it refers to an adaptation (*vikappo*). [And] in the expression "there is the opportunity to lie down" (*atthi kappo nipajjituṃ*), it refers to possibility (*sambhava*).
In such instances as these, it has the sense of a "trace" (*leśa*). In such instances as "having illuminated the entire Veḷuvana," it has the sense of "entirety" (*samantabhāva*).

However, here its intended meaning is "entirety. Therefore, in the phrase "the entire Jeta’s Grove" (*kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ*), the meaning should be understood as "the Jeta’s Grove without exception, on all sides."
"Having illuminated" means having suffused with light; the meaning is that he made it a single radiance and a single glow, like the moon or the sun.
"He approached where the Blessed One was": this is an instrumental case used in the sense of a locative.
The meaning here should be understood as: "he approached to that place where the Blessed One was. Or else, it refers to the reason why the Blessed One is to be approached by gods and humans.
For that very reason, "he approached" (*upasaṅkami*)—this is how the meaning should be understood here. And for what purpose should the Blessed One be approached?
It is with the intention of attaining various distinguished qualities, just as a flock of birds approaches a great tree that is constantly laden with fruit, intending to enjoy its delicious fruits.
Furthermore, "he approached" means that he "went. Having approached... (*upasaṅkamitvā*)... [the rest of the sentence follows].

This is an illustration of the conclusion of the approach. Alternatively, it means that having gone thus, she went to a place even closer than before, which is reckoned as being in the presence of the Blessed One;
"having paid homage to the Blessed One" means having bowed to him, having prostrated, having saluted him.

“*Ekamantaṃ* (to one side) is an indication in the neuter gender; it means to one place or to one side. Alternatively, it is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative. *Aṭṭhāsi* (stood) is a negation of sitting and so forth;
it means she took her stand, she remained standing. But how did she stand when she stood to one side?
‘Neither behind nor in front, nor too near nor too far;’”
"Not in a marsh, nor in a place with a headwind, nor where it is too low or too high;
having avoided these faults, they stood to one side. But why did he stand rather than sit?
Because of his desire to return quickly. For the deities [would have remained] for some time...
For a specific purpose, they come to the human world as a pure person might go to a place of excrement.
By their very nature, however, from a distance of a hundred leagues, the human world is repulsive due to its foul odor;
they do not take delight therein. Therefore, having performed her duty of coming, she did not sit down because of her desire to return quickly. And for whom...
They sit down for the purpose of dispelling the fatigue of postures such as walking; however, the devas have no such fatigue, and therefore he did not sit down.
Furthermore, he did not sit down out of respect for those great disciples who were standing surrounding the Blessed One.
Moreover, it was solely out of reverence for the Blessed One that he did not sit down. For when devas desire to sit down, [they do so only after receiving permission].
A seat appeared; not desiring it, and without even directing her mind toward sitting, she stood to one side.
"Standing to one side, that deity"—thus, for these reasons, she stood to one side.
She addressed the Blessed One with a verse means she spoke to the Blessed One with speech regulated by syllables, words, and composition.
The meaning is "he spoke. How so? [As in the verse: "Many gods and humans... speak to me of the supreme blessing.
This is the discourse on the origin of the inquiry regarding blessings (*maṅgala*).
In this context, it is said: "Having stated the origin, one should explain the meaning of the passage beginning with 'Thus' in its various aspects."
The table of contents has been established, and this is the occasion for explaining its origin;

therefore, having first stated the origin of the question regarding auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), I shall subsequently comment upon the meaning of these verse lines. And what is the origin of the question regarding auspiciousness?
It is said that in Jambudīpa, in various places such as city gates, assembly halls, and meeting rooms, the great multitude would gather together.
Having given gold and bullion, he had various stories told, beginning with the *Sītā-haraṇa* (The Abduction of Sītā); each story was completed after the lapse of four months.
On one occasion there, a discourse on auspiciousness arose: "What indeed is auspicious? What is seen as auspicious?
What is heard as auspicious? What is sensed as auspicious? Who knows what is auspicious?"
Then a certain man named Diṭṭhamangalika said: "I know what is auspicious. What is seen in the world is auspicious;
'seen' means a form regarded as highly auspicious. For example:
here someone, having risen early, sees a cātaka bird, or a bael-wood staff, or a pregnant woman, or children adorned and dressed up."

"Whether it be a full water-jar, or a live red fish, or a thoroughbred horse, or a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds, or a bull, or a cow, or a tawny animal, or whatever other such form one sees that is regarded as an auspicious omen—this is called 'the seen omen.
Some accepted his words, while others did not accept them. Those who...
They did not accept it and disputed with him about that.

Then a certain man named Sutamaṅgalika said: "Sirs, this eye sees both the pure and the impure, as well as the beautiful and the ugly, and the pleasant and the unpleasant. If what is seen by it is auspicious..."
It might be so; indeed, everything might be auspicious. Therefore, what is seen is not the auspicious; rather, it is what is heard that is the auspicious.
"What is heard" refers to a sound regarded as highly auspicious. For example:
here someone, having risen early, [invokes] "Vaḍḍhā," or "Vaḍḍhamānā," or "Puṇṇā," or "Phussā," or "Sumanā," or "Sirī," or "Sirivaḍḍhā," or "Today..."

"When one hears a sound such as 'an auspicious constellation,' 'an auspicious moment,' 'an auspicious day,' or 'an auspicious blessing'—or whatever else is regarded as an auspicious omen—this is called 'auspiciousness heard. Some accepted his words, while others did not.
Those who did not accept them disputed with him.
Then a certain man named Mutamaṅgalika said: "Sir, the sense of hearing indeed hears sounds that are both good and bad, and both pleasant and unpleasant.
If what is heard by it were to be auspicious, then everything would be auspicious. Therefore, what is heard is not auspicious;
rather, what is sensed (muta) is auspicious. What is called 'sensed' is that which is regarded as a blessing."

Smell, taste, and tangible object. For example: here someone, having risen early, smells the fragrance of flowers such as the lotus, or chews a tooth-stick of *phussa* wood, or touches the earth, or touches green crops, fresh cow dung, a tortoise, sesame seeds, a flower, or fruit, or properly smears himself with *phussa* clay.
"He wears a *phussa*-robe, or he wears a *phussa*-headcloth;

or whatever else of this kind is considered an auspicious omen, whether one smells a fragrance, tastes a flavor, or touches a tangible object—this is called 'auspiciousness through release' (*mutamaṅgala*). Some accepted his words, while others did not.

In that regard, the one who held the view that what is seen is the omen (*diṭṭhamaṅgalika*) was unable to convince the one who held the views that what is heard or what is sensed is the omen (*sutamutamangalika*), nor could either of those two convince the other two.
And among those people, those who accepted the word of the one who held the view that what is seen is the omen concluded, "Only what is seen is the omen.
Those who accepted the words of the ones who held the views that what is heard or what is sensed is the omen concluded, "Only what is heard and only what is sensed is the omen. Thus, this—
Discourse on auspiciousness became renowned throughout the entire Jambudīpa.
Then, people throughout the entire Jambudīpa gathered in groups and pondered what auspiciousness might be.
When the guardian deities of those people heard that talk, they likewise pondered what auspiciousness might be. Of them—
The terrestrial deities were friends of those deities; having heard this from them, the terrestrial deities likewise conceived auspicious thoughts.
The space-dwelling deities were friends of those deities; the deities of the Four Great Kings were friends of the space-dwelling deities.
In this manner, up to the Sudassi deities, the Akaniṭṭha deities were their friends.
Then, having heard of this, even the deities of Akaniṭṭha likewise gathered in dense throngs and contemplated auspicious signs.
Thus, throughout all the ten thousand world-systems, the contemplation of auspicious signs arose.
And though they deliberated, "This is an auspicious sign! This is an auspicious sign!", for twelve years they did not reach a definitive conclusion.
He stood there. All humans, devas, and Brahmas—except for the noble disciples (ariyasāvaka)—were divided into three groups according to what they had seen, heard, or inferred.
Not even a single person reached a definitive conclusion as to what constitutes a blessing (*maṅgala*) based on its true nature; instead, a clamor regarding blessings arose in the world.

This clamor is said to be of five kinds: the clamor concerning the eon (*kappa-kolāhala*), the clamor concerning a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-kolāhala*), and the clamor concerning a Buddha (*buddha-kolāhala*).
There was a tumultuous clamor of auspicious cries and a tumultuous clamor of lamentation.

In that regard, the gods of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-devas), with their heads shorn and hair disheveled, weeping-faced and wiping away tears with their hands, clad in red garments and wearing extremely hideous attire, cried out:
"After the passing of one hundred thousand years, the arising of a world-age (kappuṭṭhāna) will occur; this world will be destroyed; the great ocean..."
It will dry up; this great earth and Sineru, the king of mountains, will be consumed and destroyed.
There will be a dissolution of the world as far as the Brahma-world. "Venerable sirs, cultivate loving-kindness; venerable sirs, cultivate compassion, gladness, and equanimity.
Serve your mother; serve your father; honor the elders of the family."
“Be alert, be watchful, do not be negligent! Thus they proclaim as they wander along the paths of men. This is called the *kappa*-clamor.
Only the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) wander along the paths of men and proclaim, “At the passing of a hundred years, a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti-rāja*) will appear in the world.
This is called the *cakkavatti*-clamor. But the gods of the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*), with their Brahma-adornments—
Having adorned themselves and placed the *brahmaveṭhana* upon their heads, filled with joy and gladness, proclaiming the virtues of the Buddha, they wander along the paths of men and announce:
"In a thousand years, a Buddha will arise in the world. This is called the "Buddha-proclamation" (*buddhakolāhala*).
It is the Suddhāvāsa deities themselves who, knowing the minds of gods and humans, [announce this] after twelve years have passed.
“The Perfectly Enlightened One will proclaim the auspiciousness,” they announce as they wander along the human paths.

This is called the clamor of auspiciousness. Only the Suddhāvāsa deities, thinking, “After the passing of seven years, a certain bhikkhu will come together with the Blessed One and inquire about the practice of moneyya,” wander along the human paths and announce it.
This is what is called the clamor concerning the state of being a sage (*moneyya*). Among these five kinds of clamors, this clamor regarding auspiciousness arose in the world among gods and humans.

Then, when gods and humans had searched and searched for auspicious signs but found none, after the lapse of twelve years, the deities belonging to the Tāvatiṃsa realm gathered together and deliberated thus: "Just as..."
Just as the master of a house is the foremost among those within the household, the lord of a village among the village dwellers,
and the king among all men, even so is this Sakka, Lord of the Devas, our chief and most excellent in terms of merit,
splendor, sovereignty, and wisdom— the sovereign of two divine worlds. What if we were now to [inform] Sakka, Lord of the Devas, of this matter?

“Let us ask him. So they went into the presence of Sakka and, having paid homage to Sakka, lord of the devas—whose body was resplendent with robes and ornaments appropriate for that moment, and who sat upon a choice seat of yellow silk at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree surrounded by a retinue of two hundred and fifty million nymphs—they stood to one side and said this:
“Pray, dear sir, may you know that there are currently questions on auspiciousness.”
“Some have arisen [with this question]: some say ‘the seen is auspicious,’ some say ‘the heard is auspicious,’ and some say ‘the sensed is auspicious.
In this matter, both we and others have reached a deadlock; it would be well if you would explain it to us according to reality.
The king of the gods, who was naturally wise, asked: “Where did this discourse on auspiciousness first arise?”
“We, O King, belong to the Cātumahārājika devas,” they said. Then the Cātumahārājika devas [announced it] to the space-dwelling devas;
the space-dwelling devas to the earth-dwelling devas; the earth-dwelling devas to the devas who protect humans;
and the devas who protect humans said, “It has arisen in the human world.”
Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, asked, "Where does the Perfectly Enlightened One dwell? "In the world of men, O Deva," they replied.

"Does anyone question that Blessed One? "No one, O Deva. "How is it, sirs, that you have discarded the sacrificial fire and lit a mere glowworm, bypassing that Blessed One who is the source of every auspiciousness?"
"Think that you should question me; come, dear sirs, let us question the Blessed One, for we shall surely receive a magnificent answer to our questions.
Having thus commanded one son of the gods, "Question the Blessed One," that son of the gods adorned himself with ornaments appropriate for that moment, shining like a flash of lightning.

Surrounded by a host of deities, he went to the Great Monastery of Jetavana, paid homage to the Blessed One, and standing to one side, he addressed him with a verse while asking about the question of auspiciousness: "Many are the gods and humans...
This is the origin of the question regarding auspiciousness.
Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Bahū devā":

Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the verse lines. *Bahū* is a designation for an unspecified number; by this it is meant that there are many hundreds, many thousands, and many hundreds of thousands.
They play (*dibbanti*), therefore they are called *devā*; [they do so] by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure.

They play, or they shine by means of their own glory—this is the meaning. Furthermore, there are three kinds of gods (*deva*) by way of convention (*sammuti*), rebirth (*upapatti*), and purification (*visuddhi*).
As it is said: "There are three kinds of gods: conventional gods, gods by rebirth, and purified gods.
Among these, 'conventional gods' refers to kings, queens, and princes. 'Gods by rebirth' refers to the gods beginning from those of the Four Great Kings and those above them."
“Those called ‘pure deities’ (visuddhideva) are said to be the Arahants.
Among these, it is the deities by rebirth (upapattideva) that are intended here. They are called “human beings” (manussa) because they are the offspring (apacca) of Manu. However, the ancients say:
“They are human beings because of the abundance of mind (manasa-ussannatā). These consist of those from Jambudīpa, Aparagoyāna, Uttarakuru, and Pubbavideha.
They are of four kinds, and here those of Jambudīpa are intended. "Auspicious" (*maṅgala*) means that beings are honored (*mahanti*) by these things;

the meaning is that they attain success and growth. "They reflected" (*acintayuṃ*) means they thought, desiring—that is, wishing, longing for, and yearning for—welfare (*sotthāna*), which is the state of well-being for all [beings] regarding both the present life and the future life.
It is said that there exists "the good, the beautiful, and the auspicious" (sobhanānaṃ sundarānaṃ kalyāṇānaṃ dhammānaṃ). "Speak" (brūhi) means:
teach, reveal, declare, disclose, analyze, and make plain. "Auspiciousness" (maṅgalaṃ) is the cause of success, the cause of growth, and the cause of all prosperity.
"Supreme" (uttamaṃ) means distinguished, excellent, and bringing welfare and happiness to the entire world—this is [the meaning].
This is the word-by-word commentary on the verses.

As for the summarized meaning: that son of the gods, desiring to hear the discourse on auspiciousness (*maṅgalapañha*) from the deities throughout the ten thousand world-systems, assembled here in this world-system within a space no larger than the tip of a single hair-fiber, numbering ten, twenty, thirty, or even forty [thousand].
Having manifested fifty, sixty, seventy, or eighty subtle bodies, and having surrounded the Blessed One—
who was seated upon the prepared, sublime Buddha-throne, outshining all the devas, Māras, and Brahmas with his glory and splendor while shining brilliantly—
they stood there; and at that time, [they saw] all the humans of Jambudīpa who were yet to come.
Having known with his own mind the thoughts in their minds, for the purpose of extracting the arrow of doubt from all gods and humans, he said:
"Many gods and humans have pondered over auspicious signs, desiring safety;
speak, therefore, of the supreme auspicious sign."

"Being questioned by me with the consent of those deities and out of favor toward human beings, please speak, O Blessed One, out of compassion for us, regarding that supreme blessing which brings about absolute welfare and happiness for all of us.

3. Having heard these words of the son of the gods, the Blessed One spoke the verse beginning with "Not associating with fools. *Note: The phrase "Asevanā ca bālānaṃ" refers to the first line of the verse Dhammapada 208.*
In this context, *asevanā* means non-association and non-attendance. Regarding "fools" (*bālānaṃ*): they are called fools because they merely breathe;

the intention is that they live by the mere act of inhaling and exhaling, not by the life of wisdom (*paññājīvita*). Of those fools. Regarding "wise ones" (*paṇḍitānaṃ*): they are called wise because they discern;
the intention is that they proceed by way of knowledge regarding matters pertaining to the present life and the future life. Of those wise ones.
“Serving” (sevanā) means attending upon, waiting upon, being a companion to, associating with, and being joined with them; it is honor, namely: respect, reverence, esteem, and veneration.
“Of those worthy of worship” (pūjaneyyānaṃ) means of those deserving of worship. “This is the supreme blessing” (etaṃ maṅgalamuttamaṃ):
having combined together both the non-association with fools, the association with the wise, and the worship of those worthy of worship, he says, “This is the supreme blessing.”
Regarding what was asked by you—"Speak of the supreme auspiciousness"—it is here said: "Take this to be the supreme auspiciousness.
This is the word-by-word commentary on that verse.
However, its commentary on the meaning should be understood as follows: Having thus heard these words of the son of the gods, the Blessed One...
He spoke this verse: “And by not associating with fools. In this regard, there are four kinds of verses:

the questioned verse, the unasked verse, the verse with a sequential connection, and the verse without a sequential connection. Among these, [the first two types are illustrated by] “I ask you, Gotama of vast wisdom:
how acting is a disciple excellent? and “How indeed, dear sir, have you crossed over the flood?”

In such cases as these, verses spoken by one who has been questioned are called "verses asked about" (*pucchitagāthā*). In such cases as, "What others call happiness, that the Noble Ones call suffering," verses spoken by one who has not been questioned, according to his own inclination, are called "verses not asked about" (*apucchitagāthā*).

Furthermore, all the verses of the Buddhas are "verses with a sequence of meaning" (*sānusandhikagāthā*), because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach the Dhamma together with its basis (*sanidāna*)."

There are no verses without a specific connection (*an-anusandhika*) in this teaching. Thus, among these verses, this one is called a "questioned verse" because it was spoken by the Blessed One when questioned by the son of a deity.

And just as a clever man, skilled in the path and skilled in what is not the path, having been asked about the path, first explains what is to be abandoned and afterwards explains what is to be taken, so too is this.

“In such-and-such a place there is a forked path; there, leaving the left and taking the right,” in this way, having pointed out that which is not to be practiced among things to be practiced and not practiced, he points out that which is to be practiced.
And the Blessed One is like a man skilled in the way, as it has been said:
“‘A man skilled in the path,’ Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For he is skilled in this world, skilled in the other world, skilled in the realm of death,
skilled in the realm beyond death, skilled in the realm of Māra, and skilled in the realm beyond Māra.”
Therefore, explaining first that which is not to be cultivated, he said: “Not associating with fools, and associating with the wise.
For just as the path to be abandoned must first be left behind, so too fools are not to be associated with nor waited upon;
then, just as the path to be taken up, the wise are to be associated with and waited upon. But why did the Blessed One, while speaking of an auspicious blessing, [say this]?
Was it not said that first comes the non-association with fools and the association with the wise? It is replied:
because gods and humans, through associating with fools, have grasped this view of auspiciousness regarding such things as the seen;

and since that is actually inauspicious, [the Blessed One], by censuring that association with unwholesome friends which destroys one's welfare in both this world and the next, [taught] that which accomplishes welfare in both worlds.
By the Blessed One, who praised association with virtuous friends, it was first stated that one should avoid fools and associate with the wise.
In this context, "fools" refers to any beings endowed with the unwholesome courses of action such as the destruction of life;
they are to be recognized by way of three characteristics. As it is said in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a fool. Furthermore:
The six teachers beginning with Pūraṇa Kassapa; Devadatta, Kokālika, Kaṭamodaka, Tissa Khaṇḍadeviyāputta, Samuddadatta, Ciñcamāṇavikā, and others;
as well as Dīghavidassa’s brother and other such beings in the past—these should be understood as fools.
Like a house set ablaze by fire, they destroy themselves and those who follow their words through their own misapprehension.
Just as the brother of Dīghavid was cooked in the great hell, having fallen prostrate with a body measuring sixty yojanas for the interval between four Buddhas;
and just as five hundred families who delighted in his wrong view were reborn in his company and are likewise cooked in the great hell. And this was said by the Blessed One:

“Just as, monks, a fire released from a reed-thatch hut or a grass-thatch hut burns even gabled houses—those plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with doors bolted and windows closed—in the same way, monks, whatever fears arise, they all arise from the fool, not from the wise man. Whatever calamities arise... [and so on].”
“Whatever misfortunes there may be... [omitted] ...they do not come upon the wise man. Thus, monks, the fool is full of peril, while the wise man is free from peril;
the fool is beset by calamity, while the wise man is free from calamity; the fool is subject to misfortune, while the wise man is free from misfortune.

Furthermore, the fool is like rotten fish, and one who associates with him is like a leaf-bundle tied to that rotten fish; he becomes something to be discarded and loathed by the wise. And this has been said:
“A man who carries a rotting fish on the tip of a blade of kusa grass—both the kusa grass and the fish give off a foul odor;
so it is with the cultivation of fools.
And when Sakka, lord of the devas, was offering a boon to the wise Akitti, he spoke thus:
“One should not see a fool, nor hear one, nor dwell together with a fool.
One should not engage in conversation or discourse with a fool, nor take pleasure in doing so.
‘What has the fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.’”
“Why, Kassapa, do you not desire the sight of a fool?
‘The witless man leads himself astray; he yokes himself to what is not his burden.
A wrong course seems better to him; when rightly spoken to, he becomes agitated.’”
“He does not know the Vinaya; it is better not to see him.
Thus the Blessed One, censuring the cultivation of fools in every respect, stated, “Not associating with fools is an auspicious sign.
Now, praising the cultivation of the wise, he said, “And associating with the wise is an auspicious sign. In this context, the wise...
Indeed, those beings who are endowed with the ten courses of wholesome action, beginning with abstention from taking life, are to be known by three characteristics.
As it is said in the Sutta: "Bhikkhus, there are these three characteristics of a wise man.

Furthermore, [this applies to] the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, the eighty great disciples, and other disciples of the Tathāgata, such as Sunetta, Mahāgovinda, Vidhura, Sarabhaṅga, Mahosadha, Sutasoma, and King Nimi.
It should be understood that Ayoghara, Kumāra, Akitti, Paṇḍita, and others were likewise wise men.

Just as protection is to one in fear, a lamp in darkness, or the acquisition of food and drink to one overcome by the suffering of hunger and thirst, these [wise men] are capable of destroying all fears, calamities, and misfortunes for those who carry out their word. For it is thus:

Relying upon the Tathāgata, incalculable and immeasurable devas and humans have attained the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*), established themselves in the Brahma-world, established themselves in the world of the devas, and been reborn in the world of happy destinations.
Furthermore, eighty thousand families, having gladdened their hearts toward the Elder Sāriputta and having attended upon the Elder with the four requisites, were reborn in heaven. Likewise...
Among all the great disciples, beginning with Mahāmoggallāna and Mahākassapa, some disciples of the Teacher Sunetta were reborn in the Brahma-world;
some attained companionship with the Paranimmitavasavatti gods... and so on...
while others were reborn as companions of wealthy householders. And this has also been said:
“Monks, there is no fear for one who is wise, no calamity for one who is wise, and no misfortune for one who is wise.

Furthermore, a wise person is like the fragrance of *tagara* powder, garlands, and so forth; one who associates with such a person becomes like the leaves used to bind and wrap that fragrance. They attain a state of being cultivated and pleasing to the wise. And this has been said:
“If a man carries *tagara* powder wrapped in *palāsa* leaves...”
“Even the winds blow fragrant; such is the result of associating with the wise.
And when Sakka, lord of the devas, was offering boons, the wise Akitti Paṇḍita spoke thus:
“One should see the wise, hear the wise, and dwell together with the wise.”
“Engage in conversation with the wise man, and you will find it pleasing.
‘What has the wise one done for you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.
For what reason, Kassapa, do you long for the sight of the wise one?’”
“The wise man follows the right path; he does not yoke himself to what is burdensome.
The one who follows the good path fares better; when spoken to rightly, he does not become angry.
He understands discipline; it is good to have association with such a person.”

Thus, the Blessed One, praising the service of the wise in every way, having stated, "Service to the wise is auspicious," now, praising the honoring of those who have gradually attained a state worthy of honor through that very non-service of fools and service of the wise, said:
"And honoring those worthy of honor is auspicious. In this context, "those worthy of honor" (pūjaneyyā) refers to...
The Blessed Buddhas are so called because they are free from all faults and endowed with all virtues;
after them come the Paccekabuddhas and the noble disciples (ariyasāvakas). For even a small offering made to them leads to welfare and happiness for a long time;
in this regard, the garland-makers Sumana and Mallika are examples.
Let us state one illustration of this: One day, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then the garland-maker Sumanas, while going along after taking flowers for Seniya Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha, saw the Blessed One who had arrived at the city gate.
Having seen him—gracious, inspiring confidence, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics, and blazing with the glory of a Buddha—he thought:
"If a king were to take flowers and give a hundred or a thousand [pieces of gold], that would result in happiness only for this world;
but an offering to the Blessed One yields immeasurable and incalculable fruit."
"It brings benefit and happiness for a long time; come now, let me honor the Blessed One with these flowers.
With a mind full of faith, he took a handful of flowers and threw them toward the Blessed One. The flowers traveled through the air and remained above the Blessed One, forming a canopy of garlands.
Seeing this miraculous power, the garland-maker’s heart became even more serene, and once again...
He threw up a handful of flowers; these too went and stood there having become a floral canopy. In this manner he threw eight handfuls of flowers;
they went and stood there having become a pavilion of flowers.
The Blessed One was inside the pavilion, and a great multitude of people had gathered. Seeing the garland-maker, the Blessed One smiled.
He manifested a smile. The Elder Ānanda asked the reason for the smile, saying, "The Buddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or condition.

The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, by the power of this offering, this garland-maker will wander through the realms of devas and humans for a hundred thousand eons, and at the conclusion of that time, he will become a Paccekabuddha named Sumanissara."
At the conclusion of his speech, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:
“That deed is well done which, having been done, one does not regret;
that deed is well done at the end of which one enjoys its fruit with a joyful and happy mind.”
At the conclusion of the verses, there was a realization of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
Thus, it should be understood that even a small offering made to them leads to welfare and happiness for a long time. And this refers merely to material offerings;

what need is there to mention the offering of practice (*paṭipattipūjā*)? For those sons of noble family who, by receiving the training precepts of going for refuge and by undertaking the factors of the Uposatha, [practice accordingly...]
And when they honor the Blessed One with their own virtues, such as the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), who could describe the fruit of their offering?
For it is said that they honor the Tathāgata with the supreme form of worship. As it is said:
"Ānanda, whatever monk or nun, or lay follower male or female, practices in accordance with the Dhamma..."
“He dwells practicing with propriety, acting in accordance with the Dhamma; he honors, reveres, respects, worships, and pays homage to the Tathāgata with the highest form of worship.
Following this same principle, it should be understood that the offering of worship to Paccekabuddhas and noble disciples (ariyasāvakas) also brings about welfare and happiness.
Furthermore, among householders, the elder brother or sister is to be honored by the younger;

likewise, parents are to be honored by a son, and a husband, mother-in-law, and father-in-law are to be honored by daughters-in-law. Thus, those who are to be honored in this context should be understood.

For honoring them is indeed an auspicious sign (maṅgala), because it consists of wholesome states (kusala-dhamma) and because it is a cause for the increase of longevity and other such blessings. Indeed, this has been said:
“They will be filial toward their mothers and fathers, respectful toward recluses and brahmins, and honoring those who are elders in the family;
having undertaken this wholesome Dhamma, they will abide in it. Because of undertaking these wholesome states, they will increase in lifespan and will also increase in beauty,” and so forth.
Now, since the following summary (mātikā) has been set forth: "Having determined what is auspicious for whom, one should clarify its nature as auspicious," therefore this is said:
Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated—non-association with fools, association with the wise, and honoring those worthy of honor.
Therein, non-association with fools is [a blessing] by way of protection from fear and so forth caused by associating with fools.
Because it is the cause for the welfare of both worlds, service to the wise and worship of those worthy of honor should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*),
since— according to the method already stated in the commentary on the manifestation of their fruits— it is the cause for *nibbāna* and a happy rebirth. Hereafter, however,
without setting forth a formal outline (*mātikā*), we shall determine what constitutes an auspicious sign in each case and clarify its status as an auspicious sign.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "And the non-association with fools," is concluded.
4. Commentary on the verse beginning with "Living in a suitable locality":
Thus, although the Blessed One was requested with only one word—"Tell me the supreme blessing"—he, who gives much even when asked little, [proceeded to explain].
Just as a noble person, having spoken of three blessings with a single verse, might speak further blessings— out of a desire for the deities to hear more,
and out of a desire to direct various beings toward whatever blessings are suitable for them in their respective circumstances—
he likewise spoke many further blessings with verses beginning with “Dwelling in a suitable place” (patirūpadesavāso).
He began to speak. Regarding that, first of all, in the initial verse: *patirūpa* means suitable or appropriate.
*Desa* refers to any place where beings dwell—whether a village, a town, a city, or a province. *Vāsa* means dwelling there. *Pubbe* means previously, in past births.
*Katapuññatā* means the state of having accumulated merit. *Attā* refers to the mind; it is called the "self" (*sakala*).
Or, "one's own person" (*attabhāva*); "right aspiration" (*sammāpaṇidhi*) means his own right aspiration, the directing [of the mind], which is to say, the establishing [of it].
The rest is exactly as explained by the method already stated. This is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) here.
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood thus: "Dwelling in a suitable locality" (*patirūpadesavāsa*) refers to where the four assemblies (*parisā*) move about.
The bases for performing merit, such as giving and the rest, proceed there; the ninefold teaching of the Master shines forth;

and because dwelling there serves as a condition for beings to perform meritorious deeds, it is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*). Examples of this include the Kevala-vatta and other sites that entered the Island of Siṃhala.

Another method: what is called "dwelling in a suitable locality" refers to the region of the Blessed One’s seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and the region where he set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
The site at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree where, in the midst of an assembly twelve yojanas in extent, he shattered the doctrines of all non-Buddhist sects and displayed the Twin Miracle;

the site of his descent from the deva-world; or any other site inhabited by a Buddha, such as Sāvatthī or Rājagaha—residence there is called an auspicious occasion because it is a condition for sentient beings to obtain the six unsurpassed attainments.
Another method: In the eastern direction there is a market town named Gajaṅgala;
beyond that is Mahāsālā, and beyond that are the bordering districts, while on this side is the Middle Country. In the southeastern direction there is a river named Sallavatī;
beyond that are the bordering districts, while on this side is the Middle Country. In the southern direction is Setakaṇṇika.
The town named Nigama; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the Middle Country.
In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the Middle Country.
In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the bordering districts, and on this side is the Middle Country. This is the Middle Country.
In length it is three hundred yojanas, in breadth two hundred and fifty, and in circumference nine hundred yojanas.
This is what is called a "suitable place.
Herein, one exercises sovereignty and lordship over the four great continents and the two thousand minor islands.
Wheel-turning monarchs arise after fulfilling the perfections for one incalculable aeon and a hundred thousand aeons;

the great disciples such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna arise after fulfilling the perfections for two incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons; paccekabuddhas [arise] after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons;
and perfectly enlightened Buddhas [arise] after fulfilling the perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand aeons.

They arise there. In that place, beings who have taken up the counsel of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti-rāja) and established themselves in the five precepts (pañca-sīla) become destined for heaven.

Likewise, by establishing themselves in the counsel of the Paccekabuddhas, and especially in the counsel of the Buddhas and their disciples, they become destined for heaven and destined for Nibbāna. Therefore, in that place—
The possession of these attainments is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it serves as their requisite condition.
"Merit performed in the past" refers to the accumulation of wholesome kamma directed toward the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) in previous births;
that too is an auspicious sign. Why? Because it has been demonstrated in the presence of the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, and [is directed] toward the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas...
Or, it is because one attains Arahantship at the conclusion of even a four-line verse heard in the presence [of the Teacher].

Furthermore, a person who has performed meritorious deeds in the past and possesses abundant roots of virtue attains the destruction of the taints by developing insight through those very roots of virtue, just as King Mahākappina and his chief queen did. Therefore, it was said:
“Having performed merit in the past is an auspicious sign.

Herein, “right aspiration for oneself” means that someone here establishes themselves, who were previously immoral, in virtue; establishes themselves, who were lacking in faith, in the perfection of faith;
and establishes themselves, who were stingy, in the perfection of generosity. This is called “right aspiration for oneself.”
And this is an auspicious factor. Why? Because it is the cause for attaining various benefits, including the abandonment of enmity pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.

Thus, in this verse as well, only three auspicious factors are stated: dwelling in a suitable locality, merit performed in the past, and right aspiration for oneself. And their status as auspicious factors has already been explained in detail in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "Dwelling in a suitable locality," is concluded.
Commentary on the verse beginning with *bāhusaccañca*:
Now, regarding the phrase *bāhusaccañca*, here *bāhusacca* means the state of being well-versed in learning (*bahussuta*). *Sippa* refers to any kind of manual skill.
*Vinaya* is the disciplining of body, speech, and mind. *Susikkhita* means well-trained. *Subhāsita* means well-spoken.

Thus it has been spoken. This concludes the explanation of the indefinite [category]. "Speech" means voice, utterance. The remainder is exactly as previously stated. This is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) here.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: "Great learning" (*bāhusacca*) refers to that which is described by such methods as, "He is one who retains what he has heard, an accumulator of what he has heard," and, "In this case, someone has much that is heard: discourses (*sutta*), songs (*geyya*), and expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*)," and so forth.

The state of upholding the Teacher’s instruction is praised; because it is the cause for abandoning the unwholesome and attaining the wholesome, and because it is the cause for the gradual realization of the ultimate truth, it is called an auspicious factor (*maṅgala*). For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Monks, the learned noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons what is blameworthy and develops what is blameless; he maintains himself in purity.”
Furthermore, it is said:
“One examines the meaning of the teachings that have been mastered; as one examines the meaning, those teachings become acceptable through reflection;
when there is acceptance through reflection on the teachings, zeal arises; having developed zeal, one exerts effort; exerting effort, one weighs [the matter].”
"By weighing [the teachings], he practices; by practicing, he realizes ultimate truth with his very body and, having penetrated it with wisdom, he sees.
Furthermore, even the secular learning of a householder, if it is blameless, should be understood as an auspicious sign because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.

"Craft" (sippa) means both the craft of a householder and the craft of one who is not a householder. Therein, the "craft of a householder" refers to such things as the work of jewelers, goldsmiths, and so forth, which is free from harming others and devoid of unwholesome states;
that is an auspicious thing because it brings about welfare in this world.
The "craft of one who is not a householder" refers to the preparation of the requisites of a recluse, such as the inspection and sewing of robes, and so on. That which is...
“Here, monks, a monk is skillful in those various duties that are to be performed for his fellow celibates,” and so forth,
as described in various places. That which is called “the Dhamma that acts as a protector” should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*),
because it brings about welfare and happiness for both oneself and others in both worlds.

"Discipline" (vinaya) consists of both the discipline of the householder and the discipline of the homeless one. Therein, the "discipline of the householder" refers to abstaining from the ten courses of unwholesome action;

when well-trained therein by not falling into defilement and by establishing oneself in the qualities of proper conduct, it is an auspicious blessing because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.
The "discipline of the homeless one" refers to not committing the seven classes of offenses; that too, in the manner already described...
Well-trained means well-trained in either the fourfold morality of purification (*catupārisuddhisīla*) or the discipline of the homeless life (*anagārikavinaya*).

It should be understood as an auspicious sign because it is the cause for attaining mundane and supramundane happiness by training in such a way that one reaches *arahantship* by being established therein.

Well-spoken speech refers to speech free from faults such as lying and the like. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, speech endowed with four factors is well-spoken. Or rather, speech that is free from idle chatter (*asamphappalāpa*) is itself well-spoken. As it is said:
“The virtuous say that well-spoken speech is supreme;
to speak the Dhamma and not what is contrary to the Dhamma is the second;
to speak what is pleasant and not what is unpleasant is the third.”
"Speak the truth, do not speak falsely;
this is the fourth"—this too should be understood as an auspicious factor because it brings about welfare and happiness in both worlds.
