Furthermore, since this [verse] is included within the Vinaya itself, the Vinaya should be compiled by including it under the heading of "Vinaya. Alternatively, what is the need for this?
Here, "well-spoken speech" should be understood as the words used for teaching the Dhamma to others and so forth.

For just like dwelling in a suitable locality, this is called an "auspicious sign" (*maṅgala*) because it is a condition for sentient beings to attain welfare and happiness in both worlds, as well as *nibbāna*. And it has been said:
"The speech that the Buddha utters is secure, leading to the attainment of *nibbāna*."
“...for the making of an end of suffering; that indeed is the supreme among words.
Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: great learning, craft, well-trained discipline, and well-spoken speech. Furthermore, their status as blessings has been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, “Great learning and...,” is concluded.
Commentary on the Verse Beginning with “Service to Mother and Father” (6).
Now, regarding the phrase *mātāpituupaṭṭhānaṃ*: here, *mātāpitu* means mother and father. *Upaṭṭhānaṃ* means attending upon (*upaṭṭhahanaṃ*).
*Puttadārassa saṅgaho* means the gathering together and supporting of sons and wives. *Na ākulā* means not distracted; *anākulā*. *Kammāni*... [the tasks].
Such are the duties. The remainder is exactly as previously stated; this is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).
The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: "Mother" refers to the biological progenitor, and likewise "father.
"Attendance" (*upaṭṭhāna*) means performing service by washing the feet, massaging, anointing, bathing, and providing the four requisites.
In this regard, because parents are of great assistance to their children, desiring their welfare and compassionate toward them—
seeing their little sons return from playing outside with bodies smeared with dust, they wipe away the dust, smell their heads, kiss them,
and arouse affection; indeed, for even a hundred years, parents carry their children upon their heads.

They are unable to repay them. And because these parents and nurturers are the revealers of this world, honored as Brahmās and honored as the ancient teachers, therefore attending upon them brings praise in this life and the happiness of heaven hereafter.
For that reason, it is called an auspicious omen (*maṅgala*). Indeed, this was said by the Blessed One:
“Parents are called ‘Brahmā,’ and they are called ‘former teachers.
They are worthy of offerings from their children and are compassionate toward their offspring.
Therefore, a wise person should indeed revere and honor them.”
With food, and also with drink, with clothing and with bedding;
with anointing, with bathing, and with the washing of the feet—
by such service toward their mother and father, the wise [attain merit].
“Right here they praise him, and after death he rejoices in heaven.
Another method: “Attendance” (upaṭṭhāna) consists of five kinds—namely, providing sustenance, performing duties, establishing the family lineage, and so forth.

It should be understood as an auspicious sign (maṅgala) because it is a cause for five kinds of welfare and happiness in this present life, beginning with the warding off of evil. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In five ways, householder’s son, should a son attend upon his parents as the eastern quarter:
‘I will support those who supported me; I will perform their duties; I will maintain the family lineage; I will take charge of the inheritance;
or else, when they have passed away and become deceased, I will offer them funeral oblations. In these ways, householder’s son...”
"In five ways, parents who are attended to by their son as the eastern quarter show compassion for him:
they restrain him from evil, establish him in what is wholesome, train him in a craft, unite him with a suitable wife,
and at the proper time, hand over the inheritance."

Furthermore, he who serves his mother and father by inspiring them with confidence in three ways, by instilling in them the undertaking of virtue, or by supporting their going forth into homelessness—
he is the foremost among those who serve their parents. That service rendered to one's parents is a repayment for the assistance provided by them,
and it yields manifold benefits both in this present life and in future lives.
It is called a "mangala" (auspicious) because it is the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) of welfare.
Regarding the phrase "of children and wife": here, both sons and daughters born from oneself are reckoned as "children" (*putta*).
"Wife" (*dāra*) refers to any one of the twenty types of wives. "Children and wife" is a compound of "children" and "wife"; [the phrase means] "of that child and wife."

*Saṅgaha* (inclusion) is the act of providing assistance through such means as honoring and so forth. It should be understood as an auspicious factor (*maṅgala*) because it is a cause for welfare and happiness pertaining to the present life, such as having well-organized undertakings.
For this was said by the Blessed One: “The western direction should be understood as one’s children and wife.
Having thus mentioned children and wife there, he included them under the term *bhariyā* (wife), saying: “There are five things, householder’s son, [by which a wife is to be honored]... [and so on].
In five ways, householder’s son, should a husband attend to his wife as the western quarter:
with honor, without contempt, by not being unfaithful, by surrendering authority, and by providing ornaments.
When a wife is attended to by her husband in these five ways as the western quarter, she in turn attends to him in five ways.
She is compassionate; she is well-organized in her duties; she has won over her attendants; she is not unfaithful;
she protects what has been gathered; and she is skillful and untiring in all tasks. Or, another way [to explain it]:
"Inclusion" (*saṅgaha*) means winning over [others] through righteous acts of giving, kind speech, and beneficial conduct. That is to say:
— Giving provisions on Uposatha days, arranging for the viewing of constellations on festival nights, performing auspicious rites on auspicious days,
and providing exhortation and instruction regarding matters pertaining to the present life and the future life. This is because, according to the method already stated,
it is a cause for welfare in the present life, a cause for welfare in the future life, and a cause for being worthy of veneration even by the deities.
And it should be understood as an auspicious omen. As Sakka, lord of the devas, said:
"Those householders who perform meritorious deeds, those virtuous lay followers who support their wives in accordance with the Dhamma—to them I pay homage, Mātali" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.1.264).

"Undisturbed occupations" refers to occupations such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade that are free from the state of being "disturbed"— namely, the disturbances consisting of missing the proper time,

doing what is inappropriate, laziness, lack of excellence in initiative and energy, and failure due to misfortune— by virtue of knowing the right time, acting appropriately, being untiring, possessing the perfection of initiative and energy,
and being invincible. These [occupations] belong either to oneself, or to one's wife and children, or to slaves and laborers.
Or rather, because they are employed for proficiency and serve as the cause for obtaining an increase in wealth and grain in this very life, they are called "auspicious.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"One who acts appropriately, who is steadfast, and who exerts effort, finds wealth."
“For one who has the habit of sleeping by day, who looks for the night as the time to wake,
and who is constantly intoxicated and addicted to drink— it is impossible to live the life of a householder.
‘It is too cold,’ ‘it is too hot,’ ‘it is too late’— thus he says.”
Thus, for those young men who have neglected their duties, their goals pass them by:
“But he who here considers cold and heat no more than blades of grass,
performing his manly tasks— he does not depart from happiness.”
“As one who gathers wealth, moving like a bee, his riches go toward accumulation, just as an anthill is built up. And so forth.
Thus, in this verse, [are mentioned] service to one’s mother, service to one’s father, the support of wife and children, and being undisturbed.
And regarding "occupations," four blessings have been stated; or, by dividing the support of wife and children into two, there are five;
or, by counting the service of mother and father as one, there are three. Furthermore, their status as blessings has already been clarified in various places.
Thus ends the commentary on the meaning of this verse beginning with "service of mother and father."
Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Dānañca" (7).
Now, regarding the phrase "dānañca": it is called *dāna* because one gives (*diyati*) by means of it; what is meant is that one bestows upon another what belongs to oneself.
*Dhammacariyā* is the practice of the Dhamma, or a practice that does not deviate from the Dhamma. They know us as... [amhākaṃ]...
"These" refers to kinsmen. "Not blameworthy" means blameless; that is to say, they are irreproachable and beyond censure. The remainder is exactly as explained by the method already stated.
This is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: what is called "giving" (*dāna*) is the volition of relinquishing the ten bases of giving, such as food and so forth, preceded by a wise intention directed toward another.
Or it is non-greed associated with that [volition]. For it is by means of non-greed that one bestows that object upon another; therefore it is said:

"Giving is that by which something is given. It is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for attaining specific fruits, both pertaining to the present life and to future lives, such as being dear and agreeable to many people.
"O Sīha, a donor, a master of giving, [is] much..."
In this regard, such discourses as “He becomes dear and pleasing to people” should be recollected.
Another method: giving is twofold—giving of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*) and giving of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*). Therein, giving of material goods is of the kind already described.
However, regarding the Dhamma proclaimed by the Perfectly Enlightened One, which brings about the happiness that consists in the destruction of suffering in this world and the next:
Teaching for the sake of others' welfare is the gift of the Dhamma, and of these two gifts, this alone is the foremost. As it is said:
"The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all gifts;
the taste of the Dhamma surpasses all tastes."
“The delight in the Dhamma overcomes all delight in worldly things;
the destruction of craving overcomes all suffering.

In this regard, the auspiciousness of the gift of material goods has already been explained. However, the gift of the Dhamma is called an auspicious thing because it is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for qualities such as experiencing the benefit [of the teaching]. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, to whatever extent a bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others exactly as he has heard it and mastered it, to that same extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma in regard to that teaching,” and so forth.

Practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammacariyā*) refers to the practice of the ten courses of wholesome action. As it is said: “Householders, there are three kinds [of wholesome conduct] by way of body...”

“Practice of the Dhamma is practice of equanimity,” and so forth. Furthermore, this practice of the Dhamma should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for rebirth in the heavenly world.

For this was said by the Blessed One: “It is, householders, because of the cause of practice of the Dhamma and practice of equanimity that some beings here, with the breakup of the body after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.”
"Relatives" (ñātaka) refers to those connected through the mother's or father's side, up to the seventh generation of ancestors.

For those who have been struck by the loss of wealth or the loss of health and have come into one's presence, providing for them according to one's ability with food, clothing, money, grain, and so forth—
whether it be the acquisition of excellence in this very life, such as praise and the like, or excellence pertaining to the future life, such as rebirth in a happy destination— is [the duty].
It is called an auspicious sign by reason of its cause.

"Blameless actions" refers to deeds of good conduct of body, speech, and mind, such as undertaking the factors of the Uposatha, performing services, planting orchards and groves, building bridges, and so forth.
Indeed, these are called an auspicious sign because they are the causes for attaining various kinds of welfare and happiness.
“It is possible, Visākhā, that here some woman or man,
having observed the Uposatha complete in its eight factors, on the dissolution of the body, after death,
might be reborn in the company of the gods of the Four Great Kings. Such discourses as these are to be recollected here.
Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: giving, righteous conduct, the support of relatives, and blameless deeds. Furthermore, their status as blessings has been elucidated in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with "Giving" is concluded. [Now follows] the commentary on the verse beginning with "Abstaining from."

8. Now, regarding the terms *āratī* and *viratī*: here, *āratī* means abstaining (*āramaṇaṃ*), and *viratī* means desisting (*viramaṇaṃ*), or else it is called *viratī* because beings desist (*viramanti*) by means of it.

"Evil" (*pāpa*) refers to unwholesome states. "Intoxicant" (*majja*) is so called in the sense of causing intoxication; the drinking of intoxicants is "intoxicant-drinking" (*majjapāna*), and [abstinence] is from that intoxicant-drinking.

"Restraint" (*saṃyama*) is the act of restraining; "heedfulness" (*appamāda*) is the state of not being negligent. "In regard to states" (*dhammesu*) means in regard to wholesome states. The rest is as follows.
"This is the word-by-word commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*) according to the method already stated.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: ‘Abstention’ (*ārati*) means simply a lack of delight in evil by means of the mind alone in one who sees its danger.
‘Refraining’ (*virati*) means desisting from [evil] through body and speech by way of the doors of action; and this refraining is called ‘refraining by attainment’ (*sampattavirati*)."
It is threefold: abstinence through undertaking, and abstinence through eradication.

Among these, that which consists in a clansman’s abstinence from an available object by way of such reasoning as, "It is not fitting for me—considering my own birth, family, or clan—to kill this living being, or to take what is not given," and so forth, is called abstinence through attainment.
Abstention by undertaking is that which occurs through the undertaking of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*);
from the moment it is undertaken, the clansman no longer commits acts such as the destruction of life. Abstention by eradication is that which is associated with the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*);
from the moment it occurs, the five fears and enmities of the noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*) are pacified. As for what is called "evil" (*pāpa*), it is that which—
“Householder’s son, the destruction of life is indeed a defilement of action; taking what is not given... [and so on] ... sexual misconduct...
[and so on] ... false speech. Having thus explained in detail:
“The destruction of life, taking what is not given, and false speech are said to be [defilements];”
"And going to another's wife—the wise do not praise this.
Thus, the fourfold unwholesome action known as *kamma*-defilement is summarized by this verse; it is more evil than those [other evils].

All these [abstinences] are both *ārati* (non-inclination) and *virati* (abstention), because they are the causes for attaining various specific distinctions, such as the abandonment of fear and enmity pertaining to the present life and the future life.
It is called "auspicious. In this regard, such suttas as, "The noble disciple, householder’s son, abstains from the destruction of life," should be recollected.
Restraint from drinking intoxicants is simply another term for the abstinence from the occasion of negligence through fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants, as previously stated.

This is a synonym. For one who drinks intoxicants does not understand the meaning, does not understand the Dhamma, creates obstacles for his mother, and creates obstacles for his father, for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of the Tathāgata;
he incurs censure in this very life, a miserable rebirth in the future, and successive states of madness. Therefore, restraint from drinking intoxicants [is prescribed].
One attains the subsiding of those faults and the perfection of qualities contrary to them. Therefore, this restraint from drinking intoxicants should be understood as a blessing.
Regarding wholesome states, "heedfulness" (appamāda) means the state of not performing the cultivation of wholesome states with negligence.

“Lack of constant performance, lack of steadfast performance, sluggish conduct, abandonment of zeal, abandonment of the burden, non-repetition, non-cultivation, non-multiplication, lack of resolve, lack of application, and negligence.
Whatever negligence there is of this kind—neglecting, the state of having neglected—this is called negligence. Regarding the negligence spoken of here:
In terms of its meaning, non-forgetfulness regarding wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) by way of their opposites is to be understood here.

Because it is the cause for attaining various kinds of wholesomeness and the cause for attaining the Deathless (*amata*), it is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*). In this regard, one should recollect the Teacher’s instruction, such as: "For the heedful and ardent," and "Heedfulness is the deathless state."

Thus, in this verse, three blessings are stated: abstaining from evil, restraint regarding the drinking of intoxicants, and heedfulness in wholesome states. And their status as blessings has been explained in detail in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "Ārati," is concluded.
[Now begins] the commentary on the verse beginning with "Gāravo ca... (And reverence...).

9. Now, regarding the phrase "and reverence" (*gāravo ca*): here, "reverence" (*gāravo*) means the state of being weighty (*garubhāvo*). "Living humbly" (*nivāto*) means a lowly way of life. "Contentment" (*santuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction.
"Knowing what has been done" (*katajānanatā*) is gratitude (*kataññutā*). "At the proper time" (*kālena*) means at the opportune moment or occasion.
"Hearing the Dhamma" (*dhammassavana*) is the hearing of the Dhamma. The remainder is exactly as previously explained. This is the word-by-word commentary.

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*) should be understood as follows: "Reverence" (*gārava*) means the act of honoring, the state of honoring, and the quality of being reverential, directed appropriately toward those worthy of such treatment—namely, the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Tathāgata, teachers, preceptors, mothers, fathers, elder brothers, sisters, and so forth. And this reverence is the cause for proceeding to happy destinies and other benefits. As it is said:
"One honors what is worthy of honor, respects what is worthy of respect, and worships what is worthy of worship. By that kamma..."
"By practicing thus and undertaking thus, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. But if, with the breakup of the body...
one is not so reborn, and if one returns to the human state, wherever one is reborn, one is born into a high family.
And as it is said: "Bhikkhus, there are these seven qualities that prevent decline. Which seven? Reverence for the Teacher," and so forth; therefore, it is called a "good omen" (*maṅgala*).
"Modesty" (*nivāta*) means a lowly state of mind and a humble way of living. A person endowed with this quality has subdued pride and subdued arrogance;
like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with its horns cut off, and like a snake with its fangs extracted, he becomes gentle, amiable, and pleasant to converse with.
This is modesty. And because it is the cause for obtaining qualities such as renown and so forth, it is an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*).
It is said: "One who is humble in conduct and free from arrogance—such a person gains renown," and so forth.

Contentment (*santuṭṭhi*) means satisfaction with whatever requisites are obtained; it is of twelve kinds. Namely: regarding robes, there is threefold contentment—contentment with what is obtained, contentment with what is suitable to one's strength, and contentment with what is appropriate.
It is the same for alms-food and the other requisites. This is the explanation of its divisions: here, a bhikkhu obtains a robe, whether beautiful or ugly.
Thus he maintains himself with that alone, does not long for anything else, and even if he obtains more, he does not take it; this is his contentment with whatever robe-material is obtained.

Furthermore, if a bhikkhu becomes ill, and while wearing a heavy robe he leans forward or becomes exhausted, he exchanges it with a fellow bhikkhu of similar status and maintains himself with a light one; even so, he remains truly content.
This is his contentment with robes according to his strength. Furthermore, another monk may be one who obtains excellent requisites;

having received a costly robe such as a cloth from Benares (*paṭṭacīvara*) or the like, he gives it to those elder monks who have long been gone forth and are learned, thinking, "This is suitable for them," and then collects rags himself from a rubbish heap or from somewhere else.
Even when he wears his outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) after having made it up [from scraps], he remains content; this is his contentment with robes as they happen to be suitable.

Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives almsfood, whether coarse or refined; he sustains himself with that alone, he does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it; this is his contentment with almsfood as it happens to be obtained. Then, moreover—
A bhikkhu becomes ill; having eaten coarse almsfood, he falls into a severe sickness.
By giving that food to a bhikkhu of similar standing and consuming ghee, honey, milk, and so forth from his hand, he remains content even while practicing the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
This is his contentment with almsfood according to his strength. Another bhikkhu [receives] excellent...
When he receives almsfood, he thinks: "This almsfood is suitable for the elders who have long been gone forth and for my fellow celibates who do not obtain choice almsfood.
Having given it to them, even if he himself wanders for alms and eats a mixture of foods, he remains content;
this is his contentment with almsfood as is appropriate.

Furthermore, a bhikkhu obtains a lodging; he is content with that alone and does not take another even if a more beautiful one becomes available—this is his contentment regarding lodgings according to what is obtained. Moreover, a bhikkhu may be afflicted by illness;
while staying in a sheltered lodging, he suffers excessively from bile diseases and the like. He [then gives] that to a fellow bhikkhu...
Having given [the lodging] away, even when he dwells in a cool lodging that has come to him by chance while practicing the duty of a recluse, he remains content;
this is his contentment with a lodging according to his strength. Another bhikkhu does not accept even a beautiful lodging, thinking:
"A beautiful lodging is a basis for negligence; sloth and torpor descend upon one sitting there."
"And for one who has been overcome by sleep and is waking up again, a thought of sensual desire arises.
Having rejected that, he remains content even when dwelling anywhere—in the open air, at the foot of a tree, or in a leaf-hut;
this is his contentment with a dwelling as is appropriate.
Furthermore, here a bhikkhu receives medicinal requisites such as yellow myrobalan or emblic myrobalan. He sustains himself with that alone;
he does not long for the ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth received by others, and even when receiving them, he does not take them.
This is his contentment with whatever is obtained regarding the requisite of medicine. Moreover, if a bhikkhu is afflicted by illness and needs oil, he receives molasses instead.
Having given that to a fellow monk of similar standing and having prepared a medicinal oil from his hand, he remains content even while performing the duties of a recluse;
this is his contentment with the requisite of medicine according to his strength.
Another monk, having placed fermented urine and *harītakī* in one vessel and the four sweets (*catumadhura*) in another, says: "Take these, venerable sir."
When he is told, "If you wish," and his illness is cured by either of those two [medicines],

then, reflecting that "the so-called fermented urine and myrobalan (harītaka) has been praised by the Buddha and others," and that "it was said that one should rely on fermented urine as medicine and exert oneself therein for as long as life lasts," he [rejects] the four sweet medicines.
Even when preparing medicine with putrid urine and harītaka after having rejected [other options], he remains perfectly content.
This is his appropriate contentment regarding the requisite of medicine.
All such varieties of contentment are called *santuṭṭhi*. It is the opposite of excessive desire (*atricchā*), great desire (*mahicchā*), and evil desire (*pāpicchā*).

It should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for the abandoning and attainment of evil qualities, the cause for a happy rebirth, the constituent of the Noble Path, and the cause for being one who dwells in the four quarters and so forth. And it has been said:
"He is one who dwells in the four quarters and is free from aversion..."
"...being content with whatever little [one has]," and so forth.
What is called gratitude (*kataññutā*) is the state of knowing—by repeatedly recollecting—a benefit performed by another, whether small or great.
Furthermore, because they provide protection from the sufferings of hell and other realms, meritorious deeds alone are of great benefit to living beings; therefore...

Their recollection of benefits should be understood as gratitude (*kataññutā*). Because it is the cause for attaining various distinguished qualities—such as being praised by the virtuous—it is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*).
And it has been said: "Bhikkhus, these two persons are rare in the world. Which two?
He who acts first, and he who is grateful and mindful of what has been done."

"Listening to the Dhamma at the proper time" means that when the mind is possessed of restlessness, or is overcome by any one of the thought of sensual desire and so forth, listening to the Dhamma at that time for the purpose of dispelling those states is what is meant. Others say:
"Listening to the Dhamma every fifth day is called 'listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. As the Venerable [Ānanda] said:"
Anuruddha said: "But, Bhante, we sit together for five days every night engaged in talk on the Dhamma.

Furthermore, whenever one is able to approach a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) and hear the Dhamma that dispels one's own doubts, at that time too it should be understood as "listening to the Dhamma at the proper time. As it is said: "They..."
“Having approached from time to time, he questions and inquires,” and so forth.

This timely hearing of the Dhamma should be understood as a *maṅgala* (auspicious factor), because it is the cause for attaining various specific distinctions, such as the abandoning of the hindrances, the four benefits, and the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).
For this has been said:

“Bhikkhus, at whatever time a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma with intentness, with attention, with his whole mind, and with an attentive ear, at that time the five hindrances are not present in him. And:
“Bhikkhus, for those teachings that have entered the ear, been mastered, and been well penetrated, four benefits are to be expected.”

“Bhikkhus, these four things, when properly cultivated and properly practiced from time to time, lead gradually to the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). Which four? Hearing the Dhamma at the proper time,” and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, five blessings are stated: reverence, humility, contentment, gratitude, and hearing the Dhamma at the proper time. And their status as blessings has already been explained in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with “Reverence” is thus concluded.
Commentary on the Verse Beginning with "Patience" (Khantī):

10. Now, regarding the phrase "patience" (*khantī*): the act of enduring is patience. One who possesses pleasant speech because of his inclination toward what is favorable is "easily spoken to" (*suvaco*);
the action of one who is easily spoken to is "good-naturedness" (*sovacassaṃ*); the state of being good-natured is "good-naturedness" (*sovacassatā*). Because of the calming of the defilements...

"Ascetics. "Seeing" means looking upon. "Discussion of the Dhamma" (*dhammasākacchā*) is discussion regarding the Dhamma. The rest is exactly as explained by the method already stated. This is the word-commentary.
The commentary on the meaning, however, should be understood thus: "Patience" (*khanti*) means patience through endurance;
a bhikkhu endowed with that [patience], even when not hearing [the words] of persons who revile him with the ten grounds for reviling or who harass him with killing, binding, and so forth—
He remains without agitation, as if not seeing and as if not perceiving, like one who preaches patience. As it is said:
"In the past, there was a recluse who illuminated patience;
though he stood firm in patience alone, the King of Kāsi cut him down."
Or he attends to them as "good," because there is no fault beyond that, as in the case of the Venerable Elder Puṇṇa. As he said:
"If, venerable sir, the people of Sunāparanta abuse and revile me, then this thought will occur to me:
'These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good; these people of Sunāparanta are truly very good.'"
"O people, it is because of this that they do not strike me with their hands," and so forth.
And endowed with which [quality] one becomes praiseworthy even among the seers (isī), as the seer Sarabhaṅga said:
"Having slain anger, one never grieves."
The seers praise the abandoning of conceit;
one should endure all harsh words spoken [to them].
The virtuous say that this is the highest patience.
He is worthy of praise even by the deities. As Sakka, Lord of the Devas, said:
"He who, being strong himself, endures one who is weak—him they call the supreme patient; the weak man, however, always endures."
He is worthy of praise even by the Buddhas. As the Blessed One said:
"He who, free from malice, endures abuse, execution, and imprisonment—he possesses the strength of patience, the foremost of strengths; him I call a brahmin."
Furthermore, this patience should be understood as a blessing because it is the cause for the attainment of these and other qualities described here.
"Being easy to speak to" means that when one is addressed in accordance with the Dhamma, one does not resort to evasion, silence, or deliberation over merits and faults,
but rather acts upon what is said with the words "Very well," preceded by extreme earnestness, reverence, and humility.

It is called an auspicious omen (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for receiving exhortation and instruction from one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life, and because it is the cause for the abandoning of faults and the attainment of virtues.

As for "seeing ascetics" (*samaṇānaṃ dassanaṃ*), it refers to those whose defilements have been stilled, who have cultivated body, speech, mind, and wisdom, and who are endowed with supreme self-control and tranquility.
The approaching, attending upon, recollecting, hearing, and seeing those who have gone forth—all this is said to be "seeing" within the teaching on the lowly;
that should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*). Why? Because it is of great benefit. And it has been said:
"Monks, I say that even the sight of those monks is of great benefit," and so forth. Therefore, by a son of good family desiring his own welfare...
When virtuous bhikkhus arrive at the door of one's house, if there is anything to be given, they should be honored with a gift according to one's ability.
If there is nothing, one should pay homage by performing the fivefold prostration.
If even that is not possible, one should pay respect by raising one’s joined palms. If even that is not possible, one should do so with a clear mind and affectionate eyes.
They should be clearly observed. For by merit rooted in such vision, for many thousands of births, there will be no disease, burning sensation, swellings, or pustules in the eye;
rather, the eyes will be clear, five-colored, and beautiful, like jeweled windows opened within a celestial mansion, [dwelling] among the devas for as long as a hundred thousand eons.

And he becomes a recipient of prosperity among human beings. It is not surprising that one born as a human being, possessing wisdom, should experience such a success of karmic fruition through merit consisting of visiting ascetics performed correctly;
for even among those who have gone to the animal realm, the result of merely visiting ascetics out of simple faith is as follows:
They describe the perfection of the result:
“The owl, marked with a circle, who has lived for a very long time on Vediyaka—
how happy indeed is this Kosika, that at the break of dawn he beholds the Supreme Buddha!”
“Having placed confidence in me and in the unsurpassed Saṅgha of bhikkhus,
for a hundred thousand eons he does not go to an unhappy destination.
Having passed away from the world of the devas, impelled by his wholesome karma...”
"He will possess infinite knowledge and be renowned as Somanassa.
Discussion of the Dhamma at the proper time means that in the evening or at dawn, two monks who are experts in the Suttas discuss the Suttas with one another;
those who uphold the Vinaya discuss the Vinaya; those who specialize in the Abhidhamma discuss the Abhidhamma; and those who recite the Jātakas [discuss the Jātakas].
The Jātaka and the Aṭṭhakathā—commentaries—are discussed at various times by commentators for the purpose of purifying the mind from dullness, agitation, and doubt;
this is "discourse on the Dhamma at the proper time. Because it is the cause of qualities such as proficiency in the Āgamas, it is called an auspicious blessing (maṅgala).

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: patience, amenability to advice, visiting ascetics, and timely discussion of the Dhamma. And their status as blessings has already been clarified in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of this verse, "Patience indeed," is concluded.
Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with "Austerity."
11. Now, regarding the phrase "and austerity" (*tapo ca*): here, it is called austerity (*tapo*) because it burns away (*tapati*) unwholesome states (*pāpakā dhammā*).

"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) means the conduct of a Brahmā (*brahmaṃ cariyaṃ*), or the conduct of those who are Brahmās; what is meant is "the supreme conduct. "Vision of the Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccānaṃ dassanaṃ*) refers to the seeing of the Noble Truths.
Some say that *ariyasaccāni* is the object of the seeing (*dassanaṃ*), but that is not correct. It is called Nibbāna because one has departed from craving (*vānato*); it is the realization.
Realization (*sacchikiriyā*); realization of Nibbāna is *nibbāna-sacchikiriyā*. The remainder is exactly as previously explained; such is the word-commentary (*padavaṇṇanā*).

The commentary on the meaning (*atthavaṇṇanā*), however, should be understood as follows: "Austerity" (*tapo*) refers to restraint of the sense faculties because it burns away covetousness, dejection, and so forth, or it refers to energy because it burns away laziness.
A person endowed with these is called "ardent" (*ātāpī*). This [person]...
It should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for the abandoning of covetousness and so forth, and for the attainment of the jhānas and so forth.
"The holy life" (*brahmacariya*) is a designation for celibacy, the duty of a recluse, the teaching, and the path.
For instance, in such passages as "Having abandoned unchastity, he lives the holy life," celibacy is called the holy life. [In the passage] "In the Blessed One..."
In such passages as, "No, friend, the holy life is lived," [it refers to] the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).

In such passages as, "I shall not attain final Nibbāna, O Evil One, as long as this holy life has not become successful, prosperous, widespread, and well-known," [it refers to] the Dispensation (*sāsana*). "This very Noble Eightfold Path, monk... [and so forth].
In such passages as "The path is the holy life; that is to say, right view," it refers to the path.

However, here, because the subsequent path is included by means of the vision of the Noble Truths, everything else is also appropriate. And this should be understood as an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for the successive attainment of various specific distinctions.

The "vision of the Noble Truths" refers to the vision of the Path by way of the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four Noble Truths as taught in the *Kumārapañha*; it is called an auspicious sign (*maṅgala*) because it is the cause for transcending the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
The "realization of Nibbāna" here intends the fruit of Arhatship (*arahattaphala*) as Nibbāna.

For that too is called "Nibbāna" because it has "departed" (*nikkhanta*) from craving—which is designated as "binding" (*vāna*)—by means of the removal of the five destinies. Its attainment or its reviewing [is what is meant].
Or it is called "realization" (sacchikiriyā). However, the realization of the other Nibbāna is accomplished through the mere vision of the Noble Truths;

therefore, that is not intended here. Thus, this realization of Nibbāna should be understood as an auspicious sign (maṅgala) because it is the cause for dwelling in happiness in this very life and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: asceticism and the holy life, the vision of the Noble Truths, and the realization of Nibbāna. And their status as blessings has already been elucidated in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with "tapo ca" is finished.
[Now follows] the commentary on the verse beginning with "phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi."
12. Now, regarding the phrase "one who is touched by worldly conditions" (*phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi*): here, "touched" (*phuṭṭhassa*) means struck, contacted, or encountered.
"Worldly conditions" (*lokadhammā*) refers to those phenomena that persist as long as the world endures; what is meant is that they are phenomena that do not turn back [as long as the world exists].

"Mind" (*citta*) means the mental faculty (*mano*), the mind (*mānasa*). "Of whom" (*yassa*) refers to one who is either a novice, a middle-ranking monk, or an elder. "Does not waver" (*na kampati*) means...
It does not waver, it does not tremble. "Sorrowless" means free from sorrow, one who has pulled out the arrow of grief.

"Dustless" means free from dust, one who has destroyed all defilement. "Secure" means fearless and free from calamity. The remainder is exactly as previously explained; this is the word-by-word commentary.
The commentary on the meaning, however, should be understood as follows: he whose mind does not shake when touched by the worldly conditions (lokadhamma).
That mind of one who, when touched and overwhelmed by the eight worldly conditions such as gain and loss,
does not waver, does not shake, and does not tremble— should be understood as a "good omen" (maṅgala), because it brings about the state of the supramundane which cannot be shaken by anything.
And whose mind does not waver when touched by these? That of the Arahant whose taints are destroyed, and no one else’s. For this has been said:
“As a solid mass of rock is not shaken by the wind, So too, all forms, tastes, sounds, Odors, and tactile objects—”
“Desirable things and undesirable things do not cause trembling in one who is such (a Tādin);
his mind is steady and liberated, and he contemplates its passing away.

The state called “unshaken” (*asoka*) belongs only to one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). For that [state] is free from what is called “sorrow,” “the act of sorrowing,” “the state of having sorrowed,” and “inner sorrow.”
"Sorrow" (*soka*) is described by such passages as "internal distress, the state of brooding over the mind";
because of the absence of that, it is "without sorrow" (*asoka*). Some say this refers to *nibbāna*, but that does not connect with the preceding phrase.
And just as it is "without sorrow," so too the mind of one whose taints are destroyed is "dustless" (*viraja*) and "secure" (*khema*); for it is free from the dust of greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is "dustless" (*virajaṃ*); it is "secure" (*khemaṃ*) because of its security from the four bonds (*yoga*).

Therefore, it should be understood as an "auspicious sign" (*maṅgala*) because, by way of being grasped and demonstrated in each respective mode at each moment of its occurrence, it brings about the supramundane state—such as the non-occurrence of the aggregates—and brings about the status of being worthy of offerings and so forth.

Thus, in this verse, four blessings are stated: a mind unshaken by the eight worldly conditions, a sorrowless mind, a stainless mind, and a secure mind. And their status as blessings has already been explained in various places.
The commentary on the meaning of the verse beginning with “phuṭṭhassa lokadhammehi” is finished. Now follows the commentary on the verse beginning with “etādisāni.”

13. Thus, having explained the thirty-eight great blessings (*mahāmaṅgala*) by means of ten verses beginning with "In this way, the Blessed One [taught] the non-association with fools," the Blessed One now spoke the final verse, "Having performed such things as these," while praising these very blessings he himself had declared.
This is the commentary on its meaning: "Such as these" (*etādisāni*) means these, of such a kind, namely the non-association with fools and so forth, in the manner described by me.
"Having performed" (*katvāna*) means having done. For "having performed," "having done," and "having made" are not different in meaning. "Unconquered in every respect" (*sabbatthamaparājita*).
This means that having remained undefeated by even one among the four adversaries— the Māras consisting of the aggregates (*khandha*),
defilements (*kilesa*), volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*), and the son of a deva (*devaputta*)— he himself has conquered those four Māras. Furthermore,
it should be understood that the letter *m* here serves merely for the euphonic junction of words (*padasandhi*).

"Going everywhere in safety": having performed such auspicious rites as these, they become unconquered by the four Māras and go everywhere—in this world and the next, and in standing, walking, and so forth—in safety;
they go in safety because of the absence of those taints (*āsava*), afflictions, and fevers that might arise from associating with fools and the like; they are untroubled.
It means they go unassailed, secure, and free from fear. It should be understood that the nasal vowel here is used for the sake of metrical convenience in the verse composition.
With this line of the verse, "That is their supreme blessing," the Blessed One brought his teaching to a conclusion.
How so? "Thus, O son of the gods, because those who perform such [deeds] go everywhere in safety, therefore..."
"Take this— this thirty-eightfold [set of practices] beginning with not associating with fools— as the supreme, most excellent, and most noble auspiciousness for those who perform such deeds.
And when the Blessed One had thus concluded his teaching, at its conclusion, one hundred thousand times ten million deities attained arahantship.
They attained [the fruits]; those who reached the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, and non-returning became incalculable in number.
Then, on the second day, the Blessed One addressed the Elder Ānanda:
"Ānanda, during this night a certain deity approached me and asked a question regarding auspicious signs; I then explained to her the thirty-eight auspicious signs."
“Learn this discourse on auspiciousness, Ānanda; having learned it, teach it to the bhikkhus. The Elder, having learned it, taught it to the bhikkhus.
This has been handed down through the succession of teachers and continues to the present day:
“In this way, this holy life has become successful, prosperous, widespread, popular, and extensive, reaching as far as the world of gods and humans.”
It should be understood as "well-expounded.
Now, for the sake of proficiency through the cultivation of knowledge regarding these very auspicious factors, here is the exposition starting from the beginning:
thus, these beings who desire the happiness of this world, the next world, and the supramundane, having abandoned the company of foolish people and relying on the wise, [should proceed].
Having honored those worthy of honor, being urged toward the practice of the wholesome by dwelling in a suitable locality and by virtue of merit performed in the past,
they rightly resolved themselves; their persons adorned with great learning, craft, and discipline, speaking well-spoken words in accordance with that discipline,
they discharged the ancient debt through service to mother and father for as long as they did not abandon the state of a householder.
Purifying themselves, they incurred new debt through the maintenance of wives and children; they attained prosperity in wealth, grain, and other assets through orderly management of their affairs;
by means of giving, they secured the essence of material wealth, and by righteous conduct, the essence of life;
and through the support of kinsmen, they brought benefit to their own people, while through blameless occupations, they brought benefit to others.
Having avoided harming others by abstaining from evil and harming oneself by restraining from the drinking of intoxicants,

and having increased the side of wholesome qualities through heedfulness regarding the teachings, she— though remaining in the state of one who has gone forth after casting off the marks of a householder—
attained perfection in her conduct through reverence for the Buddha, his disciples, preceptors, teachers, and so forth, and through living in seclusion.
Having abandoned greed for requisites through contentment; having stood upon the ground of true persons through gratitude;
having abandoned mental sluggishness through hearing the Dhamma; having overcome all perils through patience; having made oneself well-guarded through readiness to listen;
seeing the application of practice through the sight of ascetics; and [resolving] regarding points of doubt through discussion of the Dhamma...
Having dispelled doubt regarding phenomena, they achieve purification of virtue through the austerity of restraint of the sense faculties;

they achieve purification of mind through the holy life of the ascetic’s duty (*samaṇadhamma-brahmacariya*); and further, accomplishing the four subsequent purifications, they—by means of this practice—reach the purification of knowledge and vision consisting in the seeing of the Noble Truths, and realize Nibbāna, which is reckoned as the fruit of Arahantship, having realized which...
Like Mount Sineru, their minds unshaken by the eight worldly conditions—just as by wind and rain—they are free from sorrow, stainless, and secure.
Those who are secure are undefeated by anyone anywhere and go everywhere in safety.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having performed such deeds, undefeated in all places, they go everywhere in safety; that is their supreme blessing.
Thus ends the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
The commentary on the Maṅgala Sutta is finished.
6. The commentary on the Ratana Sutta:
The purpose of its presentation.

Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the meaning of the Ratana Sutta, which was placed immediately after the Maṅgala Sutta with the words "Whatever beings there are here," and so forth. Having stated the purpose for its placement here,
[one should understand] that, just as one enters the water of rivers, ponds, and the like through a perfectly pure ford, this sutta [is entered] by means of a perfectly pure introduction (nidāna).
In order to demonstrate the immersion into the meaning,
[the author says]: "Having explained by what, when, where, and why this method was stated,
we shall provide a commentary on its meaning."
In this regard, since the *Maṅgala Sutta* demonstrates self-protection— by way of avoiding what is unwholesome and performing what is wholesome—

and the warding off of the taints (*āsava*) that arise from such conditions, and since this present sutta accomplishes protection for others and the warding off of the taints arising from non-human beings and other such causes,
it was therefore placed immediately after that.
This, then, is the purpose for its placement here.
Regarding the Vesālī episode:
now, concerning the statement, "By whom was this sutta spoken, when, where, and why? it is asked: "But by whom was this sutta spoken?"
"When, where, and for what reason was it spoken? It is replied: This was indeed spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by his disciples or others.

And it was spoken at Vesālī at the time when the Blessed One had been brought there from Rājagaha by the Licchavis, who requested him because Vesālī was afflicted by calamities such as famine; it was spoken for the purpose of warding off those calamities.
This is the concise answer to those questions. However, in detail, it is described by the ancients starting from the account of Vesālī.
Herein is the narrative: It is said that a conception took place in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Having learned of this, she informed the king, and the king provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy. While her pregnancy was being properly maintained,
At the time when her pregnancy had reached maturity, she entered the birth chamber. For those possessed of merit, delivery occurs at dawn;
as she was one among them, she gave birth at dawn to a lump of flesh resembling a layer of lac or a bandhujīvaka flower. Then [the king thought]:
"Other queens give birth to sons resembling golden images, but the chief queen..."
Thinking, "If this piece of meat is seen before the king, my reputation will suffer," and out of fear for that ill repute,
he placed the piece of meat in a vessel, covered it with another lid, sealed it with the royal seal,
and had it cast into the current of the Ganges. As soon as the people had discarded it, deities established a protective guard over it.
There, they inscribed upon a golden plate with natural vermilion, "The offspring of the chief queen of the King of Bārāṇasī," and bound it [to the vessel].
Then that vessel, unassailed by the dangers of waves and the like, proceeded along the current of the Gaṅgā.
At that time, a certain ascetic was dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā, supported by a family of cowherds. Early in the morning, he...
While descending into the Ganges, he saw a vessel coming toward him; perceiving it as a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*), he took hold of it.
Then, seeing the writing-tablet and the royal seal-mark upon it, he let go of it and saw that piece of flesh.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to him: "It might be a fetus, for otherwise there would be no absence of foul odor and putrefaction. He [took] it...
Having led him to the hermitage, he placed him in a clean spot. Then, after the lapse of half a month, two slabs of flesh had formed.

Seeing this, the ascetic placed him in a better spot; then, after another half-month, five pustules arose on each slab of flesh for the sake of hands, feet, and head. Seeing this, the ascetic again placed him in a better spot. Then, after the lapse of half a month...
One piece of flesh became a boy resembling a golden image, and the other became a girl. Affection for his children arose in the ascetic toward them;
milk issued from his thumb. From that time on, he received milk-rice, and having eaten the rice, he would pour the milk into the mouths of the children. Whatever entered their bellies—
All of that appeared as if contained within a vessel of precious gems. Thus did the Licchavis come to be. Others, however, say:

"Their skin became so closely adhered to one another, as if it had been sewn together. Thus, because of their smooth skin (*nicchavitā*) or their closely-adhering skin (*līnacchavitā*), they were known as Licchavis.
While raising the children, the ascetic would enter the village for alms after sunrise and return only when it was well past midday.
Knowing of this activity, the cowherds said to him, "Venerable sir, raising children is an impediment for those who have gone forth.
Give the children to us; we will raise them while you attend to your own duties. The ascetic consented, saying, "Very well."
On the second day, the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers upon it, and raised banners and flags;
as musical instruments were being played, they arrived at the hermitage. The ascetic said, "These children possess great merit; raise them with diligence.
Once they have grown, let them marry one another. Having gratified the king with the five products of the cow, [secure] a portion of land..."
"Take them and build a city; there, consecrate the boy as king," he said, and gave the boys to them.
They replied, "Very well," and taking the boys, they raised them.
As the boys grew up, while playing in places where disputes occurred, they would strike other cowherd boys with their hands and feet.
They struck them, and they wept. When asked by their parents, "Why do you weep? they replied, "These people, who have no parents and are raised by ascetics, strike us excessively.
Thereupon their parents said, "These children harass and cause suffering to other children;
they should not be kept, but should be avoided. From that time on, it is said, he...
That region was called “Vajjī,” measuring three hundred yojanas in extent. Then the cowherds, having gratified the king, took possession of that region.
Having established a city right there and consecrated the prince, who was sixteen years of age, they made him their king.
And having held a wedding for him together with that maiden, they made an agreement: “From outside...”
“A girl must be brought; no girl is to be given to anyone from here.
Through their first union, two children were born—a daughter and a son—and in this manner, sixteen times they had two children each.
Then, as those children grew up in succession, that city became unable to accommodate the abundance of their parks, gardens, residences, and retinues.
They surrounded it with a wall at intervals of one gavuta each; because it was repeatedly expanded, the name Vesālī came into being. This is the account of Vesālī.
The Invitation to the Blessed One.
Furthermore, at the time of the Blessed One’s appearance, this Vesālī was prosperous and had reached a state of great abundance.
For there were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings alone; likewise [there were that many] crown princes, generals, treasurers, and so forth. As it is said:
"At that time, Vesālī was indeed prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food."
And there were seven thousand palaces, seven hundred palaces, and seven palaces;
seven thousand gabled chambers, seven hundred gabled chambers, and seven gabled chambers;
seven thousand parks, seven hundred parks, and seven parks; and seven thousand lotus ponds, seven hundred lotus ponds, and seven lotus ponds.”
At a later time, there was a famine, a failure of rain, and a poor harvest.
First, destitute people died and were cast outside. Because of the stench of the corpses of those who had died, non-human spirits entered the city, and consequently, even more people died.
Due to that repulsiveness, a plague of snake-poisoning broke out among the beings. Thus, there were three fears: the fear of famine, the fear of non-humans, and the fear of disease.
The inhabitants of the city of Vesālī, being oppressed, approached the king and said to him, “Great King, a threefold danger has arisen in this city;
such a thing has never occurred before, even throughout seven successive royal dynasties.
We believe it has arisen now because of your unrighteousness. The king then had everyone assembled in the assembly hall.
“Examine my lack of righteousness,” he said. Examining the entire lineage, they saw nothing amiss.
Then, seeing no fault in the king, they thought, “How shall we pacify this danger that threatens us?
Thereupon, some pointed to the six teachers, saying, “It will be pacified as soon as these have entered. Others said:
“It is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world; that Blessed One, possessed of great psychic power and great majesty, teaches the Dhamma for the welfare of all beings.

By his mere entering [the city], all fears would be stilled. Because of this, they became joyful and said, “But where does that Blessed One dwell at present? Would he not come if we were to send for him? Then others...
They said, “The Buddhas are indeed compassionate; why would they not come? However, that Blessed One is currently staying at Rājagaha, and King Bimbisāra attends upon him;
he might not allow him to come. [Vaiśravaṇa replied,] “In that case, let us persuade the king and bring him here.
Then the two Licchavi kings, accompanied by a great military force and bringing many gifts, [set out].
They sent a messenger to the king with the message: "Having persuaded Bimbisāra, bring the Blessed One [to us].
They went, presented the king with a gift, and having reported the matter, said: "Great King, send the Blessed One to our city.
The king did not accept, saying: "You yourselves must decide. They then approached the Blessed One.
Having paid homage, they spoke thus: "Venerable Sir, three fears have arisen in our city;
if the Blessed One would come, there would be safety for us. The Blessed One, having reflected, [thought]:
"When the Ratana Sutta is recited in Vesālī, that protection will pervade hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems. At the conclusion of the sutta, for eighty-four..."
“...there will be a realization of the Dhamma by thousands of beings,” he consented.
Then King Bimbisāra, having heard the Blessed One’s consent and learning that the Blessed One had accepted the journey to Vesālī, had a proclamation made throughout the city.
He then approached the Blessed One and asked, “Venerable sir, do you accept the journey to Vesālī? “Yes.”
"Great King. "In that case, venerable sir, please wait for a moment until I have prepared the road.

Then King Bimbisāra, having leveled a five-yojana stretch of ground between Rājagaha and the Ganges and having constructed a monastery every yojana, informed the Blessed One that it was time for his departure. The Blessed One [set out] with the five hundred monks...
Surrounded by hundreds of bhikkhus, he set out. The king had the road for five yojanas strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors;

having raised banners, streamers, full water-jars, plantain trees, and other ornaments, he had two white parasols held over the Blessed One and one over each bhikkhu, and together with his own retinue, [he honored them] with flowers, perfumes, and so forth.
Performing worship, he had the Blessed One reside in each monastery in turn, gave great alms-offerings, and in five days brought him to the banks of the Ganges.
There, decorating a boat with all kinds of ornaments, he sent a message to the people of Vesālī:
"The Blessed One has arrived; prepare the road and all of you go out to meet the Blessed One. They [prepared] twice as much...
Thinking, “We shall perform an offering,” they leveled the three-league distance between Vesālī and the Ganges,
prepared four white parasols for the Blessed One and two for each individual monk, and while performing the offering, they arrived at the bank of the Ganges and stood there.
Then King Bimbisāra joined two boats together, constructed a pavilion, adorned it with flower garlands and other ornaments, and [established himself] there.
He prepared a Buddha-seat made entirely of jewels, and the Blessed One sat upon it. Five hundred monks also boarded the boat and sat down according to their rank.
Following the Blessed One, the king waded into water reaching up to his neck and said, "Venerable Sir, I shall remain right here on the bank of the Ganges until the Blessed One arrives."
Having spoken thus, he turned back. Above, the deities offered worship as far as the Akaniṭṭha realm;

below, the Nāga kings dwelling in the Ganges, such as Kambala and Assatara, offered worship. Having traveled a distance of one yojana along the Ganges amidst such great worship, the Blessed One entered the boundary of the Vesālī territory.
Then the Licchavi kings, doubling the honor previously shown by Bimbisāra, went out to meet the Blessed One in water reaching up to their necks.

At that very moment, at that very instant, a great cloud arose in the four quarters, its peak spreading through the darkness enveloped by the radiance of lightning, thundering with a deep rumbling. Then, as the Blessed One set his first foot upon the bank of the Ganges—
As soon as it was set down, a rain of lotuses fell. Those who wished to get wet were wetted, while those who did not wish to get wet remained dry.
Water flowed everywhere, reaching the knees, the thighs, the hips, and up to the neck;
all corpses were carried into the Ganges by the water, and the ground became completely pure.

The Licchavi kings, having had the Blessed One stay at intervals of one *yojana* each along the way, gave great alms-offerings and, performing double the usual honor for three days, escorted him to Vesālī.
When the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, Sakka, the lord of the gods, approached preceded by a host of deities.
Due to the gathering of such powerful deities, non-human beings for the most part [withdrew].
They fled. The Blessed One, standing at the city gate, addressed the Elder Ānanda:

“Ānanda, having mastered this Ratana Sutta and taking the requisites for the ritual offerings, go with the Licchavi princes and, as you wander within the triple-walled enclosure of Vesālī, perform the protective recitation.
He then recited the Ratana Sutta. [The Licchavis asked: “By whom, then, was this sutta spoken?”
The answers to these questions— "When, where, and why was it spoken?"— are described in detail by the ancients starting from the Vesālī episode.
Thus, on the very day the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, for the purpose of warding off those calamities at the gates of the city of Vesālī...
Having mastered this Ratana Sutta, the Venerable Ānanda, reciting it for the purpose of protection,
took water in the Blessed One’s bowl and walked through the entire city, sprinkling it everywhere.

As soon as the Elder had uttered the words "Whatever [beings...]," those non-human beings who had previously not fled— residing in rubbish heaps, walls, corners, and so forth— [were driven out] by the four...
They fled through the gates, but the gates were out of order. Then some, unable to find an opening at the gates, escaped by breaking through the wall.
As soon as the non-human beings had departed, the disease in the bodies of the people subsided.
Having emerged, they honored the Elder with all kinds of flowers, perfumes, and other offerings. The great multitude gathered at the assembly hall in the center of the city.
Having anointed [the hall] with all kinds of perfumes, having fashioned a canopy, and having adorned it with every ornament, he prepared a Buddha-seat there and led the Blessed One inside.
The Blessed One entered the assembly hall and sat down on the seat that had been prepared. The community of monks and the kings and people likewise [entered].
And they sat down on their respective appropriate seats. Sakka, the lord of the devas, sat down together with the assembly of devas from two celestial realms;

other devas did likewise. The Venerable Ānanda, having traversed the entire Vesālī and established a protective guard, arrived together with the inhabitants of the city of Vesālī and sat down to one side. There, the Blessed One [addressed] all of them...
"He recited that very Ratana Sutta.

At this point, the summary outline (*mātikā*) which was set forth as: "By whom it was spoken, when, where, and for what reason—having explained this method in all its aspects"—has been fully detailed.
This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with *Yānīdha*.
1. Now, because it was stated, "We shall provide a commentary on its meaning," the commentary on the meaning begins.
Others, however, say: "Only the first five verses were spoken by the Blessed One; the remainder were spoken by the Elder Ānanda at the time of reciting the *paritta*.
Be that as it may, what is the use of this investigation? In any case, regarding this *Ratana Sutta*:
We shall provide a commentary on the meaning.
"Whatever beings there are here" is the first verse. Therein, "whatever" means of whatever kind—whether of little power or great power.
"Here" means in this place; he says this with reference to the location where they have gathered at that moment. As for "beings," although...
The word *bhūta* (being) refers to: (1) that which exists, as in such passages as “there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) regarding a being”;
(2) the five aggregates, as in such passages as “Behold, monks, this as it has come to be (*bhūtamidam*)”;

(3) the fourfold material form consisting of the earth element and so forth, as in such passages as “Monk, the four great elements (*mahābhūtā*) are the causes”; and (4) one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), as in such passages as “And he who has become a consumer of time (*kālaghaso bhūto*)”.

In such passages as “All beings in the world shall cast off their physical frame,” it refers to all sentient beings. In such passages as “The destruction of the forest of living beings,” it refers to trees and so forth.
In such passages as “One perceives a being as a being,” it applies to the category of beings below the realm of the Four Great Kings.
However, here it should be understood specifically as referring to non-human beings without distinction.
“Gathered together” means assembled. “Terrestrial” means those produced on the earth. “Or” (*vā*) is used in the sense of an alternative.
Thus, having made this first alternative—namely, “whatever beings here on earth have gathered together”—he spoke again to make a second alternative:
“or those in the sky. All those beings who have been produced in the sky as well—[all these he addresses].

The meaning is: "assembled here. Furthermore, in this context, those beings produced from the Yāma realm up to the Akaniṭṭha realm should be understood as "beings in the sky," because they are produced in celestial mansions manifested in the air.
Below that, from Sineru onwards, those dwelling in trees, creepers, and so forth upon the earth, as well as those produced in the earth itself, [are included].

As for those beings, because they are all produced on the earth and on things connected to the earth such as trees, creepers, mountains, and so forth, they should be understood as "earth-dwelling beings" (*bhummāni bhūtāni*).
Thus, the Blessed One [includes] all non-human beings with the two phrases: "those that are earth-dwelling or those in the sky."
Having thus assigned [the merit], he spoke the words, "May all beings indeed be well-disposed," in order to show that he again encompasses them with a single phrase.
"All" (*sabbe*) means without exception. "Indeed" (*eva*) is used for emphasis; the intention is that not even a single one is to be excluded.

"Beings" (*bhūtā*) refers to non-human spirits (*amanussā*). "May they be well-disposed" (*sumanā bhavantu*) means may they have happy minds, having become filled with joy and gladness. The phrase "and furthermore" (*athopi*) is intended to enjoin another duty.

The two particles [in the phrase] *vākyopādāne* (in the taking up of the sentence) mean: "Let them listen attentively to my speech"—that is, having made it their core purpose, having applied their minds, and having directed their entire consciousness toward it, let them listen to my teaching which brings about divine excellence and supramundane happiness.
Thus, here the Blessed One, by means of the unrestricted expression "whatever beings have gathered here," has encompassed all beings.

Furthermore, having divided [the beings] into two categories with the words “those on earth or those in the sky,” and then having unified them again with the words “all beings indeed,” he enjoins them toward the perfection of intention (*āsayasampatti*) with the phrase “may they be well-disposed,” and toward the perfection of application (*payogasampatti*)—
and likewise toward the perfection of wise attention (*yonisomanasikārasampatti*)— with the words “let them listen attentively to what is spoken.”

And thus, directing [the listener] toward the excellence of hearing the voice of another, as well as toward the excellence of one’s own right aspiration and reliance upon true persons, and toward the excellence of the causes for concentration and wisdom,
he concluded the verse. Therefore, this is the commentary on the verse beginning with "tasmā hi."
2. Therefore, "O beings," is the second verse. Therein, "therefore" (*tasmā*) is a word expressing a reason. "Beings" (*bhūtā*) is a form of address.
"Listen" (*nisāmetha*) means "hear. "All" (*sabbe*) means "without exception. What is being said?

Since you have come here for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma, having abandoned celestial abodes as well as the excellence of enjoyments and pleasures therein—not for the purpose of seeing actors, dancers, and the like—[therefore listen].
"Therefore, all you beings, listen attentively. Alternatively, having observed their state of gladness and their desire to hear with care through the words "May they be well-disposed;

may they listen respectfully," he said: "Because, by means of your gladness and your desire to hear respectfully—through the purity of intent consisting in right self-application and appropriate attention—you have relied upon true persons and the voice of others as the proximate cause [for understanding]..."
"And being endowed with purity of practice, therefore, all you beings, listen!
Alternatively, pointing to what was stated at the end of the previous verse as "spoken," he says this by way of citing it as a reason:

"Because my spoken word is exceedingly rare to obtain—since the opportune moment is difficult to find when one has avoided the eight inopportune moments—and because it possesses manifold benefits through the qualities of wisdom and compassion."
"Because it has come forth, and desiring to speak it, I said, 'Listen to my speech'; therefore, all you who are present, listen attentively.
This is what is expressed by this verse-line.
Having thus presented the reason and directed them toward listening to his own speech, he began to state that which is to be listened to.

“Practice loving-kindness toward the human race. This is its meaning: toward this human race that is afflicted by the three calamities, establish loving-kindness—that is, a state of friendship and an inclination toward their welfare.
Some, however, read it as “mānusikaṃ pajaṃ”; that is not appropriate because the locative sense is impossible there. As for what...
Others explain the meaning differently, but that too is not tenable. The intended sense here is this: I do not say "I am the Buddha" by virtue of my sovereign power;
rather, I speak for the sake of the welfare of both you and this human race when I say, "Practice loving-kindness toward the human race. And in this regard—
“Those royal seers who, having conquered the earth with its seven divisions,
went about performing sacrifices—
the horse sacrifice and the human sacrifice— ”
The Sammāpāsa, the Vājapeyya, and the Niraggaḷa sacrifices—
even these do not equal even a sixteenth part of a well-developed mind of loving-kindness.
If one has a mind free from malice toward even a single living being and feels loving-kindness, one becomes skilled thereby.
And by feeling compassion for all beings with the mind, the Noble One performs abundant merit.
By way of such suttas as these and the eleven benefits, it should be understood that loving-kindness is for the benefit of those who practice it.
By way of such suttas as, “A person favored by the deities always sees auspicious things,” it should be understood that it is also for the benefit of those toward whom it is directed.
Thus, showing that both [gods and humans] possess the nature of being beneficial, he said, "Practice loving-kindness toward human beings.
Now, demonstrating their helpfulness as well, he said, "For they carry offerings by day and by night; therefore, protect them with heedfulness.
The meaning of this is: those humans who, by means of painting, woodwork, and so forth, create shrines for deities such as *cetiya*-trees...
Having approached, they offer a daily oblation (bali) dedicated to the deities; they also offer an oblation at night during the dark fortnights and other such times.

Or, having given "ticket-meals" (salākabhatta) and so forth, they perform the daily oblation by dedicating the merit (pattidāna) starting from the protective deities up to the deities of the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, they cause the raising of parasols, the lighting of garlands of lamps, and the holding of all-night Dhamma-listenings and other such rites.
And since they perform the *bali* offering at night by means of the transfer and dedication of merit (*pattidāna-niyyātana*), how could they not be protected?
Since they thus perform the *bali* for your sake both by day and by night, therefore protect them;
therefore, through the performance of the *bali* ritual, protect and guard those people, remove what is harmful for them, and bring them what is beneficial, being heedful.
"Keeping that state of gratitude in their hearts, they constantly remember [it]. This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "Whatever... (Yaṃkiñci).
Having thus shown how humans are of benefit to deities, [the text proceeds] for the purpose of pacifying their calamities.

And by proclaiming the qualities of the Buddha and others, he began to employ a declaration of truth (*saccavacana*) in the manner beginning with "Whatever wealth... for the purpose of the gods and humans hearing the Dhamma.

Therein, "whatever" (*yaṃkiñci*) includes everything without exception in an unrestricted sense—whatever is applicable to various conventional expressions. "Wealth" (*vitta*) means riches; for it generates prosperity (*vitti*).
"Vittaṃ" (the world here). "Idha vā" refers to the human world. "Huraṃ vā" refers to the remaining worlds beyond that;

and since this would entail the inclusion of the entire world with the exception of humans, because the phrase "or in the heavens" is stated later on, it should be understood as referring to the inclusion of all others—such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so forth—with the exception of humans and the heavens.
Thus, by these two phrases, that which belongs to human commerce and to ornament and enjoyment— namely, gold, silver, pearls, gems, beryl, coral, rubies, emeralds, and so forth—
and the wealth of the nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others who dwell in palaces made of jewels on ground strewn with pearl and gem sand,
in abodes extending for many hundreds of yojanas, is indicated. "In the heavens" means in the divine worlds of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
They are called *saggā* because beings dwell there (*ajīyanti*) due to beautiful (*sobhana*) kamma; they are also called *saggā* because they are exceedingly excellent (*suṭṭhu agga*).
"That which" (*yaṃ*) refers to whatever [object], whether it has an owner or is ownerless. "Jewel" (*ratana*) means that which leads, carries, produces, or increases delight (*rati*);
this is a designation for whatever is esteemed, of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold, and fit for use by extraordinary beings. As it has been said:
“Because it is honored, of great value, incomparable, difficult to behold, and enjoyed by beings who are not ordinary, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).

“Exquisite” (paṇīta) means supreme, best, and insatiable. Thus, by this line of verse, [it refers to] that which exists among the gods in celestial mansions made of every kind of jewel, measuring many hundreds of yojanas, such as the Sudhamma and Vejayanta halls.
This refers to that which has an owner, as well as that which has no owner— such as empty celestial palaces (vimānas) attached to those beings who,

due to the absence of a Buddha’s appearance, are filling only the states of misery (apāya), or whatever other jewels are situated in the earth, the great ocean, the Himalayas, and so forth. These are what are indicated.
"There is nothing equal to the Tathāgata": *na* is a negation; *no* is used for emphasis;
*samaṃ* means "equal"; *atthi* means "exists"; *tathāgatena* means "by the Buddha. What is meant?

Of all that has been proclaimed as wealth (*vitta*) and treasure (*ratana*), there is not even a single treasure here that is equal to the Buddha-treasure (*buddharatana*). For even that [other treasure], in its sense of being honored...
A treasure, namely: the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
When these have arisen, the great multitude does not direct its devotion elsewhere; no one takes flowers, perfumes, and so forth to go to the abodes of *yakkhas* or *bhūtas*;
rather, all people direct their devotion solely toward the wheel-treasure and the jewel-treasure.
One worships it and prays for various boons; some of those things prayed for are indeed fulfilled, yet even that jewel is not equal to the Buddha-jewel.
For if a "jewel" is so called in the sense of being highly esteemed, then only the Tathāgata is a jewel.
Indeed, when a Tathāgata has appeared, whatever gods or humans possess great influence do not find their esteem directed anywhere else [but toward him].
