They perform [offerings], honoring no one else. For instance, Brahmā Sahampati honored the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland as large as Mount Sineru;
and likewise, according to their respective capacities, did other gods, humans, King Bimbisāra, King Pasenadi of Kosala, Anāthapiṇḍika, and others.
Even after the Blessed One had attained parinibbāna, the Great King Asoka spent ninety-six koṭis of wealth for his sake.
Throughout the entire Jambudīpa, he established eighty-four thousand monasteries; what need is there to mention other acts of veneration?

Furthermore, for whom else who has attained final Nibbāna do such places as the sites of birth, enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, and final Nibbāna, or images and shrines, become objects of such veneration and respect as they do for the Blessed One? It is also in this sense of being thus venerated...
There is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Likewise, that which is a jewel by way of its great value is like, for example, Kāsī cloth. As it is said:
“Monks, even when old, Kāsī cloth is both beautiful in color and pleasant to the touch, and it is of great value.”
Even that is not equal to the Jewel of the Buddha. For if "jewel" means something of great value, then only the Tathāgata is a jewel.
Indeed, whatever even a mere scrap of rag the Tathāgata accepts becomes of great fruit and great benefit for those who offer it—just as in the case of King Aśoka.
This is his quality of being of great value. And by this statement regarding his great value, the absence of faults is established here.
This passage from the Sutta should be understood:

"But for those from whom he accepts robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, that [gift] becomes of great fruit and great benefit for them. This, I say, is because of its high value. Just as..."
“Monks, that Kāsī cloth is of great value; it is in this way, monks, that I speak of this person as being of great value.
Thus, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata even in terms of great value.
Likewise, there is also that which is a jewel in terms of being incomparable. For example: the wheel-jewel of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
There arises [a wheel] with a nave made of sapphire, a thousand spokes made of the seven precious gems, a rim made of coral, and joints made of red gold;
above every ten spokes there is a single hollow spoke intended to catch the wind and produce sound,
by which the sound produced is like that of a five-fold musical ensemble well-played by a skilled musician, at both sides of whose nave...
The passes have two lion-mouths, and their interior is hollow like the nave of a chariot wheel.
There is no maker or one who causes it to be made; it arises through kamma-conditioning from the element of heat.

When the king, having fulfilled the tenfold duty of a Wheel-turning Monarch, on the Uposatha day of the full moon, has bathed his head and observed the Uposatha precepts, he goes up to the excellent upper palace. The precepts...
While sitting there purifying himself, he saw him rising like the full moon and like the sun;
one whose voice could be heard from twelve yojanas away and whose form could be seen from a yojana away, who was being beheld by the great multitude with immense wonder,
thinking, "I believe a second moon or sun has arisen," as he approached over the city and reached the king’s inner palace.
On the eastern side, neither too high nor too low, it stands like a threshing-floor at a suitable place for the great multitude to worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Following that very [treasure], the Elephant-Treasure appears, entirely white, with red feet, and sevenfold-supported.
Possessing supernormal power, he travels through the air; he comes from either the Uposatha family or the Chaddanta family. When coming from the Uposatha family, he arrives as the eldest of all;
when coming from the Chaddanta family, he arrives as the youngest of all, one who has completed his training and is endowed with self-mastery.
Taking a retinue twelve yojanas in extent, and having traveled throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he returns to his own [abode] even before the morning meal.
He comes to the royal capital.

Following after him, the horse-treasure appears: entirely white, with red hooves, a black head, and a mane like *muñja* grass, it comes from the lineage of the king of cloud-horses. The rest here is exactly the same as for the elephant-treasure.
Following after that as well, the jewel-treasure appears. That jewel is beryl, beautiful, of noble birth, and eight-faceted.
Well-polished and long, resembling the nave of a wheel, it comes from Mount Vepulla.
Even in darkness possessed of the four factors, it illuminates the king’s banner-top for a league;
by its light, people, thinking it is day, engage in their work, seeing even down to the smallest ant.
Following that [wheel-treasure], the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratana*) also appears; she is either the natural chief queen, or she comes from Uttarakuru, or from the royal family of Madda.
She is free from defects such as being too tall, surpassing human beauty yet not reaching divine beauty.
For this queen, her limbs are warm during the cold season and cool during the hot season.
The touch is like that of cotton-wool beaten a hundred times; sandalwood fragrance wafts from his body and the scent of blue lotuses from his mouth;
he is endowed with many virtues such as rising before others.
Following him, the householder-treasure also arises: a merchant who serves as the king’s ordinary official, for whom—
As soon as the Wheel-Treasure has appeared, the divine eye manifests, by which he sees a treasure within a league in every direction, whether it has no owner or has an owner;
he approaches the king and offers this invitation: "Be free from anxiety, O Lord;
I shall perform for you whatever needs to be done with wealth."
Following that, the Jewel of the Counsellor arises as the king’s eldest natural-born son.
As soon as the Wheel-Jewel has appeared, he is endowed with an exceptional lucidity of wisdom;
having understood the minds of his assembly of twelve leagues by means of his own mind, he is capable of restraining and encouraging them. He approaches the king and makes an offering.
“Be free from anxiety, O King; I shall govern the kingdom for you.

Or whatever other such thing there may be that is a treasure by way of being incomparable—that whose value cannot be determined by weighing or estimating it as “it is worth a hundred, or a thousand, or ten million”—in that regard, even a single such treasure is not equal to the Buddha-treasure. For if...
In the sense of being incomparable, he is a treasure; indeed, the Tathāgata alone is a treasure.

For it is impossible for anyone, by weighing or evaluating him according to his virtue, concentration, wisdom, or any other quality, to define him by saying, "He has only this many virtues," or "He is equal to this," or "He has a counterpart.
Thus, even in the sense of being incomparable, there is no treasure equal to the Tathāgata.

Likewise, even that which is a "jewel" in the sense of being difficult to see—namely, a wheel-turning monarch who appears rarely, and his jewels such as the wheel and so forth—that too has no equal to the Buddha-jewel.
For if something is a jewel in the sense of being difficult to see, then only the Tathāgata is a jewel; how then could there be the status of a jewel for wheel-turning monarchs and the like?

For these [Buddhas] arise many times within a single eon (*kappa*). However, because the world remains empty of Tathāgatas even for incalculable (*asaṅkhyeyya*) eons, the Tathāgata alone is difficult to behold, arising only once in a great while.
And this was said by the Blessed One at the time of his final *parinibbāna*:
“Ānanda, the deities are complaining: ‘We have indeed come from afar to see the Tathāgata.
Rarely, only once in a great while, do Tathāgatas, Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise in the world. This very night, in the final watch, the Parinibbāna of the Tathāgata will take place;
yet this influential bhikkhu stands before the Blessed One, obstructing our view.’”
"We do not obtain the opportunity to see the Tathāgata in this final age.
Thus, in the sense that his vision is difficult to obtain, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Likewise, he is a jewel in the sense that he is enjoyed by extraordinary beings; for example, [the jewel] of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).

Indeed, that [wheel-treasure] and the others do not arise for the enjoyment even in a dream by those of low birth and inferior status— such as caṇḍālas, venas, nesādas, rathakāras, pukkusas, and so forth— even if they possess hundreds of thousands of millions of wealth or dwell on the floors of magnificent seven-storied palaces.
Rather, it arises only for a well-born Kṣatriya king who has fulfilled the tenfold conduct of a Cakkavatti.
Because it arises for the purpose of enjoyment, it is exclusively for the enjoyment of extraordinary beings; yet even that is not equal to the Buddha-ratana.
For if something is a "jewel" (ratana) by way of being enjoyed by extraordinary beings, then only the Tathāgata is the jewel.

Indeed, in the world, compared to those regarded as inferior beings—such as Pūraṇa Kassapa and others who lack the necessary spiritual support and possess perverted views—the Tathāgata alone is the jewel.
It is not for consumption even in a dream by other teachers or those of similar character; however, it is for the consumption of those endowed with the necessary supporting conditions—

such as Bāhiya Dārucīriya and other great disciples born of noble families— who are capable of attaining Arahatship at the conclusion of even a four-line stanza through their penetrating knowledge and vision.
For it is they who, while accomplishing the unsurpassed vision, the unsurpassed hearing, the unsurpassed service, and so forth, enjoy the Tathāgata.
Thus, even in the sense of being enjoyed by an extraordinary being, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, that which is a jewel in the sense of indiscriminately producing delight—such as, for example, the wheel-jewel of a universal monarch (cakravartin)—is also surpassed by him.
Upon seeing it, the Wheel-turning Monarch is delighted; in this way, it produces joy for the king.
Furthermore, the Wheel-turning Monarch takes a golden pitcher in his left hand and sprinkles the Wheel-treasure with his right hand, saying:
"May the noble Wheel-treasure turn! May the noble Wheel-treasure conquer!"
Then the Wheel-Treasure, emitting a sweet sound like a fivefold musical ensemble, proceeds through the air toward the eastern direction;
the King, the Wheel-turning Monarch, follows right after it with his fourfold army,
twelve yojanas in width, neither too high nor too low, passing beneath the tops of tall trees and above the tops of short trees.
From the upper part [of the tree], he receives gifts such as flowers, fruits, and young shoots from the hands of those who have come;

and when rival kings arrive with the utmost humility, saying, "Come, Great King," and so forth, he proceeds while instructing them in the manner beginning with, "Living beings must not be killed. However, wherever the king desires to eat...

If he wishes to take his midday rest, the Wheel-Treasure descends from the sky and remains upon a level stretch of ground—capable of withstanding all tasks such as bathing water—as if fixed upon an axle.
Then, when the king’s mind turns toward departing, it proceeds making sounds just as before;
hearing that sound, the assembly, even if twelve leagues in extent, travels through the air. Such is the Wheel-Treasure.
Gradually he plunges into the eastern ocean; as he plunges in, the water recedes for a distance of one *yojana* and stands as if forming a wall.
The great multitude takes the seven treasures according to their desire.
Then the king, taking a golden pitcher, sprinkles water [on the ground], saying, "From this point on, let my kingdom begin."
It turns back. The army is in front, the Wheel-Treasure is behind, and the king is in the middle. At every place where the Wheel-Treasure halts, the water fills it completely.
By this very means, it proceeds across the southern, western, and northern oceans as well.
Having thus traversed the four quarters, the Wheel-Treasure ascends into the sky to a height of three yojanas. Therein—

By the power of the Wheel-Treasure (*cakraratna*), the King, having achieved victory over his enemies, remained established as ruler over Pūrvavideha—adorned with five hundred minor islands and measuring seven thousand *yojanas* in circumference;
likewise, Uttarakuru, measuring eight thousand *yojanas*; Aparagoyāna, measuring exactly seven thousand *yojanas*;
and Jambudvīpa, measuring ten thousand *yojanas*. Thus, he ruled over the four great continents adorned by two thousand minor islands.
He gazes upon a single world-system as if it were a forest of full-blown white lotuses.
As he gazes thus, no small measure of delight arises within him. In this way, too, that wheel-treasure produces delight for the king; yet even that is not equal to the Buddha-treasure.
For if a "treasure" is so called in the sense of producing delight, then the Tathāgata alone is the treasure—what then would this [wheel] accomplish?
What is the Wheel-Treasure? For the joy produced by all the treasures beginning with the Wheel-Treasure does not approach even a fraction, a part, or a portion of the divine joy of the Tathāgata;
and superior and more sublime than even that joy is the joy of the first meditative absorption experienced by the countless gods and humans who practice his instruction.

It generates delight in the second, third, fourth, and fifth jhānas; delight in the base of infinite space, the base of infinite consciousness, the base of nothingness, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and it generates delight in the path of stream-entry, the fruit of stream-entry, and the paths and fruits of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship.
Thus, in the sense of generating delight, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this so-called "treasure" (ratana) is of two kinds: sentient and insentient.
Among these, the insentient consists of the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) and the jewel-treasure (maṇiratana), or whatever else such as gold and silver not bound to sense-faculties (anindriyabaddha).

The sentient consists of those beginning with the elephant-treasure (hatthiratanādi) and ending with the counselor-treasure (pariṇāyakaratana), or whatever else of a similar nature that is bound to sense-faculties (indriyabaddha).

Thus, of these two kinds, the conscious jewel is declared to be the foremost. Why? Because the unconscious jewels—such as gold, silver, gems, and pearls—are brought forth for the purpose of adorning conscious jewels, such as the elephant-jewel and others.
The conscious jewel is also twofold: the animal jewel and the human jewel. Of these, the human jewel...
It is declared to be the foremost. Why? Because the treasure of the animal realm is subordinate to the treasure of human beings.
The treasure of human beings is also twofold: the female treasure and the male treasure. Among these, the male treasure is declared to be the foremost. Why?
Because the female treasure enters into the service of the male treasure. And as for the male treasure...
There are two kinds of jewels: the jewel of the householder and the jewel of the homeless one. Among these, the jewel of the homeless one is declared to be supreme.

Why? Because even a universal monarch (cakravartin), who is the foremost among the jewels of householders, having prostrated with the five limbs, attended upon, and served the jewel of the homeless one endowed with virtues such as morality, attains celestial and human prosperity.
...one attains the perfection of Nibbāna.

Thus, the jewel of the homeless life is twofold, according to the noble ones (ariya) and worldlings (puthujjana). The jewel of the noble ones is also twofold, according to those in training (sekha) and those beyond training (asekha).

The jewel of those beyond training is also twofold, according to those who are dry-insight practitioners (sukkha-vipassaka) and those whose vehicle is serenity (samatha-yānika). As for the jewel of those whose vehicle is serenity...

There are two kinds [of disciples]: those who have attained the perfection of a disciple and those who have not. Among these, the one who has attained the perfection of a disciple is declared supreme.
Why? Because of the greatness of his qualities. Even compared to the jewel of a *paccekabuddha*, the jewel of a disciple who has attained perfection is declared supreme.
Why? Because of the greatness of his qualities. For even many hundreds of disciples like Sāriputta and Moggallāna are [not equal to] a single *paccekabuddha*.
They do not approach even a hundredth part of the [Buddha’s] qualities. Even compared to the jewel of the Paccekabuddhas, the jewel of the Sammasambuddha is declared supreme.

Why? Because of the greatness of his qualities. For even if all of Jambudīpa were filled with Paccekabuddhas sitting cross-legged, each touching the next, they would not equal even a fraction, a portion, or a sub-portion of the qualities of a single Sammasambuddha.
They approach it. For this was said by the Blessed One: “Bhikkhus, as far as there are beings—whether footless... [and so on]...
the Tathāgata is declared to be the foremost among them,” and so forth. Thus, in any manner whatsoever, there is no jewel equal to the Tathāgata.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “There is none equal to us; there is no one like the Tathāgata.”
Thus, having spoken of the Blessed One’s incomparability with other jewels by means of the jewel of the Buddha,
he now speaks— so as to pacify the calamities that have arisen for those beings— not on account of birth, clan, lineage, or the beauty of his complexion and so forth,
but rather on account of his qualities such as the aggregates of virtue and concentration throughout the world, from the Avīci hell up to the peak of existence.
Relying on the incomparable nature of the Buddha-jewel, he utters a word of truth: "This jewel of the Buddha is sublime;
by this truth, may there be well-being.
Its meaning is: whatever wealth or jewel exists here, or in the world beyond, or in the heavens—whatever it may be.
Because it is not fully equal to those various qualities, the Jewel of the Buddha is sublime.
If this is true, then by this truth may there be well-being for these living beings; may there be the presence of beauty, health, and freedom from calamity.
And here, just as it is said: "The eye, Ānanda, is empty of a self or of what belongs to a self..."
In such passages as “or,” the meaning is “either by way of selfhood (attabhāvena) or by way of what belongs to self (attaniyabhāvena).

For otherwise, it would follow that the eye being either the self or belonging to the self would not even be prohibited. Likewise, in the phrase “the jewel is excellent,” the meaning should be understood as “the state of being a jewel (ratanattaṃ) is excellent” or “the quality of being a jewel (ratanabhāvo) is excellent. For otherwise, it would not be established that the Buddha is a jewel.
For it is not the case that where a jewel exists, the designation "jewel" is not established.

Rather, wherever there exists a jewel—defined by its being honored and so forth, or connected by whatever means—and because it is designated as a "jewel" by depending upon that state of being a jewel, therefore, due to the existence of that jewel, the designation "jewel" is established. Alternatively:
"‘This too is a treasure in the Buddha’—by this expression as well, the meaning should be understood as ‘the Buddha alone is the treasure.
As soon as these verses were spoken by the Blessed One, safety was established for the royal family and fear was stilled.
The command of these verses was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems."
Commentary on the Verse “Destruction and Dispassion”: 4.
Having thus spoken the truth by means of the Buddha’s qualities, he now begins to speak by means of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna with the words, “Destruction and dispassion.
In this context, because through the realization of Nibbāna, lust and the other defilements are destroyed and utterly exhausted; because—
Or rather, it is called "destruction" (khaya) because it is merely the non-arising, cessation, and destruction of those [defilements];

and it is called "dispassion" (virāga) because it is dissociated from lust and the rest both by way of association and by way of object, or because when that [state] is realized, lust and the rest become utterly detached, departed, and shattered.
Furthermore, because its arising is not perceived, it is so called.
There is no aging, nor is there alteration of what stands; therefore, because it is not born, does not decay, and does not die, it is called "the Deathless" (*amata*).
Furthermore, in the sense of being supreme and in the sense of being insatiable, it is called "exquisite" (*paṇīta*).

"That which he attained" (*yadajjhagā*) means that which he reached, found, and acquired; he realized it through the power of his own knowledge. "The Sakyan Sage" (*Sakyamuni*) is so called because he was born into the Sakya clan.
He is a Sakyan because he is endowed with the qualities of a sage (*moneyya-dhamma*); thus, a Sakyan who is a sage is the "Sakyamuni.
"Concentrated" means one whose mind is concentrated by means of the concentration of the Noble Path (*ariya-magga-samādhi*).

"There is nothing equal to that Dhamma" means there is no class of phenomena whatsoever equal to the Dhamma attained by the Sakyamuni, which is named by terms such as "destruction" (*khaya*) and so forth. Therefore, it is also said in another sutta: "To whatever extent..."
“Monks, whether phenomena are conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be their foremost,” and so forth. Thus,
having stated that the phenomenon of Nibbāna is unequalled by other phenomena, the Blessed One now [praises] the jewel of the Nibbāna-dhamma by means of its qualities of destruction (*khaya*),
dispassion (*virāga*), peace (*santa*), and excellence (*paṇīta*), for the purpose of pacifying the calamities that have arisen for those beings.
Relying upon his peerless nature, he utters this word of truth: “This too is a sublime jewel in the Dhamma;
by this truth, may there be well-being! The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as stated for the previous verse.
The command of this verse, too, was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
Commentary on the verse beginning with *Yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho*.
Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Dhamma of Nibbāna, he now begins to speak by way of the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path with the words, “*Yaṃ buddhaseṭṭho*.
Therein, he is called “Buddha” according to the method beginning with “one who has awakened to the Truths” (*bujjhitā saccāni*), and he is supreme and praiseworthy.
He is both supreme and a Buddha, thus he is the "Supreme Buddha" (*buddhaseṭṭho*);

or, among the Buddhas—namely, the *anubuddhas*, *paccekabuddhas*, and *sutabuddhas*—he is supreme, thus he is the "Supreme Buddha. That Supreme Buddha praised that which [is the Eightfold Path], saying:
"The Eightfold [Path] alone is the best of paths for attaining the security of Nibbāna," and: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you noble right concentration."
And in such ways as "with its proximate cause and its requisites," he praised and elucidated it here and there.
It is called "pure" (*suci*) because it effects the complete eradication of the stains of the defilements (*kilesa*).

They call it "the immediate concentration" (*ānantarika-samādhi*) because it invariably bestows the fruit immediately following its own occurrence; for indeed, in the case of the path-concentration (*magga-samādhi*), [it is not so].
There is no obstacle whatsoever that could prevent the arising of his fruit once it has arisen. As it is said:
"Suppose this person were practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, and it were the time for the world-age to end;
the world-age would not end until this person had realized the fruit of stream-entry."
"This person is called one who can endure for an eon. Indeed, all persons possessing the path are those who can endure for an eon.

Regarding the phrase "there is nothing equal to that concentration": there is no concentration whatsoever—whether of the fine-material sphere or the immaterial sphere—that is equal to that pure *ānantariya* concentration praised by the Supreme Buddha. Why? Because of its having been cultivated by them.
Because even for one reborn here and there in the Brahma-world, rebirth in the hells and other realms can still occur;
whereas for a noble person (ariya-puggala), because this concentration of arahantship has been developed, the total eradication of all rebirth is possible.
Therefore, it is said in another sutta: "Bhikkhus, as far as there are conditioned phenomena... [etc. ...the Noble Eightfold Path..."
“The Path is declared the foremost among them,” and so forth.

Having thus stated that the immediate concentration (*ānantarika-samādhi*) is unequalled by other concentrations, the Blessed One now, in the same manner as before, utters a word of truth based on the incomparable nature of the Jewel of the Dhamma of the Path: “This too, in the Dhamma…” and so on.

"Let it be so. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
This concludes the commentary on the "Ye Puggala" verses.
6. Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Dhamma of the Path, he now begins to speak by way of the qualities of the Saṅgha with the words, “Those individuals.
Therein, “those” (*ye*) is an indefinite enumeration. “Individuals” (*puggalā*) means beings (*sattā*). “Eight” (*aṭṭha*) is the numerical limit of them;

for they consist of the four who are practicing the path (*paṭipannā*) and the four who are established in the fruit (*phale ṭhitā*), thus making eight. “Praised by the virtuous” (*satam pasatthā*) means praised by true persons (*sappurisehi*).
They are praised by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, disciples of the Buddha, and other gods and humans. Why? Because they are endowed with co-nascent qualities such as virtue (*sīla*).
For them, there are co-nascent qualities such as virtue and concentration, just as there are co-nascent color and fragrance in flowers like the *campaka* and *vakula*.
Therefore, like flowers endowed with color, fragrance, and so forth, they are dear and pleasing to gods and humans.
And they are worthy of praise. Therefore it is said: “The hundred and eight persons who are praised.
Alternatively, *ye* (those who) is an indefinite enumeration. *Puggalā* means sentient beings (*sattā*). *Aṭṭhasataṃ* (hundred and eight) is the limit of their number.

For there are three types of stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*): the one-seeder (*ekabījī*), the family-to-family (*kolaṃkolo*), and the one who returns seven times at most (*sattakkhattuparamo*). [They are distinguished] in the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness...
There are three types of once-returners who have attained the fruit. All of them together amount to twenty-four by way of the four paths. There are five in the Aviha realm:

those who attain Nibbāna in the interval, those who attain Nibbāna upon landing, those who attain Nibbāna with exertion, those who attain Nibbāna without exertion, and those who go upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Likewise, there are five each in the Atappa, Sudassa, and Sudassī realms. And in the Akaniṭṭha realm, there are five.
Furthermore, there are twenty-four non-returners (anāgāmin), excluding those who go upstream (uddhaṃsota).

There are two types of arahants: the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) and the one whose vehicle is serenity (samathayānika). Including the four who are established on the path (maggaṭṭha), there are fifty-four.

All of these, when doubled according to whether they belong to the lineage of faith (saddhādhura) or the lineage of wisdom (paññādhura), total one hundred and eight. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
"These four pairs" means that all those individuals previously mentioned in detail—whether eight or one hundred and eight—are summarized as follows:
one pair consists of the one standing on the path of stream-entry and the one established in its fruit;

likewise, up to the one standing on the path of arahantship and the one established in its fruit, there are four pairs. "They are worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyā*); here, "they" refers to the aforementioned...

This is the specific description of those who were previously mentioned without specification. Those individuals who, in detail, are said to be eight or one hundred and eight, or in brief, four pairs—all of them are "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*), meaning they are worthy of sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*).
A "sacrificial gift" (*dakṣiṇā*) refers to that which is given after having faith in both the action and the result of the action, thinking: "This is my work as a physician..."
Disregarding such thoughts as, "He will perhaps give me a gift, or send me a message," the gift that is being given is what is meant;

those persons endowed with qualities such as virtue who are worthy of it are called "arahants," and these [monks] are of such a kind; therefore they are called "those worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyā*).
They are "disciples of the Sugata" because the Blessed One is endowed with a beautiful gait and has gone to a beautiful state.
He is the Sugata because he has gone well and spoken well; [the phrase] belongs to that Sugata.
They are called *sāvakā* (disciples) because they all listen to his word. Granted, others also listen, but having listened, they do not perform the duty that ought to be done;

these, however, having listened and performed the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammappaṭipatti*) that ought to be done, have attained the paths and fruits; therefore, they are called "disciples."
...are so called. Regarding the phrase "gifts given to these bear great fruit":

even small gifts given to these disciples of the Sugata become of great fruit because, by virtue of the recipient, they attain the state of purity of the sacrificial offering (*dakṣiṇā-visuddhi*). Therefore, it is also said in another sutta:
"Bhikkhus, to whatever extent there are assemblies or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared to be the foremost among them."
"Namely, these four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples...
[as before] ...it is the supreme fruit.
Thus the Blessed One, having described the qualities of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of all those established on the paths and in the fruits, said:
Now, relying on that very same quality, he employs a declaration of truth (saccavacana), saying, "This too [belongs] to the Saṅgha.

Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with *ye suppayuttā*.

7. Having thus spoken the truth by way of the qualities of the Saṅgha through those established on the path and those established in the fruit, he now begins to speak by way of the qualities of those very individuals whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), who experience the bliss of the attainment of the fruit, starting with the words, “Those well-yoked.
Therein, “those” (ye) is an indefinite term of reference. “Well-yoked” (suppayuttā) means thoroughly yoked; [to] manifold...
The meaning is that, having abandoned seeking, they began to apply themselves to insight (vipassanā) by relying on a pure livelihood.
Alternatively, "well-applied" means endowed with perfectly purified bodily and verbal exertion; by this, he shows their aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha).
"With a firm mind" means with a firm mind, that is, with a consciousness joined to stable concentration (samādhi); by this—

He shows them the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*). "Having gone forth" (*nikkāmī*) means having become indifferent toward both body and life, one has gone forth from all defilements by means of energy dominated by wisdom (*paññādhura*).
By this, he shows them the aggregate of wisdom (*paññakkhandha*), which is endowed with energy.

"In the teaching of Gotama" (*gotamasāsanamhi*) means in the teaching of the Tathāgata Gotama himself by virtue of his lineage (*gotta*). By this, [he excludes] even the various kinds [of teachings] outside of this...
This shows the absence of emergence from the defilements due to the lack of qualities such as skillful application in those performing the austerity of immortality.
"Tesaṃ" (of them) is a term of explanation referring back to those previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase "pattipattā," here "patti" means that which is to be attained (*pattabbā*);
"to be attained" means worthy of being attained—that which, having been reached, one becomes one who has attained ultimate security from bondage; this is a designation for the fruit of arahantship.
"Foot-soldiers of foot-soldiers" means those who are foot-soldiers among foot-soldiers. "The Deathless" refers to *nibbāna*. "Having plunged in" means having entered [it] by way of its object.
"Having obtained" means having gained it. "Frugally" means without spending even as much as a *kākaṇika* coin through waste.

"The state of extinction" refers to the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), wherein the distress of the defilements has been stilled. "Enjoying" means experiencing it. What is being said? Those who, in this teaching of Gotama...
Being well-applied due to their perfection in virtue, possessing a firm mind due to their perfection in concentration, and being free from desire due to their perfection in wisdom,
they plunge into the Deathless by means of this right practice. Consuming the extinction known as the attainment of fruition—
obtained effortlessly— they are said to have "attained what was to be attained."

Thus, having described the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of those individuals whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) as they experience the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), the Blessed One now employs a word of truth (saccavacana) based on that very quality, saying: "In this Saṅgha also...
Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. The command of this verse also extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷa).
"Accepted by non-human beings.

Thus, having spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha through the qualities of individuals whose taints are exhausted— just as in the commentary on the verse beginning "Like the post of Inda"— he now [speaks] by way of what is evident to many people.
He began to describe the qualities of a stream-enterer with the words, “Just as a city gate post. In this context, “just as” (*yathā*) is a word used for comparison.

“City gate post” (*indakhīla*) is a designation for a pillar made of solid wood that has been driven into the ground after digging eight or ten cubits into the earth inside the threshold for the purpose of securing the city gate. “Into the earth” (*pathaviṃ*) means into the ground. “Fixed” (*sita*) means...
Having entered within, it is supported. "Siyā" means it would be. "By the four winds" means by the winds coming from the four directions.
"Unshakable" means incapable of being shaken or moved. "Tathūpamaṃ" means of such a kind.
"A true person" (sappurisa) means a supreme person. "I say" means I speak. "He who sees the Noble Truths through direct penetration" means he who...
Having plunged into the four noble truths with wisdom, one sees them. In this context, the noble truths are to be understood according to the method already explained in the *Kumārapañha*.
However, the summarized meaning here is as follows: just as a city-gate post, because its socket is deep, is fixed in the earth by four [sides]...
One should be unshakable by the winds; I declare this true person to be just like that.

Why? Because he too, like a city gatepost, is unshakable by the four winds—that is, by the winds of the doctrines of all other sectarians—and cannot be shaken or moved from that vision by anyone. Therefore...
It is also said in another sutta: "Bhikkhus,
just as if there were an iron pillar or a city gatepost, deeply rooted with a firm base, immovable and unshakable—
even if a violent wind and rain should come from the eastern direction, it would neither tremble nor shake."
He would not be shaken. Even from the west... [and so on] ...from the south, or even from the north, he would not be shaken.
Why is that? Because of the depth of this pillar, monks, and because the door-post is firmly planted.
In the same way, monks, whatever recluses or brahmins understand as it really is: "This is suffering"... [and so on] ..."this is the way leading to its cessation."

“They understand; they do not look to the face of any other ascetic or brahmin, thinking, ‘Surely this venerable one knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. For what reason? Because, monks, the four noble truths have been well-seen.
Thus the Blessed One, having spoken of the quality of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of a stream-enterer who was evident to many people, said:
Now, relying on that very same quality, he employs a word of truth (saccavacana): "This too is in the Saṅgha.

Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously stated. With this verse as well, the command was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷas).
This concludes the commentary on the verse beginning with "Ye ariyasaccāni."

9. Having thus stated the truth based on the Saṅgha by way of the qualities of a stream-enterer (sotāpanna) without distinction, [the text now addresses] those three types of stream-enterers: the one-seeded (ekabījī), the family-to-family (kolaṃkolo), and the one who returns seven times at most (sattakkhattuparamo).
As it has been said: "Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer...
he produces only one more existence and makes an end of suffering; this is the one-seeded. Likewise, [he is reborn] in two or three families..."
“Having run and wandered through [the cycle of existence], one makes an end of suffering; this is the ‘one who goes from family to family’ (kolaṅkolo).
Likewise, having run and wandered seven times among gods and humans, one makes an end of suffering;

this is the ‘one for whom there are seven births at most’ (sattakkhattuparamo). Thus he began to speak of the qualities of the one with the fewest remaining births, the one for whom there are seven births at most, starting with the words: “Those which are the Noble Truths.”
In this context, "the noble truths" is exactly as previously explained.
"They illuminate" means that by means of the radiance of wisdom, they dispel the darkness of the defilements that obscures the truths, making them manifest and clear to themselves.
"By one of profound wisdom" means by one whose wisdom is immeasurable, whose wisdom finds no foothold for the knowledge of the world including its devas; it is said, "by the Omniscient One."
"Well-taught" means they have been excellently taught through various methods such as concise and detailed expositions,

complete and partial presentations, and so forth. "Even though they may be greatly negligent" means that even if those individuals who have discerned the Noble Truths become greatly negligent by resorting to grounds for negligence such as divine sovereignty or the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch,
nevertheless, by means of the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, [they abandon] the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*).
By means of cessation, having set aside name-and-form that would otherwise arise throughout the beginningless cycle of existence across the seven realms of being,
because those have ceased and passed away, they do not take up an eighth existence; rather,
having begun insight meditation within the seventh existence itself, they attain arahantship.

Thus, having described the virtue of the Jewel of the Saṅgha by way of its being supreme even for those who have attained the state of being reborn seven times at most, the Blessed One now employs a declaration of truth (saccavacana) based on that very virtue, saying:
"This too [belongs] to the Saṅgha. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
Commentary on the *Sahāvassa* Verse (10):
Having thus spoken the Truth based on the Saṅgha by virtue of not taking up an eighth existence after seven at most,
he now [speaks] of that same person’s excellence over other individuals who have not abandoned the grasping for existence, even regarding those seven existences.
He began to speak by way of its quality, saying, “sahāvassā. In this context, *sahāva* means “together with.

*Assa* refers to one of those mentioned in the phrase, “Your reverence does not take an eighth [birth]. *Dassanasampadāya* means by way of the attainment of the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*).
For the path of stream-entry is the very first seeing of Nibbāna, by virtue of the perfection of the task that must be done after having seen Nibbāna.
It is called "seeing" (*dassana*); the manifestation of that within oneself is the perfection of seeing (*dassanasampadā*).

Together with that very perfection of seeing, these three qualities are abandoned. In the phrase "these three qualities are abandoned" (*tayo assu dhammā jahitā bhavanti*), the word *assu* is a mere particle used for the purpose of filling out the meter, as in such expressions as "This, Sāriputta, is my [experience] regarding the great repulsive food. Therefore, it is together with his perfection of seeing...
The meaning here is that these three things have been abandoned and are relinquished.
Now, in order to show the states that have been abandoned, he says: “Personal-existence view, doubt, and whatever there is of virtue-and-observance.
In this context, while the body—known as the pentad of the aggregates of clinging—is still present, [there is] that which has twenty bases...
"View" refers to the view of a personal body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*). Alternatively, it is the "view regarding that body," hence *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*;
the meaning is: views existing with respect to a body of the aforementioned kind. Or again, it is the "view that there is a self in the body," hence *sakkāyadiṭṭhi*; the meaning is:
a view occurring in the form "there is a self consisting of form and so forth" while a body of the aforementioned kind exists. And because of its abandonment—
All modes of view have indeed been abandoned, for that [wisdom] is their root. Because it allays the disease of all defilements, wisdom is called "the cure";
since this has departed from that wisdom-cure, or since this is departed from the wisdom-cure, it is "vicikicchita" (doubt).
This refers to the eightfold basis as described by the method beginning with "he is uncertain regarding the Teacher."
This is a designation for doubt (*vimati*). Because that [doubt] has been abandoned, all forms of perplexity (*vicikicchita*) are also abandoned, for it is their root.

Regarding such passages as, "Outside of this [dispensation], purification comes through the virtue of recluses and brahmins, purification comes through vows," the term *sīlabbata* refers to the virtue consisting of the cow-virtue, dog-virtue, and so forth, and the vow consisting of the cow-vow, dog-vow, and so forth.
It is said that because that [craving] has been abandoned, all forms of asceticism—such as nakedness, shaving the head, and so forth—are also abandoned.
For that [craving] is their root; therefore, at the very end of that section, it is stated: "Whatever there may be.

Furthermore, here, the perfection of the vision of suffering abandons the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), the perfection of the vision of its origin abandons doubt (*vicikicchita*), and the perfection of the vision of the path and the vision of Nibbāna...
"It should be understood that virtue and observance are abandoned.
Commentary on the verse beginning with "From the four states of misery": 11.
Having thus shown the abandonment of the cycle of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*), [the text now shows] the cycle of result (*vipākavaṭṭa*) which exists when that cycle of defilements is present.
It must be so; showing that with the abandoning of that [defilement], there is also the abandoning of this [result], he said:

"And liberated from the four states of misery. In this context, the "four states of misery" (apāya) are the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the asura-hosts. The meaning is that even while taking up existence within the seven [planes of] becoming, he is liberated from these.

Having thus shown the abandonment of his cycle of karmic results (*vipākavaṭṭa*), he now says, "He is incapable of committing the six transgressions," while demonstrating the abandonment of the cycle of karma (*kammavaṭṭa*) which is the root of that cycle of results.

In this context, "transgressions" (*abhiṭhānāni*) refers to gross offenses; he is incapable of committing these six. And regarding those, [the Buddha said]: "Monks, it is impossible, it is out of the question..."

It should be understood that the acts of killing a mother, killing a father, killing an arahant, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṅgha— along with the act of professing another teacher— as described in the Ekaka-nipāta by way of the passage beginning, “If a person endowed with right view were to deprive his mother of life,” and so forth, are [the five heinous crimes].
For although a noble disciple endowed with right view does not deprive even an ant or a termite of life, [he would certainly refrain from these acts].
Moreover, these [statements] were spoken for the purpose of censuring the state of being a worldling (*puthujjana*).
For a worldling, because he is not endowed with right view, commits even such highly blameworthy transgressions; one who is endowed with vision, however, is incapable of committing them.

And here, the mention of "incapability" is for the purpose of showing that he would not commit them even in another existence. For even in another existence, this person—[is incapable of committing them].

Even one who does not know the state of being a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka) does not, by the very nature of things (dhammatā), commit these six bases—namely, the six beginning with the intentional taking of life—or the five enmities, together with the instruction of another teacher;
it is with reference to these that some read, "the six and six bases. And here, the examples of the noble disciples, the village children, and the fish-catchers are given.

Thus, having described the quality of the Saṅgha-ratana by way of the distinguished virtues of a noble disciple who has taken up seven existences—even when compared to other individuals who have not abandoned the grasping for existence—the Blessed One now utters a declaration of truth based on that very same quality, saying, "This too is in the Saṅgha.
The meaning of this should be understood in the same manner as previously explained. Regarding this verse as well:
The command was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
Thus, even though he took up seven existences, he was distinguished by his superior qualities from those individuals who have not abandoned the grasping for existence.

Having stated the truth regarding the foundation of the Saṅgha, he now begins to speak of the quality of one endowed with vision (*dassanasampanna*)—that such a person is not only incapable of performing the six grounds [of defeat], but is also incapable of concealing even a minor evil deed once committed;
thus, even for one who dwells in negligence, because of the virtue of not concealing what has been done, it is said: "Even though he performs an evil deed."

The meaning of this is as follows: although one who is perfected in vision might, due to a lapse of mindfulness, fall into a state of negligence, he would—setting aside that which the Blessed One spoke with reference to the intentional transgression of a worldly offense, namely:

"Whatever training rule has been laid down by me for my disciples, my disciples do not transgress it even for the sake of their life"—refrain from other things such as building a hut or sleeping in a group of four.
He commits a bodily evil deed censured by the Buddha, characterized as a transgression of the prescribed rules (*paṇṇatti-vajja-vītikkama*);
or he commits it through speech, such as teaching the Dhamma while standing on a high seat or higher than five or six words, idle chatter, harsh speech, and so forth;

or indeed, he commits an evil deed through the mind, such as giving rise to greed or hatred toward anything, accepting gold and other valuables, or failing to exercise proper reflection regarding the use of robes and other requisites. He is incapable of concealing that [deed]; he does not [think], "This..."

Having recognized that it is "unfit" and "not to be done," if one conceals it even for a moment, but at that very instant reveals it to the Teacher or to wise fellow-celibates and makes amends according to the Dhamma, or restrains oneself with the thought, "I shall not do it again"—why is this?
Because incapacity [for such an act] has been declared for one who has seen the Truth (diṭṭhapada); even for such a person...
The meaning is that it has been stated that a person who has committed an evil deed but conceals it— one who has seen the state of Nibbāna and is endowed with vision—
is incapable [of such concealment]. How so?
“Bhikkhus, just as a young, tender infant lying on its back, having stepped on a coal with its hand or foot,

quickly withdraws it, even so, bhikkhus, it is the nature of a person endowed with right view that even if they should commit an offense for which an expiation is prescribed, they quickly emerge from it. This is the natural law.”
"Then he quickly teaches, reveals, and makes plain [the fault] to the Teacher or to wise fellow-celibates;
having taught, revealed, and made it plain, he undertakes restraint for the future.
Thus did the Blessed One describe the quality of one who dwells heedlessly yet is possessed of vision, by virtue of his lack of concealment regarding what has been done, as a jewel of the Saṅgha.
Having spoken of the quality, he now employs a declaration of truth (saccavacana) based on that very quality, saying, "And this too in the Saṅgha.

Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. The command of this verse was also received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (cakkavāḷa).
Commentary on the *Vanappagumba* Verses (13).
Having thus spoken the truth based on the Saṅgha by describing individuals included within the Saṅgha according to their various types of qualities,
[the author] now, while the Blessed One was elucidating the qualities of the Triple Gem, speaks here in brief— whereas elsewhere...
And the Dhamma of the scriptures was taught in detail; relying upon that, he again began to speak the Truth with reference to the Buddha:
"Just as when the tops of the forest thickets are in full bloom. Therein, a *vana* (forest) is a collection of trees established in close proximity.
A *gumbo* (thicket) is that which has grown up with roots, heartwood, sapwood, bark, branches, and foliage; a *pagumbo* is a thicket [so grown]. Of the forest...
*Vanappagumbo* means a tree in the forest (*vane pagumbo*). This is expressed as *vanappagumbe*, for it is also permissible to speak in this way, just as in such cases as:

"there is [a state] with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitakka-savicāra*)," "there is [a state] without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitakka-vicāramatta*)," or "in pleasure, in pain, in the living being (*jīva*)," and so forth.
*Yathā* is a word signifying a comparison. *Phussitagga* means that its tips are covered in blossoms; it is one upon whose branches and twigs flowers have appeared.
The meaning [of this] has already been stated according to the method previously explained as “at the tip of the blossomed [trees]. “In the first month of the summer” means:
among those four months of summer, in one of those four summer months. If you ask, “In which month?
It is in the first summer, that is to say, in the month of Citta (Citra). For that is called both “the first summer” and “the young spring.”
And so it is said. Beyond that, the meaning of the words is self-evident.

However, this is the summary of the meaning here: just as in the early spring known as the "first summer," in a forest dense with various kinds of trees, a thicket—so called by the synonym for a young tree or shrub—with its tips and branches in full bloom, is exceedingly beautiful.

Just so, because it is exceedingly beautiful with the various kinds of flowers that are the distinctions of meaning—namely, the aggregates, bases, and so forth; the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, and so forth; or the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and so forth—it is like that [lotus].

Because it illuminates the path leading to Nibbāna, this excellent Dhamma of the scriptures leads to Nibbāna; and it is not for the sake of gain, nor for the sake of honor and the like, but solely out of great compassion.

"With a heart uplifted, he taught for the supreme welfare of beings. Regarding the phrase "for the supreme welfare" (*paramaṃ hitāya*), the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*) is used here for the sake of metrical ease in the verse composition.
However, the meaning is this: "he taught for the supreme welfare, that is, for Nibbāna.
Thus, having spoken this Dhamma of the scriptures—which is like a forest thicket with its tops in full bloom—the Blessed One now [proceeded] with that very same...

Relying upon the Buddha’s resolve, he utters the word of truth: “This too is in the Buddha. Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. However, it should be applied thus:

“This jewel of the Buddha—consisting of the Dhamma of the scriptures (pariyatti-dhamma) of the aforementioned kind—is sublime. In this verse as well, the command extends throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).
"Accepted by non-human beings.
Thus, having spoken the truth concerning the Buddha through the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*), the Blessed One now [speaks] through the supramundane Dhamma (*lokuttara-dhamma*).

He began to speak: “The Excellent One, the Knower of the Excellent. In this context, “the Excellent One” (*vara*) refers to that which is desired by those inclined toward the sublime, thinking, “Oh, may we too become like this!
Alternatively, it means “the Excellent One” in the sense of being supreme and best because of his possession of excellent qualities. “Knower of the Excellent” (*varaññū*) means the knower of Nibbāna.
For Nibbāna is the “Excellent” among all phenomena in the sense of being the highest; and this [Buddha] himself, at the foot of the Bodhi tree—

Having penetrated [the truth], he realized it. "Varado" means the giver of the excellent Dhamma—pertaining to penetration and pertaining to purification—to the group of five, the group of thirty, the matted-hair ascetics, and other gods and humans.
He is called "Varāharo" because he has brought forth the excellent Path (varassa maggassa āhaṭattā).
For that Blessed One, from the time of Dīpaṅkara onwards, was fulfilling the thirty perfections (pāramīs).
He brought forth the ancient, supreme path followed by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past; therefore, he is called "Varāhara" (the Bringer of the Supreme).
Furthermore, he is "Vara" because of his attainment of omniscience; "Varaññu" because of his realization of Nibbāna; "Varada" because of his bestowing the bliss of liberation upon sentient beings;
and "Varāhara" because of his bringing forth the supreme practice. There is no one superior to him in these supramundane qualities.
He is "unsurpassed" (anuttara) because of the absence of any superior quality. Another method:
he is "excellent" (vara) through the fulfillment of the foundation of tranquility; "knower of the excellent" (varaññū) through the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom;

"giver of the excellent" (varada) through the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity; "receiver of the excellent" (varāhara) through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth; and he "brought forth" (āhari) the excellent Truth of the Path.
Likewise, he is excellent (*vara*) by virtue of his abundance of merit; he is a knower of the excellent (*varaññū*) by virtue of his abundance of wisdom;

he is a giver of the excellent (*varada*) to those desiring Buddhahood by providing them with the means thereto; he is a taker of the excellent (*varāhara*) to those desiring the state of a Paccekabuddha by taking away the obstacles thereto;

he is unsurpassed (*anuttara*) because of his peerlessness in various respects, or because, being himself without a teacher, he acts as a teacher to others; and he taught the excellent Dhamma (*dhammavara*) to those desiring the state of a disciple.
It is for that purpose, because of the teaching of the sublime Dhamma endowed with qualities such as being well-expounded. The rest is according to the method already stated.

Thus, having described his own quality by means of the ninefold supramundane Dhamma, the Blessed One now, relying on that very quality, utters a word of truth (saccavacana) based on the Buddha: "Idampi buddhe" (This too is in the Buddha). Its meaning is as follows: [as previously stated...]
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. However, it should be applied in this way:
"The jewel of the Buddha is sublime because he has realized the supramundane Dhamma which is excellent, because he gave [it], because he brought [it] forth, and because he taught [it].
Furthermore, the command of this verse was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
Commentary on the Khīṇāsavagāthā 15.
Thus, having spoken the truth based upon the Dhamma of the scriptures and the ninefold supramundane Dhamma by means of two verses, establishing the theme of the Buddha,
the Blessed One now [speaks] regarding those who heard that Dhamma of the scriptures and followed it according to what was heard.
And having practiced accordingly, they attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma;

relying on their quality of having reached Nibbāna without residue, he again began to speak the Truth with reference to the Saṅgha, saying: "The old is destroyed. Therein, "destroyed" (khīṇa) means cut off.
"The old" (purāṇa) means that which is ancient. "The new" (nava) means that which is currently occurring. "There is no further becoming" (natthi sambhava).
"Non-manifestation of what does not exist. "With minds detached" means with minds free from lust. "In future existence" means in a renewed birth in a future period.
"They" refers to those for whom the old is exhausted and there is no new becoming, and who have minds detached from future existence;
these are the bhikkhus whose taints are destroyed. "With seeds destroyed" means with their seeds cut off. "Without desire for growth" means devoid of the desire for growth.
"They go out" means they are extinguished. "The wise" means those endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*). "Just as this lamp": it is like this lamp.

What is meant? That ancient, past karma of sentient beings, which has arisen and ceased, yet remains undestroyed because the moisture of craving has not been abandoned and is thus capable of bringing about rebirth—that ancient [karma]...

The karma of those [Arahants] has been exhausted by the path of Arahantship because the moisture of craving has been dried up; thus, like a seed burnt by fire, it is incapable of yielding a result in the future.
Furthermore, the karma that is currently arising for them through such acts as worshiping the Buddha is called "new";
yet even this is incapable of yielding a fruit in the future because the root of craving has been severed, just like the flower of a tree whose roots have been cut.
Those for whom there is no further arising, and whose minds have become dispassionate toward future existence through the very abandoning of craving—
those bhikkhus with taints destroyed are "those whose seed is destroyed," because the rebirth-linking consciousness mentioned here as "kamma is the field,
consciousness is the seed" has been destroyed by the destruction of kamma. As for the desire that previously existed for growth in the form of renewed existence...
It was so. Because it has been abandoned precisely through the abandoning of its origin, it does not exist at the time of death as it did before;

thus, due to the absence of desire for growth and because they are endowed with steadfastness (*dhiti*), these wise ones (*dhīrā*)—with the cessation of the final consciousness—extinguish like this lamp that has gone out.
They do not again enter the path of conceptual designation (*paññatti-patha*) such as "possessing form" or "formless," and so forth. At that time, it is said...
When the lamps were lit for the purpose of worshipping the city deities, one lamp went out;
showing this, he said, "Just as this lamp.
Thus the Blessed One [spoke] regarding those who heard the Dhamma of the scriptures mentioned in the two preceding verses, following what they had heard.

Having practiced accordingly, they attained the ninefold supramundane Dhamma; having spoken of their quality of attaining Nibbāna without residue (*anupādisesa-nibbāna*), he now concluded the teaching with the words, "This too is in the Saṅgha," while employing a declaration of truth (*saccavacana*) based on that very quality.
Its meaning is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained; however, only...
This too should be connected thus: "In this manner, the jewel of the Saṅgha—consisting of bhikkhus whose taints are exhausted and known as Nibbāna—is sublime.
Furthermore, the command of this verse was received by non-human beings throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of world-systems.
At the conclusion of the teaching, there was safety for the royal family; all calamities were pacified, and eighty-four thousand living beings attained realization of the Dhamma.
Commentary on the Three Verses Beginning with *Yāni-dhātī*: 16.
Then Sakka, Lord of the Devas, thought: "The Blessed One has ensured the safety of the city by employing a declaration of truth based on the virtues of the Triple Gem;
I too, for the sake of the city's safety, [shall do likewise] based on the virtues of the Triple Gem."
Thinking, "It must be spoken," he recited at the conclusion three verses beginning with "Whatever beings there are here. In this context,
because the Buddha has come just as one should come when those intent on the welfare of the world have exerted themselves,
and because he has gone just as they should go, and because he has understood just as they should understand, and because—
He is called "Tathāgata" because he knows things as they truly are, and because he speaks exactly according to how things are. Furthermore,
because he is exceedingly honored by gods and humans with external offerings such as flowers and perfumes, as well as by internal practices such as the practice in accordance with the Dhamma,
he is like Sakka, the lord of the gods, who [surpassed] the entire assembly of deities with himself.
Combining these together, he said: “To the Tathāgata, worshipped by gods and humans, to the Buddha, let us pay homage; may there be well-being.

Furthermore, regarding the Dhamma: it is called the *Tathāgata* because the path-dhamma has gone (*gata*) in such a way—that is, by one who must proceed by means of the power of the pair consisting of serenity and insight (*yuganaddha-samatha-vipassanā*), cutting off the side of the defilements. The *Nibbāna*-dhamma also has gone in such a way.
When penetrated by wisdom, it leads to the destruction of all suffering;

because he has understood it in that way, as realized by the Buddhas and others, he is therefore called "Tathāgata. Furthermore, because the Saṅgha also has gone (gata) by those various paths in the same manner as those practicing for their own benefit must go, he is therefore called "Tathāgata. Therefore, in the remaining two verses as well—
"It is said: 'We pay homage to the Tathāgata and the Dhamma; may there be well-being! We pay homage to the Tathāgata and the Saṅgha; may there be well-being!
The remainder is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, having spoken these three verses, Sakka, lord of the gods, circumambulated the Blessed One and returned to the city of the gods.
He departed together with the assembly of devas. The Blessed One, however, taught that same Ratana Sutta on the second day as well;
again, there was a penetration of the Dhamma for eighty-four thousand living beings.
He taught it in this manner until the seventh day, and on each successive day, there was likewise a penetration of the Dhamma. The Blessed One remained at Vesālī for exactly half a month.

Having stayed there, he informed the kings, "Let us go. Then the kings, with double the honor, led the Blessed One back to the bank of the Ganges in three days. The Nāga kings born in the Ganges thought, "The humans are paying honor to the Tathāgata;
why should we not do so? and [prepared] boats made of gold, silver, and jewels.

Having had thrones made of gold, silver, and jewels prepared, and having filled the water with a covering of five-colored lotuses, they entreated the Blessed One, saying, "Please show us your favor. The Blessed One consented;
he boarded a ship of jewels, and five hundred bhikkhus boarded five hundred ships. The nāga kings—
They led the Blessed One, together with the community of monks, into the abode of the nāgas. There, the Blessed One indeed taught the Dhamma to the assembly of nāgas throughout the entire night.
On the following day, they offered a great almsgiving of divine hard and soft foods;
the Blessed One, having expressed his appreciation, departed from the nāga abode.
The earth-dwelling deities thought, "Since humans and nāgas are paying honor to the Tathāgata, why should we not do so?
Having thus reflected, they raised parasols and super-parasols upon the forest thickets, trees, mountains, and other features.
By this very means, a magnificent distinction of great honor was established as far as the Akaniṭṭha Brahma-abode. King Bimbisāra, along with the Licchavis...
When he arrived, he performed double the honors he had previously shown. Just as described before, he conducted the Blessed One to Rājagaha over the course of five days.
When the Blessed One had reached Rājagaha, after the meal, while the monks were assembled in the pavilion, this discussion arose among them:
"Oh, how great is the power of the Buddha, the Blessed One, that on whose account [the people] from the near side of the Ganges..."
"And for eight yojanas on all sides, having leveled the ground—both lowlands and highlands—and strewn it with sand, it was covered with flowers;
the waters of the Ganges for a distance of one yojana were covered with lotuses of various colors;
and from there up to the Akaniṭṭha realm, parasols and double-parasols were raised on high. The Blessed One, having understood this occurrence, said:
Having emerged from the Fragrant Chamber, the Blessed One proceeded by means of a miracle appropriate for that moment and sat down upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the circular pavilion.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you seated here at present?
The bhikkhus reported everything to the Blessed One, and the Blessed One said this: "Bhikkhus, this particular offering is not..."
“It was reborn through the power of my own merit, not through the power of the nāgas, devas, or brahmās;
rather, it was reborn through the power of a small gift given in the past. The bhikkhus said, “We do not know, venerable sir, what that small gift was.
It would be well if the Blessed One would tell us so that we might know it.”
The Blessed One said: "In the past, monks, there was a brahmin named Saṅkha in Takkasilā.
He had a son, a young brahmin student named Susīma, sixteen years of age.
One day, he approached his father, paid homage to him, and stood to one side. Then his father said to him, 'What is it, dear Susīma? He replied, 'I wish, father..."
“Father, go to Bārāṇasī and learn a craft. “In that case, dear Susīma, there is a brahmin named so-and-so who is my friend;
go to him and learn from him,” he said, and gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas.
Taking that money, he paid homage to his parents and, traveling by stages, arrived at Bārāṇasī according to the proper etiquette for visitors.
Having approached the teacher and paid homage, he introduced himself.
The teacher, recognizing him as "the son of my friend," accepted the young man and performed all the duties of hospitality.
Once he had dispelled the fatigue of the journey, he placed the thousand kahāpaṇas at the teacher’s feet and requested permission to learn the craft. The teacher—
Having made the opportunity, he caused him to learn.

Learning both quickly and extensively, and retaining each thing learned without loss—just like oil poured into a golden vessel—he brought the twelve-year craft to completion in only a few months. He...
While reciting his lesson, he saw only the beginning and the middle, but not the end.
Then, having approached his teacher, he said, "I see only the beginning and the middle of this craft, but not its conclusion. The teacher replied, "I too, my son, am exactly like that.
He then asked, "Teacher, who then knows the conclusion of this craft? [The teacher replied: "At Isipatana..."
"Father, there are seers; they might know," he said. "I shall go to them and ask, Teacher? "Ask, my son, as you please.
He went to Isipatana, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, "Venerable sirs, do you know the conclusion?
"Yes, friend, we know it. "Then teach it to me as well. "In that case, friend—"
“Go forth; it is not possible for one who has not gone forth to train. “Very well, venerable sirs, let me go forth, or having done whatever you wish, let me know the conclusion.

Having ordained him, they were unable to direct him to a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), so they [instructed him] on the higher conduct (ābhisamācārika) in such a manner as: “It should be worn thus; it should be put on thus,” and so forth.
They trained him. While training there, because he was endowed with the necessary spiritual potential (*upanissaya*), he soon attained the enlightenment of a *paccekabuddha*.
Throughout all of Benares, he became renowned as "Susīma the *Paccekabuddha*," reaching the pinnacle of gain and fame and surrounded by a complete retinue.
Because he had performed an action conducive to a short lifespan, he passed away into final *parinibbāna* before long.
The Paccekabuddhas and the great multitude of people, having performed the funeral rites for his body and taken the relics,
established a stupa at the city gate.
Then the brahmin Saṅkha, thinking, "My son has been gone for a long time, and I do not know his fate," desired to see his son.
Having departed from Takkasilā and traveling by stages to Bārāṇasī, he saw a great multitude of people gathered together.
Thinking, "Surely among so many, there might be one who knows news of my son," he approached them and asked:
"Is there a young brahmin named Susīma who has come here? Do you perhaps know his whereabouts? They replied, "Yes."

"Brāhmaṇa, we know," they said, "that in this city there was one who, having mastered the three Vedas in the presence of a brāhmaṇa, went forth in the presence of paccekabuddhas, became a paccekabuddha, and attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue;
this stupa has been erected for him. He then struck the ground with his hand.
Having wept and lamented, he went to that cetiya courtyard, cleared away the grass, brought sand in his upper robe,
and scattered it over the courtyard of the Paccekabuddha’s cetiya. He sprinkled water from his water-pot all over the ground,
made an offering with wild forest flowers, and hoisted a banner of his upper robe atop the stupa.
“Having fastened his own sunshade, he departed.
Having thus related the past, he concluded the Jātaka by connecting it with the present and spoke this Dhamma discourse to the bhikkhus:
“It may be, bhikkhus, that you might think: ‘Perhaps Saṅkha the brahmin at that time was someone else.’”
But this should not be viewed in such a way. At that time, I was the brahmin Saṅkha.

I cleared away the grass from the courtyard of the shrine of the Paccekabuddha Susīma; as a result of that deed, they made the road for eight yojanas level and pure, removing all stumps and thorns. I scattered sand there, and as a result of that—
As a result of that, they scattered sand over a road eight *yojanas* long.
Because I performed an offering there with forest flowers, as a result of that, they created a carpet of various flowers on both land and water along a road nine *yojanas* long.
Because I sprinkled the ground there with water from my water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), as a result of that, there was a rain of lotuses in Vesālī.
It rained. I had hoisted a banner upon that cetiya and fixed a parasol there;
as a result of that, banners have been hoisted and parasols and super-parasols raised all the way up to the Akaniṭṭha realm.
Thus, monks, this particular excellence of my worship was produced neither by the power of the Buddhas, nor by the power of the nāgas, devas, or brahmās.
"Furthermore, it was produced by the power of giving up a mere trifle. At the conclusion of this discourse on the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:
"If, by giving up a small pleasure, one sees a vast happiness, the wise man should renounce that small pleasure, clearly perceiving the vast happiness."
The commentary on the Ratana Sutta in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*, is completed. 7.
The commentary on the *Tirokuṭṭa Sutta*.
The Purpose of its Placement:

Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the meaning of the *Tirokuṭṭa-sutta*, which was placed immediately after the *Ratana-sutta* with the words, "They stand beyond the walls," and so forth. Having stated the purpose for its placement here, we shall provide the commentary on its meaning.
In this regard, although this *Tirokuṭṭa-sutta* was not spoken by the Blessed One in this specific sequence, it was previously taught in various ways.

The practice of wholesome deeds has been demonstrated; therein, for the purpose of showing that one who falls into negligence— even if reborn in a place superior to the realms of hell or the animal womb—
will nevertheless be reborn among such *petas*, and therefore one must not be negligent here,
as well as for the purpose of pacifying the calamities of Vesālī which were afflicted by those spirits, the *Ratana-sutta* [was spoken].
It has been stated; or rather, it is stated for the purpose of showing that among those [passages], some are of such a nature.
This should be understood as the reason for its placement here.
The Discourse on Rejoicing (Anumodanākathā).
Furthermore, its commentary on the meaning is as follows:
“By whom, where, when, and why— The wall-penetrating [power] was manifested;
Having explained all of that in due order, [The commentary] is now being composed.”
"It is well done; therefore, I shall do exactly that.
But by whom was this proclaimed, where, when, and for what reason? It is said:
it was proclaimed by the Blessed One at Rājagaha on the second day, for the purpose of offering a blessing to the King of Māgadha. This is the meaning of this [passage].
To illustrate the meaning of "elimination" (vibhāvana), this detailed exposition should be told here:
Ninety-two aeons ago, there was a city named Kāsi. There, a king named Jayasena reigned.
He had a queen named Sirimā, and in her womb the Bodhisatta named Phussa was conceived; subsequently, he attained full enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).
He attained full enlightenment. King Jayasena, having conceived the sense of possessiveness, thinking, "My son has gone forth and become a Buddha;
the Buddha is mine alone, the Dhamma is mine, the Saṅgha is mine," attended upon him himself at all times and gave no opportunity to others.
The three uterine half-brothers of the Blessed One, who were his younger brothers, thought:
"Buddhas indeed arise for the welfare of the entire world, not for the sake of a single person alone; yet our father gives no opportunity to others.
How then might we obtain the chance to attend upon the Blessed One? It occurred to them: "Come now, let us [do something]..."
“Let us employ a stratagem,” they said. They caused the border region to be made as if it were in rebellion.
Then the king, hearing that “the border is in revolt,” dispatched his three sons to pacify the border. Having pacified it, they returned;
the king was pleased and granted them a boon, saying, “Take whatever you wish. They replied, “We wish to attend upon the Blessed One.”
They said. The king said, “Set this aside and take another. They said, “We have no need for anything else.
[The king said,] “In that case, take it after making a limit. They requested seven years; the king did not grant it.
Likewise six, five, four, three, two, one; seven months, six, five, four—down to...
They requested three months. The king said, “Take them,” and gave his consent.
Having received the boon, they were exceedingly joyful; they approached the Blessed One, paid homage, and said:
“Venerable sir, we wish to attend upon the Blessed One for three months; may the Blessed One grant us this favor.”
“Let us spend the three-month rains retreat here. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Thereupon, they sent a letter to an official in their own country, saying:
“The Blessed One is to be attended upon by us for these three months;
starting with the construction of a monastery, provide everything necessary for the Blessed One’s service. That official prepared all of it and reported back to them. They—
Having dressed themselves in saffron robes, they respectfully attended upon the Blessed One with two thousand five hundred male servants;
then, leading him to the countryside and having presented him with a monastery, they settled him there.
