Among them was a treasurer’s son, a householder, who together with his wife was faithful and possessed serene confidence. He [attended] the community headed by the Buddha...

He respectfully gave what was to be given to the Saṅgha. An official appointed in the countryside took that [gift] and, together with eleven thousand men from the countryside, caused the gift to be distributed with due respect.
Among them, some of the countrymen had hostile minds; having created an obstacle to the gift, they consumed the things to be given themselves.

And they burned the refectory with fire. When the invitation was concluded, the princes, having paid great honor to the Blessed One, placed the Blessed One at their head and went back to their father's presence. It was there, upon arriving, that the Blessed One passed into final nibbāna.
The king, the princes, the official appointed over the countryside, and the treasurer all passed away in due course.
Having done so, they were reborn together with their retinue in the heavenly realms, while those whose minds were obstructed were reborn in the hells.
Thus, as these two groups passed from heaven to heaven and from hell to hell, ninety-two eons elapsed.
Then, in this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, those people with obstructed minds were reborn among the hungry ghosts (petas).
At that time, people would give gifts for the sake of their deceased relatives and dedicate them, saying, "May this be for our relatives.

Those relatives would then obtain prosperity. Then these other departed spirits (petas), seeing this, approached the Blessed One Kassapa and asked: "Venerable sir, might we too obtain such prosperity?"
The Blessed One said: "You shall not receive them now; however, in the future there will be a Buddha named Gotama.
At the time of that Blessed One, there will be a king named Bimbisāra, who was your kinsman ninety-two aeons ago.
He will give a gift to the Buddha and dedicate it for your sake; then you shall receive them. When this had been said...
It seems that those words spoken to the petas, "You shall receive it tomorrow," were as if they had been uttered [in anticipation].
Then, after one interval between Buddhas had passed, our Blessed One appeared in the world.
Those three princes, together with those two thousand five hundred men, fell from the world of the gods and were reborn in brahmin families in the kingdom of Magadha.
Having been reborn, they eventually went forth as forest recluses (isipabbajjā). At Gayāsīsa, there were three matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila):
one was a man appointed to a district office, one was King Bimbisāra, and the treasurer was a householder named Visākha, who was a great merchant;
his wife was Dhammadinnā, the daughter of a merchant. In this way, all the remaining retinues [were likewise reborn].
They were reborn as the very retinue of the king.
After our Blessed One had appeared in the world and, having passed seven weeks, had gradually arrived at Bārāṇasī and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
starting with the group of five monks, he [was surrounded] by a retinue of two thousand five hundred up to three...

Having instructed Jaṭila, he went to Rājagaha. There, as King Bimbisāra approached him that very day, he established him in the fruit of stream-entry, together with ninety-one Magadhan brahmins and householders.
Then, having been invited by the king for a meal on the following day, the Blessed One consented; on the second day, by Sakka...
As Devānaminda went before him, he proclaimed:
“Tamed together with those formerly matted-hair ascetics who were tamed, liberated together with those who were liberated—
the Blessed One, with the hue of refined gold, has entered Rājagaha.”
Being thus extolled with these verses and other such praises, he entered Rājagaha and accepted a great almsgiving at the king’s residence.
Those hungry ghosts stood surrounding him with the hope, "Now the king will dedicate the gift to us; now he will dedicate it!
Having given the alms, the king thought only of a place for the Blessed One to dwell, wondering, "Where indeed might the Blessed One stay?"
He did not dedicate that gift to anyone. The pretas, their hopes shattered, let out a most terrifying shriek in the king’s palace during the night.
The king fell into a state of fear, agitation, and terror; then, when the night had turned to dawn, he informed the Blessed One:
“I heard such a sound. What, venerable sir, will become of me? The Blessed One—
He said: “Do not fear, Great King; no evil shall befall you.

However, there are some of your ancient kinsmen who have arisen among the *petas*, and for an entire interval between Buddhas they have wandered about hoping for you alone, thinking, ‘Having given a gift to the Buddha, he will dedicate it to us.
You did not dedicate [the merit] to them yesterday; with their hopes cut off, they raised such a cry.”
He said, "But now, venerable sir, if it is given, would they receive it? "Yes, great king," [the Blessed One replied].
"In that case, venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my gift for today; I shall dedicate it to them. The Blessed One consented.
The king went to his residence, prepared a great almsgiving, and had the time announced to the Blessed One. The Blessed One [went] to the royal palace.
Having arrived, he sat down upon the prepared seat together with the community of monks.

Those hungry ghosts, thinking, "Perhaps we might receive something today," went and stood behind walls and other such places. The Blessed One acted in such a way that they all became visible to the king.
As the king was offering the water of dedication, he dedicated it, saying, "May this be for my kinsmen. At that very moment—
For those departed spirits, lotus-covered ponds appeared.
Having bathed and drunk there, their exhaustion, fatigue, and thirst were allayed, and they became golden-hued. The king gave them rice gruel, hard food, and meals, dedicating them;
at that very moment, divine rice gruel, hard food, and meals appeared for them. They [partook of] those...

Having partaken [of the food], their faculties became refreshed. Then, having given them robes and lodgings, he assigned them. For them, divine garments, divine vehicles, divine palaces, divine coverlets, divine beds, and various ornaments appeared.
The Blessed One made a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāsi*) so that their prosperity might become manifest to everyone.
The King was exceedingly delighted. Then, the Blessed One, having finished eating and being invited to do so, for the purpose of giving a blessing (*anumodana*) to the King of Māgadha...
“Standing beyond the walls,” he spoke these verses.
At this point, the matrix—“by whom, where, when, and why the ‘beyond-the-walls’ was proclaimed, having proclaimed all of that”—has been analyzed both in brief and in detail.
[End of] the commentary on the first verse.
1. Now we shall provide a commentary on the meaning of this *Tirokuṭṭa Sutta* in due order. To begin with, in the first verse:
*tirokuṭṭa* refers to the far side of walls. *Tiṭṭhanti* (they stand) is a term for maintaining a standing posture, in the sense of precluding sitting and other such postures.
By this, it is shown that just as one might go to the far side of a rampart or the far side of a mountain...
“They say, ‘He goes unhindered across walls and across mountains’;
so too here, he says ‘standing beyond walls’ regarding those standing on the far side of a wall. And ‘at junctions and crossroads’:
here, ‘junctions’ (sandhi) refers to four-way streets, as well as house-junctions, wall-junctions, and light-shaft openings. ‘Crossroads’ (siṅghāṭaka) refers to...”
“Trikonas” (triangular junctions) are what is meant; having grouped them together with the preceding [term], he said “and at junctions and crossroads.
“Standing by the doorposts” means they stand leaning against the doorposts of city gates or house doors.
Regarding the phrase “having come to their own home,” here “one’s own home” refers to either the former home of one’s kinsmen or that which has been made one’s own through ownership.
Even a house where they have previously lived. Since both of them come with the perception that it is their own home, he says, "Having come to their own home.
This concludes the commentary on the second verse.

2. Thus the Blessed One, having come to the residence of Bimbisāra—the former home of his kinsmen where he had never before stayed—with the perception that it was his own home, saw those standing against the walls, at the junctions, at the crossroads, and by the doorposts, experiencing the fruit of envy and stinginess;
some of them, with long beards and hair in disarray, with darkened faces, their limbs and members loose, hanging, emaciated, rough, and black.
In various places, they resemble palm trees scorched by forest fires;
some have their bodies consumed by flames of fire that, produced by the friction of the sticks of hunger and thirst, rise from their bellies and issue from their mouths;

others, because the cavity of their throats is as small as the eye of a needle and their bellies are as vast as mountains, cannot consume even when they obtain food and drink to their heart's content.
Showing the king many hungry ghosts (petas) with bodies that were extremely hideous, deformed, and terrifying— unable to eat due to their incapacity,
tormented by hunger and thirst, finding no other flavor, and some of them, having obtained the pus, blood,
and lymph trickling from each other’s or other beings’ burst boils and pustules, tasting it as if it were nectar— he said:
Having said, "They stand at the outer walls, at the junctions and crossroads,
and they stand by the doorposts, having come to their own homes," he then spoke the second verse,
beginning with "Amidst abundant food and drink," to demonstrate the cruelty of the deed committed by them.
In that context, *pahūte* means "not small," "abundant," or "as much as desired" (*yāvad-atthika*).
For the substitution of the letter *ha* for the letter *bha* occurs, as in such examples as *pahu santo na bharati*. Some, however, read it as *bahūte* and *bahūke*;
these are merely scribal errors. *Anne ca pānamhi ca* means "in food and drink. *Khajje ca bhojje* [means "in hard food and soft food"].
"And chewables and edibles"—by this he shows the fourfold food by way of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted.
"Set out" means standing near; it is said to mean prepared, arranged, and placed ready.
"None of them remembers them, [namely] beings"—none of those beings born in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) remembers them, whether mother, father, or son. Why?

What is the cause? It is due to the condition of karma; specifically, it is due to the condition of miserly karma—such as the withholding of gifts or the refusal to give—which was committed by oneself.
For that karma does not allow those relatives to remember [the deceased].
Commentary on the Third Stanza.
3. Thus, even when abundant food, drink, and other requisites were presented, the Blessed One—

showing that among those departed ones who wander about hoping for their relatives, thinking, "Perhaps they will give something intended for us," there was not even the slightest recollection on the part of any relative regarding the karma they had committed which results in extremely bitter retribution— said:
“Though abundant food and drink, and various kinds of solid and soft foods are set before them,
no one remembers those beings because of the condition of their own karma.

Having said this, he then spoke the third verse, “Thus do they give for their relatives,” praising the gift given on behalf of the king’s kinsmen who had been reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya).
In this context, "evam" (thus) is a word of comparison. Its connection is twofold:
[it refers to] those beings who, even when not being reminded, give to certain relatives out of the condition of their past karma;

and it refers to those who are compassionate in this way, thinking, "Just as you, O Great King, have given, so do they give pure, excellent, timely, and permissible food and drink to their relatives. Those who are thus...
"And compassionate" means: "giving" means they give, dedicate, and bestow. "Of kinsmen" means of those related through the mother’s side and the father’s side.
"Whoever" means whoever they may be—sons, daughters, or brothers. "Compassionate" means desiring their welfare and seeking their benefit.
"Pure" means stainless, beautiful to behold, pleasing to the mind, righteous, and acquired in accordance with the Dhamma.
"Exquisite" (*paṇīta*) means supreme and best. "At the proper time" (*kālena*) means at the time when the departed relatives have come and are standing beyond the walls and so forth.
"Suitable" (*kappiya*) means appropriate, fitting, and worthy of being used by the Noble Ones (*ariya*).
"Drink and food" (*pānabhojana*) refers to both drink and food; here, by way of drink and food, all things that may be given are intended.
Commentary on the First Half of the Fourth Stanza: 4.
Thus the Blessed One, praising the food and drink given by the King of Magadha out of compassion for his kinsmen who had become ghosts, said:
“Thus do those who are compassionate give to their kinsmen;”
Having said, "Pure, excellent, timely, and permissible food and drink," he spoke the first half of the fourth verse—
*“This be for your relatives!”*— to show the manner in which what is given becomes theirs, connecting it with the first half of the third verse:
“Thus do those who are compassionate give to their relatives;”
“May this be for your relatives; may your relatives be happy.

In this regard, by the word *evaṃ* (thus) used in the sense of manner, an illustration of the manner in which the gift should be given is made, namely: “They give in this way, saying ‘May this be for your relatives,’ and not otherwise.
Therein, *idaṃ* (this) is an indication of the object to be given. *Vo* (to you) is as in the passage: “But are you, Anuruddhas, living in harmony, in mutual affection?”
In such expressions as “yehi vo ariyā,” the word *ca* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*), not a genitive case ending.

“May it be for kinsmen” means may it be for those kinsmen who have arisen in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*). “May kinsmen be happy” means may those kinsmen born in the realm of hungry ghosts be happy while experiencing this [merit].
Commentary on the Second Half of the Fourth Stanza and the First Half of the Fifth Stanza (4–5).
Thus, the Blessed One, showing the manner in which what is to be given should be offered to relatives reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*), said:
"May this be for your relatives; may your relatives be happy. Furthermore, because [he said]: "May this be for your relatives..."
Even when it is said, "Let it be so," an action performed by one person does not yield its fruit to another;
rather, that object being given specifically for their sake becomes a condition for the wholesome karma of those relatives.
Therefore, showing how wholesome karma produces its fruit for them at that very moment regarding that same object, he says: "And they there..."
He spoke the second half of the fourth verse and the first half of the fifth verse, beginning with “When there is abundant food and drink.
Their meaning is as follows: those deceased relatives come from all directions and gather together—meaning they assemble or come together as one—at the place where that gift is being given;
having thus properly arrived and assembled, [they think], “These are our relatives, for us...”
"Having come properly for the purpose of designating the gift for the welfare [of others]"—this is what is meant.
"When there is abundant food and drink" means when that food and drink is being designated for oneself and it is abundant.

"They express gratitude with care" means having full faith in the fruit of karma, not neglecting the result of action, and with a mind of reverence and undistracted thought, they say: "This gift of ours..."
"May it be for their welfare and happiness"—thus they rejoice and offer their appreciation, becoming filled with rapture and gladness.
This concludes the commentary on the fifth verse and the first half of the sixth verse.
Thus the Blessed One, demonstrating how wholesome karma that produces fruit at that very moment exists for those reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, said:
Having said, “And those departed relatives who have gathered there,
amidst an abundance of food and drink, will properly offer their thanks,” he further spoke concerning those relatives,
regarding the experience of the fruit of wholesome kamma produced by depending upon them:

Demonstrating the manner of praise, he spoke the second half of the fifth verse, beginning with “May they live long,” and the first half of the sixth verse, beginning with “And the honor rendered to us.
Their meaning is as follows: “May they live long” means may they be long-lived and possess a long lifespan. “Our kinsmen” (no ñātī) means our relatives.

"Of whom [is it] the cause? means by depending on whom, for whose sake. "We receive" (*labhāmasa*) means we obtain. They speak while referring to the prosperity obtained by themselves at that very moment.

For the offering (*dakkhiṇā*) succeeds through three factors: by the deceased's own act of rejoicing (*anumodana*), by the donors' dedication (*uddesa*), and by the excellence of those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya-sampadā*);
thus, it becomes productive of fruit at that very moment. In this regard, the donors...
It is a specific cause. Therefore they said, "We receive [this] because of you.
And by those who dedicate this gift while saying, "This is for your relatives," honoring has been performed toward us as well. Furthermore, the givers are not without fruit;
since the karma consisting of the act of relinquishment is performed within a particular mental continuum, it yields its fruit right there, and thus the givers are not without fruit.
Here it is asked: "Do only relatives reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts receive [offerings], or do others receive them as well?
It is replied: This has been explained by the Blessed One himself when questioned by the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi;
what need is there for us to say anything more on this matter? For it has been said:
“Master Gotama, we brahmins give gifts and perform acts of faith, saying:
‘May this gift benefit our deceased relatives and kin; may our deceased relatives and kin enjoy this gift.
Does that gift, Master Gotama, actually benefit the deceased relatives and kin? Do those deceased relatives and kin [indeed receive it]?”
“They enjoy that gift. “In this case, Brahmin, it is appropriate in one instance, but not in another.
“But what, Master Gotama, is that appropriate instance, and what is the inappropriate one? “In this case, Brahmin, someone is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...he holds wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in hell. It is in such a case that it is not appropriate.”
Whatever is the food of beings in hell, by that he sustains himself there, by that he remains there.
This, brahmin, is the situation where, for one who stands therein, that gift does not benefit them.
But here, brahmin, someone is a destroyer of life... [as before] ...he holds wrong view; such a person, upon the dissolution of the body...
After death, he is reborn in the animal realm. There, he subsists on whatever food animals of the animal realm eat;
there, he persists by means of that. This too, brahmin, is an impossible situation where, for one who has taken his stand therein, that gift does not benefit him.
“But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he holds right view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of human beings... or he is reborn in the company of devas.
Whatever is the food of the devas, by that he sustains himself there; by that he remains there. This too...”
“Brahmin, it is impossible that for one standing in such a state, that gift would be of benefit.
On the other hand, Brahmin, suppose someone here is a destroyer of life... [and so on] ...up to... he holds wrong view;
with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya). Whatever food there is for beings in the realm of hungry ghosts, by that...”

He sustains himself there; by that he remains there. Or else, whatever they send to him from here—whether friends, companions, relatives, or kinsmen—he sustains himself there; by that he remains there.
This, brahmin, is the situation in which, for one who stands therein, that gift is beneficial.
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased kinsman has not been reborn in that place, who then enjoys that gift?
“Brahmin, there are other deceased kinsmen of his who have been reborn in that place;
they enjoy that gift.”
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased kinsman has not been reborn in that place,
and other deceased kinsmen of his have also not been reborn in that place, who then consumes that gift? “Brahmin, it is impossible and there is no occasion for it that,
throughout this long stretch of time, that place should remain devoid of those [beings].”
“...by their departed kinsmen and blood relations. Moreover, O Brahmin, even the donor is not without fruit.
This concludes the commentary on the sixth verse and the beginning of the seventh verse.

Thus, the Blessed One, praising King Māgadha by way of the prosperity of his deceased kinsmen reborn in the realm of the *petas*, showed him: “Great King, these are your kinsmen; they are delighted by this perfection of giving and praise it thus.”
“May our kinsmen live long, for whose sake we receive [this offering];
may the honor rendered to us be made, and may the donors not be without fruit.
Having said this, he further spoke regarding another cause for those reborn in the realm of the hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) to obtain prosperity, such as agriculture, cattle-rearing, and so forth.

Demonstrating that there is no existence [of food] here through what is given, and showing the state of mere subsistence, he spoke the second half of the sixth verse, "For there is no plowing there," and this seventh verse, "Nor is there such trade.
Herein is the commentary on the meaning: "Indeed, Great King, in that realm of the *petas* there is no plowing, depending upon which..."

Those hungry ghosts (petas) might obtain prosperity. "Cattle-herding does not exist here" means that not only agriculture, but cattle-herding as well does not exist here in this realm of hungry ghosts, which they might rely upon to obtain prosperity.
"Trade of such a kind does not exist" means that even trade of such a kind does not exist, which could serve as a cause for their obtaining prosperity. [Regarding] gold...
They do not buy or sell with gold; there is nothing of that kind there which could serve as a cause for their obtaining prosperity.

They subsist on what is given from here. "The departed who have passed away there"—this means they merely subsist and maintain their individual existence on what is given from here by kinsmen or friends and associates.
"The departed" (petā) refers to beings reborn in the realm of the departed (pettivisaya). "Who have passed away" (kālagatā) means...
"Passed away at the time of their own death"—or alternatively, the reading is "kālakatā," meaning those whose time has come, those who have met their end. "Tahin" means in that realm of the *petas*.
Commentary on the Eighth and Ninth Couplets of Verses (8–9):

Having thus stated, "The deceased *petas* there subsist on what is given from here," he now speaks this pair of verses beginning with "Water rained upon a height" in order to clarify that matter through similes.

The meaning of this is as follows: just as water rained down by clouds upon a high plateau or elevated ground flows toward the lowlands—flowing, moving toward, and reaching whatever part of the ground is low and sloping—in the very same way, a gift given from here benefits the departed (petas);
that is to say, it comes into being for them and manifests. For it is just like the lowland.

The realm of the departed (petaloka) is the place for the flow of water; it is the place for the preparation of gifts. As it is said: "This, brahmin, is the place where, for one who stands there, that gift is effective.

And just as rivers carrying water, filled by the convergence of mountain clefts, gullies, branches, sub-branches, small pools, and great pools, fill the ocean, so too does the gift given from here [fill the world of the departed] in the manner previously described.
"It is beneficial for the *petas*.
This concludes the commentary on the tenth verse.
Thus, by means of similes, the Blessed One [established] this meaning: "The *petas* who have passed away there subsist on what is given from here."
Having thus explained this, he spoke the verse beginning with "He gave to me" to show that a clansman should give a gift while recollecting these objects of recollection for those hungry ghosts;
for although they have come to their kinsmen's homes overcome by the hope, "We shall receive something from here," they are unable to say, "Give us such-and-such.
Therefore, a clansman should give a gift while recollecting these specific bases for recollection on their behalf.
The meaning of this is as follows: [one regards someone] as "wealth" or "grain" because they gave such-and-such to me;
as "a task" because they undertook it for me by exerting themselves; as "a relative" because they are a kinsman on my mother’s or father’s side;
as a "friend" because of their capacity to provide refuge through affection; and as "such-and-such a companion" because he was a playmate with me in the dust.
And thus, recollecting all [the ancestors] in this way, one should give a gift (dakkhiṇa) to the departed (petā); the gift should be offered. Another reading is: “petānaṃ dakkhiṇā dajjā.
Its meaning is as follows: “dajjā” means “one should give. What is it that should be given? It is the offering (dakkhiṇā) to the departed.
Therefore, it is said that one should recollect what was done previously according to the method beginning with “He gave to me,” and so forth. This occurs in the context of the instrumental case.
The singular number is to be understood.
Thus, in the eleventh verse commentary,
the Blessed One, demonstrating the bases for recollection that serve as the causes for the dedication of offerings to the departed (*peta*), said:
“‘He gave to me, he did for me; my kinsmen, friends, and companions—may one give an offering for the sake of the departed, recollecting what was done in the past.
Having said this, [the Buddha] further addressed those who, having lost a kinsman, remain solely intent on weeping, grieving, and so forth, and do not act for their benefit.

Showing that when they give anything, their weeping, sorrow, and so forth result only in self-torment and do not accomplish any benefit for the *petas*, he spoke this verse beginning with "For neither weeping... (*na hi ruṇṇaṃ vā*).
Therein, "weeping" (*ruṇṇa*) means crying, the state of having cried, or the shedding of tears; by this, he indicates physical exhaustion. "Sorrow" (*soka*)...
"Socanā" (sorrowing) and "socitattaṃ" (the state of being sorrowful): by this, he shows the exhaustion of the mind. "Yā caññā" (and whatever else):
that which is other than weeping and lamentation. "Paridevanā" (lamentation): the wailing of one afflicted by the loss of kinsmen;
the extolling of virtues in such a manner as, "Where, O my only son, dear and beloved? By this, he shows the exhaustion of speech.
Commentary on the Twelfth Verse (12):
Thus the Blessed One [taught] that "weeping, sorrow, and whatever other lamentations there may be—all these do not benefit the departed;
they are merely a source of self-torment for those who remain as kinsmen. This refers to weeping and the rest.

Having shown the state of being useless [of the previous offerings], and now showing the state of being purposeful regarding the offering given by the King of Māgadha, he spoke this verse beginning with “And yet this offering.
Its meaning is as follows: “And yet, Great King, this offering which you have given today on behalf of your own circle of kinsmen—”
Because the Saṅgha is the unsurpassed field of merit for the world, therefore, when one is well-established in the Saṅgha, it conduces to the welfare of the departed being for a long night;
it is said that it "succeeds" and "bears fruit. And as for the phrase "it conduces":
it conduces immediately upon the occasion; it conduces at that very moment, not after a long time. For just as [the seed] at that very moment...
When something occurs immediately, it is said, "It occurs to the Tathāgata at that very moment";
likewise here too, things that become available at that very instant are said to "become available at that moment. Or rather, regarding what was said:

"This, brahmin, is the occasion where, for one standing upon it, that gift becomes effective"—therein, among those divided into various classes such as the hungry, the thirsty, those living on scraps, those subsisting on what is given by others, those with parched craving, and so forth—
"It is beneficial in its proper place" means that just as one who gives a kahāpaṇa coin is said in the world "he gives by the kahāpaṇa," so it is here.
And in this interpretation of the meaning, "it is beneficial" (upakappati) means it manifests or arises.
Commentary on the Thirteenth Stanza.
13. Thus the Blessed One, demonstrating the beneficial nature of the offering given by the king, said:
“This offering, when given, is well-established in the Saṅgha;
it conduces to his welfare for a long time and is immediately effective.”
Furthermore, having said this, because this duty toward relatives (*ñātidhamma*)—
consisting in performing the services that must be performed by relatives for one another— was demonstrated, made manifest, or illustrated by the giver of this offering,
you too must fulfill the duty toward relatives in the same way by performing the services that must be performed by relatives for one another, and not in vain.
By saying "one's own self must be tormented by weeping and so forth," one honors the departed with a sublime offering through their attainment of divine prosperity;
and by satisfying the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with food, drink, and other requisites, one bestows strength upon the monks;
and by generating the volition of generosity accompanied by qualities such as compassion, one produces no small merit.
Because merit has been performed, the Blessed One, gladdening the king with these qualities as they truly are,
said: "Thus this duty toward kinsmen has been demonstrated,
and a sublime offering has been made to the departed."
"And strength has been bestowed upon the monks;
by you, no small merit has been set flowing.
With this verse, he brought the teaching to its conclusion.
Alternatively, with this verse-line, “And thus this duty toward kinsmen has been demonstrated,” the Blessed One instructs the king with a discourse on the Dhamma.
For here, by the very demonstration of the duty toward kinsmen, he encourages him with the thought, “And the honoring of the departed has been performed in a sublime manner.
Indeed, in this context, “sublime” is a term of praise, and it serves as an encouragement to perform such honor again and again.
With the words, "And strength has been bestowed upon the bhikkhus," he inspires him. For here, the bestowing of strength is itself the gift;
thus, "the bestowing of strength" refers to the inspiration that increases his enthusiasm. With the words, "By you, no small merit has been performed," he encourages him.
For here, the proclamation of the performance of merit serves as a praise of his qualities according to their true nature.
It should be understood as "inspiring" because it produces inspiration.

At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand living beings attained penetration of the Dhamma through wise exertion, being moved by the description of the danger of rebirth in the realm of hungry ghosts (*pettivisaya*). On the second day as well, the Blessed One [addressed] gods and humans...
He taught this very *Tirokuṭṭa* [Sutta]; in this way, until the seventh day, there was a similar realization of the Dhamma.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Tirokuṭṭa Sutta* in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
8. Commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta:
The Reason for Its Placement.
Now, as for this Section on Treasure (Nidhikaṇḍa) which was placed immediately after the section on the wall (*tirokuṭṭa*) beginning with, “A man deposits treasure,” regarding that—
“Having explained the reason for the placement of the ‘Treasure’ chapter here, and having illustrated its origin (*aṭṭhuppatti*), we shall provide a commentary on its meaning.
In this regard, the reason for its placement here should be understood as follows: for this ‘Treasure’ chapter was [spoken] by the Blessed One...
Because this pair, although not explicitly mentioned, is associated with the expression of thanksgiving (*anumodanā*) that was spoken by Tirokuṭṭa, it has therefore been included here.

Alternatively, it should be understood that this is included here for the purpose of showing the failure of those devoid of merit through Tirokuṭṭa, and the success of those who have performed merit through this [text]. This is the reason for its inclusion here.
The Origin of the Discourse:
As for its origin—there was, it is said, a certain householder in Sāvatthī who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments.
He was faithful and confident, dwelling at home with a mind free from the stain of stinginess. One day...
On that day, he gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. At that time, the king was in need of wealth;
he sent a man to him, saying, "Go, sir, and bring such-and-such a householder.
Having gone, the man said to that householder, "The king summons you, householder. The householder, endowed with qualities such as faith...
While serving the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with his own mind, he said: "Go, good man, I shall come later;

for now I am standing here as if depositing a treasure. Then the Blessed One, having finished eating and being invited to do so, in order to express his appreciation to that householder and to show that the excellence of merit is, in the ultimate sense, a treasure, [spoke].
He spoke these verses beginning with, “A man deposits a treasure. This is the origin of this account.
Thus, having spoken [the previous section], here is the reason for the placement of the *Nidhikaṇḍa*:
“Having illuminated the occasion for the discourse (*aṭṭhuppatti*), we shall provide an exposition of its meaning.
Commentary on the First Verse (1):
Regarding the phrase “A man deposits a treasure” (*nidhiṃ nidheti puriso*): it is called a “treasure” (*nidhi*) because it is deposited (*nidhīyati*); that is, it is placed, guarded, and protected.
Wealth (*attha*). It is fourfold: stable (*thāvara*), mobile (*jaṅgama*), limb-like (*aṅgasama*), and following (*anugāmika*).
Therein, "stable" refers to gold or silver situated on the ground or in the air, or a field, or a site, or whatever else of a similar nature that is devoid of postures;
this is the stable treasure. "Mobile" refers to female and male slaves.
Elephants, cattle, horses, mares, goats, sheep, chickens, pigs, or whatever else of a similar nature connected with modes of deportment—

this is the "mobile treasure" called the field of action (*kammāyatana*) resembling a limb. It includes the field of craft (*sippāyatana*), the sphere of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*), and great learning (*bāhusacca*),
or whatever else of a similar nature that, having been mastered and acquired, is bound to one's own person like a limb or a member of the body.

This is the treasure that is like a limb. That which is called "following" consists of merit consisting of giving, merit consisting of virtue, merit consisting of development, merit consisting of hearing the Dhamma, and merit consisting of teaching the Dhamma;
or whatever other such merit follows along here and there as it were, bestowing a desirable fruit—this is the following treasure. But in this context, the "stable" is intended.

*Nidheti* means he deposits, arranges, or guards [it]. *Puriso* means a human being. While it is true that a man, a woman, or even a eunuch may deposit a treasure, here the teaching is given under the heading of "man";
however, in terms of meaning, the inclusion of all of them should be understood here as well. *Gambhīre odakantike*:
it is "deep" (*gambhīra*) in the sense of being something to be plunged into; it is "near water" (*odakantika*) by virtue of its proximity to water.
It is water-reaching (*odakantika*). There is that which is deep but not water-reaching, like a pit five or six spans deep in a dry region of land;
there is that which is water-reaching but not deep, like a pit one or two cubits deep in a low-lying pool;
and there is that which is both deep and water-reaching, [like a pit] in a dry region of land as long as it will remain filled with water until now.
It is like a deep pit; with reference to this, it was said: "in a deep place near water. Regarding the phrase "when a matter or duty has arisen":

that which does not deviate from the purpose (*attha*) is "purposeful" (*atthaṃ*); what is meant is that it brings about benefit and welfare. That which is to be done is "duty" (*kiccaṃ*); what is meant is simply some task to be performed.
"Arisen" (*uppannaṃ*) is the same as "arisen" (*samuppannaṃ*); what is meant is that it has presented itself as something to be accomplished.
"It exists" means when that purpose or task has arisen. "It will be for my benefit" is an indication of the motive for the hoarding.
For he hoards it with this intention: "When some task conducive to my welfare arises, it will be for my benefit; it will serve for the accomplishment of that task of mine.
Indeed, it should be understood that the very accomplishment of the task is what constitutes "benefit" (attha) when that task has arisen.
Commentary on the Second Verse:
Having thus shown the purpose of the store by demonstrating the intention for attaining what is beneficial, he now spoke the following to demonstrate the intention for removing what is harmful: 2.
"Whether from a king who has spoken harshly, or from a thief who has oppressed him..."
“Either for the sake of wealth, or for the release from debt, or in times of famine, or in times of misfortune.

The meaning of this should be understood by connecting, as appropriate, the two phrases containing the word *bhavissati*—namely, “it will be for my benefit” and “or for the release from debt”—with the phrase *pamokkhāya*.
Herein, the construction is as follows: a person does not merely deposit a treasure with the thought, “It will be for my benefit,” alone.
But when I am reviled by enemies or adversaries in such ways as "This man is a thief," or "He is an adulterer," or "He is a smuggler," it may lead to my release from the king;
or when I am oppressed by thieves through the seizing of wealth via housebreaking and the like, or by taking me alive with the demand,
"Give this much gold and bullion!"— [in such cases, one might resort to theft].
It will lead to my release from a creditor or a thief. I have creditors who will press me, saying, "Pay the debt," and it will lead to my release from that debt when I am pressed by them.
There comes a time when there is famine, a scarcity of grain, and alms are difficult to obtain;
in such a situation, it is not easy for one of little means to subsist. In such a case...

"Or there will be a famine for me when it arrives; or when such misfortunes arise—whether from fire, water, or unloving heirs—as when such misfortunes have arisen, I shall have [this treasure]," thinking thus, a man deposits a hoard.

Having thus shown, by means of two verses, the twofold purpose of depositing a hoard—namely, the intention to acquire wealth and the intention to avoid misfortune—he now spoke to conclude that very twofold purpose:
“For this purpose, indeed, a treasure is deposited in the world.

Its meaning is as follows: that which was shown as the attainment of benefit and the avoidance of harm—by means of such thoughts as “it will be for my benefit” and “to protect me from ill-treatment by the king,” and so forth—for the sake of this, that is, for the sake of accomplishing these [aims], in this [world]...
In the world of space, whatever is called a "treasure"—whether it be gold, silver, or other varieties—is that which is stored, deposited, and kept for one's own use.
Commentary on the Third Verse:
Now, since even such a treasure, though thus deposited, serves to accomplish the intended purpose only for those possessed of merit and not for others, he spoke as follows to illuminate that point:
3. “Though that treasure be well-hidden, deep by the water’s edge, it does not serve him at all times, nor for everyone.
The meaning of this is: though that treasure is well-hidden—that is, though it has been properly buried and placed there—[it is still not sufficient].
It is said. How well? It is said to be "well" as long as it remains in a deep place near water and is reckoned as being placed there;

it is not the case that for every person and at all times it serves him—that is, for the person by whom it was placed, even the whole of it does not serve him or succeed at all times, being incapable of performing the functions as described.
"It does not exist" is what is meant. However, it is only sometimes and for someone that it is beneficial, or perhaps it is not beneficial at all.
And here, the word "taṃ" should be regarded as a mere particle used to fill out the meter, as in such expressions as "yathā taṃ appamattassa ātāpino.
Alternatively, having made a change in gender, "taṃ" was said where "so" ought to have been said; for when it is stated in this way—
Thus, that meaning is easily understood.
This concludes the commentary on the fourth and fifth verses.
Having thus stated, "It is not the case that everything is suitable for everyone at all times," he now speaks in order to show the reasons why it is not suitable:
4. “Either the treasure shifts from its place, or his mindfulness fails him;
or else the nāgas carry it away, or others take it from him.
5. Or even unwelcome heirs dig it up while he is looking on.”
The meaning of this is as follows: either the place where the treasure is well-stored moves away, departs, or disappears from that spot;
or, although it is insentient, it goes to another place due to the exhaustion of merit;
or its perception becomes confused, such that it no longer knows the place where the treasure was stored; or else, urged by the exhaustion of merit, the *nāgas* [guardians] [move it].
Or they remove that treasure and move it to another place; or even *yakkhas* carry it off, taking it wherever they wish;
or while he is looking on, unpleasant heirs dig up the ground and extract that treasure.
Thus, by these causes such as its removal from its place, that treasure does not serve him.

Having thus explained the causes recognized by the world—such as falling from one’s position and so forth—as reasons for the non-occurrence [of prosperity], he now says: “When there is a depletion of merit, all this perishes,” in order to show that single cause known as the depletion of merit which is the root of even these aforementioned causes.
Its meaning is as follows: at whatever time there is a depletion of the merit that produces the attainment of wealth, it provides an opportunity for demerit that leads to the loss of that wealth.
Having done so, it remains; then, whatever store of wealth consisting of gold, bullion, and other riches was deposited by the one who buried the treasure—all of this perishes.
Commentary on the Sixth Stanza.
Thus, having spoken of the worldly treasure— which, though deposited with various intentions, fails to conform to those intentions and is liable to destruction in many ways—

the Blessed One now began this Chapter on Treasure (Nidhikaṇḍa) as an expression of thanks to that householder, in order to show that the perfection of merit is, in the ultimate sense, a treasure. Demonstrating this, he said:
6. “For whomsoever, by means of giving, virtue, self-restraint, and self-mastery, a treasure is well-laid up—whether it be for a woman or for a man.
In this context, “giving” (dāna) is to be understood according to the method already stated in the passage: “Giving and righteous conduct. As for “virtue” (sīla):
Non-transgression regarding body and speech; or rather, all virtue (sīla), such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha with its five factors and ten factors, is intended here by the term "virtue.
"Restraint" (saṃyama) means the act of restraining;

it is said to be the warding off of the mind’s movement toward various objects, and this is a synonym for concentration (samādhi). One who is endowed with that restraint is "restrained in hand," and so forth.
In the passage, “restrained in body, restrained in speech, the most excellent of those restrained,” he is called the “most excellent of those restrained.

Others say: “Restraint (*saṃyama*) is the act of restraining; it is said to mean ‘restraint’ (*saṃvara*). This is a designation for the restraint of the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).”* “Taming” (*dama*) is the act of taming;
it is said to mean “the pacification of the defilements. This is a designation for wisdom (*paññā*). For wisdom, in some contexts, is simply called wisdom itself.
It is called "dhamma" in such passages as, "He who listens gains wisdom. In some instances it is "truth," as in, "Truth, Dhamma, fortitude, and generosity.
In some instances it is "self-control," as in, "If there were truth, self-control, and generosity, nothing would be found superior to patience.
Having thus understood giving and the other virtues, the meaning of this verse should now be understood by synthesizing them as follows: for one...

Just as a treasure consisting of wealth is stored by placing gold, silver, pearls, or gems together in one place, so too is a treasure consisting of merit stored within the single continuum of consciousness— such as at a cetiya— by means of these four qualities: giving, virtue, self-restraint, and self-control, whether by a woman or a man.
Or, it is well-deposited because of its excellent execution upon the site.

Thus, having shown by means of this verse beginning with “For whom [there is] giving” that the perfection of merit is, in the ultimate sense, a treasure, the Blessed One now spoke, showing that site whereon the treasure is deposited such that it becomes well-deposited: [The commentary on the seventh verse. Thus, having shown by means of this verse beginning with “For whom [there is] giving” that the perfection of merit is, in the ultimate sense, a treasure, the Blessed One now spoke, showing that site whereon the treasure is deposited such that it becomes well-deposited:
7. "In a shrine (*cetiyamhi*), or in the Saṅgha, or in an individual, or in guests, or likewise in one's mother, father, and eldest brother.

In this context, it is called a *cetiya* because it is to be accumulated (*cayitabba*); that is to say, it is to be honored (*pūjetabba*). Or, it is a *cetiya* because it is piled up (*citatta*). Furthermore, this [shrine]...
A *cetiya* is of three kinds: a *paribhoga-cetiya*, an *uddissaka-cetiya*, and a *dhātu-cetiya*.
Among these, the Bodhi tree is a *paribhoga-cetiya*; a Buddha image is an *uddissaka-cetiya*; and relic shrines or stūpas containing relics are *dhātu-cetiya*s.
"The Sangha" refers to anyone among those headed by the Buddha and so forth. "An individual" (*puggala*) refers to those among the laity and the ordained.
"Whoever": there is no fixed day for him; he arrives on this or that day, thus he is an *atithi*. This is a designation for a guest who has arrived at that very moment.
The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Having thus understood the *cetiyas* and so forth, the meaning of this verse should now be understood by synthesizing it as follows: whoever...
That treasure is said to be "well-deposited"; it is well-deposited in these objects. Why?

Because of its capacity to yield desirable fruits for a long time. For indeed, by giving even a single flower at a shrine (*cetiyamhi*), people become recipients of desirable fruits for a long duration. As it is said:
"Having offered a single flower, for eighty million eons..."
“I do not recognize an unhappy rebirth; this is the fruit of giving flowers.
And: “If one sees that vast happiness comes from the relinquishing of limited happiness,” so it is said.
Thus, according to the method stated in the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta, the Velāma Sutta, and others, the distribution of the fruits of giving is explained with respect to the objects such as the Saṅgha.

It should be understood. And just as the occurrence of giving and the manifestation of its fruit have been shown in relation to shrines and so forth, so too—in each case as appropriate—there is the occurrence of virtue (*sīla*) by way of conduct and restraint (*cāritta-vāritta*) undertaken with respect to this or that object; of self-control (*saṃyama*) by way of the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*);
and of self-mastery (*dama*) by way of the attention and reflection of insight (*vipassanā-manasikāra-paccavekkhaṇa*) based upon those same objects.
And the manifestation of the fruit should also be understood.

Thus, having shown the various bases such as the cetiya for the store of merit consisting of giving and so forth—which is being deposited—by means of the eighth verse, the Blessed One... [end of fragment]
Now, demonstrating the distinction of that well-hidden treasure among these objects over one hidden deep in the earth or at the water's edge, he said: 8.
“This treasure is well-hidden, invincible, and follows one along.”
"Leaving behind what is to be left behind, one goes taking this along.
Therein, by the first line, he points out that well-deposited treasure through giving and so forth: "This is a well-deposited treasure.

"Invincible" (*ajeyyo*) means it cannot be seized by others after being conquered; there is also the reading "invulnerable" (*acceyyo*), for which the meaning is "to be honored" (*accitabbo*) or "worthy of honor" (*accanāraho*).
The meaning is that it should be accumulated by one who desires welfare and happiness. And in this reading, having connected it as "this treasure should be buried," and then showing the inquiry "Why?
by connecting it with "Because when well-buried, it follows [the owner]," [the sense is established].
Otherwise, the state of being buried would be predicated of what is already well-buried, yet that which is well-buried is not something to be buried; for it is only that which has been buried...
It is "that" (so). It follows along, thus it is "following" (*anugāmika*); the meaning is that even when one goes to the next world, it does not abandon him by bestowing its fruit here and there.

Regarding the phrase "having abandoned, one goes taking this," the meaning is said to be: when the time of death has arrived, having abandoned all enjoyments which must be left behind, one goes to the next world taking this treasure; such is its significance. And that...
This is not tenable. Why? Because wealth cannot be taken away. For those various forms of wealth are only to be abandoned;

they are not things that can be taken away, whereas those specific destinations (gatis) are what can be gone to. Therefore, if this were the intended meaning, he would have said, "having abandoned wealth, one goes to specific destinations.
Consequently, the meaning here should be understood thus: "or a treasure is displaced from its place."
In this and other such ways, having abandoned death, when enjoyments pass away, one goes taking this [wealth] with one.
For because it is something that follows one along, one does not abandon it.

Herein, it might be argued: "In the phrase 'among those things to be gone to' (*gamanīyesu*), the meaning is 'among those things to be traversed,' not 'among those things passing away. That is not necessarily so.

It should be understood thus: for just as in the phrase "the noble ones are leading out" (*niyyānikā*), the meaning is "those who lead out" rather than "those to be led out," so too here the meaning is "while they are going" rather than "those to be gone to.
Alternatively, because at the time of death this person does not even get to touch his wealth when he wishes to give it away to someone, therefore—
Therefore, those enjoyments must first be abandoned by the body, and afterwards one must go with a mind free from longing; that is what is meant by "they must be transcended.
Thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "having first abandoned them by the body, [one should proceed] with regard to those enjoyments which are to be departed from by the mind.
In the first sense, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*), [meaning]: "among those enjoyments which are to be abandoned and departed from."
"Having extracted and taken this very same wealth of the storehouse of merit from there, one goes. In the latter sense, the locative case is used to indicate a characteristic by means of a state.
For, by the fact that possessions are subject to departure, the fact that this storehouse of merit is also subject to being taken and departing is characterized.
Commentary on the Ninth Stanza.
Thus, having demonstrated the distinction between this treasure of merit and a treasure placed at the edge of deep water, the Blessed One—
like a merchant of magnificent goods who inspires the buyers by praising the qualities of his wares—
further praised the qualities of the treasure of merit he himself had taught, [arousing] gods and humans toward that treasure of merit.
Inspiring enthusiasm, he said:
9. “A treasure not shared with others, a hoard that thieves cannot carry away— The wise person should perform meritorious deeds, for such a treasure follows one after death.”

In this context, *asādhāraṇam-aññesan* means "not common to others" (*asādhāraṇo aññesaṃ*); the letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasaṃdhikaro*), as in expressions such as *adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā*.
*Acorāharaṇo* means "not to be taken away by thieves"; the meaning is that it cannot be seized by thieves.
*Nidhi* means "that which is to be stored. Thus, having praised the quality of the treasure of merit with these two phrases—
Then, with two [verses], he generates enthusiasm therein: “A wise person should perform meritorious deeds, for they are a treasure that follows one.
The meaning of this is: because meritorious deeds are a treasure that is not shared with others and cannot be stolen by thieves.
And it is not merely a treasure that is unshared and cannot be stolen; rather, “this treasure is well-deposited, invincible...”

Regarding the phrase "the following treasure": since that which is called the "following treasure" here consists of nothing other than merits, therefore a wise person—one endowed with intelligence and endowed with steadfastness—should perform, or indeed do, these merits.
Commentary on the Tenth Stanza.

Thus, having inspired enthusiasm among gods and humans for the treasure of merit through this description of its qualities, the Blessed One now spoke—briefly showing what fruit is bestowed upon those who, having been inspired, accomplish the performance of meritorious deeds—as follows:
"This treasure grants all desires to gods and humans.
Now, since the quality of granting all desires belongs to that which is bound to aspiration, it does not exist without aspiration. As it has been said:
“Householders, if a practitioner of the Dharma, a practitioner of equanimity, should wish:

‘Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might arise in the company of wealthy kṣatriyas,’ it is indeed possible that after the breakup of the body, after death, he will arise in the company of wealthy kṣatriyas. Why is that?”
What is the reason? Because he is one who lives according to the Dhamma, one who lives righteously. Likewise:

"He might dwell having himself, through direct knowledge, realized and attained in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. What is the reason for that? Because he is one who lives according to the Dhamma, one who lives righteously.
And thus it has been said:
“Here, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, he is endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
It occurs to him: ‘Oh, that after the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in the company of wealthy kshatriyas!
He exerts that mind, fixes that mind, and directs that mind [toward that goal].”
“He develops them. Those volitional formations and modes of abiding, thus developed and thus cultivated, lead to rebirth there,” and so forth.

Therefore, showing that the cause for that [rebirth] being the granter of all desires is the aspiration—which consists of the equipment for development through the exertion of the mind and resolution according to the method of one’s wish—he said:
“Whatever they aspire to, all that is obtained by means of this.
This is the commentary on the eleventh verse.
Now, demonstrating specifically and individually what it is that is obtained by means of this, he spoke the verses beginning with “Goldenness, a beautiful voice,” and so forth.
In this regard, first of all, in the initial verse, "goldenness" means having a beautiful complexion and skin resembling gold; that too is obtained through this treasure of merit. As it is said:
"Bhikkhus, when the Tathāgata—in a previous birth... [omitted] ...formerly being a human being—was free from anger and possessed little distress;
even when spoken to much, he did not become resentful, did not become angry, did not harbor ill will, and did not remain fixed in resentment."
He manifested neither anger, nor hatred, nor resentment; rather, he became a donor of fine, soft rugs, coverlets, and exquisite linens, cotton fabrics...
[and so on] ...silk fabrics... [and so on] ...and exquisite woolen blankets.
Because of having performed and accumulated that karma... [and so on] ...having come to this state of existence, he acquires this mark of a Great Man.
“He is golden-hued, with skin like refined gold.
By this, one also attains what is called the "excellent voice," which is the voice of Brahmā, sounding like the song of the *karavīka* bird. As it is said:
“Monks, whatever harsh speech the Tathāgata abandoned in a previous birth... having abandoned harsh speech...”
He abstained from that speech which is harsh... [and so on] ...he became one who speaks such speech as is gentle and pleasing to the ear...
Because he performed and accumulated that action... having come to this state of existence, he acquires these two marks of a Great Man:
he has a long tongue and a Brahma-voice, speaking like a karavīka bird.
“Goodly configuration” (*susanthāna*) means a state of being well-configured; it is said to be the arrangement of the limbs and members in places that are even, well-rounded, and appropriate.
That too is obtained by this [perfection]. As it is said: “Monks, when the Tathāgata, in a former birth...

having been a human being in the past, was one who desired the welfare of many people, desired their benefit, desired their comfort, and desired their security from bondage, thinking: ‘How might they increase in faith...’”

"May I increase in virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, wealth and grain, fields and lands, bipeds and quadrupeds, children and wives, slaves, laborers, and servants, and in kinsmen, friends, and relatives"—while performing that action...
[as before] ...he acquires these three marks of a Great Man: his upper body is like that of a lion, and he has a broad chest.
“...and with a symmetrical trunk,” and so forth.

Following this method, one should bring forward from here and there the scriptural passages that establish the attainment of this treasure of merit for those who follow; however, I have abbreviated them for fear of excessive prolixity. Now, I shall provide an explanation of the remaining terms. Regarding “surūpatā” (handsomeness):
here, the entire body should be understood as “rūpa” (form), according to the passage: “Space enclosed [by the elements] is designated simply as ‘rūpa’...”

In such passages as “he goes,” etc., what is meant is that the beauty of that form (*rūpa*)—its handsome appearance (*surūpatā*), its being neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too pale—is expressed.
“Sovereignty” (*ādhipacca*) means the state of being a lord (*adhipati*); the meaning is the status of a master by virtue of being a wealthy Khattiya, and so forth.
“Retinue” (*parivāra*) refers to the excellence of one’s kin and attendants for householders, and the excellence of one’s assembly for those who have gone forth from the household life.
“Sovereignty and retinue” means sovereignty together with retinue. Herein, it should be understood that by means of [the qualities such as] golden hue and so forth, excellence of body is expressed;
by sovereignty, excellence of wealth; and by retinue, excellence of kinsmen and attendants.
Regarding the statement, “By this, everything is obtained—that which they aspire to, all that is obtained by this”—therein:
This shows that it should be understood that all these qualities, such as the specific excellence of possessing gold mentioned first, are obtained by means of this [merit].
Commentary on the Twelfth Stanza:

Having thus shown, by means of this stanza, the prosperity among gods and humans obtainable prior to the attainment of sovereignty through the power of merit, he now speaks this stanza beginning with “padesarajjaṃ” (local sovereignty) in order to show both types of royal prosperity.
In this context, "local sovereignty" (*padesarajja*) refers to rule over a single region of the earth without having attained even a single continent in its entirety.
"Sovereignty" (*issariya*) means the state of being a lord; by this, he shows the sovereignty of a continent-turning monarch (*dīpacakkavatti*).

"The happiness of a wheel-turning monarch is dear" means that the happiness of a wheel-turning monarch is desirable, lovely, and pleasing; by this, he shows the sovereignty of a universal monarch who rules over the four quarters (*cāturantacakkavatti*).
“Devesu rajjaṃ” means sovereignty among the gods; by this, the divine sovereignty of humans such as Mandhātā and others is also shown.
With the phrase “api dibbesu,” he shows the divine sovereignty even for those who have arisen in the celestial bodies (kāyas) which, because they exist in the heavens (divi), are called “divine.
By this, everything that is desired is obtained: whatever they aspire to, all that [is gained] by this.
It is said, “it is obtained”; therein, this second point shows that all this—specifically, regional sovereignty and so forth—is to be understood as being obtainable by means of this [merit].
Commentary on the Thirteenth Verse.
13. Having thus shown, by means of this verse, the attainment of sovereignty among gods and humans that is to be obtained through the power of merit,
he now spoke this verse, "And human prosperity," while demonstrating the attainment of Nibbāna by briefly placing before it the prosperity described in the two preceding verses.
This is the word-by-word commentary on that [verse]: it belongs to humans, thus it is *mānussī*; being human, it is *mānussikā*. Attaining is *sampatti*.
The world of the devas is *devaloka*; in that world of the devas. It goes (*yāti*) to complete exhaustion.
It is called *rati* because they delight (*ramanti*) by means of it—whether it has arisen internally or exists externally as an instrument—[namely] pleasure and the basis for pleasure.
This is a designation. The word "and" (ca) is indefinite; together with the preceding attainment, it has the sense of inclusion.
Nibbāna itself is the attainment of Nibbāna.
This, however, is the commentary on the meaning: that which is this human attainment and [that which is] in the world of the gods, expressed by such terms as "golden-hued," and so forth.
And whatever delight has been mentioned, all of that, as well as this other attainment of Nibbāna to be reached by way of being a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*) and so forth—
all this is obtained by means of this [path] in its entirety, even specifically in this third case. Alternatively,

that which was not previously stated by terms such as "gold-like" (*suvaṇṇatā*), but rather expressed by such passages as "the brave and mindful dwell here in the holy life" (*sūrā satimanto idha brahmacariyavāso*), etc.— [all that is obtained].
Furthermore, by this method, all of this is obtained specifically: the human prosperity distinguished by discernment (*paññāveyyattiya*) and so forth;
the other [prosperity] in the world of the gods, which consists in the delight of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so on; and the attainment of Nibbāna in the manner already described.
Thus should the explanation of the meaning here be understood.
Commentary on the Fourteenth Stanza:

14. Having thus shown, by means of this stanza, even the attainment of Nibbāna—which is to be obtained through the power of merit and reached by way of being a follower by faith (*saddhānusārī*) and so forth—he now shows that which is to be attained by way of being one possessing the threefold knowledge (*tevijja*) and being liberated both ways (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).
Showing that very means for him, he spoke this verse:
“Having attained excellence of friends. This is the word-by-word commentary upon it: it is called *sampadā* because by means of it one succeeds and attains the manifestation of virtues;
a friend itself as excellence is *mittasampadā*; that is, *taṃ mittasampadaṃ*. *Āgamma* means relying upon. *Yoniso* means by way of skillful means (*upāya*). *Payuñjato* means...
[It is] for one who practices yoga. It is called *vijjā* because by means of it one discerns; it is called *vimutti* because by means of it one is liberated, or because it itself is liberated.
*Vijjāvimuttiyo* refers to both clear knowledge (*vijjā*) and liberation (*vimutti*). Mastery over clear knowledge and liberation is *vijjāvimuttivasībhāvo*.
This, however, is the commentary on the meaning: having attained the perfection of friendship, [one approaches] either the Teacher or some other person worthy of respect...

Having relied upon a fellow practitioner of the holy life and received from him both exhortation and instruction, one who applies oneself thoroughly to practice according to what was taught [attains] the three types of higher knowledge, such as the recollection of past lives. Regarding that, as it is said: "What therein is liberation?
It is the mind's resolute intent and Nibbāna," there is likewise the liberation consisting of the eight meditative attainments and Nibbāna.
Likewise, through non-delusion, mastery is attained; this too is the fourth specific instance where "all this" is obtained by means of this [wisdom].

Commentary on the Fifteenth Stanza (15): Thus, by the power of the merit conducive to the wings of enlightenment—namely, the branches of clear knowledge, liberation, and mastery—which was previously described in this stanza, that which is to be obtained is attained.

Having thus shown the attainment of Nibbāna to be reached by way of the state of one liberated both ways through the threefold knowledge (*tevijja-ubhatobhāga-vimutta*), he now shows how all those who have attained mastery over true knowledge and liberation— whether possessing the threefold knowledge or liberated both ways— obtain the majesty of qualities such as the analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*).
And it is through this perfection of merit that they obtain that majesty of qualities in various ways, by way of its being the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*).
That too is obtained; therefore, showing that as well, he spoke this verse: “The analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) and the liberations (*vimokkha*).

When it is said, “From which [arises] the wisdom that has reached differentiation regarding the Dhamma, its meaning, its language, and its eloquence,” that is called the analytical knowledge (*paṭisambhidā*);
and these eight liberations, according to the method beginning with “one possessing form sees forms,” and this [wisdom] of the Blessed One—
The disciple-parami is that which accomplishes the attainment of a disciple to be reached by disciples; likewise,

the state of a Pacceka-Buddha which accomplishes self-enlightenment, and the stage of Buddhahood which accomplishes the state of being the supreme among all beings— all this fifth category, in its entirety,
should be understood as obtainable through this [perfection].
Commentary on the Sixteenth Stanza:

16. Thus, having demonstrated with these five stanzas in detail what was stated by the Blessed One—that "whatever they aspire for, all that is obtained by this"—he now [shows] that all this is indeed designated as the treasure that grants every desire.
Praising the attainment of merit, he concluded the teaching with this verse:
"Thus it is of great benefit. This is the word-by-word commentary upon it: *evaṃ* (thus) is a demonstrative indicating a past state. *Mahatthikā* means that which has a great purpose;
what is meant is that it conduces to a great goal. *Mahiddhikā* is also a reading for this term. *Esā* (this) is a term of reference.
By this [verse], beginning with "He who, by giving and by virtue... and ending with "...the wise man should perform meritorious deeds," he indicates the attainment of merit (*puññasampadā*).
*Yadidaṃ* is a particle used in the sense of bringing something to mind;

by means of it, he brings to mind what has been indicated as "this" (*esa*), using the form "which is this" (*yā esā*) to point it out. *Puññānaṃ sampadā* is "the attainment of merits. *Tasmā* is a word expressing a reason.

The steadfast are those possessed of firm resolve. "They praise" means they extol. "The wise" are those endowed with wisdom. "The state of one who has performed merit" refers to the condition of having accomplished meritorious deeds.

Now, this is the commentary on the meaning: Having thus described the goal to be attained through the power of the perfection of merit—beginning with a golden complexion and ending with the stage of Buddhahood—the Blessed One now presents that very same matter in summary, by way of that very meaning.
Praising the great benefit of the perfection of merit of the kind already described, he said:
"This perfection of merit—which I have taught in the manner beginning with 'For one who, by giving and by virtue'—is of great benefit because it brings about such a great purpose;
therefore, through my quality of being untiring in teaching the Dhamma for the welfare and happiness of beings as it truly is..."
And the wise and learned praise the performance of merit in its many aspects— both through what is explicitly stated here,

such as "a treasure not shared with others, a hoard that thieves cannot carry away," and through what is unstated, such as the words, "Monks, do not fear merits; this, monks, is a designation for happiness, namely, merits"— yet they do so without partiality.
At the conclusion of the teaching, that lay follower, together with many people, was established in the fruit of stream-entry.
Having gone into the presence of King Pasenadi of Kosala, he reported this matter to him. The king, being exceedingly pleased, expressed his approval, saying:
"Excellent, householder! Excellent indeed, householder! You have deposited a treasure that cannot even be taken away by those like me. Thus he commended him.
"He performed a great worship.
Thus ends the commentary on the Nidhikaṇḍa Sutta of the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
9. Commentary on the *Mettasutta*.
The Purpose of its Inclusion:
Now, the turn has come for the commentary on the *Mettasutta*, which was placed immediately after the *Nidhikaṇḍa*. Having stated the purpose for its inclusion here, following that—
“Since these [factors] have been explained by whom, when, where, and for what reason,
we shall provide an exposition of their meaning after first clarifying the introduction.

In this context, since the excellence of merit consisting of generosity, virtue, and so forth was described in the section on the treasure-store (*nidhikaṇḍa*), and that [merit] was performed through loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward sentient beings...
It is of great fruit, being capable of leading one as far as the stage of Buddhahood; therefore, it is for the purpose of showing the benefit of that perfection of merit, or else because,
after entering the Dispensation through the Refuges and becoming established in virtue by means of the Training Rules,
it demonstrates the meditation subject capable of abandoning lust by way of the thirty-two aspects, and the meditation subject capable of abandoning delusion by way of the Questions of the Youth.
Through the recitation of the Maṅgala Sutta, there is the auspiciousness and self-protection resulting from its occurrence; through the Ratana Sutta, there is corresponding protection against others;

through the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta, there is the perception of certain spirits among those mentioned in the Ratana Sutta, as well as the misfortune of those who are negligent regarding the aforementioned attainment of merit;
and through the Nidhikaṇḍa, there is that which serves as the antidote to the misfortune mentioned in the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta.
Although prosperity has been shown, the meditation subject capable of abandoning hatred has not yet been shown;
therefore, this *Mettasutta* has been placed here in order to show that meditation subject capable of abandoning hatred.
For in this way, the *Khuddakapāṭha* becomes perfectly complete. This is the purpose for its inclusion here.
The Purification of the Sources (Nidānasodhana):
Now, as for this [verse]:
"That by which, when, where, and why these are explained..."
"Having cleared away its introduction, we shall provide an exposition of its meaning"—thus the matrix (mātikā) was set forth.
In this regard, this *Mettasutta* was spoken by the Blessed One himself, not by his disciples or others;
and that was at the time when monks, harassed by deities on the slopes of the Himalayas, came into the presence of the Blessed One.
It was spoken at Sāvatthī for the sake of those bhikkhus’ protection and for the sake of their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Thus, first of all, the brief exposition of these words and the clarification of the introduction (*nidāna*) should be understood.
In detail, however, it should be understood as follows: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī when the [rains] were near...
At the time of the entry into the rains retreat, on that occasion, a number of bhikkhus from various kingdoms,
having received a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from the Blessed One and desiring to enter the rains retreat here and there, approached the Blessed One. Therein,
the Blessed One [taught] the elevenfold meditation subject on the foul (asubha), according to the animate and inanimate, for those of a lustful temperament (rāgacarita).

For those of a temperament characterized by hatred, there are the fourfold meditation subjects beginning with loving-kindness; for those of a deluded temperament, the meditation subjects beginning with mindfulness of death;

for those of a discursive temperament, mindfulness of breathing, the earth-kasiṇa, and so forth; for those of a faithful temperament, the meditation subjects beginning with the recollection of the Buddha;
and for those of an intellectual temperament, the analysis of the four elements and so forth—in this manner, [the teachings] correspond to the eighty-four thousand types of temperament.
He taught the meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Then, about five hundred bhikkhus, having received a meditation subject from the Blessed One,
went by stages in search of suitable lodgings and alms-resorts, eventually reaching a border region contiguous with the Himalayas.
They saw a mountain with a rocky surface resembling blue glass gems, adorned with cool, dense shade and groves of dark-blue forests;
its ground was strewn with sand like networks of pearls and silver bands, and it was surrounded by reservoirs of pure, pleasant, and cool water.
Then those bhikkhus, having stayed there for one night and performed their bodily duties at the break of dawn, went for alms to a certain village not far from that place.
They entered. The village was composed of a thousand families living in densely packed dwellings; and the people there were faithful and devout.
Because it was rare for those in the border regions to see renunciants, they were filled with joy and gladness upon seeing the monks.
Having fed them, they requested, "Venerable sirs, please stay right here for the three months of the rains," and they constructed five hundred meditation huts.
Having had it built, they prepared all the necessary requisites there, such as beds, chairs, water-jars, and vessels for drinking and washing.
On the following day, the bhikkhus entered another village for alms. There too, people attended upon them in the same manner and requested that they spend the rains retreat.
The bhikkhus, consenting with the words "provided there is no obstacle," entered that forest grove.
Exerting energy throughout the entire day and night, having divided the watches into segments and dwelling with abundant wise attention,
they approached the roots of trees and sat down. By the spiritual power of those virtuous bhikkhus, the tree deities, their own power overcome,
descended from their respective celestial mansions, took their children, and wandered here and there, just as if [they were] by kings.
Or, when royal ministers have gone to a village residence and lodgings have been taken in the houses of the villagers,
those people leave their homes and, dwelling elsewhere, watch from afar, wondering, "When will they depart? In the same way, the deities,
having abandoned their respective celestial mansions, wander here and there and watch from afar.
“When will the venerable ones depart? Then they thought to themselves:
“The monks who have entered their first rains retreat will certainly stay for the three months; however, we cannot go away and live with our children for so long.
Come now, let us show the monks a terrifying object. During the night, they [prepared] for the monks...
At the time for performing the duties of a recluse, they conjured terrifying forms of *yakkhas* and stood right before them, making a dreadful noise.
When the monks saw those forms and heard that sound, their hearts trembled;
they became discolored, turning pale and wan. Because of this, those monks were unable to make their minds one-pointed.
They were unable [to focus]; because their minds were distracted and they were repeatedly agitated by fear, their mindfulness lapsed.
Then, while they were thus forgetful, [the devas] presented them with foul-smelling objects.
By that foul odor, their brain seemed as if it were being crushed, and intense pains arose in their heads; yet they did not realize what was happening.
They informed one another.
