Then one day, at the time of the senior elder of the Saṅgha’s attendance, when they had all assembled, the senior elder asked:
"Friends, for you who have entered this forest grove for these few days, why is the color of your skin so exceedingly pure?"
“Formerly your complexion was clear and your faculties were serene; but now you are thin, discolored, and jaundiced.

What is it here that is unsuitable for you? Then one bhikkhu said: “Venerable sir, at night I see and hear such and such terrifying objects, and I smell such a scent; because of that, my mind does not settle.”
“...he attains concentration. By this very means, they all reported that situation to him. The Elder of the Sangha said:
“Friends, two times for entering the rains-residence have been prescribed by the Blessed One. Furthermore, this lodging of ours is unsuitable;
come, friends, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One and ask about another suitable lodging. “Very well,” [they replied].
“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the elder, and having all tidied their lodgings and taken up their bowls and robes, they set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Because they were unstained by worldly things, they did not even take leave of anyone among the families before departing.
Gradually reaching Sāvatthī, they came into the presence of the Blessed One.
When the Blessed One saw those bhikkhus, he said this: “Bhikkhus, I have laid down a training rule that one should not go on a journey during the rains;
why then are you going on a journey? They reported everything to the Blessed One.
As the Blessed One reflected, he perceived that throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, there was not even a place large enough for a four-legged stool that would serve as suitable lodging for them.
He did not see it. Then he said to those bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, you have no other suitable dwelling place;
while staying right there, you will reach the destruction of the taints.
Go, bhikkhus, dwell depending on that very same dwelling place. But if you desire safety from the deities, [recite] this protective chant.”
“Learn this, for it shall be a protective charm (*paritta*) and a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for you. Thus he spoke this sutta.
Others, however, say that after saying, “Go, monks, and dwell depending on that very same lodging,” the Blessed One said:
“Furthermore, the forest-dweller must know how to maintain [the practice]. That is to say: in the evening...”

By way of application, there are two on loving-kindness (*mettā*), two on the protective formulas (*paritta*), two on the foulness of the body (*asubha*), two on mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), and the attention directed toward the eight great objects of spiritual urgency (*mahāsaṃvegavatthu*).
These eight great objects of spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, death, and the four types of suffering in the woeful states (*apāya*);

alternatively, they are birth, aging, sickness, and death as four, with the suffering of the woeful states as the fifth, and the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭamūlaka*) in the past.
"In the future, suffering rooted in the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*); in the present, suffering rooted in the search for nutriment.

Thus, having explained the means of protection, the Blessed One spoke this sutta for the sake of loving-kindness (*mettā*), for the sake of a protective chant (*paritta*), and for the sake of the jhāna that serves as a basis for insight (*vipassanā*) for those bhikkhus.
Thus, even from the perspective of the detailed exposition, [the meaning is established] by these [factors]: "by whom it was spoken," "when," "where," and "why."
The illumination of the words and the purification of the introduction (nidāna) should be understood.

To this extent, that matrix (mātikā) which was established thus—“By which, when, where, and because of what these are illuminated; having purified the introduction”—has been explained in its entirety.
Commentary on the First Stanza.
1. Now, because it was stated, "We shall provide an exposition of the meaning of this," the exposition of the meaning of this Sutta—whose introductory context has thus been cleared—is commenced.
Therein, regarding the first verse, "What is to be done by one skilled in the goal," this is the word-by-word commentary:
"What is to be done" (*karaṇīya*) means that which ought to be performed; the sense is "that which is worthy of being done. "Goal" (*attha*) refers to the path of practice (*paṭipadā*), which...
Or whatever is beneficial to oneself—all that is called "meaning" (*attha*) because it is to be approached (*araṇīya*); "to be approached" means to be resorted to.
By the phrase "by one skilled in meaning, skilled in what is beneficial, and clever regarding benefit," this is what is meant.
*Yaṃ* is the unspecified nominative; *taṃ* is the specified accusative; or both *yaṃ* and *taṃ* are nominative forms. *Santaṃ padaṃ* is the accusative form.
In this context, "peaceful" (*santa*) is by way of its characteristic; "the goal" (*pada*) is by way of what is to be attained—this is a designation for Nibbāna.
"Having fully realized" (*abhisamecca*) means having fully arrived at. "Sakka" means one who is capable; it is said to mean one who is competent and able.
"Uju" means endowed with uprightness. "Suhuju" means perfectly upright. "Suvaco" means one in whom speech is easy. "Assa" means he would be. "Mudu" means endowed with gentleness.
"Not conceited" means one who is not conceited (*anatimāni*).

Here, however, is the commentary on the meaning: regarding the phrase "What ought to be done by one skilled in the goal, having realized that state of peace," there is indeed what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
In this context, briefly stated, the three trainings are what ought to be done.
Failure in virtue, failure in view, failure in conduct, and failure in livelihood—such things as these are not to be done.
Likewise, there is one skilled in what is beneficial and one skilled in what is harmful. In this regard, he who has gone forth in this teaching does not apply himself rightly;
he is of broken virtue and maintains his life by resorting to the twenty-one kinds of wrong search.

Namely: the gift of bamboo, the gift of leaves, the gift of flowers, the gift of fruits, the gift of tooth-sticks, the gift of water for rinsing the mouth, the gift of bathing facilities, the gift of bath-powder, the gift of clay;
flattery, bean-soupery, servility, running errands on foot, medical practice, acting as a messenger, going on errands, giving alms-food in exchange for alms-food, and the science of geomancy.
Astrology and the science of bodily marks. He frequents six kinds of improper resort:
namely, the resort of prostitutes, widows, elderly maidens, eunuchs, bhikkhunīs, and taverns.
And he dwells in association with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and the disciples of sectarians, through an inappropriate intimacy with householders, or...

But he frequents, associates with, and attends upon those families that are faithless, lacking confidence, like bottomless pits, abusive and insulting, and desiring neither the welfare nor the benefit, comfort, or security of the bhikkhus...
[and so on] ...of the female lay disciples; such are the families he serves.
This is one who is unskilled in what is beneficial.
But he who, having gone forth in this dispensation, applies himself rightly, abandons wrong livelihood, and— desiring to be established in the fourfold purification of virtue—
fulfills the restraint of the Pātimokkha with faith as its head, the restraint of the senses with mindfulness as its head, purity of livelihood with energy as its head,
and the use of requisites with wisdom as its head: he is skilled in the goal.
Or else, by means of purifying the aggregate of offenses committed by beings, one achieves restraint according to the Pātimokkha;

by means of the non-arising of covetousness and other unwholesome states toward objects encountered at the six sense-doors, one achieves restraint of the faculties; by means of avoiding improper search and by partaking of requisites praised by the wise and described by the Buddha and his disciples, one achieves purity of livelihood;
and by means of reflecting as previously described, one achieves the partaking of requisites during the performance of the four postures.
He also purifies his clear comprehension by reviewing [the act] in terms of its purposefulness and so forth. This person too is skilled in the goal.

Or else, just as a cloth that has become soiled is cleansed by means of alkaline water, a mirror by means of ash, and gold by means of the furnace-mouth, so too virtue is purified by means of knowledge; knowing this, he [purifies it] with the water of knowledge.
Washing it, he purifies his virtue. Just as the quail protects her egg, the yak protects its tail,
a woman with an only child protects her beloved only son, and a one-eyed man protects that one eye,
so too does he, being exceedingly heedful, protect his own aggregate of virtue, reviewing it morning and evening, even down to the slightest detail.
He does not see his fault. This one, too, is skilled in the goal.
Or again, one who, having established himself in virtue that brings freedom from remorse, undertakes the practice for the suppression of the defilements;

and having undertaken it, performs the preliminary work of the kasiṇas; and having performed the preliminary work of the kasiṇas, produces the meditative attainments—this one, too, is skilled in the goal.
Furthermore, he who, having emerged from attainment and having comprehended formations (*saṅkhāra*), attains Arahantship—he is the foremost among those skilled in the goal (*atthakusala*).

In this context, those "skilled in the goal" who have been described as being established in virtue that brings about non-regret, or as following the method for the suppression of defilements (*kilesa*), are intended here by the term "skilled in the goal. And such persons as these—
The Blessed One, referring to those bhikkhus, spoke the words "What is to be done by one skilled in the goal" as a teaching based on a single individual.
Then, for those who had developed doubt as to what that which is to be done was, he said: "Having realized that state which is peace.
This is the intended meaning here: [he spoke of] that peaceful state of Nibbāna, praised by those awakened after the Buddha, by way of its penetration.
"By one who desires to dwell having fully realized that which is to be done.
Here, the word "that" (*yam*) from the first part of this verse-line refers back by context to "that which is to be done" (*karaṇīyam*), namely, "having fully realized that peaceful state.
However, since this reading is incomplete, it should be understood that the phrase "by one who desires to dwell" has been added.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "having realized the state that is peace" (*santaṃ padaṃ abhisamecca*): having known through mundane wisdom—by way of oral tradition and so forth—that the state of Nibbāna is "peace," one who desires to attain it [realizes] what is to be done;
this follows from the context. Thus, the intended meaning here should be understood as: "that which is to be done by one skilled in the goal.
Alternatively, when it is said, "what is to be done by one skilled in the goal," [the question arises]: "What?"
To those who were reflecting, he said: “Having realized that state which is peace. Its intended meaning (adhippāya) should be understood as follows:
having realized with mundane wisdom (lokiya-paññā) that state which is peace, whatever is to be done—that which ought to be done—has been stated as “that which is fit to be done” (karaṇīya).
But what is it? What else could it be than the means for attaining that [peace]? Indeed, this is so by virtue of its fitness to be performed.
This was stated by the very first phrase, which illustrates the three trainings. For indeed, in the commentary on its meaning, we said:
"There is what ought to be done; there is what ought not to be done. In this regard, in brief, the three trainings are what ought to be done.
However, because it was taught with extreme brevity, some of those monks understood it, while others did not. Therefore, for those who did not...
In order to make known that which has been understood—specifically, what must be done by a forest-dwelling bhikkhu—he spoke this half-verse:
“He should be capable, upright, and very upright; he should be easy to speak to, gentle, and not conceited.
What is meant? One who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or having realized it through mundane wisdom...
A forest-dwelling bhikkhu who practices for its realization,
being endowed with the second and fourth factors of striving and becoming indifferent to both body and life, would be able to practice for the penetration of truth; likewise,
regarding the undertaking of the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*, the observance of duties, and so forth, as well as the mending of his own bowl and robes, those things which—
Regarding the various duties toward fellow practitioners of the holy life, as well as other such matters, he should be capable, skillful, and diligent.
Even while being capable, he should be upright by way of possessing the third factor of striving.
And even while being upright, he should not, merely through that initial state of uprightness or his uprightness during youth, fall into complacency, but [remain so] for as long as life lasts.
By making it firm again and again, it becomes more perfectly straight. Or, it is straight through honesty (*asaṭhatā*) and perfectly straight through the absence of deceit (*amāyāvitā*).
Or, it is straight through the abandonment of crookedness of body and speech, and perfectly straight through the abandonment of crookedness of mind.

Or, it is straight through not disclosing non-existent qualities, and perfectly straight through not tolerating gain arising from non-existent qualities. Thus, by means of contemplation upon the object and its characteristics...

By means of the first two and the third training rules, and through purity of application and intention, he should be straight and very straight. And not only should he be straight and very straight, but he should also be easy to speak to.
For when a person is told, "This should not be done," he says, "What have you seen? What have you heard? Who are you to speak to me after having heard it? What does my preceptor [think]?"

If one says, "The teacher is seen and trusted," or if one harasses him by remaining silent, or if, having accepted the advice, one does not act accordingly, that person remains far from the attainment of distinction. But he who, being exhorted, says, "Excellent, venerable sir, well said;
for one's own faults are indeed difficult to see; please exhort me again when you see me in such a state," [is one who draws near].
Out of compassion, he says, "It has been a long time since I have received instruction from you," and he practices according to what has been taught;
such a person is not far from the attainment of distinction. Therefore, by accepting the words of another and acting accordingly, one should be easy to speak to.

And just as he is easy to speak to, so too should he be pliant. "Pliant" means that when being appointed by householders to tasks such as going on errands or delivering messages, he should not remain stiff by failing to show pliancy in those instances;

rather, he should be pliant in his observance of duties and in the entire holy life (*brahmacariya*), like well-refined gold that is fit for use in various applications. Alternatively, "pliancy" means being free from frowning.
With an open face and pleasant speech, he should be one whose conduct is hospitable and who is easy to approach, like a pleasant bathing place.
Not only should he be gentle, but moreover, he should not be conceited;
he should not look down upon others on account of grounds for pride such as birth or clan, but should dwell with a mind equal toward all, like the Elder Sāriputta toward the son of a Caṇḍāla.
Commentary on the Second Verse: Thus,

having spoken of a certain duty specifically for a forest-dwelling bhikkhu who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or who is practicing for its attainment, the Blessed One, wishing to speak further beyond that, said:
And he spoke the second verse: “*Santussako cā*.
Therein, one is called “contented” (*santussako*) because one is contented by the twelvefold contentment mentioned here under the heading “contentment and gratitude.
Alternatively, *tussako* means “one who is pleased”; thus, one is “pleased with what is one’s own” (*sakena tussako*) and “pleased with what is sufficient” (*santena tussako*).
One who is content with what is equal is a "santussaka" (one who is easily satisfied).
In this context, "one's own" (*saka*) refers to the fourfold requisites that were specified in the ordination assembly by the words, "depending on alms-food," and which one has accepted for oneself;
whether they are excellent or not excellent, given with care or without care, at the time of receiving them or at the time of using them—[one is satisfied with such].

One who maintains oneself without showing any alteration [in one's livelihood] is called "content with what one has. That which is obtained and exists for oneself is called "what is available" (*santa*);
being content with that very availability, not longing for more than that, and abandoning excessive desire, one is called "content with what is available.
Equanimity (*sama*) means the abandonment of attraction toward the agreeable and aversion toward the disagreeable.
Because he is satisfied with all objects of experience in an even manner, he is called "one who is satisfied in an even way" (*samena tussako*).
He is "easily supported" (*subharo*) because he is nourished by ease; that is to say, he is well-nourished.
For a bhikkhu who, even when people fill his bowl with rice, meat, boiled rice, and so forth, displays a sour face and a state of dissatisfaction, or [behaves] right in their presence—
If, after receiving alms-food, he shows displeasure by asking, "What have you given? and gives it instead to novices, householders, and so forth, he is difficult to support.
Seeing this, people avoid him from afar, thinking, "This monk is difficult to support; he cannot be maintained.
However, one who, having received anything—whether coarse or refined, little or much—is satisfied and has a serene face...
Having offered [the alms], he sustains himself; such a one is easy to support. Seeing this, people become exceedingly confident, thinking, “Our venerable one is easy to support;
he is satisfied even with very little; we ourselves shall nourish him. Having given their word, they do so nourish him.
It is such a person as is intended here by the term “easy to support.”
"One who has little business" (*appakicco*) means one who is not occupied with various tasks such as delighting in work, delighting in talk, or delighting in socializing;
or rather, it means one who is free from duties such as new construction, providing for the Sangha’s use, instructing novices, or supervising monastery attendants throughout the entire monastery.
It is said that he performs his own tasks, such as cutting his hair and nails or preparing his bowl and robes, and is devoted solely to the duties of the ascetic’s practice (*samaṇadhamma*).

"Light in livelihood" means one whose mode of living is light. This refers to one who does not depart like a certain monk with many belongings, who at the time of setting out for another region departs after having people carry away much—alms bowls, robes, rugs, oil, molasses, and so forth—as head-loads or hip-loads;
rather, it refers to one who has few requisites, possessing only the eight requisites of a recluse, such as the alms bowl and robes.

He avoids [unwholesome things]; at the time of departing for another region, he departs taking [only] what is necessary, like a winged bird—such a person is intended here by the term "one who lives lightly.
One whose faculties are peaceful is "peaceful in faculties" (*santindriyo*); this means that his faculties are not agitated by passion and so forth toward desirable objects and the like.
"Clever" (*nipako*) means wise, discerning, and possessed of wisdom; [this refers to] the wisdom that guards one's virtue (*sīla*).

The intended meaning is that he is endowed with the wisdom that examines robes and other requisites, as well as the wisdom that thoroughly understands the seven kinds of suitability regarding dwellings and so forth.

"Not impudent" (*appagabbho*) means free from impudence; the sense is that he is devoid of the eight grounds for bodily impudence, the four grounds for verbal impudence, and the many grounds for mental impudence.

The eight grounds for bodily impudence consist of [behaving improperly] in relation to the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, the dining hall, the sauna, the bathing place, the path to almsround, and entering into houses.
Improper conduct by way of the body is as follows: for instance, here someone sits in the midst of the Saṅgha with his legs crossed or with one foot placed over the other, and so forth.
Likewise in the midst of a group, in an assembly of the fourfold congregation, and likewise toward senior persons.
Furthermore, in the dining hall, he does not give a seat to those who are senior, and he obstructs the seats of those who are junior.
Likewise, in the sauna (*jantāghara*), he lights fires and so forth without asking permission from those who are senior.
And regarding the bathing place, as it has been said: "One should bathe according to the order of arrival, without making the distinction of 'junior' or 'senior,'" he disregards this as well;

having arrived later and entered the water, he disturbs both the seniors and the juniors. Furthermore, on the path of alms-round, for the sake of obtaining the best seat, the best water, and the best alms-food—
He walks right in front of those who are senior, striking arm against arm.
Upon entering a house, he enters before the seniors and engages in physical play with the juniors—such things as these.
What is called verbal impudence in four instances is the utterance of inappropriate speech within the Saṅgha, a group, an individual, or a house.
For example: here someone speaks Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without having asked for permission;
likewise, in a group of the aforementioned type or toward an elder person, when questioned by people there, he answers without asking the elder;
and furthermore, within a house, [he asks]: "Lady so-and-so, what is there? Is it rice-gruel or solid food?"
He speaks such things as: "Food," or "What will you give me? "What shall I eat today? "What shall I consume? "What shall I drink? and so forth.

"Immodesty of mind in various matters" (*anekaṭṭhāna-manopāgabbhiya*) means that even without committing transgressions through body or speech in those various situations, one engages in various kinds of unbecoming thoughts through the mind alone, such as sensual thoughts and the like.
"Not greedy for families" (*kulesvananugiddho*) means that regarding those families he visits, he is not [driven] by craving for requisites or by inappropriate intimacy with householders.

Or, it is said: "not being greedy, not sharing in sorrow, not sharing in joy, not being happy when others are happy, not being pained when others are pained, and not personally undertaking exertion when duties and tasks arise.
And regarding this verse, the word "assā" (of her) which is stated in the phrase "suvaco cassā" (and she is easy to speak to), that word [is to be construed] with all the preceding terms.
"He should be contented and easy to support"—thus it should be construed.
This concludes the commentary on the third verse.
Thus the Blessed One [spoke] for one who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or who desires to set out for its attainment.
Having specifically explained what must further be done by a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, the Teacher now wishes to explain what must not be done, and thus spoke this half-verse:
“One should not perform even the slightest thing by which the wise might censure others. Its meaning is as follows:
while performing these duties in this manner, whatever bodily, verbal, or mental misconduct there may be that is trivial or base—
It is said: "One should not practice even that which is minor. By saying this, it is meant that one should not practice anything at all—not only what is gross, but even what is slight or minute.
Then, he shows the disadvantage of such conduct as being visible in this very life: "thereby the wise would censure others."
And here, because those who lack understanding are not an authority, for they may perform what is blameless or what is blameworthy, or what is slightly blameworthy or what is greatly blameworthy;

whereas only those with understanding are an authority, for they speak dispraise of one who deserves dispraise and praise of one who deserves praise after having investigated and scrutinized the matter. Therefore, it is said: "those others who possess understanding."
Thus, with these two hundred and fifty verses, the Blessed One— having explained the sphere of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhānūpacāra*) by way of its duties and non-duties,
specifically for one who desires to dwell having realized the state of peace, or who desires to set out for its attainment, particularly for a forest-dweller,
and by way of the "forest-dweller" including all those who wish to dwell taking up a meditation subject— [spoke as follows].

Now, for the purpose of warding off that fear of deities for those bhikkhus, and for the purpose of a meditation subject by way of jhāna that serves as a basis for insight (vipassanā), he began to speak a discourse on loving-kindness (mettā) in the manner beginning with, "May they be happy and secure.
In this context, "happy" (sukhino) means endowed with happiness; "secure" (khemino) means possessing security, which is to say, fearless and free from calamity.
"Exists. "All" means without exception. "Beings" means living creatures.

"Happy-minded" means those whose minds are happy. And herein, one should be understood as "happy" through bodily happiness, "happy-minded" through mental happiness, or as "secure" through the absence of both kinds of suffering and all fears and calamities.
But why is it stated thus? It is for the purpose of showing the mode of developing loving-kindness (*mettā*). For in this way:
Loving-kindness should be developed with the thought: "May all beings be happy," or "May they be secure," or "May they be at ease in mind.
Having thus shown the development of loving-kindness in brief, from the stage of access up to the limit of absorption, [the author] now [proceeds] even in detail.
To demonstrate this, he spoke the two verses beginning with "Whatever beings... Alternatively,
because a mind that has become habituated to diverse objects does not settle in unity at the very outset, but rather settles gradually after following along with the various distinctions of objects,
[the Buddha] spoke thus after following along with the distinctions of objects such as the pairs and triads of moving and stationary beings.
He spoke the two verses beginning with "Whosoever" (*ye keci*) for the purpose of establishing [the mind]. Alternatively,
since the mind dwells happily upon whatever object is clear (*vibhūta*) to a person, he— desiring to establish the minds of those bhikkhus upon whichever object was clear to them—
spoke [these verses] which illustrate the distinctions among objects such as the pairs and triads of the moving and the stationary (*tasa-thāvara*).
He spoke these two verses beginning with “ye keci.

For herein there are four dyads: the dyad of the moving and the stationary, the dyad of the seen and the unseen, the dyad of the distant and the near, and the dyad of those who have come to be and those seeking existence;
as well as [the application] of the six terms beginning with "long" to three instances of the middle term and two instances of the "minute" term.
Because of the possibility of these three states, he illustrates three triads: long, short, and medium; large, minute, and medium; and thick, thin, and medium.

In that context, "whatever beings" (*ye keci*) is an expression meaning without exception. "Beings who are living things" (*pāṇabhūtā*) means those who are both living things (*pāṇā*) and beings (*bhūtā*).
Alternatively, they are called "living things" (*pāṇā*) because they breathe; by this term, he includes five-aggregate beings who are bound to inhalation and exhalation.
They "are" (bhavanti), thus they are "beings" (bhūtā); by this term, he includes beings of the one-aggregate and four-aggregate realms. They "exist" (atthi), meaning they are present or found.

Thus, by the phrase "whatever breathing beings exist," having shown all beings together who are to be included by the triads of the Duka, he now shows them by including them all within this dyad: "whether moving or stationary, or whatever else remains. In that context, they "tremble" (tasanti), thus they are "moving" (tasā);
this is a designation for those possessed of craving and those possessed of fear. They "stand still" (tiṭṭhanti), thus they are "stationary" (thāvarā).
This is a designation for the Arahants who have abandoned craving and fear. Because there is nothing remaining for them, they are called "without remainder" (*anavasesa*);
that is to say, all of them. And what was stated at the end of the second verse should be connected with all the dyads and triads:
"Whatever living beings there are—whether trembling or stationary, all without exception—may all these beings be happy-minded."
"Thus, as far as beings exist or seek existence, may all these beings be happy-minded.
Now, regarding the six phrases beginning with "long" (*dīghā*), which illustrate the triad of long, short, and medium [stature]:
"long" refers to those with long physical forms, such as nāgas, fish, and crocodiles; for in the great ocean, there are even nāgas measuring many hundreds of *vyāmas*.
The individual bodies (*attabhāva*) of fish, crocodiles, and other such creatures may measure many *yojanas* in size.
"Great" refers to those with large bodies: in the water, fish, turtles, and so forth; on land, elephants, *nāgas*, and so forth; among non-human beings, *dānavas* and others.
And it is said: "Rāhu’s individual body. For his body is four thousand eight hundred *yojanas* in height.
The arms are twelve hundred *yojanas* in measure, the distance between the eyebrows is fifty *yojanas*, as is the space between the fingers;
the palms of the hands are two hundred *yojanas*. "Medium-sized" refers to the individual bodies of horses, oxen, buffaloes, pigs, and so forth.
"Short-statured" refers to beings such as dwarfs within their respective species, whose proportions are inferior to those that are long or medium-sized. "Subtle" refers to...
Beings produced in water and so forth, whose subtle bodies are beyond the range of the fleshly eye and are objects of the divine eye—
such as lice and the like— or furthermore, those beings in various species who are smaller in measure than large or medium-sized creatures,
should be understood as "subtle" (aṇuka). "Gross" (thūla) refers to beings such as snails and conchs, whose bodies are large and rounded.
Commentary on the Fifth Stanza (5).
Having thus shown beings without exception by means of three triads, he now shows them again by grouping them together through three dyads beginning with "those seen or those unseen.
In this context, "seen" refers to those who have previously come within the range of one's own eyes; "unseen" refers to those...
[Beings] residing in other oceans, other mountains, other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*), and so forth.

However, by this pair [of verses], “Those who dwell far away or those who dwell not far,” he shows beings dwelling both far from and near to his own personal existence (*attabhāva*). These are to be understood by way of those without feet and those with two feet.
For beings dwelling within one's own body are "near," while beings dwelling outside the body are "far. Likewise...
Those dwelling within the precincts are "nearby"; those dwelling outside the precincts are "far away.
Those dwelling in one's own monastery, village, district, island, or world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) are "nearby"; those dwelling in another world-system are said to be "dwelling far away.
"Beings" (*bhūtā*) means born, produced, or manifested. They are those who have already come into being and no longer count as being subject to future rebirth.

This is a designation for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*). "Seekers of becoming" (*sambhavesī*) means those who seek future existence; this is a designation for trainees (*sekha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*) who, because they have not abandoned the fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*), seek further rebirth.

Alternatively, among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), egg-born and womb-born beings are called "seekers of becoming" as long as they have not yet broken the shell of the egg or the membrane of the womb.
Those beings who have emerged outside after breaking through the eggshell or the womb-membrane are called "beings" (*bhūta*).

Those born from moisture and those of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) are called "seeking existence" (*sambhavesī*) during the first moment of consciousness; from the second moment of consciousness onward, they are called "beings.
Alternatively, by whichever posture they are born, as long as they have not yet reached another [posture], they are called "seeking existence"; beyond that, they are "beings."
Commentary on the Sixth Stanza: 6.

Thus, having demonstrated the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward sentient beings by means of two and a half stanzas beginning with “May they be happy,” through various modes as a wish for the attainment of welfare and happiness for those monks, the Blessed One now [proceeds] by way of wishing for the non-occurrence of harm and suffering.
Showing this, he said: “One should not deceive another. This is the ancient reading; however, they now read it as “paraṃ hi,” which is not elegant.
In that context, *paro* means another person; *paraṃ* means another person. *Na nikubbetha* means one should not deceive. *Nātimaññetha* means...
One should not think of transgressing it. "In any place" means in some location, such as in a village, a village field, in the midst of kinsmen, or in the midst of a guild, and so forth.
"This" refers to this [precept]. "Anyone" means any person whatsoever—whether a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or one gone forth;
whether happy or suffering, and so forth. "Malice and perception of resistance" refers to [actions] through bodily and verbal gestures.
[It is] through resentment, mental distortion, and the perception of aversion.

For where one should say "through resentment and the perception of aversion," it is said "resentment and the perception of aversion," just as where one should say "liberated through right knowledge," it is said "right knowledge and liberated," and just as [in the phrase] "through gradual training, gradual performance, and gradual practice."
It should be said: "Gradual training, gradual performance, gradual practice.
"One should not wish suffering for another" means one should not desire suffering for another. What is meant?
One should not cultivate loving-kindness merely by way of the mental attention, "May they be happy or secure," and so forth; rather, [one should think], "O, may any person whatsoever..."
One should develop this while reflecting thus: "One should not deceive any other person with frauds such as trickery;

one should not despise any other person in any place on account of the nine grounds for conceit, such as birth; and one should not wish suffering upon one another through mutual resentment or perceptions of aversion.
Thus, reflecting in this way, one should practice meditation.
Commentary on the Seventh Stanza (7).

Having thus shown the development of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) by way of the aspiration for the non-arrival of harm and suffering, he now says, "Just as a mother [her own son]," in order to illustrate that very same thing through a simile.
Its meaning is as follows: just as a mother [regards] her own son—her biological son born from her own body—and specifically that one and only son...
One should protect them with one's life; for the sake of warding off the arrival of suffering upon them, one should even sacrifice one’s own life to protect them.

In this way, one should cultivate this mind called loving-kindness toward all beings—repeatedly generating and increasing it—and cultivate it as immeasurable by way of having immeasurable sentient beings as its object, or by way of pervading a single being without exception.
Commentary on the Eighth Verse (8).
Having thus shown the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*) in all its aspects, he now says, "And loving-kindness toward the whole world," in order to demonstrate its further expansion.

In that context, one who "measures" (*mijjati*) and "protects" (*tāyati*) is a "friend" (*mitto*); he feels affection through the inclination toward welfare and guards [others] from the arrival of harm.
And this is the meaning. The state of a friend is *mettā*. "In the entire world" means in the world of beings without exception. It exists in the mind (*manasi bhavanti*);
it is called "mental" (*mānasa*) precisely because it is associated with consciousness (*citta*). "Cultivate" means increase. "It has no measure" is *aparimāṇa*;
it is so called because its object consists of immeasurable beings. "Above" means upwards; by that, the formless realm (*arūpabhava*) is indicated.
It grasps. "Below" (*adho*) means downward; by that, it grasps the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*). "Across" (*tiriyam*) means the middle;

by that, it grasps the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*). "Unconfined" (*asambādham*) means free from confinement; it is said to be one whose boundaries are broken. A "boundary" (*sīmā*) is called an adversary;
the meaning is that they proceed even against such a person. "Harmless" (*averam*) means free from enmity; it means free from the manifestation of hostile volition even intermittently.

The meaning is as follows. "Without enemies" (*asapatta*) means free from adversaries. For a person who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings, and has no adversary whatsoever; therefore, because that mind of his is free from adversaries, it is called "without enemies.
Indeed, "adversary" (*paccatthika*) and "enemy" (*sapatta*) are synonymous terms. This...
The word-by-word commentary follows.
Here, however, is the clarification of the intended meaning:

as for what was said, "In this way, one should cultivate an immeasurable mind toward all beings," this means that one should cultivate—that is, develop—an immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward the entire world.
One should cause it to reach increase, growth, and abundance; one should bring it to perfection. How?

Above, below, and across—above as far as the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), below as far as the Avīci hell, and across as far as the remaining directions. Or, above, pervading the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
below, the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*); and across, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) without exception. And while developing it in this way, just as...
It is unconfined, without enmity, and without adversaries; thus, one should cultivate it while effecting the absence of confinement, enmity, and adversaries.
Or rather, that perfection of cultivation is "unconfined" because it pervades all space throughout the world;
it is "without enmity" through the removal of malice toward oneself and others; and it is "without adversaries" through the removal of malice from others toward oneself.

One should cultivate and increase that boundless mind of loving-kindness—unconfined, free from enmity, and without ill-will—toward the entire world, encompassing all three dimensions: above, below, and across.
Commentary on the Ninth Verse.

9. Having thus shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness (*mettā*), he now says, "Standing, walking... [etc. ...one should resolve," in order to show that for one dwelling devoted to that development there is no restriction regarding the postures (*iriyāpatha*).

Its meaning is as follows: while developing this mind of loving-kindness in such a way, one does not impose a restriction on the postures—as in the passages beginning with "sitting down, having folded the legs crosswise, and set the body erect"—but rather remains at ease, dispelling any discomfort caused by whichever particular posture may arise.
"Whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, as long as he is free from drowsiness,
he should then resolve upon this mindfulness of loving-kindness meditation (*mettā-jhāna-sati*).
Alternatively, having thus shown the expansion of the development of loving-kindness, he now says "standing," demonstrating mastery (*vasībhāva*).

They walk. For one who has attained mastery (*vasippatta*), whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down—whatever posture he wishes to maintain this mindfulness of the *mettā*-jhāna, or whether standing, walking... [and so on] ...or lying down—his standing and other postures do not act as obstacles;
rather, it is simply to the extent that he maintains this mindfulness of the *mettā*-jhāna.
If he wishes to resolve, he resolves having dispelled his drowsiness for that duration; there is no sluggishness in him regarding that.
Therefore it was said: “Standing, walking, or sitting, or lying down as long as he is free from drowsiness—therein one should resolve upon this mindfulness.
This is the intention: that which was stated as “one should develop a mind of loving-kindness toward the whole world,” that—

Just as one would develop it—whether by means of the postures in standing and so forth, or without even taking up standing and so forth, to whatever extent one might wish to resolve upon this mindfulness of the *mettā*-jhāna—to that extent, having become free from drowsiness, one should resolve upon this mindfulness.

Thus, demonstrating mastery over the development of *mettā*, he enjoins one to that abiding in *mettā* with the words, "one should resolve upon this mindfulness. Now, praising that abiding, he says: "This is called the sublime abiding here."
The meaning of this is as follows: That abiding in loving-kindness (*mettāvihāra*) which was praised starting from "May they be happy or secure" up to "one should resolve upon this mindfulness"—
because it is free from fault among the four divine, brahma, and noble modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha-vihāra*), and because it brings about welfare for both oneself and others,
it is called here in the Noble Dhamma and Vinaya a "brahma-abiding" (*brahmavihāra*), meaning the most excellent abiding.
"Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down— as long as he is free from drowsiness— he should maintain this mindfulness continuously, constantly, and uninterruptedly.
Commentary on the Tenth Stanza.

10. Thus the Blessed One, having shown those bhikkhus the development of loving-kindness in its various modes, now—since loving-kindness, because it has sentient beings as its object, is close to the view of self—demonstrates to those bhikkhus the attainment of the plane of the Noble Ones by making that very jhāna of loving-kindness the foundation, through the means of suppressing the thicket of views: “And views... [he said].
With this verse, “Not approaching,” he concluded the teaching.

Its meaning is as follows: having emerged from that dwelling in the jhāna of loving-kindness—which was praised as “this, they say, is the sublime dwelling here”—those states such as applied thought and sustained thought that were present therein, and the material phenomena following upon their bases and so forth, [he did not approach].
Having comprehended this delimitation of name-and-form, and without adopting the view that "this is merely a heap of pure formations;

no being is found here," one gradually becomes virtuous through supramundane virtue and becomes endowed with the vision known as the right view of the path of stream-entry, which is associated with supramundane virtue.
Thereafter, regarding those sensual desires based on material objects...

Greed, which is the defilement of sensual desire, has not yet been abandoned; however, by means of the paths of the once-returner and the non-returner, having removed, eliminated, and pacified that greed for sense pleasures through its attenuation and its complete abandonment, one indeed never again enters a womb.
It is certain that one does not enter a womb again, but having been reborn in the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa), attains Arahantship right there.
“Having reached [this state], he attains final Nibbāna.
Having thus concluded his teaching, the Blessed One said to those bhikkhus:
“Go, bhikkhus, dwell in that very grove, and on the eight days of the month when the Dhamma is heard, strike the gong for this discourse.”
"Strike it and drive them away; deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, engage in discussion, and offer expressions of appreciation.
Cultivate, develop, and frequently practice this very meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). Then those non-human beings will no longer show you that terrifying object;
instead, they will become desirous of your welfare and desirous of your benefit. Having assented to the Blessed One with the words "Very well," they...
Rising from their seats, they paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him to the right, went to that place,
and did as instructed. And the deities, filled with joy and gladness, thinking, "The venerable ones desire our welfare and seek our benefit," swept the lodgings themselves,
prepared hot water, and performed massages for the backs and feet.
They established a guard. Those monks, too, having cultivated that very same loving-kindness and having made that very same [meditation] their foundation, began insight meditation;
and within that very month, they all attained the supreme fruit, Arahantship, and at the Great Pavāraṇā ceremony, they performed the Pavāraṇā of purity.
Thus has the Tathāgata, skilled in the goal and Lord of Dhamma,
spoken regarding the purpose that is to be accomplished;
having performed it and experienced the supreme peace of heart, [one should dwell].
Those of perfected wisdom realize the state of peace.
Therefore, one who desires to dwell having realized that peaceful state— the deathless, wonderful, and beloved by the noble ones— [should apply themselves].
"A wise person should constantly strive for that which is beneficial,
which consists of the divisions of pure virtue, concentration, and wisdom.
Thus ends the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha*.
The commentary on the *Mettasutta* is finished.
Concluding remarks:
And up to this point, that which was stated—
“Having paid homage to the Triple Gem, the most worthy of veneration,

I shall compose a commentary on the meaning of some of the Minor Works. In this regard, [the Minor Works consist of] the *Saraṇa*, the *Sikkhāpada*, the *Dvattiṃsākāra*, the *Kumārapañha*, the *Maṅgalasutta*, the *Ratanasutta*, the *Tirokuṭṭa*, the *Nidhikaṇḍa*, the *Mettasutta*, and so forth.
Thus, the commentary on the meaning of the *Khuddakapāṭha* in its ninefold division has been completed. Therefore, it is said:
“By me, who desired the endurance of the True Dhamma, while composing this commentary on the meaning of the *Khuddakapāṭha*, whatever merit has been acquired—”

"By the power of this [merit], may these people swiftly attain growth, increase, and abundance in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble One. [Thus it was said] by one adorned with the qualities of supreme purity in faith,
wisdom, energy, and virtue, and endowed with a multitude of qualities such as moral conduct, decorum, gentleness, and humility.
One who is endowed with the analytical clarity of wisdom capable of penetrating and plunging into both his own tradition and the traditions of others;

one who possesses unimpeded radiance of knowledge regarding the Teacher’s Dispensation—the Dhamma classified into the three Piṭakas along with their commentaries; one who is a great expounder of the six [types of] exposition;
and one who speaks with reasoned and supreme speech, adorned with the beauty of sweet and noble words emerging from the bliss produced by perfection of expression.

This was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa— so designated by his teachers— an ornament of the lineage of the Mahāvihāravāsī Elders who were lamps of the Theravamsa, whose intellects were well-established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with qualities such as the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā),
and who was a preeminent poet and foremost among debaters, possessing vast and purified wisdom; and it serves as an adornment for that lineage.
The Commentary on the Khuddakapāṭha, named *Paramatthajotikā*:
"May it remain as long as there exist in the world those seekers of the means to cross over the world,
showing to noble sons the method for the purification of virtue and the rest."
"Even the name 'Buddha'— of that Pure-Minded One,
the Tathāgata, the World-Chief, the Great Seer— prevails throughout the world.
— From the *Paramatthajotikā*, the Commentary on the Minor Works.
The commentary on the *Khuddakapāṭha* is finished.
